scram!”
Akechi blinks. Opens his mouth. Closes it.
“Court.” He starts, “Has never been in recess.”
It should make sense. The Velvet Room is a ‘reflection of his heart’, or whatever bullshit Igor
feels like spewing on the day – why would its doors ever close? His mind doesn’t let up, so
neither should the forces set to judge it.
So, it doesn’t make sense that its doors are suddenly obstructed. So, no, court can’t be in

Akechi raises an eyebrow, then pauses.

In an instant, and with a twisting crack, Akechi feels the two extra presences within his soul
torn out with all the grace of a haphazard attempt at surgery. Loki and Robin bristle and panic
at the contact, pressing far, far, way from the intrusion.
Shiji-Ouki and Mithras appear in the corners of Akechi’s vision, leaving behind gore and scar

Akechi thinks he sees José’s frown deepen even as his vision spins. He tries to push himself
off the tracks – when did he fall over? – and gets nowhere.
The pulsing reds of Mementos blur and shift, and Akechi can’t tell if the walls are cracking,
breaking off in chunks, stabbing through the personas he had convinced to his side with
jagged edges. His ears ring, and he clamps his hands over his head, and he can’t, he can’t“Oh.” José’s voice says, and everything stops, “That’s different than I was expecting.”

moved at all.
“I,” A new voice rings, and Akechi’s eyes suddenly snap to the chains and blue fire that
wreath the product of the fusion, “Am Atropos. The thread of life shall ever come to an end,
and it is by my shears that the edges fray. I am thou, thou art I.”
She bows her head, and she dissolves into the shape of a mask, flickering between onyx black
and crimson red, shape undecided, and she flies forward, and settles into place.
“That wasn’t I was trying to make,” José says, sounding entirely unbothered, “But, hey! I
think it turned out great! That one’s pretty strong.”
“Right.” Akechi mumbles, still orienting himself.
“All’s well that ends well!” José cheers, “That’s the saying, right?”
Akechi feels untethered. The part of him that isn’t steeped in spite and stubborn selfdestruction thinks that he should have waited to do this. He ignores it.
He still feels like shit.
“Thank you.” Akechi manages to grit out around the disorientation, because he still feels
awful, but José hasn’t done anything to deserve the brunt of Akechi’s mood, and he can
imagine Sumire’s disappointed frown and Ren’s sad, forgiving, smile, and Akechi just wants
all of this to stopThe Star grows to rank seven.
José looks delighted as the sound of breaking chains fades, “Oh! I wasn’t sure if it would do
that. I’m happy it did, though!”
“Yeah.” Akechi mutters, managing to stagger to his feet. His insides don’t feel right. It’s like
Atropos doesn’t fit. He’s sure it’ll settle later. “Thanks.” He says again.

“No problem!” José declares as he hops back into his car, “See you later! And good job,
mister!”
He peels away, the tires screeching against the train tracks, and Akechi tries to shove
everything back into place.

Time, flowers, and choices

Sugimura’s shadow looks down at the three of them as one might at ants crawling over their
shoes. Which, Sumire thinks, from the perspective of a shadow as enormous as Sugimura’s,
might not be an entirely inaccurate comparison.
Noir has her grenade launcher slung over her shoulder, aimed up at the shadow, feet rooted

see her posture drawn taught, even as far away as she is.

scoff.

Chapter 52
Chapter Summary

Flowers, and silence.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Morgana doesn’t understand Akechi in the slightest.
He had thought that Akechi was a menace to deal with before all this, what with the boy’s
abysmal kitchen and overall bare apartment, but now?
Well. Those things still stand, but now Akechi apparently can’t even muster up the decency
to be polite to someone doing him a favour.
‘Dropping the pretence’, He had called it. Morgana can only scoff.
(But, at the same time, the idea of an Akechi that’s all polite smiles and vapid pleasantries
doesn’t sit quite right.
Frankly, it never really has.
…
Maybe the pretences were already halfway to breaking before the return of Ren and Akechi’s
memories smashed through the rest of the glass.)
But, there’s only so long that Morgana can grumble to himself about someone before he starts
getting bored. And at this point, it’s turning into procrastination from the task at hand.
This isn’t Morgana’s first trip delivering a calling card. He was the primary distributor for
Madarame’s, too. And clearly, he did an excellent job, if the oh-so-competent trio of black
masks are asking for his help.
Flicking his tail and readjusting the card in his mouth, Morgana leaps up onto a windowsill of
a sheer apartment block wall. Then another, then another, until he’s reached the fourth floor.
With a dexterity that Morgana is sure would be impressive even for people with opposable
thumbs, he flicks open the latch of the window, and slips inside, stopping the momentum
with his tail to keep it from closing again.

He skirts along the walls of the apartment -gilded in gold and artefacts and trinkets that even
Morgana considers to be a bit gaudy- and quietly drops the calling card on a large dining
table. He skitters back, concealing himself near the open window, ready to escape in a flash.
It only takes a minute or so of waiting for the man who Morgana assumes is Haru’s fiancé to
return home.
With an expression of practiced disdain, Sugimura scowls, and glares over at the card on the
table as he spots it. He spits something under his breath as he swipes the card, looking ready
to throw it in the trash, before he stutters in his motion.
“Sir Haruto Sugimura-?” He hisses, “What- What the hell is this?!”
And just before Morgana can leap away, confident in a job well done, the air distorts.
Greenery, shrouded in vivid reds and deep purples pulses in the corners of his vision, melting
from above in thick strands.
Where the ceiling once rested is an expanse of sky. And where Sugimura once stood, is a
towering giant, so tall that Morgana can’t see his head above the clouds, the only indication
that it’s there at all are two piercing golden pricks of light, diffused in the smog.
“There’s no room for weeds in this place.” The shadow seethes, “Perhaps it’s time to prune.”
And the distortion fades.
Morgana shudders as the world shifts back into place, slipping through the window and
gently latching it shut as Sugimura screeches panicked profanities to the empty room.

status ailment by working more like a Dispel Magic.

“I’m surprised.” Goro says with put-upon shock, “You? Condoning violence?”
Sumire thwacks him on the arm, “I’m plenty violent.”
“Yes, I suppose you are. Your codename isn’t so far off the mark, either.” Goro says blandly.
Sumire laughs, “Yeah.” She pauses, “I’m- I’m really mad at Ren-senpai too, you know.”
“I figured.”
“No, I mean-” Sumire huffs, “I don’t want you to think that- well. You might be the only one
that hates him. But I haven’t forgiven him, is my point.”
“Is this your promise to take my side in any leadership arguments?” Goro drawls, voice
dripping with sarcasm.
“Uh.” Sumire grins sheepishly, “Can I take it at a case-by-case basis?”
“I don’t control what you do.” Goro points out flatly.
“Yeah.” Sumire smiles slightly, before she slumps, “I- I honestly don’t know how to talk to
Ren-senpai anymore.”
“Is that so.”
Sumire grimaces at the response, but presses on anyway, “Well- I just idolised him for so
long, that…” She swallows, “I think it’s more than just… the fact that he betrayed everyone.”
That catches Goro’s attention, “Oh?”
“Well…” Sumire starts, “My sister- I really looked up to her too. So much so that I wanted to
be her, and, well, you already know all that.” She swallows as the words tumble out of her
mouth, “And then with Doctor Maruki, I idolised him, too. I guess I didn’t see everything he
did as a betrayal, at the time, because I technically wanted it.”

“Have some self-respect.” Goro snips.
Sumire laughs, “Well I have that now.” She rolls her fingers around her glass, “It was only
after Ren-senpai said he was taking the deal that I realised how much the idea of being forced
to be Kasumi again scared me. Then I got mad at Doctor Maruki.”
She takes a small sip of water, “I guess my point is- I always… attach myself to people. But
I’m not attached to Ren-senpai anymore, and- I’ve never had to… deal with that. Kasumi
died before I got myself together, and I think I’ve seen Doctor Maruki all of twice in this
timeline.”
“But Ren is still here.” Goro finishes.
“Yeah.” Sumire mumbles, “It sounds kind of weird when I say it out loud. And I don’t…”
Goro raises an eyebrow when she trails off, and nudges her with his elbow, “And?”
“I don’t want to do that to you, or Haru-senpai.” Sumire finishes, “I want to be equal. Not
reliant.”
Goro nods slowly. “I suppose I can’t speak for how you feel.” He starts, “But you should
know that I do see you as a valuable ally.”
“Not an equal?” Sumire asks, half teasing, half insecure.
Goro presses his lips together, and stares at the ground. “I thought Ren was my equal. Hell, I
thought he had thoroughly surpassed me. It pissed me off.” He admits, “But it turns out that
was all for nothing.” He looks up, “I think, by this point, it’s safe to say your resolve is
stronger.”
Sumire feels a smile break out across her face.
(And, with the sound of breaking chains in Akechi’s mind, the Magician grows to rank ten.)

Shido stares at him for a beat. “Two months.” He says, “It’s been two months, and not only
have you failed to provide me with names, you can’t even lock down if they’re alive.”
Akechi’s mind darts in a few threads.
The first, is that he could use that comment. ‘Sorry, sir! It seems the Phantom Thieves died in
some cold corner of the Metaverse, never to be seen again. No-names, too. Nothing to worry
about!’ -He immediately shoots the thought down. The second Akechi tries to say it, Shido
will no doubt dismiss it outright.
The second, is that Shido is an irrational bastard, and won’t listen to any reason Akechi can
provide or attempt to fabricate.
“Your value is diminishing.” Shido interrupts Akechi’s thoughts. An idle comment, as though
he were speaking about the weather, rather than issuing a blatant threat.
And so, the third thread is that Akechi is fucked.
But, he already knew that.
The problem is that he can’t see the time on the clock.
“I can start investigating other palaces.” Akechi offers, “It’s possible that the thieves have
avoided the bait with Okumura because they have other priorities.”
Shido scoffs, “Are you going to throw darts at a wall and hope you’ll hit something? I hope
you have a better suggestion than that.”
Damn. “I’ll start placing more emphasis on my investigation in reality, as well. Perhaps my
focus on catching them in the Metaverse has narrowed my sights.”
“Perhaps.” Shido echoes.
Akechi swallows, “I’m sure that the thieves will come around to targeting Okumura at some
point, either way.” Maybe.
The nebulous deadline hanging over his head is looking shorter and shorter by the minute.

“I should hope so.” Shido drawls, “The Phantom Thieves are rather convenient, you
understand.”
“Of course.”
“Good.” Shido continues, “Then you’d better find a way for things to get back on track.”
Akechi nods stiffly.
“So long as we’re on the same page.” Shido waves a hand, “Dismissed.”
The Devil grows to rank seven.
Akechi is fucked.
Thankfully, he’s on break for carrying out hits. A small mercy, granted by the reasonable
workload that his current assignment is supposed to provide.
But that also means that Akechi really isn’t contributing anything, in Shido’s eyes.
He can’t make any grand declarations, can’t provide any excuses, because Akechi doesn’t
know what the plan is, and he might complicate things even further if he jumps the gun.
(Small mercies, silver linings; he can count them on one hand. This is the first time he’s seen
Shido since he regained his memories of the last timeline, and all it’s done for him is let him
keep his head above water.
Can anything be done, this late?)
Akechi grits his teeth, and finds himself hoping that plans start happening sooner rather than
later.
***
It’s tradition, at this point, to take stock of the cruise liner in Shido’s head after a meeting.
Akechi tries not to think about the last time he was here. A difficult task, when salt and iron
assault his senses in an oppressive haze, the tittering laughter and clinking of champagne
flutes making his trigger finger itch.
The cognition hasn’t shown its face.
Despite their last encounter ending with a few too many bullets, Akechi knows that
cognitions tend to be annoyingly persistent. It only takes a stray thought for another to
materialise after being destroyed. So the only question that remains is where is it?
Maybe it finally took a hint.
Unconvinced with his own train of thought, Akechi begins to wander the halls of the ship,
avoiding shadows and rat puzzles. He eventually opens the door to the restaurant, shooting

the cognition guarding it to dust before it can ask something inconvenient.
The restaurant is filled with people milling about, scooping fake food into their fake mouths
in their fake ship, and Akechi almost has it in him to be impressed at the unnecessary detail.
“I was wondering if you would show up again.”
Akechi clenches his jaw, and takes a breath.
“Honestly,” The voice says again, filtering in from the stage elevated a metre or so off the
ground, “I thought after last time, you’d stay away for good.”
Akechi turns his head.
The cognition wearing his likeness is facing away, seated at one of the two grand pianos,
tapping at the keys in some elegant, improvisational, melody.
“I don’t play piano.” Akechi comments tiredly.
The cognition hums, pausing its performance, “Perhaps the captain sees it as a skill that suits
you. Or, perhaps, he thinks that learning would finally give you some class.”
“Are you asking for another bullet to the head?” Akechi asks, saccharine. He hopes so. It
would probably be good stress relief.
The cognition laughs, turning around, “I didn’t think you had it in you! Perhaps I shouldn’t
be surprised, though. It was probably cathartic.”
Akechi sneers, hopping up onto the stage. “Sure. You’ve made yourself enough of a nuisance
that killing you is especially satisfying.”
“I could say the same to you, you know.” The cognition inspects its hands. It tilts its head
with a small, condescending smile, “That isn’t quite what I was referring to, though.”
Akechi knows exactly what it was referring to, but he doesn’t care to dignify the implication
with an acknowledgement.
“Why did you come here, anyway?” The cognition sighs, “You know everything there is to
know that this place could possibly tell you.”
Akechi wishes he had an answer to that. “Is that really the case?” He pushes instead.
The cognition grins maliciously, “Oh, don’t tell me- are you hoping to find something that
contradicts what you already know?” It gives a performative sigh, “Poor, poor, attack dog, so
desperate for affection that-”
Akechi slams the cognition against the piano, the instrument releasing a discordant protest,
bringing his serrated sword to its throat, “Maybe I should wrap this up.”
The cognition rolls its eyes, “Do what you want. We both know it won’t be permanent.”

Akechi grits his teeth, pressing his blade a little closer, “It will be, one day.”
The cognition gets an odd look in its eye. “Hm.” it hums shortly.
“What?” Akechi hisses.
“Nothing.” It says, voice flat.
“Bullshit.”
“Is this going to become a tradition?” The cognition interrupts, pointing to the sword at its
throat, “You speak with the captain, you come visit, you kill me, I come back?”
“I would prefer if steps one and four were revised.” Akechi drawls.
“But you still want to come visit?” The cognition simpers with a flashy smile. It drops the
expression, “I can hardly complain. It gets boring around here- especially now I don’t have a
list of jobs to get through.”
“What even are you?” Akechi snarls, “You’re not real, how the hell can you even get bored?
Aren’t you supposed to be too busy singing the praises of your beloved captain?”
“I wonder…” It hums.
Akechi narrows his eyes.
It’s unsettling, how different this cognition is to the one that killed him. Shido, supposedly,
still thinks of him in the same insulting (pathetic, condescending, piece of shit-) manner as
last time, so what changed?
The Sword of Damocles lowers a little further.
The cognition shifts slightly, “Are you going to keep me pinned to this piano for the rest of
time?”
Akechi slits its throat.
Predictably, the Tower grows to rank six.
Akechi doesn’t move, staring as bits of black smoke and dust drift to the floor.

Futaba doesn’t have it in her to complain when Yusuke shows up at her house unannounced.

“Whuh?” Is the eloquent sound she musters in response.
“I did come here for a purpose, but I found myself struck with too many ideas to risk losing

“That took you,” Futaba checks the time, “Nearly half an hour.”
Yusuke’s eyes widen, “Truly? It felt like longer.”
Futaba sighs.
“Back to the matter at hand,” Yusuke continues, neatly tucking all his art supplies away, “I

“Oh, I’m fine.” Futaba says to the ceiling, “Peachy.”
“Is that so?” Yusuke hums, “I suppose you were the one to first attempt to bridge the gap
between our two groups.”
“Sure was.” Futaba says, puffing out her chest in excessive bravado.
Yusuke gives her a flat look, “Are you really alright?”
Futaba slumps, defeated. Her acting skills never were that great, and Inari has the unfortunate
honour of being barely socially aware enough to see right through her. “M’ fine.” She
mumbles.
Yusuke hums knowingly. “I know that I have no qualms in working with the others, but I am
not a victim of any of their misdeeds.” He says, a clear invitation for Futaba to start spilling
her guts.
“Yeah, yeah.” She huffs, “But it’s not really-”

She cuts herself off before she reaches the root of the problem.
Well. She cuts her voice off. She’s not quite quick enough to catch her thoughts.
She doesn’t have a problem with Sumire. She doesn’t! She thought she did, but then that
turned out to be about three people jumping the gun with circumstantial evidence. Problem
solved, water under the bridge, other similar proverbs.
Futaba doesn’t have a problem with Haru, either. All the same baggage as with Sumire,
solved and forgotten even faster since there wasn’t any history there to begin with. The only
thing that Futaba can begrudge is the snide comment about her motherWhich halts the train at Futaba’s actual problem.
“I dunno what to do about Akechi.” Futaba mutters.
“I don’t think you’re alone in that feeling.” Yusuke points out.
Futaba shrugs, “Sure. But it’s not like anyone else has a solution to go with that.”
“That’s also true.” Yusuke concedes.
“Part of me just hopes he’s an asshole.” Futaba whispers, mostly to herself, “That the time we
spent working together was one-hundred-percent fake, and he’s just the absolute worst.”
Yusuke huffs something that sounds almost like a laugh, “I can see why that would make
things easier. I certainly…” He frowns, and cuts himself off with a shake of the head, “I have
to say that in this instance I hope that is not the case.”
“How come?” Futaba mumbles with a pout, slightly annoyed at being disagreed with.
“I believe that Akechi-kun and I have things to discuss.” Yusuke explains airily, “It would be
rather difficult to achieve this if he is, as you say, just an asshole.”
Futaba grins slightly at successfully getting Inari to swear.
“And besides,” Yusuke continues, “Yoshizawa-san and Okumura-san seem to enjoy his
company. I doubt this would be the case for no reason at all.”
“Yeah.” Futaba clicks her tongue, conceding the point. “But, also…”
Yusuke tilts his head, “Also?”
Futaba swallows, “There was… When Makoto and I were trying to figure out what Akechi’s
deal was, when he was part of the team, I, uh, fell down a couple of rabbit holes, and… I
asked Sojiro a bit about my mom.”
Yusuke narrows his eyes, and nods slowly.

“And, um,” Futaba continues, voice growing smaller, “Apparently she was… experimenting
on people. Kids.”
Yusuke’s mouth forms a little ‘o’, and he looks stricken, “Ah.”
“Yep.” Futaba finishes with a popping sound.
Yusuke grimaces, “And you believe that Akechi-kun…?”
Futaba shrugs, “I don’t know.” She says truthfully, “I’d have to ask.”
Which is the problemYusuke hums lowly, a considering look on his face.
“And, what if-” Futaba chokes out, “What if I do ask him, and he tells me something that-”
She swallows, “I love my mom, but what if-?”
“He tells you something that stains your image of her?” Yusuke finishes.
“Yeah…” Futaba breathes out.
Yusuke doesn’t seem to have an answer to follow that. Futaba isn’t surprised, but she can’t
help but feel disappointed.

The twins have stood guard over the entrance to the Velvet Room for over a week at this

The inmate, meanwhile, should be experiencing far more in the way of inconvenience.
But, it doesn’t seem like he has.
In fact, the twins haven’t seen him pass the entrance to any of the Velvet doors placed in the
Metaverse at all since they’ve taken to barricading them. If they were to flaunt their own
pride, they would say that the inmate relies on them so heavily that he simply doesn’t dare
step foot in the cognitive world without their aid at his side.
But, Pride is a sin, so they once again have to concede that this is not the case.

The last they saw the inmate was in that back alley in the human world, eyeing the twins with

by the promise of not seeing the inside of his cell for an indeterminate amount of time.

shoulder.
Odd, that a sudden chunk of previously unregistered personas were suddenly made manifest,
moments before their master ordered that the doors be sealed.

“This isn’t…” Justine mumbles under her breath. Caroline ignores her, her fists clenching
tightly around her baton.
It doesn’t mean anything. The scattered memories and strange lists that plague their thoughts
are falsehoods, fragments of nothing, designed to distract them.
They ignore the feeling of the Strength and Temperance nested in their heart.

Just two paces away, or perhaps an infinite space, a god watches with interest.
The cards have spoken at last, and the two chosen wildcards have finally proven themselves
useful. A total victory is the only outcome that matters- it is hardly a win if it is by the skin of
one’s teeth.
How easy it will be to drag the players forward on strings, roping their chaos back in line. To
rebel is to doom themselves- there is only one path that will bring them the furthest, and that
path is as ruinous as all the rest.
But, first, the waiting game.

Had, being the operative word, as he receives an unfortunate phone call one foot out the door.

Bad sign. “Oh?”

Shido drawls.

Sumire had been worried that she’d have to report a murder when Ren practically leapt out of
his chair to chase after Goro. She thinks that might have been an overreaction, when she sees
Ren come back, looking entirely unscathed. Though, by the relieved slumps of some of the
other thieves, she wasn’t the only one with concerns.
Following that, it doesn’t take long for all the non-Leblanc residents to slowly trickle out in
twos and threes. Sumire makes to stand at the same time Haru does, and they fall into step as
they wander the streets in the direction of Yongen station.
“That went well.” Sumire decides out loud.
Haru giggles slightly, “all things considered, I suppose. I was worried that there would be
more arguments.”
“Me too.” Sumire admits, “But I think everyone was more concerned about the situation
rather than each other.”
Haru hums in agreement, “I just hope that those problems don’t come up in the future.”
Sumire is almost certain that they will. “Yeah…” She says anyway.

Haru smiles, “I know it’s a bit naïve. I haven’t been the friendliest towards everyone, either.”
She sighs, “I’ve been a bit stressed.”
“I can imagine.” Sumire huffs, “How is… everything going, by the way?”
Haru lifts her shoulders in a half-shrug, “It’s… going.” She laughs, “I haven’t seen Sugimura
in person, but he did call my father in tears. I think that my father has been a bit distracted
trying to make sure that nothing reaches the press. Even if political and business marriages
are still commonplace enough, it’s not a good look for him if Sugimura confesses what kind
of person he is.”
“Maybe that will be helpful for his palace?” Sumire muses, “If he’s distracted, I mean.” She
frowns, “Or, it might make it worse.”
“I suppose we’ll find out.” Haru hums. She bites at her lip, “I’m… not as conflicted as I
thought I would be about changing my father’s heart.”
Sumire tentatively tilts her head in question, “Yeah?”
Haru frowns, “I- well. I don’t think Goro-kun is wrong, when he says that there really isn’t
much of a difference between killing someone and changing their heart. But I’m not sure if
he’s entirely right, either. The action just… feels different.”
Sumire has never been fully confident in her opinions about changing hearts. At first, her
thoughts had been put through a blend of what she believed Kasumi would feel- a mix of
opinionated musings about the state of society and several layers of irony about what it
means to be saved.
She supposes that there would have been a week in early January where she would have
welcomed the Phantom Thieves’ methods whole-heartedly, if only to make her forget.
Though, she hadn’t quite been conscious or coherent enough to reflect on it.
And now…
The key difference between the Phantom Thieves and Maruki, Sumire thinks, is that Maruki
is indiscriminate.
But, even still, what someone deserves is subjectiveSumire is going to give herself a headache if she keeps thinking about this. Which is
unfortunate, since it’s hardly unimportant.
“I’m honestly not sure how I feel about it.” Sumire admits, “I mean- Maruki was kind of
killing me, wasn’t he? But you’re right, it feels different.”
Haru looks to consider this, “You’re... right. But, even so,” she continues, “I- I didn’t kill
Sugimura. It didn’t feel like mercy, but still…” Her frown deepens, “I think… I did it for me,
far more than I did it for his benefit.”

A nice alternative, then. An easy solution to dust off their hands and claim no blood has ever
stained them.
But, Sumire corrects, that’s uncharitable.
A mental shutdown and a change of heart are both violent assaults on the mind, forcing a
shadow to change, to an end of crushing guilt or complete nonexistence. For Haru, the end
would have been the same in either case. The result she needed could have been achieved
through death as it would have been through a tearful confession. And yet, even with
vengeance on her mind, she chose to let him live.
Maybe Sumire is looking for an answer that doesn’t exist. She herself knows that the thought
of being an accomplice to murder scared her far more than helping change a heart. She didn’t
even bat an eye- it’s only when her thoughts drift to Maruki that the discomfort sets in.
Sumire nods slowly, “I understand.” Even if she can’t articulate it.
Haru’s lips tilt up, “Isn’t it a bit sad? I started out wishing that I could make my father
remember the man he used to be, to love me again.” She sighs, “I know a change of heart
won’t accomplish that. I think the good things about him died a long time ago. Maybe that’s
why it feels different.”
Mind or matter? Was Sumire truly, effectively, dead while under Maruki’s spell? Kasumi
certainly hadn’t been brought back to life, so what remained? A stilted puppet with a paintedon smile and a body it couldn’t understand?
Sumire doesn’t think she’s cut out for philosophy.
“I guess…” She mumbles, and can’t find an end to the sentence. She sighs, “In an ideal
world,” She grimaces at the phrasing, “None of this would be necessary.”
And isn’t that just the point? They don’t live in an ideal world. They can’t. But that doesn’t
mean they should sit back and do nothing, should injustice back them into a corner.
Goro had decided he would rather die, than have his mind altered beyond recognition. Sumire
had decided she would rather not exist at all, when Maruki first gave her the choice. She
hadn’t quite reached Goro’s level of self-sacrifice when she changed her mind, but she had
resolved she wouldn’t take her fate lying down.
Maybe the morality of the situation hardly matters.
“And yet, it is necessary.” Haru muses, lips dipping back into a frown, “I suppose there’s
nothing to be done. But I think it makes me feel better if it’s my own choice, rather than a
stepping stone to a larger goal.”
“It can be both.” Sumire points out.
Haru laughs, “I suppose it can.”
Life, as ever, comes served in opposites and extremes.

Akechi hadn’t wanted to speak with Ren. In fact, the only way he convinced himself to not
make a scene out of showing up to the meeting was by resolving to ignore Ren’s presence
entirely.
Of course, that held relatively well until Ren decided to chase after him like he hadn’t fucked
up everythingBy the time Akechi manages to escape the situation, he’s fuming.
Going to check on the cognition of him that lives in the cruiser of Pride in times like these is
a bad habit he’s trying to kick, so he instead decides to fall back on his other bad habit, and
decides to take a spontaneous trip to Mementos.
He gives a token effort towards not putting himself in excessive danger. But, there’s only so
much he can do when (He wishes Ren would stop talking, stop existing in his line of sight,)
Mementos is generally a dangerous place, (He’s not giving Ren another fucking glove. Who
the hell does he think he is? What the hell did Ren even think it meant-?) after all, andAkechi thinks it might be time to call it, as his internal monologue starts taking on the
cadence of the most polished version of the detective prince.
Digging his sword out of the oozing remains of the last shadow he just vivisected, he sighs,
and starts stalking in the direction that Robin pings as the exit.
He only gets three steps before he hears the rumbling of an engine.
He presses his lips together, wondering whether wading through a conversation of cryptic
nonsense is something he can endure at this time. He eventually decides that if it becomes too
much, he can just leave. José will hardly be offended.
He gives the Star a strum, and hears the screeching of tires in the near distance.
“Oh, Mister!” Comes José’s telltale greeting, his car skidding to a stop, “I thought you might
have been here.”

“Hello, José.” Akechi greets in turn, “I take you aren’t busy?”

whenever I want!”
“How convenient.”

“No, not as of yet.” Akechi shakes his head, “Though your last fusion was rather helpful,

“No, I understood it plenty.” Akechi sighs, “I suppose I’m simply questioning the validity of
your claims.”
What use is a system of fate, after all, that boils down to the ‘consequences of actions’ when
there are certain actions they must take, all the same? It can hardly be called their decision, if
the alternative is certain death or the end of the world.
José frowns, like he’s never been told he’s wrong before, “What do you mean?”
“How much do you know about the thing at the bottom of Mementos?” Akechi asks, leaning
forward.
José opens his mouth, looking as though he’s about to confidently respond, before he pauses.
He closes his mouth, and looks perplexed, “The… thing at the bottom of Mementos?
There’s… there is something- I think? But…”
Great. Akechi sighs, “Nevermind.”

Akechi raises an eyebrow, “And?”
“And?”
“Are you going to elaborate?” Akechi asks, slowly.
“I can’t.” José says.
Okay then.

Akechi is starting to feel a headache coming on.

“Yes.” Akechi grits out.
José laughs, “Well, that person definitely isn’t wrong about this, Mister. I told you:

Akechi, begrudgingly, can concede that point.
In all likelihood, that person, whoever the hell they may be, only cares about avoiding the

Akechi scoffs, thinking of blood and vengeance and broken promises, “Of course it does.”

Akechi thinks of darts, and gloves, and coffee.
None of it mattered. Not at all, and yet,
“Maybe,” He swallows, “Maybe it does change things, a bit.”

The apathy that Akechi is so practiced in is starting to slip.
He had, foolishly, assumed that keeping every bit of fire, every bit of hatred, that so

before the fate of the world was at stake.

Akechi, over the years, has learned not to be optimistic.
He prefers the term realist, over anything else, especially with regard to his own actions. It’s

feel its sting.

event. Akechi sincerely doubts this place is airtight to begin with.
Despite his willingness to cooperate, Morgana keeps giving him the side eye.
“We didn’t have to split up, you know.” He says, as the group wanders down a hall that
creaks and groans at an alarming volume. Akechi sends the walls a glare, as Haru regards
them cooly, and Sumire huddles a little closer to the centre of the group.
“I believe we did, actually.” Akechi snipes back.
Morgana grumbles under his breath, before sighing. “Is working with Joker really that bad?”
Akechi presses his lips together, “I didn’t think it would be.”
Haru steps over a stray sheet of metal, “I suppose it’s hard, when someone has broken your
trust.”
Sumire gives a short hum.
Morgana makes a face, “I get you can use that reasoning, Violet. But, Crow, didn’t you betray
Joker first?”
“It’s different.” Akechi says immediately.
“Why?”
“First off,” Akechi starts, “I think Joker is a moron, for whatever forgiveness shtick he has.
That’s his problem. But, it is still different. I betrayed you all in November because I couldn’t
bend from what I had to do. Joker wouldn’t, either, so we were at an impasse. All part of the
game.” He waves his hands in a showy arc, scoffing.
Morgana frowns, not looking entirely convinced, “…And with Maruki?”
“There shouldn’t have been a problem with Maruki.” Akechi spits, “We were on the same
page, and that was the point.” He grits his teeth, “Ren is the one that folded. One little threat,
and… we were so close.” He cuts himself off before he feels the urge to bite through his
tongue.
Sumire walks forward, brushing against his shoulder. She sends him a small, sympathetic
smile, a bit of melancholy around her eyes.
“So, you just think Joker is an idiot, full stop.” Morgana rolls his eyes, “Well, can’t argue
with that logic.” He mutters.
“Then don’t.” Akechi says snippily.
“Just- can’t you just talk to each other?” Morgana protests.
“A tired argument.” Akechi sneers. “Just drop it, will you? This isn’t getting anywhere.”

“You can’t try and resolve this at all?” Haru pushes gently.
“Joker already tried that.” Akechi says, “I found his attempt lacking.”
“When he ran after you, the other day?” Morgana tilts his head, “What did he say?”
“Something inane and sentimental.” Akechi says dryly, “I’m not interested in his apologies.
I’m not convinced he even means them.”
Sumire opens her mouth, and then clicks it shut. She swallows, and tries again, “I think… he
does mean them.” She frowns, looking conflicted, “But… I can’t tell if he’s sorry for the
choice or sorry for the aftermath.”
Morgana goes quiet, ears flattening against his head. “…I’m not sure, either.”
“Is this something you’ve discussed with him?” Haru asks quietly.
“Yeah.”
A beat. Then, a few more.
“Sometimes,” Akechi begins slowly, tongue heavy with the weight of a confession, “I can
look at Joker, and almost forget what he did. I can weigh one aspect against the other, and
pretend that everything good is worth more. But I don’t want to forget. I said that I’d never
forgive him, and that is a promise I intend to keep.”
Morgana doesn’t speak for a moment. “Right,” He says, walking a little faster to keep pace.
“Can you… try again?”
Akechi rolls his eyes, “To what end?”
“I dunno.” Morgana kicks at the ground, “To what end are you gonna keep this up?”
Akechi doesn’t know.
Haru straightens out her back, “Well, for now, we have a solution.”
“Yeah…” Sumire hums, “…I guess we’ll join back up when the paths converge, again? Or
when we send the calling card.”
Akechi huffs under his breath. “Well. It can hardly go worse than our previous encounter
with a palace ruler.”
Morgana frowns, “Sugimura, huh?” He blinks, “Hey, wait! I thought you guys said that went
off without a hitch!”
“Um-!” Sumire squeaks, suddenly looking very embarrassed. Haru coughs delicately into her
hand.

“It hardly matters now that it’s said and done.” Akechi says primly, hoping to dismiss the
topic entirely.
“Nuh uh.” Morgana immediately protests, apparently hoping to present himself as a whiny
child, “I thought you guys were- I don’t know! Super competent!”
“We are!” Sumire insists, “But… unforeseen circumstances?” She offers weakly.
Akechi snorts, and resigns himself to a barrage of prying and mildly condescending
questions.
It is, he thinks, at the very least, a distraction from having to think about Ren any further.
***
With how quickly Akechi sped down the tunnel that looked like about five safety hazards
rolled into one, Ren would have almost thought that he’s a fan of scrap metal. And possibly
the vacuum of space.
Taking a second look at the remaining tunnel, however; Ren grimaces at the passing
similarity to Shido’s cruiser. He doesn’t particularly want to explore this place either.
Red carpet -the kind that has probably been in use a few decades too long- is placed overtop
of the once-smooth floors. Dirty wooden panelling slowly begins to replace the blue-grey
metal sheets, faded and musty.
Ren internally rescinds his past comparison to the cruiser of Pride. This corner of Okumura’s
cognition is far too run-down to compare.
“Okay…” Futaba hums from above, “By the looks of it, the other guys are just stuck with a
bunch of hallways. Boring stuff.”
“You’re keeping an eye on them?” Makoto asks.
“Uh, duh.” Futaba scoffs good-naturedly, “What kind of navi would I be if half our squad
died while I wasn’t paying attention?”
“That’s cool and all, but how’re we doing?” Ryuji speaks up, hands folded behind his head,
“Like, what’re we walkin’ into?”
“It kinda reminds me of some… I dunno.” Ann frowns as she looks around the hall, “A
museum, weirdly? Not like Madarame’s, or anything. Some kind of science museum?”
Yusuke tilts his head, humming, “I suppose that would fit with the theme.”
“Something like that.” Futaba agrees dismissively, “But watch out, we’re headed into some
kind of lobby, I think."
Sure enough, the hall funnels outwards. The room opens into a half-dome structure, split
down the middle by a receptionist’s desk, and two staircases that meet in the middle to lead to

a higher floor. Along the edges of the room, strange platforms projecting holographic
blueprints flicker and spark.
“Could’ve sworn those used to be earlier.” Ren mumbles to himself, jerking his head towards
the holograms.
“Well, the palace is all funky now.” Futaba says simply, “Got any idea what this is supposed
to represent, oh Time Traveller?”
“Not a clue.” Ren admits, shoving his hands in his pockets as he takes in the view, “This
entire place used to be a sweatshop factory with a sci-fi coat of paint.”
“I think the coat of paint stayed the same.” Makoto hums, “Though that doesn’t particularly
help us.”
“So, should we get to checking it out?” Ryuji asks, stretching out his arms, “There aren’t any
shadows here.”
“Can confirm.” Futaba chimes in, “Just a bunch of cognitions. The receptionist, some randos
milling about, and, hm.”
Ren narrows his eyes, “What’s up?”
“There’s… I think it’s another cognition? It’s a little further in. It feels kinda weird, though.”
“It’s simply a cognition though, right?” Yusuke tilts his head, “Should we be concerned?”
“Yes.” Ren says, “It’s like Oracle’s palace- the cognitions here are going to be a pain. Last
time, Okumura almost only threw cognitions at us.”
“Gotcha.” Futaba drawls, “On your guard, people! The scrubs in here don’t seem hostile,
though. I think the receptionist is just here to- well. Receive?”
“Should we talk to it, then?” Ann asks, “Ugh, it’ll be so nice to go through a palace where not
everything is trying to kill us.”
“Go ahead.” Ren says, “We can split up in pairs to case the room. Oracle, keep an eye on
everyone.”
“You got it! Inari, you’re with me! Bodyguard duty!” Futaba cheers, Necronomicon doing a
little spin.
Yusuke sighs, “I suppose that’s alright.”
“Skull! You’re with me!” Ann says brightly, “You can back me up if it gets dicey.”
“Fiiine.” Ryuji drawls, pouting, but not doing much to fight it.
Makoto huffs a laugh, before turning to Ren, “Where to, Joker?”

Ren tilts his head, “Check out the stairs, maybe? We won’t go past the door.”
Makoto nods, “Sounds good to me.”
They head up the stairs, none of the cognitions making any move to stop them. Behind them,
Ren can hear Ann start chatting up the receptionist, Ryuji occasionally chiming in.
As they reach the outcropping with a set of wooden double doors, Ren rolls out his shoulders,
“I’m surprised you were okay with us all splitting up.”
Makoto jumps, blinking in surprise, “Oh.” She starts, “Well- I had a conversation with Noir,
this afternoon.”
“Yeah?”
“Yeah.” She echoes, face pained, as she appears to try and find her words, “She suggested
that our groups are never going to really be able to work together. She talked about how that
doesn’t mean we can’t-” She huffs, like she thinks it’s absurd, “That we can’t work alongside
one another.”
Ren taps at the double doors idly, “I’m guessing you don’t agree?”
“I just don’t see the difference.” Makoto says primly.
Ren can’t pretend it doesn’t sting, to hear that Haru thinks their groups have no chance of
fully cooperating. He supposes they have found a work around, but how long will that last?
When the paths converge? Will their first real taste of teamwork be tested while they’re
trying to take down Okumura’s shadow? Ren doesn’t think that will be the best training
grounds.
“I guess it depends on the circumstances.” Ren offers.
Makoto makes a face, “You know, I never realised how much of a diplomat you were until
recently.”
Ren smiles in a way he hopes is charming, “Not a fan?”
“It just doesn’t seem like you.” Makoto narrows her eyes, and Ren feels a bit like he’s being
dissected, “You get along well with everyone, but you stood your ground when we all
questioned the company you keep. Now, though…”
Ren knows.
“I know.” He says, seeing no reason to be dodgy, “It’s- yeah.”
Makoto gives him another piercing look, “…You always seem to be on Crow’s side.”
Ren grimaces, “Not always.”

It’s true. True enough, at least. Ren thinks that before December, last time, they were both
more than willing to place the game, to place winning, above the other.
It didn’t feel much like winning in Shido’s palace.
He didn’t get any satisfaction from taking Maruki’s deal, either. No- then, Ren was desperate,
scrambling for anything that would give him what he wanted, more than willing to pay the
price.
He isn’t entirely sure if the feeling has faded. It twists his stomach and leaves a sour taste on
his tongue.
“Queen, I’ll be honest.” Ren laughs self-deprecatingly, “I have no idea what I’m doing.”
“I kind of gathered that by this point.” She says dryly.
“Gee, thanks.”
“That’s not-” Makoto frowns, “I mean, it’s not like I know what I’m doing, either.” She
laughs weakly, “I feel more out-of-touch than ever.”
Ren eyes the lobby below them, Yusuke and the looming form of Necronomicon flitting
between the holograms, Ann and Ryuji making a friend out of the cognition at the front desk.
“…At least no one seems too down.” Ren says.
“Which is exactly why I’m feeling out of touch.” Makoto deadpans. Ren snorts. “…I really
don’t see the point of working with them if this is the only way we can do it.” She says.
Ren shrugs. “It’s not like we could stop them from going into the palace. Especially not
Crow.”
Makoto huffs, “That’s-”
“And besides,” Ren continues, “What would they do, if we told them to get lost? Try and
clear Shido’s palace?” He takes a steadying breath, “Even if they got out of that all okay, it
would put us in a bad position, probably.”
Makoto rolls her eyes, “So we’re all stuck, just like we thought.”
Ren smiles wryly, “No way around it.”
Ren isn’t sure if he wants a way around it. Being backed into a corner sucks. Being trapped
on the one path isn’t great, either. But, still,
God, Ren wishes there was a way to rebuild the bridge between him and Akechi. The other
seems adamant on burning any scaffolding Ren lays, however.
…He should probably have learned his lesson about making wishes, at this point.

(If he could just fix thisDoes he have to force the issue? How?
He needs more than just the opportunity. But then what?)
Snapping himself out of his thoughts with a deep sigh, he turns his attention back to the door.
Not wanting to poke any wasps’ nests by opening the doors, he activates his third eye to try
and get a glimpse of anything glaringly important beyond the threshold.
Ren frowns, as he sees an outline of blue.
“Guys.” He shouts to the room, and the present thieves all turn their heads, “Anything
interesting?”
“Not really.” Futaba says, moving towards the raised outcropping as Ann, Ryuji, and Yusuke
climb the stairs, “The holograms just kind of look like blueprints for a bunch of space stuff.
Weirdly burger themed, too.”
“It is difficult to tell whether or not the blueprints are depicting past achievements or future
projects.” Yusuke adds.
“Oh, I think it’s both!” Ann chimes in, “The receptionist was going on about how this place
is dedicated to Lord Okumura’s legacy.” She drawls in a mocking tone.
“The cognition seemed kinda on-edge, though?” Ryuji says, “I dunno if it was just me,
though.”
“No, I got that too.” Ann quickly nods, “Like, whenever we got to talking about how well the
space station is doing, he got super defensive.”
“Was it a cognition of anyone in particular, do you think?” Makoto asks.
Ryuji shrugs, “Doubt it. Or, Okumura didn’t bother remembering the guy’s name. Or face.
It’s just some robot.”
“Checks out, I guess.” Futaba hums, “Well! I’ve got good news, anyway. I think I can get a
whiff of a safe room not too far beyond these here doors.”
“We should get a move on, then.” Ren gestures towards the door, “Anyone wanna do the
honours?”
Ann snorts, “Joker, if you want to be dramatic about it, just say so.”
Ren grins, “Well- I’d like to be dramatic, then.”
“Please, go ahead.” Yusuke frames Ren and the door with his fingers.
Ren laughs, and pushes the doors open with both hands, making sure he has a small run-up to
let his cloak fly behind him.

He loses most of the wind in his sails as he sees what his third eye was highlighting before.
Striding confidently through the halls is a robot Ren did not expect to encounter. Not quite as
robotic as all the others, a smart blazer and pencil skirt, and a helmet of pink metal shaped
into the fluffy locks of Haru Okumura; Ren blinks in shock.
Now this is very early.
“Uh, is that…?” Ann gapes.
“Looks like it.” Makoto grimaces.
Yusuke sighs, “He doesn’t see his daughter as human, then?”
“She looks… a little more human than the rest?” Ryuji offers, not sounding particularly
convinced.
Futaba makes a soft sound that doesn’t quite read as agreement.
The robot taps at the clipboard in her hands. She looks up, tilting her head as she catches
sight of the gaggle of thieves crowding the entry to the hallway.
She walks forward, “Are you here to see the museum?” She asks flatly.
Ren frowns, as another thread of his memory of this palace pulls loose.
This is different- not just where this cognition of Haru is appearing, but her entire shape and
demeanour. Last time the cognition had first appeared as the same, blue-skinned alien
Okumura’s shadow takes the form of, before having transformed into a destructive robot at
her father’s command.
The symbolism was fairly cut and dry. Now, with the original as a comparison, Ren has no
idea what this new version of Haru living in Okumura’s head is supposed to represent.
“There are several tours available.” The cognition continues, “A view of the majesty of
Okumura Foods is at your disposal, should you wish.”
Ren’s ears strain, as he can’t quite decipher the cognition’s tone. If he didn’t know any better,
he could almost interpret her words as sarcastic.
But, that can’t be, right? Okumura views his daughter as much a tool as he does his workers.
The man probably couldn’t comprehend the possibility that his daughter has snark within her
capability.
But, his palace is different. Ren presses his lips together in frustration.
“Uhh, y-yeah!” Ann chokes out, “We’d… totally love one of those… tours.”
“Excellent.” The cognition nods sharply, “You may register for one just ahead.” She gestures
to a desk protruding from the wall, the shimmering door to a saferoom just beyond, “I will be

your tour guide.”
Everyone exchanges a look. Ren clears his throat, “I guess we’d better go register then, huh?”
“…I suppose it’s the only way to proceed.” Makoto concedes.
Ren walks forward, and signs Joker on a list of names. The cognition nods approvingly,
quickly marking off the name in the same row.
“Well then.” The cognition bows stiffly, “Shall we begin?”

Chapter Summary

Cognitions, festivals, and dreams.

After a quick pitstop in the saferoom, Ren leads the thieves to follow the cognitive Haru
through the… tour.
Ren has no idea what this is supposed to consist of. He’d almost prefer the airlock puzzles, if
it meant knowing where they stand with the cognitions of this place.
“Uh, were cognitions this… friendly? Last time?” Ann asks in a whisper.
Ren shakes his head, “Not in the slightest.”
“Guess it means we can avoid a fight?” Ryuji suggests, rubbing the back of his neck.
“Hopefully.” Futaba calls from above. Necronomicon dissipates, and she drops back to the
floor, “Unless we piss her off, I guess.”
“Then we won’t do that.” Makoto says simply.
“Welcome to the grand tour of the Okumura Foods empire.” The cognitive Haru interrupts,
gesturing broadly as they enter a large room, an enormous bay window on one end, the view
opening to the expanse of space. Along the edges, pedestals with glass casing hold various
objects, lengthy plaques to the sides of each.
“Okumura Foods began as a humble satellite, launched by the late father of Lord Okumura.”
The cognition walks crisply, striding past several of the smaller exhibits, Ren and the others
trailing behind, “Small, but unsuccessful. It was the current Lord’s expertise that allowed for
this empire to truly raise off the ground.”
“So this tour will be spoken largely in metaphors, then.” Yusuke sighs.
“She calls her dad Lord?” Ann makes a face.
Makoto frowns, “Doesn’t something seem off, to you?”
Ren shrugs. The distinction between off as in ‘Okumura is an asshole’ and off as in
‘Something isn’t adding up’ is blurry at the best of times.

The cognition pauses at a pedestal, presenting a UFO in the shape of a burger bun, “In a fit of
genius, Lord Okumura devised Big Bang Burger, rapidly expanding the satellite into the
famed spaceport renowned today, a beacon of industry.”
“Well, at least Mr. CEO knows how to keep a brand recognisable…?” Futaba offers,
sounding unenthused.
The cognitive Haru moves to the next pedestals, gesturing to a sheet of paper that looks like a
contract, a page of schematics, and small-scale model of the entire palace, “Okumura Foods
continued to expand, brokering intelligent deals among the powerful, the sheer potential of
the empire bending allies to the Lord’s whims.”
“Layin’ it on a little thick, don’t ’cha think?” Ryuji mumbles.
Next, holographic dioramas of unfamiliar spaceships and stations, all derelict and crumbling.
“Business competitors were swiftly crushed under the Lord’s heel, past deals coming to call
as even the mysterious attack dog of Lord Okumura’s most powerful ally came to do his
work.”
Ren grimaces. Ann gives a small gasp, “Oh, is she talking about-?”
“Looks like it…” Makoto presses her lips together as they continue forward.
“Today, Okumura Foods stands as a monolith,” The cognition waves her arm in a grand arc,
“A testament to the efforts of our leader. And now, for the future,”
Ryuji groans, “There’s more?”
Yusuke sighs, “This really is a bit much.”
“We did sign up for this.” Futaba points out, not sounding particularly thrilled, “Maybe we
shoulda checked if there was an express tour.”
“Probably.” Ren agrees, boredom starting to overtake his nerves.
The cognitive Haru pays their complaining no mind, “Okumura Foods plans to tread a new
frontier- the realm of politics, and new strides in scientific advancement.”
Yusuke straightens up, “Oh, this might be…?”
“Is Okumura into science?” Futaba asks, confused, “Like, beyond his weird space obsession?
I can’t tell if that’s just part of the distortion or not.”
Ren frowns, “I don’t remember there being anything significant, last time. But there was
never any mention of this either.”
“Success breeds jealousy,” The cognition states, walking past even more exhibits, “And it
wasn’t long before Lord Okumura’s partners became his opponents. Many have seen
Okumura Foods’ riches and power- deals have been retracted, sabotage runs rampant; thieves

and assassins, all controlled by the Lord’s enemy in politics, each stake their claim on the

“Oookay.” Ann blows a raspberry, “Well, at least we know what’s running through this guy’s

Ren narrows his eyes. Is Okumura suspicious of his employees? …Is he suspicious of Haru?
Something has been slightly off about this cognition that he can’t quite put his finger on. No
longer does Okumura see his daughter as an unfailingly loyal tool to be kept at his right hand;

Ren wonders how closely guarded the knowledge of Haru’s engagement was. He hadn’t

Ren kind of wishes that Haru was here to answer that kind of question, but alas.
“Lord Okumura’s greatest opponent seeks to destroy the grand empire he has built,” The

Futaba splutters, nearly tripping over her own feet, “Hey- whoa whoa whoa, is this trying to

someone like your sister has.” He nods to Makoto.

longer the paths are going to be separated, or if only one of them will lead to the treasure. So,
buckle up, folks!”
Morgana huffs, “Yeah, yeah.” He turns to Sumire and Haru, “I guess we’ll… fill Akechi in,
next we infiltrate the palace.”
“This afternoon, you mean.” Ren says, scratching behind Morgana’s ears.
“Yeah. That.” Morgana agrees, while clearly pretending not to enjoy the pets.
“First, though,” Makoto interrupts, “I asked you all here so you could help me out.”
“For what…?” Ann asks, eyeing the three boxes on the table with a suspicious frown.
“The school festival.” Makoto says, prying open the boxes’ lids, fishing out a small sheet of
paper, “There was a vote to determine who we’ll try to invite to the panel we do every year,
and there’s a lot to tally.”
“Oh, yeah.” Ren shoots the boxes a look, “I remember this.”
“That’s still so weird dude.” Ryuji mutters.
Makoto raises an eyebrow, “Oh? Care to spare us some time and tell us what the outcome
is?”
Ren shrugs, pushing his glasses up his nose, “It was Akechi. But, that was right after
everyone thought we killed Okumura, so everyone was pretty thrilled about the idea of him.
Now, public opinion is still pretty split.”
Ann groans, and flops forward on the table, “So we’ve still gotta count them?”
Futaba cackles through the receiver, “Sucks to be you guys!”
“It’s not that many.” Sumire says, perhaps a little too charitably. The boxes really are quite
full.
“The sooner we start counting, the sooner we’ll be finished.” Haru says, not quite in
agreement. She fishes a vote out of the closest box, and tilts her head curiously, “My. This
one just says: ‘Phantom Thieves’.”

Makoto breathes out a long-suffering sigh, “I… really hope they won’t all be like that. It
would be such a waste of time.”
“Not necessarily.” Ren grins- the one Sumire knows as ‘trouble’, “We’re right here, after all.
We wouldn’t even need to pay anyone.”
“Hey, good point, dude!” Ryuji claps Ren on the back. He pauses, “…I mean. We could still
get paid though, right?”
Morgana looks seconds from clawing holes in everyone’s clothes, “Don’t be stupid! There’s
no way we can give an interview!”
“Yeah, Ryuji.” Ann snipes. She tilts her head, “Though, Mona, how would you join in on the
interview? I guess we’d have to translate?”
“Not you too…” Morgana whines, as Makoto pinches the bridge of her nose.
“Please. Can we please get this done.” She begs.
After that, beyond a few other conversational detours, the votes are all quickly counted.
Sumire frowns at the results.
“A pretty even split.” Ren observes.
“Quite.” Haru hums, “Does this mean that Goro-kun and the Phantom Thieves are equally
popular, at this point?”
“Kind of concerning, since we haven’t even done anything yet.” Futaba grumbles.
“People are starting to get impatient.” Makoto says simply, “If anything, it could work in our
favour. I hope.” She adds, “They could also be asking for Akechi to appear so they may…
express their grievances. We can’t be sure. Either way, we can hardly invite the Phantom
Thieves of Hearts to give a panel, so I suppose we’ll have to ask Akechi if he’s willing.”
Several heads turn to either look at Sumire or Haru, while Morgana turns to look at Ren, who
pointedly ignores him.
Sumire slowly reaches for her phone, “…Right now?”
Ann blinks, “I guess? Why not, right?”
“He might be busy.” Haru warns.
“Then someone can just text him, or whatever.” Ryuji waves a hand.
Sumire shrugs, and dials Goro’s number. It only takes two rings for him to pick up.
“Sumire?” Goro’s voice comes through.

“Um, hi!” Sumire says, suddenly feeling very awkward about having a phone call with an
audience. “I hope you weren’t busy…?”
“I was.” Goro says, with a bite that Sumire has learned not to take seriously, “But since it’s
you, I suppose I’ll make the time.”
Sumire tries not to feel too happy about that comment, but still finds herself giggling in
response, “Well, thank you. Um, I needed to ask you something. Most of us are here- can I
put you on speakerphone?”
“Go ahead.”
Sumire clicks the button, and places her phone on the table, “So, there’s a panel for Shujin’s
school festival, and-”
“Absolutely not.” Goro cuts her off.
Makoto makes a face, “Might I ask why?”
“Simply put, I have no reason to. It doesn’t benefit anyone, least of all us.” Goro explains,
“Last time I agreed to come because I used it as an opportunity to blackmail you all. You
invited me since you were trying to fish for information. Since that is no longer needed,
neither is my presence at your festival.”
Ann pouts, “So you’re just gonna leave us floundering for another guest? The other vote was
for the Phantom Thieves, you know!”
“I hear there is an abundance of those at Shujin.”
“Get serious!” Morgana complains.
“That aside,” Makoto sighs, “We genuinely don’t have another option. All the other votes are
for people who definitely won’t tolerate an unprofessional panel at a high school festival.”
“It’s mostly singers and idols.” Haru comments, idly picking up a handful of the small strips
of voting paper, “…I think there are some fictional characters here, too.”
Goro huffs, “Just cancel the panel, honestly. It would be a major risk for me to give a talk
similar to last time while public opinion is still so nebulous.”
“Don’t risk it, if you think it’s a bad idea.” Ren chimes in quietly.
“That’s what I’m doing, genius.” Goro scoffs, and Ren’s lips twitch up.
“So, if you won’t give a panel…” Sumire fiddles with her glasses, “Will you come to the
festival, anyway?”
There’s a very pointed pause. “Sumire.”
“Come on!” Ann cheers, “It’ll be fun!”

“Didn’t I just say that it’s ill-advised for me to-”
“I don’t know…” Haru hums, tapping her chin performatively, “It’s not as though you would
have to pander to any audience expectations, whatever they may be. You would just be
spending time with us. The festival will likely be rife with people gossiping in the halls, too.”
Goro’s answering sigh is defeated, “Are you truly that desperate for my company?”
“Please?” Sumire pushes one last time, unable to keep the triumphant grin out of her voice.
There’s a scoff, “Fine. I’ll be lying low, though. Don’t expect me to stick around the whole
time, either.”
“That’s all we could have hoped for!” Ann declares brightly.
Ryuji snickers, apparently having enjoyed the show, “See you there, dude.”
Goro hangs up after an irritated click of the tongue, and a clipped, “See you in the palace.”
The dial tone beeping loudly throughout the room.
Sumire tucks her phone away, as Makoto frowns wearily at the spread of shredded paper over
the table.
“…I guess I’ll-” Her expression becomes pained, “Try, to explain to the student council that
the panel is cancelled. Or get a teacher to do a speech or something.”
“You’ll figure it out.” Futaba’s voice crackles, unsympathetic, and Makoto groans into her
hands.
***
To say that infiltrating her father’s palace is uncomfortable is not entirely accurate.
To use a stronger descriptor, (disgusting, revolting, utterly horrendous) doesn’t quite capture
the feeling, either. Such thoughts are far too intense.
No, what Noir feels as she surveys the dilapidated remains of the spaceport that orbits in her
father’s head is far closer to resigned curiosity than anything else. A detached itch that begs
to be scratched, smeared with apathy and buried under the weight of the task at hand.
“This place used to be just a factory, right?” Mona asks, filling the silence as they trek
onwards, “I wonder if some of that’s still the same.”
“Probably, right?” Violet muses, tapping her finger against her chin, “I don’t think that
Sugimura’s change of heart would have changed how he thinks of his workers.”
“No…” Noir agrees, “According to the others, though, he seems suspicious of those close to
him.” Suspicious of her, apparently. She isn’t sure how to feel about that. Though she
supposes her father isn’t wrong, exactly.

“I suppose we’ll find out whether that extends to the rank-and-file employees as we
progress.” Crow remarks.
Noir supposes they will.
There’s a part of her that wishes she could have seen the cognition of her. Just to see- just to
understand exactly what it is her father thinks of her. Though, by the sounds of it, the
cognition is difficult to read.
The other part of her is infinitely grateful that she hasn’t seen it. But, she’s sure that this grace
afforded to her won’t last forever.
They move forward, taking down shadows with ruthless efficiency as they do. Having Mona
as a secondary healer makes Noir realise just how stretched thin Violet had been before; now
that she’s free to attack as she pleases, shadows fall with alarming speed at her blades.
“Hello.” Crow says pleasantly during one battle, after the last shadow has been knocked
down, “I have a deal for you.”
“What?!” The shadow, a woman in a white dress with devil’s wings, shrieks, “You shot me!
Why would I accept a deal from you?!”
“It seems-” Mona cuts himself off as Violet starts to speak her advice at the same time.
“…It seems kind of irritable.” Violet continues, after Mona gives her a gentlemanly nod to go
ahead. She laughs, “I think you’d get along if you just be yourself!”
Crow scowls at her, eliciting another giggle, and turns back to the shadow, “How about this?
Listen to my deal, and I won’t shoot you again.”
“Ooooh woooow, you’re so scary!” The shadow drawls, snickering, “I guess that’s not bad,
but can’t you sweeten the deal?”
Noir lifts her grenade launcher a little higher, “I’d be careful, if I were you. You’re in no
position to make demands.”
The shadow scoffs, her laughter dissipating, “Geez! What is everyone’s problem, today!”
“You’re in our way.” Crow says flatly, “Surely you can appreciate how generous we’re being.
You can even make yourself useful by joining me.”
The shadow tilts her head, “Wow, you’re kind of an asshole. You kind of remind me of- oh, I
remember now!” The shadow flies back up, facing Crow with a smile, “My name is Lilim,
and I’m from the sea of mankind’s hearts! I’ll become your mask, so use me well!”
Lilim transforms into lights, flickering between the shapes of Crow’s masks, before flying
forward. Crow grimaces as the light disperses, not nearly as pained as Noir remembers this
process having been in the past, though he still looks to be shaking off a mild headache.
“…Huh.” Mona blinks, “You really are just like Joker.”

Crow makes a face, “Sure.”
“Anything good on that one?” Violet asks, peering at Crow’s mask as though she can still see
the outline of the persona.
Crow shakes his head, “Not particularly. She’s too weak to hold a candle to Robin or Loki.
Atropos, at the very least, has some useful support skills to counter the power gap.” He
shrugs, “I suppose I’ll fuse it into something later.”
Eventually, the scenery starts to shift.
“Ah, now here’s something familiar.” Crow hums, as the hallways propped up with
scaffolding and what Noir can only assume is magic, opens into a far more open expanse.
Conveyer belts and production lines, manned by cognitive robots that flail about in a panic,
robotic shadows patrolling the paths.
Noir narrows her eyes at the sight.
“…Are you alright, Noir?” Mona speaks up, catching a glimpse of her expression.
Noir blinks, “Oh! Oh, I’m alright. I suppose I’m just…” She frowns at the sight again,
“Not… surprised, at this, but…”
“…It’s still not great to see?” Violet guesses, a sympathetic smile on her face.
Noir readjusts her hat, contemplative, “Not quite? Yes, but I think it’s more…” She sighs, “I
had been so caught up in my own problems, that I stopped thinking about everything else my
father has done. It all seemed so… distant, while I had other things on my plate.”
Crow hums, staring out at the view, “You were busy.”
Noir laughs, “That’s very kind of you.” She remarks, “It’s just I’ve had a lot of reasons to feel
I’m being selfish, of late.”
“It’s not your fault!” Mona insists, “Your fiancé sounded terrible- it’s not selfish to help
yourself!”
Violet nods enthusiastically in agreement, “And besides, we’re doing something about it now,
aren’t we?”
Haru feels her smile grow wider, “Thank you Mona, Violet.” She takes a deep breath, “Shall
we continue?”
Crow nods, “If we’re ready.”
Making progress through this section of the palace is largely a matter of stealth. Alerting one
cognition or shadow would mean alerting far more- not an impossible fight, given their
group’s strength, but not a pleasant one.
“Maybe those airlock puzzles are still intact, if this is all the same…” Violet muses.

“What was so bad about the airlock puzzles!?” Mona yells, “I swear, Joker shudders every
time they come up!”
“They’re just annoying.” Crow explains with a disinterested shrug, “It’s hardly important
anyway- look.”
He points, and at the end of the path is a saferoom, as well as two other hallways. One,
sporting a familiar weathered wood and musty carpet, the other retaining the space factory
aesthetic, though looking a tad more put-together than the path prior.
“Have the paths converged?” Noir asks, walking forward to peer down the other hall.
“Looks like it.” Mona nods, “I don’t think the others are here just yet, though. Should we
wait in the safe room?”
“That’s fine.” Crow nods, “We’ll probably leave the palace once they arrive, anyway.”
Noir and Violet give their agreements, and the four of them file into the saferoom, taking
seats around the table.
“How much further do you think we have to go?” Violet asks, looking between Crow and
Mona.
Mona hums contemplatively, tilting his head, “I’d say… not that far? We could probably
secure the route in one more infiltration.”
“Robin agrees.” Crow says with a nod. He sighs, “It looks like we’ll be teaming up for this
last stretch.”
Mona narrows his eyes, “Are you gonna be a problem?”
Crow scoffs, “I’ll reign it in.”
“Hopefully it won’t be too long between here and the treasure…” Violet murmurs, sounding
wary.
“Speaking of,” Mona perks back up, “How soon after the change of heart are we gonna fake
Okumura’s death?”
“I’d like to organise it as soon as it takes effect, honestly.” Noir speaks up, “I’d rather not
strain the limits of what little time we have.”
“That’s good, I think.” Violet nods, “I’m sure everyone else will agree too.”
“I suppose that makes the real question how much breathing room we’re going to give the
public before we make a move after that…” Noir hums.
“Faking my death serves as something of a replacement for faking Joker’s,” Crow begins,
“But I believe waiting for late November would be pushing it. I think we should, at the very
least, loop Sae-san in first before we make any big moves like that.”

Violet nods, before frowning, “What do you think Shido will do, once you’re presumed
dead?”
“Who knows?” Crow shrugs, carefully unaffected, “We’ll have to stay on our toes.”
Noir leans back, and looks at the ceiling of the safe room, “We will.”
She can only hope everything goes to plan.
***
The infiltration ends, without much fanfare, as Ren’s half of the thieves arrives at the safe
room where the two paths have converged; Akechi, Sumire, Haru, and Morgana catching
everyone up on their discussions and musings.
It’s easy, if not a little tense, everyone avoiding the elephant in the room of the groups having
to rejoin again- leading two separate infiltrations down the same hallway seems like a recipe
for confusion more than anything else, in Ren’s opinion.
But that’s a problem for tomorrow, as they all agree to call it a day.
(It’s always a problem for later-)
With that weight on his shoulders, Ren falls into a restless sleep.
There isn’t a transition, anymore. Nothing of the sort- the barrier between memory in both
dreams and waking has faded entirely, leaving only the slight disorientation of existing in a
space that isn’t entirely real.
That, and the utter confusion of Ren having no idea what he’s doing here.
“Hello?” Ren calls to the visage of a nondescript Mementos tunnel- a sight he’s seen more
than once in these dreams. But Ren had assumed with hindsight that those were his
subconscious, the persistent nag of his lost memories beneath the rubble, trying to break free.
So there is absolutely no reason for him to be here now.
Not to mention“Well, look who decided to show up.” Crow- no, Metatron’s voice snarks, and Ren whirls
around, taking in the sight of his Justice-bound persona and Aeon arcana, back to wearing
Akechi’s likeness.
Ren blinks, “Did- did I fuck up again, or something?” His mind races for an explanation,
“What-?” He gestures helplessly as he can’t find his words.
Metatron rolls his eyes, removing his helmet and running a hand through his hair, “I needed
to talk with you. It’s hard to do, when I’m in the same space as all your other personas. Only
our strongest emotions and words can reach you from there- otherwise you’d be
overwhelmed, no doubt.”

Ren can’t help the way his lips quirk up, “So you decided to find a loophole?”
“It’s hardly a loophole if there are no rules against it.” Metatron says with a scoff.
Ren laughs, and shoves his hands in his pockets, “So? What did you want to talk about?”
Something low-stakes, Ren hopes. Though he isn’t so naïve to assume that’s the case.
Metatron tilts his head, narrowing his eyes, “You know,” He starts, a little too intense to be
conversational, “I suppose I didn’t have high hopes of what you would do, once you
remembered what you had forgotten.”
Ren feels like that’s probably an insult. He frowns, “…Yeah?”
A sigh, “I’m telling you that you’re being pathetic.” Metatron grits.
Ren scowls, “About what? I’m trying- we have a plan to make sure everything else turns out
fine. What more do you need?”
“Ah, yes, your plan.” Metatron says with derision, “How well is that working out for you?”
“We haven’t run into any problems yet.” Ren glares.
“Haven’t you?” Metatron counters, “Isn’t your team falling apart at the seams? You’ve
gotten away with it, for now, but how long is that going to last?”
Ren bites at his lip, “It’s not like that’s something I can-” He cuts himself off, thinking of
declarations of hatred and meaningful glares, arcana still off-kilter, “I’m giving him space.”
Ren says quietly, knowing Metatron will understand what he’s referring to.
“Are you, now?” Metatron says, sounding more tired than accusatory. He sighs, “Tell me,
Joker, how well has ‘giving Goro Akechi space’ worked out for you in the past?”
Ren opens his mouth, confident answer on the tip of his tongue,
And clicks his jaw shut.
“Are you going to sit around and wait for him to make a move?” Metatron drawls, “Do you
think he ever will?”
Ren swallows, “I thought you were mad at me for everything, too.”
“Oh, I am.” Metatron sneers, “But you forget what I represent. I don’t get to pick and
choose; everything that built the Justice is a part of me.”
“Right.” Ren murmurs, rolling his lips together.
Ren considers this. He had figured, for many reasons, including but not limited to the sword
that had been quickly pressed to his throat the moment that he and Akechi had regained their
memories of the previous timeline, that pushing his luck would be nothing but ill-advised.
He’s already pushed it quite a bit, in fact, and Ren is certain he’ll get burned if he keeps at it.

But, even so,
Such a risk had never stopped him before, so why the hell is he letting it stop him now?
Metatron must see something in his face, as the persona grins, “Well, look at that. We get
along so well when you listen to me.”
Ren rolls his eyes, “Feels like that should be a two-way street.”
“You’re an idiot, though.” Metatron hums, bursting into a cackle as Ren scowls at him.
“Yeah, yeah.” Ren mumbles, “I- yeah. I get what you’re saying.”
Ren would rather be six feet under than let his relationship with Akechi die in such a
miserable fashion; fraying away thread by thread and dunked in bitter resentment. If two
murder attempts and a foundation of lies and games didn’t sour it, then Ren will make sure
this won’t, either.
So, he just has to fix it. Really fix it.
“I’m glad you understand.” Metatron straightens up, sounding almost genuine.
Ren tugs himself out of his thoughts -as much as he can, in a dream- and twists his fringe
between his fingers, “Any advice?”
“For repairing the relationship you fucked up?” Metatron raises an eyebrow, “Not at all.”
Ren takes a deep breath, “That seems uncharitable.” Akechi is the one refusing to give Ren
an inch.
“Allow me to rephrase, then.” Metatron gives a cheerful little shrug, “I am thou, thou art I,
and I have no idea. Good luck, Joker.”
And Ren wakes up.
He drags a hand down his face with a muffled groan.
He should ask Ann for help.
