Maruki jumps, surprised, “Oh- Amamiya-kun?”
“Hi, doc.” Ren says, flat.
Ren is pretty sick of this too, now that he thinks about it.
“I didn’t expect it’d be you in here,” Maruki says, sounding amazed, “I thought you’d be out
enjoying the festival with your friends. Though I guess in retrospect I did hear your voice, I
just didn’t connect it to- oh!” His eyes catch on Akechi, “Aren’t you…?”
“Hm.” Is all that Akechi offers, apparently not deeming Maruki worth the effort of his
princely mask.
“You keep famous company, Amamiya-kun!” Maruki laughs, oblivious to or ignoring the
atmosphere, “Oh- but, oh, you were shouting- is everything alright?”
“Just fine.” Ren says, one hand still on the door, “We were having a conversation.”
“Oh, well…” Maruki laughs awkwardly, in that way he often does, “Don’t let me interrupt
you? Oh, but- this place is off limits for the festival, and in general I think, so-”
“We’ll be quick.” Ren interrupts, “Promise.”

Ren hears something like a muffled scoff behind him, and valiantly ignores it.
“Well…” Maruki grimaces, looking a little conflicted. He eventually relents with a sigh, “I
suppose I trust you, Amamiya-kun.” He chuckles, “Maybe you can pay me back by helping
out with my research some more? Or even just stopping by for regular counselling. It’s been
while!”
“Will do.” Ren will not. “I’ll see you around.” He will continue to actively avoid him.
“Good to hear.” Maruki says with an earnest smile, “See you, Amamiya-kun! And you as
well, Akechi-kun, it was nice meeting you.”
Akechi’s face splits with a smile so plastic that Ren thinks he must be making it look fake on
purpose, “Likewise.” He says, voice entirely saccharine.
Maruki, again either oblivious or pointedly ignorant, smiles and waves as he takes a step
back, “Enjoy the rest of the festival! I hear there’s an afterparty, if you’re interested.”
“Yep.” Ren mumbles, and quickly closes the door again, locking it. He strains his ears, and
only relaxes as he hears Maruki’s footsteps disappear down the hall.
“Well.” Akechi eventually says, dry as the desert, “Do you hear it yet?”
“Hear what?” Ren sighs, only half turning around.
“The resemblance is uncanny.” Akechi drawls, “Glasses and hair that’s never seen a brush? I
think you’re cramping his style.”
Ren half laughs, smiling miserably, “I thought I was supposed to sound like him, not be his
long-lost relative.”
Akechi tilts his head, thinking performatively, “I suppose. I could also hunt through my
phone for one of Shido’s drunken voicemails. I wonder how similar you would sound to
him?”
Ren freezes, “You’re crossing a line.” He says lightly, like they’re just friends joking around.
“Am I?” Akechi says innocently, coy as he’s ever been.
“Yes.” Ren hisses, “He ruined my life- he ruined your life- don’t- I hate him just as much as
you do, don’t compare us just because you’re pissed.”
“He did ruin my life.” Akechi agrees easily, “But you and Maruki took a very solid crack at
ruining my death, too. One I could escape from, if I was desperate. The other, well.”
Ren scoffs, incredulous and just a touch hysterical, “Don’t make it sound like I’m worse than
him.”
“No, I suppose you’re not.” Akechi hums, and Ren really hates how easily he took control of
this conversation, “You’re definitely more pathetic, though.” He narrows his eyes, “After all

this, it’s almost like you're still convinced you haven’t done anything wrong.”
This is a test. It’s not even thinly veiled- Akechi’s trials never are.
“I-” Ren chokes, “It’s okay though -now- isn’t it? You’re not dead. You’re not going to die.
We’re going to get through this.”
Swing and a miss. Strike one, or one thousand. Ren doesn’t think either of them are really
counting.
“You think that just because Sumire miraculously got the chance to kick the can down the
road, that all is well?” Akechi sneers, his airy taunts slipping.
Ren grimaces, “Better her than either of us, right?”
Akechi snorts, and Ren takes it as a victory, “For you, maybe. If I woke up back in April, the
first thing I would have done is kill you.”
A lifeline. Ren almost smiles. “You haven’t killed me, though.”
Akechi narrows his eyes, “I didn’t wake up in April. I woke up in October.” He says slowly,
like he’s questioning Ren’s intelligence.
“You’ve still had the chance, though.” Ren points out, getting somewhere, “You had a sword
to my throat, and you didn’t kill me. Why?”
“Perhaps I don’t think you’re worth the effort.” Akechi spits.
“Liar.” Ren says simply.
“Don’t turn this on me.” Akechi snarls, “If your intention was to gear up to some big
apology, you’re doing a terrible fucking job.”
Point. “Is that something you want from me?” Ren asks, genuinely.
“I don’t want anything from you.” Akechi says, sounding so, so tired, “I wanted you to not
take the deal. I was certain you wouldn’t.” He scoffs, “It was a rather unpleasant shock, to
realise you weren’t the person I thought you were at all.”
A moment,
“I’m still me.” Ren says quietly.
“Are you?” Akechi accuses, “Really? Are you? You take a gun to your head with grace, but
the second it’s turned around the challenge is suddenly too much. Why?”
There is something Ren could say. It would be painfully, catastrophically true. He couldn’t lie
if he tried.
He doesn’t say it.

“Your life isn’t-” This is too familiar for Ren’s liking.
“I’m not playing this game with you.” Akechi spits, “We’re not doing this again. You want
things to be normal? Convince me that you wouldn’t make the same choice, if the
circumstances presented themselves once again.”
Ren’s mouth goes dry. He swallows. “I never wanted to put you in a cage.” You know that,
right? You have to know that, you have to“I thought I said convince me.” Akechi growls, and grits out, “Your attempt is lacking.”
And Akechi turns on his heel and leaves, throwing the door open, fury in his step and
frustration baked into every line of his body.
And RenRen thinks, about November, half-heartedly reaching out for something he knew wasn’t
possible, making sure the game was set in his favour. He thinks about December, pounding
his fists against a watertight door with the mortifying knowledge that he was too late, that he
irrecoverably fucked up- rigged the game and watched patiently as the other player spooled
out more than enough rope to hang himself with.
He thinks about January, the blissful ignorance of thinking he had a second chance, reaching
out again and again with a desperate fervour, begging the other in the safety of his mind,
don’t run from me, don’t you dare hide, I can fix this, I can make this work, one month and
then we have the rest of our lives.
(February, where he made a choice)
And now,
The blood that binds the Justice, fractured, but not broken.
I’m not letting you slip away, Ren thinks to Goro’s retreating back. Somewhere, in the depths
of Ren’s mind, he feels the silver of Metatron’s face curl into a smile.
***
“Sooo, that kinda sucked.” Ann drawls out, as she exits the haunted house attraction with the
rest of the present thieves.
Sumire, in the privacy of her own mind while her classmates are still withing earshot, agrees.
She isn’t so confident to think that if she contributed more, then the exhibit would have
turned out better, but really, what they got was a pretty sad showing.
“I had hoped for a little more, yes.” Haru sighs, “What else are we missing? We tried most of
the food stalls yesterday…”
“I think the play is already halfway through by now.” Makoto chimes in, “I’m not sure if
they’re doing more than one run through, so we might have to cut our losses on that front.”

“Man…” Ryuji groans, “This is so lame.”
“The afterparty wasn’t too bad.” Sumire adds, “But we have to wait a little longer for that.”
Futaba hums, “I kinda just wanna go home, to be honest.”
Makoto grimaces in what Sumire assumes is supposed to be a sympathetic smile, “Well, if
Ren doesn’t want to leave, you can ask one of us to take you home.”
Futaba sighs, “If Ren wants to stick around I guess I can wait. Maybe.”
“Where the hell is Ren?!” Morgana complains, “He disappeared ages ago!”
Sumire figured it was pretty obvious, considering who else is missing.
Ann laughs stiltedly, “Yeah, gee, I wonder!”
It seems like the thieves take that as a collective not their business, and dissolve back into
chatter. Sumire takes the opportunity to walk up to Ann’s side.
“Um, so,” Sumire starts, unsure how worried she should be, “Do you actually know where
Ren and Goro went?”
Ann startles, and then deflates, “Okay, well, not really. But Ren asked me for advice the other
day! So I guess he’s probably trying to-” She waves her arms, “Put it into action.”
“Ah.” Sumire hums flatly, “Well, if we find a corpse…?”
Ann snorts, “We’ll know what happened then. I’m sure it’ll be fine! Let’s not talk about those
idiots- thinking about them too much stresses me out.”
Sumire laughs into her hand, “I get that.” She looks around, “How should we waste some
time?”
Ann’s smile looks more like a grimace, “Oh boy, we’ve been stretched so thin that even the
words ‘wasting time’ freak me out. I’ve had to cancel a couple photo shoots just because of
how busy we’ve been.”
“Me too, actually.” Sumire frowns, “Oh- not photo shoots,” She laughs, “But I have had to
call out of a lot of practice sessions with my club. I think my coach is starting to get annoyed
with me.”
Ann presses her lips together, “That sucks… I’m really worried about getting a reputation for
being flaky. But it’s not like I can get a doctor’s note to be like Sorry! I was off stealing
hearts in the metaverse! No I can’t tell you what that is!” She blows a raspberry.
Sumire giggles under her breath, “Doesn’t Ren-senpai have a doctor he goes to? Maybe we
can beg her for something.”

“God, I wish.” Ann pouts, “But that would be super suspicious if anyone bothered to look
probably, and ugh- I’m not cut out for this!”
“I’m not much of a tactician either.” Sumire admits, though she supposes it’s probably
obvious, “I-” She sighs, “I’ve been kind of getting away with being absent a lot in practice,
since… Kasumi died at the start of the year. It’s not like I’ve been telling anyone that’s why
I’ve been missing practice, but- I don’t know. I really don’t like using her as my excuse,
especially when it isn’t true.”
Ann tilts her head curiously, “Is it not true?” She blanches, “Oh my god, that was probably
super insensitive. Sorry! Ignore me!”
Sumire flashes her a small smile, “It’s alright. I don’t mind. It’s…” She huffs, “I didn’t take
any time off, at first, in the original 2016.” She explains, “I just… went to practice, did
terribly, and then felt even more miserable.”
Ann tugs on one of her pigtails, “So is it like… it’s been nearly two years for you, so it’s
kinda- duller? Or something?”
Sumire does not want to think about how it’s been technically nearly two years since Kasumi
died- her chest tightens at the thought, and she breathes in sharply to try and dispel it. “I- I
guess that’s part of it. But- it was only a few weeks after… that, that Dr Maruki made me
think I was Kasumi. So then I spent nearly a whole year being miserable at practice, but I
didn’t even understand why.”
Ann frowns, “So did… Sumire, as like, a concept, just not exist for you?”
Sumire shakes her head, “No, it’s-” She laughs self-deprecatingly, “It’s kind of funny,
honestly. In my head, I was Kasumi Yoshizawa, and my younger sister had died in an
accident just a few months ago. But- I guess it would have been my cognition of Kasumi, that
she didn’t let something like that get to her. I was sad, but…”
Not nearly as devastated as Sumire had been, when she saw red painting the road, washing
out with the rain.
“Wow, that is…” Ann puffs out her cheeks, “Freaky. All of it is. I guess- like, it did kind of
happen to me, right? You said that Maruki gave all of us perfect little realities for a bit, but
it’s not like he turned me into a different person.”
Sumire bites her lip, “I thought a lot, about why Dr Maruki didn’t just… bring Kasumi back
to life, when he became a god.” She says quietly, “He did it for other people, but he just… let
Sumire stay dead. Kind of.” She’s trying not to give herself a headache.
Ann hums, considering, “…Maybe he didn’t want to change what he already gave you? He
already actualised you wayyy earlier, so…”
Sumire smiles unhappily, “I think I used that excuse at first, too. But- I think it might be
because I wasn’t happy while Kasumi was alive, either.”

Ann’s expression crumples, “Oh…”
Sumire bites at her lip a little harder, “Um- sorry, I didn’t mean to- uh, dump this on you, I
guess,”
Ann shakes her head furiously, “No, no! It’s okay!” She pats Sumire’s shoulders, “Get it all
out! I’d be like, the biggest hypocrite if I couldn’t take it- I dump all my stuff on Ren all the
time! I mean, I’ve been trying to be a bit better about it, since I don’t want him to be my
therapist, but that usually means going to Ryuji since Shiho’s got more than enough to worry
about, and- yeah.” She laughs, “It’s perfectly okay.”
Sumire smiles in relief, “That’s- good. Thank you, Ann-senpai.”
Ann waves her hands, flustered, “It’s no problem, seriously! And- oh!” She jumps, “Uhh,
what time is it?”
Sumire checks her phone, “Just after five.”
Ann groans, “Oh thank god, think they’ve cleared out the gym for the afterparty, yet?”
“…By now, probably?” Sumire casts her mind back, fishing for the memory, “At least, I
think we’ll be able to loiter before it starts.” She giggles, “They had a whole production by
the dance club, last time.”
“Ooo, that sounds fun,” Ann titters, and then waves to all the other thieves, “Hey, guys! We
can probably go to the gym now, instead of just wandering around!”
There are several relieved groans and cheers, and they pivot their general meandering to
follow the paths to the practice building.
“Um…” Ann speaks up at some point, her and Sumire still a little separated from the others,
“Hey, really, thanks for telling me all that.” She laughs a little, and tugs at her hair, “I know
we’re not super close, but I’d like to be!”
Sumire blinks, “Oh! Well- thank you as well, Ann-senpai.” She gives a short bow with an
awkward but genuine smile, “I’m glad.”
Ann smiles cheerfully in turn, and they continue walking forward.
***
After a while, and a bit of loitering in the corner of the gym as other students slowly filter in,
Sumire spots Goro rejoining the group, scowl etched on his face.
She sidles up to him, “Were you talking with…?”
Goro’s scowl deepens, “Don’t ask me how it went.” He snaps.
Sumire grimaces, “…That bad?”

“What do you think?” Goro mutters without much heat.
Sumire pats his arm reassuringly, and supposes that now isn’t the time. Not too long after, she
sees Ren quietly step back into the group as well. Ann steps up to presumably mirror
Sumire’s prying, and Ren’s answering frown tells her all she really needs to know.
“I hope the festival wasn’t too bad for you.” Sumire eventually says, feeling a little guilty at
how she pushed for him to show up in the first place.
“It was bad.” Goro says bluntly, and Sumire winces. “I much preferred last time, when I got
to blackmail everyone.” He adds.
Sumire laughs, and Goro shoots her a look. “Do you want to know something embarrassing
about me so that you can take another shot at it?”
“I know plenty of embarrassing things about you.” Goro fires back immediately.
“Huh?” Sumire gapes caught off guard, “Like what?!”
“You snore, for one.” Goro says dryly, and Sumire pouts. “And, oh, do you recall? When you
were so caught off guard by my demeanour that you loudly asked if I was always a ruthless
sort of person-”
“I get it!” Sumire quickly interrupts. She really didn’t expect this to get turned around on her,
but she’ll take it if it lightens the mood, “There are probably-”
Sumire feels the air grow tense, as she spots some students suddenly whispering in groups,
wide-eyed and staring at their phones.
Ah.
She doesn’t take out her own. She thinks she knows what she might see.
At her side, Goro’s eyes narrow. “Haru-san.” He says, any semblance of light-heartedness in
his voice drained away, “Did your father happen to call a press conference this morning, by
any chance?”
“I stayed at Sumi-chan’s place again, so I don’t know.” She answers quietly.
“I see.” Is the blank response.
Some of the other thieves, who were chatting idly away, start to pick up on the mood.
“Is- is it happenin’?” Ryuji asks, looking downtrodden.
“There’s only one way to find out.” Makoto points out stiffly.
No one takes out their phone.
“I don’t think I wanna see.” Futaba says.

“It would be unpleasant, yes.” Yusuke agrees, looking uncomfortable.
Haru takes a shaky breath. Sumire quickly grabs her hand, and gives her an equally shaky
smile.
Ann chuckles without humour, “I guess the day’s over, then.”
“It might not be- that.” Ren points out softly. He gives a half-hearted grin, “Maybe Shido
tripped and died.”
Goro snorts, and then looks very annoyed at himself for having such a reaction. It kind of
makes Sumire want to laugh too.
“If only.” Makoto agrees weakly.
“The student council prez hoping someone trips and dies?” Morgana teases half-heartedly,
the energy usually in the air entirely sapped, “Who replaced you with an evil clone?”
Futaba brightens slightly at that, “Look at you, kitty!” (“I’m not a cat!”) “I think I’ve finally
made you cultured!”
“I would have made that joke before I met you, thank you very much!” Morgana huffs.
Haru giggles slightly at their antics. Sumire squeezes her hand a little tighter, and takes a
small comfort in the slightly wider smile.
The whispering around the gym gets a little louder. More students look around in confusion,
taking out their phones, if only to fit in. It doesn’t take long for those students to go wideeyed as well.
Sumire nearly jumps three feet in the air when Goro’s phone starts ringing. He slowly takes it
out of his pocket with a resigned exhale, and brings it to his ear after eyeing the caller ID.
“Sae-san? Is there something you need?”
Sumire can hear sharp and frantic words through the receiver, a little too quiet to truly make
anything out.
“What happened with Okumura?!” Goro exclaims, entirely performative, expression a little
too flat for the tone to be real, “I- yes, of course, I’ll be there right away.” A pause, “I’m at
Shujin, at the moment; some friends- yes I understand.”
The other thieves exchange looks, as Goro pauses again.
“I’ll see you soon, Sae-san. I promise we’ll get to the bottom of this.” He finishes off,
flashing an interview smile probably out of habit more than anything, and ends the call.
“Well.” Goro rolls out his neck, “The time bomb went off.”
“…I take it my sister wants you at the precinct?” Makoto asks, dour.

“That would be correct.” Goro says, readjusting his tie. “I’m sure to her, this confirms all her
theories about the Phantom Thieves. Which- ha.” He breathes something that might be a
laugh, “I’ll try and… curb her enthusiasm, a bit. We hardly want her to arrest us on the spot
come the time where we sit down and talk it out.” He adds in a lower voice.
“Right.” Haru agrees quietly, and Sumire can hear her phone buzzing in her pocket. She
swallows, “I think I might need to take my leave, as well. It would be odd if I had no reaction
to my father…”
Ren tugs at his fringe, “…I’ll try and find a recording of what just happened. It wouldn’t hurt
to know how much Okumura managed to get out in his confession before… whatever
happened.”
Hearing it phrased like that almost makes Sumire wish she had sucked it up and watched the
press conference. The time bomb has gone off, yes, but they don’t even know what it was
made of.
Morgana’s ears flick, “…Should we all head home, then?”
“I doubt they’ll cancel the rest of the school festival over this,” Makoto says, “But I don’t
think any of us are really up for festivities.”
Sumire presses her lips together, “No, not really.” She admits.
Ren shoves his hands in his pockets, “Let’s go home, then.” He says quietly, and everyone
can only nod.
***
Despite his words, Ren doesn’t leave immediately. Neither do most of the other thieves,
blending with the rest of the crowd as they hold hushed conversations in corners. Akechi
does leave immediately; unsurprising, since he has places to be.
Haru stands by herself, frowning helplessly at her phone.
“Hey.” Ren says, moving to stand at her side.
Haru looks up, and blinks, “Oh. Hello, Ren-kun.”
“You alright?” He cuts to the chase.
Haru laughs weakly, “I assume if I said yes, you wouldn’t believe me.”
Ren smiles guiltily, “Yeah. I wouldn’t.”
Haru’s own smile becomes a little more genuine, “At least you’re honest.”
“I try to be.” He says, apropos nothing. Does he? Peripherally, he supposes, but living a life
of pseudo-crime doesn’t typically lend to the truth being the best option. And, as Morgana
would probably remind him, he isn’t the most open in personal situations, either.

Haru gives him a look, as though she is also experiencing Ren’s internal monologue.
“Usually.” Ren tacks on, even though that’s also blatantly false.
Haru giggles behind her hand with a bit less energy than Ren would normally expect from
her, “If you say so.”
“But seriously,” Ren pivots, not wishing to dwell on that any longer, “If you need to talk to
someone, or something-” He pauses, “Well- I guess you have Sumire and Akechi for that.”
“I do.” Haru concedes, “Though that doesn’t mean I wish to be secretive with you, Ren-kun,”
She tilts her head, “I suppose I’ve just already talked it out.”
“Fully?” Ren asks, a little sceptically.
Haru shakes her head, and exhales shortly with what might be amusement, “Perhaps not. I-”
She smiles ruefully, “I’ve already said it in so many words, but I’m mostly frustrated with
myself.”
“Don’t be.” Ren says quickly, “It was a group effort. And I’m our leader,” Mostly, “So if the
blame has to fall to one person, let it fall to me.”
“That would be the logical way to feel about this, yes.” Haru says agreeably, “But I can’t
force myself to feel that way, unfortunately. And I don’t want to blame you for everything,
Ren-kun. That wouldn’t be fair.”
Ren rubs the back of his neck, “Well. Thanks.”
Haru’s lips twitch again, “Not at all. It was foolish to expect that everything would go as we
planned. Or that it would be easy.”
Ren almost snorts, “Yeah. Yeah, it probably was. Everything started going wrong about now
last time, too. Maybe we’re cursed?”
Haru laughs, sounding a bit surprised. “Goodness, I hope not! That would make everything
rather difficult.”
“No kidding.” Ren mumbles, not thinking about cruise ships and klaxon alarms, “I think we
just- got overconfident. Didn’t expect the shadow to be invincible.”
Haru sighs, “No. We didn’t. It’s funny, isn’t it? I honestly expected my father to be a bit of a
pushover.”
Ren does snort, this time, “I wish. I’d say that I hope the next palace ruler is, but I don’t want
to jinx it.”
Haru laughs slightly, “Maybe it can be an early Christmas wish.”
“For Yaldabaoth to stop making things difficult?” Directly or indirectly- Ren doesn’t know
nor care, he just wants it to stop, “Fitting, since we fought him on Christmas eve.”

Haru’s laugh fills out a little more, “My, what good timing.” Her eyes flick down to her
phone as it buzzes, “I… think I should go.”
Ren inclines his head, “Good luck, Haru.”
She smiles, “Thank you.” She takes a sharp breath, and straightens up, “I’ll keep you all
updated.”
“Remember to ask if you need help.” Ren reminds her.
Haru nods gratefully, “I will, don’t worry.” She waves shortly, and turns around, “Goodbye,
Ren-kun.”
“Bye.” Ren mumbles, even as Haru can’t hear him as she leaves.
After a moment, Futaba creeps up to his side, and tugs on her sleeve, “Are we going?”
“Yeah, yeah.” Ren runs a hand through his hair, and tries to breathe deeply.

It’s odd.
Takuto doesn’t know what he did, really. He had suspected that Amamiya was avoiding him,
but had chalked it up to paranoia. He had seemed uncomfortable, when Takuto had ran into
him today, though, so maybe the theory does hold some water.
And with Goro Akechi, too. Takuto didn’t know Amamiya kept such high-profile company,
honestly! Or, he was vaguely aware, and after a little prying months prior had been politely
and quickly told it was none of his business. That’s all fair, he supposes. He’s a counsellor,
not a warden.
It was still surprising, though. If he were the type to gossip, he’s sure he’d be bouncing off
the walls with excitement. Akechi hadn’t seemed particularly enthused to see him either,
though.
…Maybe Akechi heard about him from Amamiya, and has something against counsellors?
The detective isn’t an idol, but he’s certainly close, and he’s heard all sorts of things about
mental health in those kinds of professions, so maybeOr, maybe, he had just been offput by being interrupted.
That’s… far more likely than whatever unprompted spiral of psychoanalysis Takuto was on,
he decides.
He hates you. He is opposed to your ideology.
And just when he thought he could have some peace and quiet. Not that he really minds that
much.

The voices (or rather, voice, singular) in his head are rarely so specific, so it’s interesting to
hear them use so passionate a descriptor, with the teenage detective he’s never met before.
The only other people that’s really happened with are one Ren Amamiya and one Sumire
Yoshizawa.
AndWell.
Takuto tries not to think about her, too often, but she always creeps back in his thoughts
despite his efforts.
Shaking his head as though to clear it, Takuto sighs. He swears he didn’t used to be such a
busybody- maybe it’s just a side effect of the job.
If there’s an opening to learn more, he’ll take it. If there’s an opening to help, then…
Don’t jump the gun.
They’ll tear you to shreds while you can’t defend yourself.
That’s awfully vague. And a bit concerning. He’s only ever heeded the advice of- he should
really come up with a better name than The Voice In His Head. It’s on the tip of his tonguemaybe something starting with ‘A’? A passing thought, and the other syllables illude him.
Supposed danger or no; if he can help, he will. How could he ever not?

Chapter 65
Chapter Summary

Going through the motions, second takes, and a clock hits zero.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

It’s been a while since Akechi has spent any meaningful time in the precinct or prosecutor’s
office.
He’s spent time, sure. But most of it has been occupied with nothing cases that the SIU
director sends his way as the cases of mental shutdowns and psychotic breakdowns have a
dry spell. Surely some would consider it a nice break, but most of it is just drawing fake dots
between fake evidence, and Akechi feels an awful lot like Shido is squeezing his neck,
wringing out any last drop of usefulness Akechi can provide for the conspiracy while he’s
occupied.
Akechi doesn’t want to know what Shido thinks of this unprecedented change of plans. He
doesn’t think ‘I didn’t want this to happen, either!’ will placate the man.
But first, he has to placate Sae.
“I knew it.” Sae hisses between her teeth, rewinding the recording of Okumura’s press
conference and subsequent psychotic breakdown over and over.
Akechi had quickly watched it in the bathroom before meeting up with Sae, if only to avoid
revealing his first reaction. He had watched, detached, as Okumura had cut himself off
halfway through his sobbing speech about his abysmal work health and safety policies, eyes
glazing over, launching himself at journalists and camera men, screeching about traitors and
divinity all in one breath.
Four people were injured. One needed to be carted off to hospital, sporting a concussion from
being cracked over the head with a camera.
Akechi can’t quite tell if he cares.
Annoyingly, Okumura’s sudden obsession with the gods turning against him may cause a
dent in the validity of his confession once he snaps back to his regularly scheduled change of
heart. It might spare his life, at least.
“The Phantom Thieves have revealed their hand.” Sae mutters, glaring at her laptop with
furious intensity, “Bit the hand that fed them, by the looks of it. I knew Okumura was

involved in this somehow. Too many of the psychotic breaks benefited him.” She snorts,
“Guess he got what was coming to him.”
In the privacy of his mind, Akechi can only agree. He would never tell Haru that, though.
And really, a change of heart is already enough of a horrific rearranging of the mind to serve
as a punishment.
But, beyond that, Sae’s little spiral is moving a little too quickly for his tastes.
“Are you entirely sure, Sae-san?” Akechi cuts in, “A change of heart and a psychotic
breakdown occurring at the same time isn’t exactly sufficient evidence to claim that they’re
perpetrated by the same party. We don’t even know how they occur.”
Sae only falters for a moment, “It’s a little too convenient to be a coincidence.” She decides,
“They found a calling card on the premises. The house servants are saying his daughter found
it in the mail. Security footage checks out.”
He may as well go the full nine yards. “How is a calling card sufficient evidence for the
Phantom Thieves being responsible for the psychotic breakdown, though?” He pushes,
“Unless it proudly declared that they were going to break Okumura’s mind as punishment for
his crimes, it’s as absurd as claiming the thieves responsible for any misfortune that happens
to their targets just by way of association.”
Sae grits her teeth, still not meeting his eyes, “Unless you have a better explanation, then this
case is as good as solved, Akechi. I just need to find them.”
Akechi wonders how much he can get away with running his mouth before one of Shido’s
men tries to suffocate him in the breakroom. Likely not much, he decides.
“Sae-san,” He says, as gentle as he can muster, “You know your logic is flawed.”
Sae sneers at him, “And? I thought you agreed with me, Akechi; the Phantom Thieves are
dangerous.”
Akechi tries not to feel too irritated by the dropped honorific. “On principle, perhaps,” He
agrees carefully, “But if you’re only trying to catch them because you believe they’re
responsible for the bloodier incidents plaguing us, then I urge you to reexamine some
things.”
“What does it matter?” Sae snaps, and oh, what Akechi wouldn’t give to burn that casino in
her head to the ground.
“It matters quite a bit, I’d argue.” Akechi says pleasantly.
“You’d argue.” Sae echoes, mocking, “The Phantom Thieves have made a mockery of us.
Running circles while making us look like fools.” She huffs a laugh, “Well, they’re not so
righteous now.”
“Are you jealous, Sae-san?”

Sae’s head snaps up, “Excuse me?”
“Are you jealous?” Akechi repeats, “The Phantom Thieves got to some of your bigger cases
before you got the chance. They saved the school your sister attends from a problem you
didn’t even know existed.”
“I don’t know what you’re implying.” Sae mutters, jaw tensed, “But I think you should quit
while you’re ahead.”
It’s times like these that Akechi feels three times his age. Speaking to Sae when she’s like this
is surely giving him grey hairs.
“Besides,” Sae continues, “It’s more than just Okumura. Do you remember Kobayakawa?
The principal at Shujin?”
Akechi does, in fact. Killing someone twice leaves quite the impression. “I do.”
“They found a calling card in his office, just today.” She says, conspiratorial, “He died from a
mental shutdown. Twice is a pattern, Akechi.”
“I’m fairly sure twice is still a coincidence, actually.” Akechi says brightly, “And we’re going
in circles. Yet again, a calling card is all the evidence you have.”
Sae raises an eyebrow, “We could argue about the Phantom Thieves’ modus operandi all day,
but even you have to concede that a calling card is part of their shtick.”
“It is.” Akechi agrees, “But I also happened to pass by a plethora of calling cards just this
morning, sold for a negligible handful of yen apiece.”
Sae presses her lips together.
“It is rather annoying,” Akechi concedes, “That the Phantom Thieves are entirely
anonymous. Much like Medjed, it is difficult to pinpoint what acts actually belong to the
group, and which are another’s doing entirely.”
Sae scoffs, “Are you attempting to argue that some of the changes of heart aren’t done by the
Phantom Thieves at all?” She glares, “Or are you trying to argue they don’t exist?”
“Not at all,” Akechi shakes his head, “The changes of hearts themselves are downright
supernatural in nature. If more than one group of people knew how to utilise that power, we’d
have a far easier time catching them, I think. Or at least be able to discern their methods.” He
leans forward, “I’m saying, that using a piece of paper that can be purchased in a variety of
stores is a flimsy connection to other crimes.”
“Then what do you want from me?” Sae snarls, “If that’s your reasoning, then we’re no
closer to solving this case than we were months ago.”
Now that, Akechi has no response to. Nothing that he can say here, at least.

“Surely there are other ways to wrap up cases beyond throwing crimes at the wall and hoping
they stick.” Akechi drawls, not quite able to keep the derision out of his voice.
Sae glares at him, clearly finished with this conversation. Akechi is amazed she hasn’t told
him to find somewhere else to do his work.
But the casino and its stacked decks remains sturdy, nonetheless.
Supressing a sigh, Akechi supposes that this will become a round of pointedly ignoring each
other until they quietly pack up their things and leave. Not wanting to piss Sae off any more
than he already has, Akechi does just that.
His phones buzzes.
Unknown Number: 7:00pm. Usual place.
Well. How kind of him not to call Akechi while he’s busy at work.
He takes a sharp breath, the tension that had dissipated from needling Sae returning in full
force. He grits his teeth, and tries to keep it in.
Sae looks up, eyes narrowed. “Bad news?” She asks, voice still bitter.
Akechi carves his best smile into his face, “Nothing of the sort. Though I’m afraid I’ll have
to leave earlier than I anticipated.”
Sae scoffs, before she frowns, something passing over her face. “Why?”
“Just some personal business, nothing to be concerned about.” Akechi deflects.
Sae narrows her eyes even further, typing something on her laptop with increased ferocity,
“You seem off-put.”
“Do I?”
Sae releases a sharp huff of breath, “Are you still playing games, Akechi?”
“I assure you; I’ve been entirely serious all night.” Akechi says, a little snippily, “I’m sorry
that I have to leave early.”
“That wasn’t what I-” Sae’s expression twists, “I know you do this on purpose. You’re not
nearly as slick as you think you are.” She scowls, “I think fame went to your head.”
Akechi can only laugh at that, “Perhaps it did.” He concedes, “Though it’s not entirely
relevant. Would you like to do my interviews for a change? They get awfully repetitive.”
“My point, is that you think you’re smoother than you are.” Sae snaps back, not looking
nearly as amused, “Something upset you, and now you’re hiding it. That only makes you
more suspicious, you know.”

“Am I being interrogated?” Akechi asks, “Ask away, I suppose. But know I have to leave in
ten minutes.”
Sae gives him a searching look, “That’s short notice.”
“I apologise.”
“I meant from whoever texted you.” She glares, and eventually rolls her eyes, “Whatever. Do
what you want. I’m not your boss.”
“…Good luck on your work, Sae-san.” Akechi eventually decides to say. He throws up a
small wave, “Think about what I said.”
Sae gives him a pointed look, and mutters something under her breath, turning back to her
work.
Akechi turns as well, marching out of the precinct, wondering if he’d be able to see how
close the sword is to his neck if he looks up.
And, ringing in a half-forgotten chord, the Moon grows to its seventh rank.

The ride back home is quiet. Ren doesn’t feel much like starting conversation, especially with
Futaba’s nose already buried in her phone, and the fact that talking with a cat may raise some
eyebrows. The other passengers on the train don’t pay them any mind, whispers darting about
Okumura and the Phantom Thieves.
Safe to say, their popularity is in the dumps. It’s familiar. And almost comforting, that
something went to plan.
Ren nudges Futaba as the train reaches Yongen, and they both trail off, meandering towards
Leblanc.
“You’re not gonna head straight home?” Ren asks, nudging her shoulder.
“Nah.” She says simply.
“Are you going to stay the night, or something?” Morgana pops his head out of Ren’s bag.
“Uh, and sleep where?” Futaba snarks with only half her usual energy, “I just wanna see if I
can get some curry.”
“If Sojiro’s not there, I can get you some.” Ren offers, and Futaba nods.
He feels tense. Unsurprising, considering everything. That isn’t quite enough to chase the
feeling away, though.
The lights are still on inside Leblanc, though the sign is flipped to closed. Ren frowns,
opening the door, and sees Sojiro scowling down at something on the bar.

Sojiro looks up, “You’re back.” He comments.
“Hey, Sojiro,” Futaba calls, “We’re-” She shrinks back slightly at his expression, “…back?”
Sojiro clears his throat, somewhere between a huff and a scoff, “I found this,” He holds up a
black and red card, and Ren grimaces, “While I was cleaning your room.”
Ah.
Ren silently curses himself for forgetting about this.
“I was going to confront you about it yesterday.” Sojiro continues, gaining some momentum,
“But you looked so damn miserable I figured it wasn’t a good idea.”
“You kept it?” Morgana hisses at Futaba.
“I-” She chokes, her shoulders folding in.
“I can explain.” Ren cuts in, taking a step forward.
“You’d better.” Sojiro glares, “Hell, why do you know what’s going on here, kid?”
The foresight of having already had this conversation does wonders for Ren’s resolve to cut
to the chase.
“You already know what it is, right?” Ren asks, “You read it.”
Sojiro snorts, “Yeah. A calling card. From the guys that made that CEO lose it on live TV
two hours ago.”
Ren grimaces, “That’s…”
“I thought it was weird, when Futaba started leaving her room out of nowhere, made a bunch
of friends her age.” Sojiro grits out, “I thought, hey! Maybe I did something right for once.
Maybe taking in another kid was the push she needed to make some connections. Maybe
you’re just a tenacious little bastard and wouldn’t leave her alone until she got out of her
head.”
Ren smiles weakly, “Sort of.”
“You’d better not be implying what I think you’re implying.” Sojiro says lowly, taking off his
glasses to press a hand to his forehead.
“T-they changed my heart!” Futaba blurts, “The Phantom Thieves. I asked them to.”
Sojiro gapes, “You asked- Futaba, what were you thinking?”
“I couldn’t get out.” She chokes, stilted, “It- I felt like I was going to die. I thought
everything that happened to mom was all my fault.” She sucks in a deep breath, “But the
Phantom Thieves helped me see it wasn’t.”

“They’re still dangerous,” Sojiro growls, “Anonymous- you have no idea who they are-”
“She knew who we were.” Ren cuts in, and Morgana gives a defeated groan.
Sojiro slams his hand on the bar, “Goddamnit, kid!” He shoves his glasses back on, “Does
probation mean anything to you!?”
“You don’t sound surprised.” Ren says quietly, sidestepping everything else.
Sojiro scoffs, “I’m trying to be. But- god, kid, I’m not an idiot.” His jaw clenches, “Your
friends are a colourful bunch. Just- you dragged Futaba into this!”
“That was all me!” Futaba blurts, taking a step forward, “I reached out to them,” She repeats,
“I needed help, and they did! And then I joined them, ‘cause I needed to know what really
happened to mom.”
“To Wakaba?” Sojiro echoes, bewildered, “Is that why you were asking-? Futaba, you need
to stop- you have no idea what you’re getting yourself into.”
Futaba clenches her fists, “I do! I know what happened to her! If you really think she killed
herself then you’re lying to yourself as much as I was!”
At that, Sojiro deflates.
“You know, huh?” He mutters, “Don’t get me wrong, I’ve taken a couple of shots in the dark,
but I’ve never been stupid enough to act on it.”
Ren tugs at his fringe, “S’that why you opened the café?”
“How the hell did you get that out of what I just said?” Sojiro scoffs, “But sure. Things were
dicey, even before Wakaba died. Not like that was enough to make me believe her when she
got all paranoid.”
Futaba shrinks in on herself, “Oh.”
Sojiro sniffs, “You kids… Lemme guess, I’ll go through my whole spiel about how idiotic
you’re being, and it’ll go in one ear and out the other.”
Ren smiles the only way he can, “Yeah, pretty much.”
“God damnit.” Sojiro mutters again. He scoffs, waving an arm violently, “The least you
could do is explain yourself. How did this happen? What the hell happened to that CEO- was
that you? What did you do?”
Ren grimaces, “That was… a mistake. We messed up, with that one.”
“We were trying to change his heart.” Futaba explains quietly, perhaps unnecessarily, “And
we were trying to save his life, too.”

There’s another stream of muttered how did this happen, how did you kids get involved,
idiots, stupid, that all blends together under Sojiro’s breath. Ren decides to let him get it off
his chest.
Sojiro fires off more questions, sounding increasingly resigned and defeated as they go
round. Ren confirms; no, they aren’t behind the mental shutdowns and psychotic
breakdowns, Okumura was a one-off, a mistake. He opts to leave out the cursory explanation
of time travel, if only to avoid sending the man to an early grave.
There comes a point where he has to mention Shido.
“We have a plan.” Is what Ren leads with, and decides to not mention that the plan is half in
shambles.
Sojiro snorts, “Care to elaborate?”
Futaba kicks her boots against the ground, “Do you want the short version, or the version
where we have to explain the cognitive world to you?”
“Cognitive-?” Sojiro cuts himself off, “Of course. Why not.”
“Short version?” Ren pushes.
Sojiro clicks his tongue, and moves to start messing with the coffee siphons, “Please.”
“Masayoshi Shido is behind the mental shutdowns and psychotic breakdowns.” Ren starts,
and Sojiro nearly shatters a mug on the ground.
“You can’t seriously think you can face that man.” Sojiro growls.
“He killed mom.” Futaba protests, “We’re going after him.” She wrings her hands together,
“And you don’t sound that surprised.” A running theme, Ren thinks.
“That’s because I’m not.” Sojiro says, as he angrily goes back to making coffee, “I know that
man. Which is why I know he’s not above making some teenagers conveniently disappear.”
“Oh, we know.” Ren says wryly. “He’s responsible for my probation.”
Sojiro does shatter a mug, this time. “Not surprised, not surprised…” He grumbles, and
begrudgingly waves for Ren to continue.
He tries to explain their plan in as simple terms as he can, which turns out to be quite difficult
when trying to dodge the broadest parts of the cognitive world. On the fly, he decides to cut
out the two gods they’re going to have to fight, too.
He does say: They’re getting Sae Niijima on their side at all costs.
He does say: Come December, Masayoshi Shido will be a shell of the man he once was.
He stretches the truth: Masayoshi Shido will be their last target.

“Is this why you were so sketchy around the redhead girl? God, and the detective, for that
matter.” Sojiro spits out at one point, looking exhausted.
“Akechi’s one of us.” Ren leaves out everything else about Akechi. That’s for another time,
he thinks. “And Sumire, too.”
“Jesus.” Sojiro says, emphatic.
Futaba had, sometime during the explanation, taken a seat on one of the stools and slumped
against the bar. Now, she swings her feet back and forth idly, “Do you want the list of
members, or something?”
“I can guess.” Sojiro dismisses. “The fluffy one a member?”
“Who, Mona?” Futaba says with a token attempt at levity, holding up Morgana despite his
yowls of protest.
“No, not the cat.” Sojiro scoffs, “I meant the girl. With the fluffy hair?”
“Haru’s one of us.” Ren confirms. He smiles, awkward, “But, Morgana’s a member too.”
“You’re joking.” Sojiro says, tone making it abundantly clear that he doesn’t find it
particularly funny.
“Someone translate for me!” Morgana complains, “Or just take the chief into the Metaverse
so I can introduce myself!”
Ren is sticking to his plan of not giving Sojiro a heart attack, so he opts not to do that.
“Cognitive stuff.” He shrugs, “Morgana can talk, but you can only hear him if you’ve heard
him in the cognitive world.”
“Anything goes.” Sojiro spits, clearly channelling all his frustration into how harshly he sets
down the two coffee cups on the bar, “Anything goes.”
“Anything goes.” Ren murmurs into his mug, taking a sip. It’s more bitter than usual.
Sojiro takes a long, bracing breath. “Alright.” He says eventually, “Here’s how this is going
to go.”
Futaba and Ren share a look.
“I’m holding you to it, when you say that Shido is going to be your last target. No and’s, if’s,
or but’s.” He lights a cigarette, “I’d tell you to back off right away, but by the sounds of it,
you kids have twisted the knot so tight that it’s too late for that.”
“That’s right.” Ren says, unapologetic.
Sojiro takes a drag, and Futaba wrinkles her nose at the smell, “Watch it.” He warns, and
sighs, “That’s my condition. I’ve still got… contacts. If you need ‘em, ask. And,” He

punctuates with a second drag of the cigarette, “If you’re backed into a corner, no righteous
hero bullshit. Run. Get the hell out of there. Do what you have to.”
Ren gives a rueful smile, and thinks of Okumura, “We already have.”
“Good.” Sojiro makes a face, “You’re one-hundred percent confident that a change of heart’ll
stick on Shido?”
It has before. If it doesn’t, Ren will make it. “We are.”
Sojiro snorts, like he finds Ren’s confidence hilarious, “Anything goes,” He mumbles one
last time.

There’s a sense of finality, as Akechi clicks the door to Shido’s office shut behind him. It’s a
small comfort that there’s no sudden addition of unfamiliar men in black suits that may or
may not be hiding tattoos and guns under the fabric.
A small comfort. Shido could always have a gun neatly tucked away in his desk drawers. The
man seldom likes to dirty his own hands, but maybe Akechi is just special.
At least Loki seems to find the thought amusing.
“Akechi.” Shido greets him, “I saw your handiwork.”
“Mm.”
Shido looks at him, long and hard, before snorting. “That’s it?” He laughs a little more, like
they’re two friends in on a joke, “You’ve got guts, Akechi! I have to give you that.”
Akechi smiles placidly, “Shall we cut to the chase, sir?”
Shido’s grin becomes almost mocking, “Shall we? I admit,” He stands, and strides over to the
liquor cabinet that stands to the side of his desk, “I believe I have misjudged you.”
Akechi eyes the clock hanging above a set of filing cabinets, and wonders if it’s ticking down
the time he has left.
Or maybe it’s just a normal clock.
Akechi doesn’t blink, as Shido opts for brandy, this time, “Really? With your insight?” He
doesn’t bother hiding the sardonic lilt. No point, anymore.
Shido chuckles, “See, this,” He jabs a finger in Akechi’s direction as he sits back down, “I
had wondered where this was. Aren’t teenagers supposed to be rebellious? It’s a bit late to
start now, you know.”
He could be referring to Akechi’s age, or his position. The subtext doesn’t seem to matter so
much as the neon sign blaring danger warnings at every word. “What is it that you were

expecting?” Akechi asks mildly.
Shido gives him a piercing look. “You’re not an idiot, Akechi. Far from it.” It doesn’t sound
much like a compliment. “I thought we had an understanding, really.”
“I thought talking in circles was my prerogative.” Akechi says, eyebrows raised as Shido
swirls the brandy in its glass, not taking a sip.
“You’re right about that.” Shido hums, “You’re good at your job, because you’re not stupid.
You understand what needs to be done. You, unlike some of my other, ah, partners, know that
there is a level of commitment needed to meet my expectations.”
Akechi tilts his head, and smiles, “Do you find yourself questioning my intelligence, Shidosan?”
Shido taps his fingers against his desk, “We really do seem to be on the same page.” He
agrees. He leans back, glass still in hand, “I expected you to need guidance- you’re still a kid.
You’re independent, though, that was a pleasant surprise.”
Akechi bites the inside of his cheek to stop himself from doing something overly rash. He
treads water, determined not to give into the waves and slip below.
Shido makes a sound halfway between a scoff and another laugh, “I’ve been curious, what
you’ve really been up to this year. I haven’t changed, and neither has our deal. So why have
you?”
“Are you sure it’s just something you didn’t notice?” Akechi asks, already knowing the
response. He would be a fool to forget how the devil builds the tower.
He shouldn’t draw this out. He can’t help feeling indulgent, though.
“Quite sure.” Shido fires back, “You weren’t born a good liar, Akechi, and you certainly
weren’t a good liar at fourteen.” He waves a hand, “I had thought it was irrelevant, though.
You take your time, when you want to act on your own, and, well,” He grins, “There’s the
understanding, too.”
Akechi gets it. He’s had it said to his face, in no uncertain terms, by both a blank-faced
puppet and a disturbingly bright-eyed marionette with half its strings cut.
He’s the unwitting protagonist of a rather unfortunate math problem. If two people are
holding a knife each; person A will always aim for the gut, and person B will always forgo
the knife and try to kick person A out of a tower, how long until person B dies from blood
loss?
Akechi doesn’t think he’s quick enough with his arithmetic to get the answer before the
number is already zero.
“I don’t think,” Akechi says slowly, “That this has exactly been cutting to the chase.”

“Perhaps not.” Shido agrees, finally taking a small swig from his glass, “I suppose I’ll ask,
then: why did you fuck up with Okumura?”
Not how, or what happened. Akechi sees how it is. “Not enough time.” He settles on, “The
palace was collapsing. Shadows aren’t like people. They can take a beating before they really
die. A psychotic break is much faster.”
“You couldn’t have tried harder?” Shido asks, mild as he’s ever been.
Akechi shrugs. He may as well lean into the teenage belligerence now that Shido expects it of
him. “I could have. But, then there would be a very good chance that I would be dead,
crunched into non-existence from the collapse of Okumura’s cognitive world, and the shadow
whisked away safely to Okumura Proper’s head. And then all you’d be left with would be an
uninterrupted confession of Okumura’s myriad sins, the change of heart entirely successful.”
He threads his fingers together, “I figured this was the next best thing.”
Shido hums, “Clever.” He swirls his drink contemplatively, “I’ll give you that, Akechi. That’s
fair.” He leans forward, “I think you can still make it up to me, though.”
If Akechi pushed hard enough, would the window behind Shido shatter? “Shoot.” He says.
“I think I’ve figured it out.” Shido says, “It’s obvious, in hindsight. The only thing different,
this year, has been the Phantom Thieves.” He takes another swig, “I’d think nothing of it; but
I suppose now that you’ve seen them…”
Is a drop from this high survivable? Akechi isn’t sure what he wants the answer to be.
Depends on if he’s aiming for an escape or homicide, he supposes. “Sir?”
Shido barks a grating laugh, “I’d ask if the leader is your type, but that’s not relevant, is it?”
It’s somewhere between a genuine question and a threat. “Of course not.”
Shido places his glass on the desk with a crisp clink. “You can make it up to me, by telling
me their names.”
Akechi hums, throat dry. “They wear masks, sir.”
“Their leader, at least.” Shido drawls, because he definitely knows how absolutely full of shit
Akechi is, “Don’t bullshit me. You would have looked them up.”
Well.
Akechi pulls a name out of his ass. “Akira Kurusu.”
The Devil, hilariously, grows to rank eight.
Shido nods, “There, that wasn’t so difficult, was it?”
Akechi has no idea if Shido actually believes him. The jig will be up fairly quickly either
way, the second Shido does a cursory check to find that Akira Kurusu doesn’t exist. Or, some

random citizen with terrible luck and an unfortunate name will be arrested and used as a
scapegoat.
Akechi figures that Shido sees right through him.
He tilts his head, and gives a wry smile, “Is all forgiven?”
Shido chuckles, “Of course. Safe trip home, kid.”
Shido used to call him ‘kid’ a lot, back when Akechi first offered his services. He stopped
doing it, after displeasure must have seeped through the cracks in Akechi’s mask one too
many times.
He had thought the change was a sign of respect. Proof that they were equals.
What a joke.
He’s out of time.
Akechi smiles, and turns on his heel, clicking the door shut with some vague sense of finality.
He waves to the receptionist, and wonders if she’ll gossip to her friends about having seen
the detective prince the night he vanished, and oh, isn’t that terrifying! It could have been me!
What a poor boy, so young, too.
He slips his phone out of his pocket, and keeps a furious stride through to the train station,
making sure he turns heads.
Crow: Apologies for the short notice, but we’re out of time.
Crow: How quickly can any of you make and deliver a calling card?
***
The panicked fervour that Morgana observes in Ren would probably be funny if he wasn’t
experiencing the same thing.
Ren’s face had blanched so quickly, staring at his phone, that Morgana had honestly thought
for a second that someone had died. He guesses that someone could die, though, so same
difference.
Morgana had to claw at Ren’s leg after he had spent too long mulling over what sin to put on
Crow’s Not-Calling-Card, probably trying to strike a balance between what would be the
least offensive while also genuinely considering what would be accurate.
After Morgana had moved to start biting his ankles to hurry it up, Joker! Ren finally settled

they need to go, go, go.
Which leads to now, where Morgana is grumbling to himself, wondering how this is the
second time he’s had to run to Akechi’s apartment for calling card related business. He leaps

up the fire escape, trying to remember if Crow leaves his windows unlocked.
This turns out to not be an issue, as Morgana sees Akechi flitting about once he reaches the
right floor.
Morgana bats a paw at the glass, “What are you doing?!” He hisses.
That gets Akechi’s attention, as he startles, eyes narrowing as he sees Morgana angrily
lashing his tail. He strides over to the window, slipping it open and grabbing Morgana by the
scruff to get him inside.
“Wha- hey!” Morgana yowls. He will not be manhandled.
“Hello to you too.” Akechi snipes back, which is rich, “You were fast.”
“Of course I was fast! I’m-” Morgana stops puffing out his chest as he recognises the red
herring for what it is, “No, answer my question first! What are you doing here?! Aren’t the
yakuza or something after you?!”
“Theoretically.” Akechi answers primly, already back to pacing about the apartment, rifling
through drawers and shelves, “But they aren’t here yet, and you seem to be forgetting I can
melt into another reality on a whim.”
“Not if you don’t have your phone on you.” Morgana snarks, padding over to the coffee table
to place down the calling card.
“Then it’s a good thing I do have my phone on me.” Akechi barks from another room. He
barrels back out, a laptop under his arm.
“Did you come here to grab your things?” Morgana asks, incredulous, “That’s so risky! Can’t
you just be a minimalist or something?!”
“We can’t all live in dusty attics.” Akechi sneers.
“Do you really want to have something electronic on you?” Morgana pushes, because this is
all ridiculous, “What if it’s bugged!”
“You could say the same for my phone.” Akechi points out, “Even so, I’d like to keep it long
enough to get F-” He cuts himself of with an eyeroll, “Someone, who would be willing to
help me, to back up its data before tossing it in the nearest river.”
“What’s on it?” Morgana asks, eyeing it suspiciously.
“There are pros and cons to keeping paper or digital copies of evidence.” Akechi begins, with
the air of a storyteller, “Evidence against Shido, that is, not for my job. Ex-job.” He amends
with a grimace, “So, I opted for a bit of both. Nothing backed up to the cloud or connected to
the internet, of course, but if Shido’s men got their hands on this,” He drops the laptop on the
couch unceremoniously, “It’s nothing they don’t already know, but…”
He trails off, as goes back to running around the apartment like a man possessed.

“Is it enough to get him convicted for stuff?” Morgana shouts, “And you said you had paper
copies of stuff too?”
“Right here.” Akechi calls back, running over to dump an accordion folder on the couch next

Morgana hums, “Right…” He looks around the apartment, “So this is it, huh?”
“What could you possibly be referring to?” Akechi grits out, pulling on a hoodie over his

“We’re faking your death, obviously.” Morgana rolls his eyes, “It kinda snuck up on us,

“No kidding.” Akechi snorts, “I had wanted to delay this. I wonder if the public will even be

Morgana blinks. He hadn’t thought about that, actually. “…How long until someone figures

Akechi shrugs, “However long it takes for my school to get suspicious, or until Sae tries to

Morgana’s ears press against his head at Akechi’s tone and biting laugh. “You met with him

He demanded the name of the leader of the Phantom Thieves-”

you?”
“No…?”

Morgana narrows his eyes, “You don’t sound fine.”
“Do I ever?” Akechi mutters. At least he’s self-aware, Morgana thinks.
“Not really.” Morgana says, opting for blunt honesty. He watches as Akechi shoves some

“That would be entirely too suspicious.” Akechi dismisses, “And I couldn’t possibly infringe

Morgana’s tail twitches at the reminder. “Oh… right…” He paws uncomfortably at the couch

“Heard it all before.” Akechi mutters under his breath.
Morgana snorts, “Yeah, I bet.” His tail twitches again, “I really was useless in that fight… I
had no idea what to do.”
“Sometimes.” Akechi starts, “Fighting a palace ruler is like solving a puzzle. Other times, it
requires brute force. I had assumed we were dealing with the latter, when it seems it was, in
actuality, more akin to the former.” He turns, “Rest assured I don’t think you’re alone in how
you’re feeling. I suggest you take it up with someone else.”
Morgana rolls his eyes, “Wow, you’re sooo comforting.”
“Take it up with someone else.” Akechi repeats, unrepentant.
“Yeah, yeah.” Morgana leaps off the couch, and moves to the kitchen counter to gain some
more height, “I don’t think you’d be infringing on Haru’s hospitality if you asked to stay with
her. She doesn’t seem mad at you.”
“It’d still be suspicious. She has house servants to contend with. No doubt her place will be
swarming with police in the coming days.” Akechi reminds him. A pause, “And, I don’t…”
Morgana’s ears flick, “You don’t?”
Akechi scoffs, “How many times must I have this conversation?” He mutters to himself, “I
don’t feel bad for what I did to Okumura.”
Morgana considers this. “You saved us.” He says slowly, “But, not even a little?”
“Certainly not for the man himself.” Akechi says cooly. “But- shit.” He runs a hand through
his hair.
“You do feel bad.” Morgana accuses.
“I’m not explaining myself correctly.” Akechi shakes his head, “I feel bad for Haru-san. Her

Morgana makes a face, as much as he can, “…What, like, having friends?”
Akechi scoffs.
“You’ve been friends with Haru and Yoshizawa for ages, though!” Morgana yowls, not

Morgana rolls out his shoulders with a huff, “I really don’t get you.” A sentiment he’s

“That’s-!” Morgana can’t think of anything to say. Maybe it would be insulting. He didn’t

Akechi is just so annoyingMorgana thinks they’ve lost the thread.
He still thinks Akechi’s stupid.

Akechi’s face twists, looking more affronted than Morgana’s ever seen him. “Excuse me?”

“Please shut up.” Akechi hisses.
“Then get it together!” Morgana shouts, hopping off the kitchen counter to bat at Akechi’s

Akechi’s face twists even further, and Morgana really hopes that he’s above killing a cat.
Not a cat.
“Is that all.” Akechi drawls slowly.

“You’re sleeping in Mementos?” Morgana says, because it’s so absurd that it bears repeating,

(And, in Akechi’s mind, the Hermit grows to rank six.)

It’s odd.
Or, perhaps not. Things have been changing for a long time.
It had been quite the shock, being flung into the bloody seas without so much as a how do
you do. It had been even more surprising that he had survived the encounter, dragging salt
and brine onto the deck, running a gloved hand through his dripping hair.
It’s a good thing none of this is real. The leather would have been ruined, otherwise.
Goro isn’t quite sure where he stands, anymore. The captain is still The Captain, but, well,
saying it these days feels like an act of mockery more than deference.
He feels off. Malleable. He’s rather sure cognition isn’t supposed to work like this, but what
does he know?
As much as the captain, probably. Which is weird in and of itself; none of the other
cognitions have ever quite reached this. Not the traitors nor the easily bought nor the fiercely
loyal.
Just him.
He smirks. My, what a way to make him feel special.
He could do without the half-drowned thing, though.
The captain wants him dead. The captain also knows he isn’t. Or, is fairly sure he isn’t. He
was never much of a guest to begin with, so this doesn’t change that much, Goro supposes.

Or, not him. The other one. The one that gets all the fun. He can’t begrudge the other him’s
success that much, though, since it’s what saved him from being dragged leagues below. A
disgusting death. He’s delighted to have avoided it.
Ah, now that’s a thought. He’s died twice now, at the hand of the real him, for all that
monicker is worth. Would it be more permanent, now that the captain wants him dead? Or is
he simply that resistant in the captain’s mind?
He finds himself not eager to find out. Another change. The captain must have pegged the
real him as suicidal. Past tense, it seems- Goro had felt…
Well. Being tossed off the side of a cruise ship was an unpleasant experience.
He thinks he’ll be hung up on that for a while.
What would happen to him, if the real Goro Akechi died without the captain knowing it? For
all Goro knows, the real him is dead, and the captain is living a delusion that someone of his
blood has to be made of stronger stuff.
Unlikely. Blood has never done Goro -either of them, really- any favours.
He supposes he’d just exist as he is now, until a passing line of information makes him blink
out of existence- shift forms or shift minds. Both are horrifying.
Hm.
He has to hide from the shadows, now. The other cognitions finally acknowledge his
existence, too. An intruder on his own ship. What is there to be done?
Waiting, perhaps. He furrows his brow, and tries to pull on the- thing. He doesn’t know what
it is, really. He thinks the captain has one, too. He’s laughed about it before. Maybe Goro
can’t pinpoint it since he isn’t a shadow.
Maybe he’ll ask, the next time the real him shows up.

It takes quite some time before Akechi can shake off the cat.
Morgana initially insists on bringing all the sensitive documents they collected from his
apartment to Leblanc, or the Sakura residence, or somewhere in the real world, somewhere
where they aren’t at risk of melting into the sludge of Mementos.
Akechi argues that keeping them in the real world isn’t really all that much better. They have
no idea how long any of this is going to be in stasis, and whoever ends up storing this
information would be living with a target on their backs for potentially months. Morgana
eventually concedes to this argument, coupled with that despite the fact that he does have
thumbs in the Metaverse, he would still struggle to drag everything to where it needs to go.
And so, Akechi is left standing outside of the reflection of Shibuya station, Morgana
scampering off to report to Ren.
Home sweet home is the only wry thought he can muster, as his Metaverse outfit burns across
his body, stepping down the station steps and onto the first floor.
This place is disgusting. In all his time doing work in these tunnels, he’s made it a point never
to spend the night amongst the rot and filth that pulses along the walls. He’d find a place to
sleep in topside Mementos, but then the thieves might have a difficult time tracking him
down, and the thought of sleeping somewhere as open as station square makes his skin crawl.
So, bloodstained tile it is. He thinks he’s slept in worse places, but he doesn’t care to
reminisce.
Maybe he just won’t sleep.
“What are you doing here, defendant?!”
Akechi sighs through his nose as quietly as he can. An affronted scoff tells him he isn’t as
quiet as he hoped.
He turns, and gives a sarcastic salute to the twins barring the courtroom door.

Caroline rolls her eye, but surprisingly doesn’t threaten violence.
“We’re curious, defendant.” Justine says serenely, “And, it has been some time.”
“I come here alone rather frequently.” Akechi points out, “You’ve never shown interest
before. And, it hasn’t been all that long.”
Caroline snorts, “I guess not. But you didn’t explain yourself!”
Akechi furrows his brow, trying to remember what she’s talking about.
Justine seems to take pity on him, as she waves her hand, and a glowing blue tarot card
manifests in from of her, The Temperence, Akechi can tell even without reading it.
“Last we spoke, it seems we barely saw each other at all.” Justine explain idly, “And yet our
bond still grew. It is not unheard of, for bonds to grow unevenly, but it is… disconcerting, to
say the least.”
Ah, yes. Curious, are they? Akechi thinks this might be a good thing.
“Do you want me to explain what happened on my end?” He asks, walking forward.
“What do you think!?” Caroline snaps, whacking her baton against the ground. “We’ve been
wracking our brains, and we’ve got nothing! It’s weird!”
Akechi huffs, “Alright then. We did have a conversation that you seem to have forgotten. I
asked you about some… sensitive information, it seems, and you simply stopped. You both
appeared to be in pain, and once it had passed you had forgotten the encounter entirely.”
The twins both exchange an unsettled look.
Caroline narrows her eye, “What was the information?”
“I think,” Akechi begins, slowly, “That if I were to say it again, you would forget you asked.”
Caroline scowls, but seems to accept this. Justine frowns.
“The Velvet Room exists between dream and reality, mind and matter.” She says, like Akechi
hasn’t heard it before, “And so do its residents. We appear only to those whom we choose.
Wildcards, such as yourself, being one such example.”
“We show ourselves to everyone when we’re out and about.” Caroline interjects, “You’d look
real weird if you were talking to thin air.”
Akechi raises an eyebrow, “You don’t garner odd looks for your attire?”
“On occasion.” Justine nods, “But not enough to stimulate distress within the human mind.
Those with stronger wills may notice something out of place, but we do not exist to disturb
your reality.”

Funny, considering what their current master is attempting to do.
“Caroline,” Justine turns to her sister, “Do you think this could be related to…?”
Akechi narrows his eyes, “Related to what?”
Caroline stomps her foot, “None of your business, defendant!”
“It could be his business.” Justine counters calmly, “Theoretically, the inmate and the
defendant should be on equal footing, and we have spoken with the inmate about this at
length.”
Caroline makes a face, “I guess…”
“What,” Akechi repeats, “Are you talking about?”
Justine taps her clipboard, “There is a list we were working off of. A way to grow closer to
the inmate via his arcana with us, the Strength.”
“We gave him a bunch of challenges for fusing personas with specific skills.” Caroline

Akechi snorts.
“But we don’t know where the list came from.” Justine continues. “I had thought Caroline
wrote it.”
“And I thought Justine wrote it.” Caroline huffs, “So you see the problem.”
Akechi is starting to get the picture.
Lavenza, now that he thinks about it, had looked remarkably like the twins before him. It
doesn’t pass his attention, that the twins are missing an opposite eye a piece, and that their

An inkling of an idea of exactly who Lavenza might be, and how the false god

Perhaps, they are quite alike.
The Temperance grows to its sixth rank at the thought.
Caroline gives an affronted scoff, and Justine raises an eyebrow, as the Temperance card still

Ren would probably know for certain what’s going on with the twins, he thinks, as he jogs

Surely you can handle speaking to him for the sake of information? Robin goads.
Akechi grits his teeth.
Certainly not tonight.

Sumire wonders how easy it is to have a heart attack. She think she gets halfway to
experiencing one when Goro sends his half-cryptic message to the group chat, informing
them that they’re out of time.
Sumire had paced back and forth for nearly an hour before Ren had texted everyone
confirming that all is well; according to Morgana, Goro is sleeping in Mementos for now.

The thought makes Sumire wring her hands. It seems uncomfortable, for one. Not just from
sleeping on the floor, too- she would definitely be unable to sleep with the general
atmosphere of creaking groans and rattling chains. Unpleasant is something of an
understatement.
But, maybe she could…
She has school tomorrow. It’s a terrible idea.
She resigns herself to doing it anyway, as she starts shoving some clothes, along with a
blanket, into the duffle bag she uses for gymnastics.
She’s never snuck out of the house like this before. She decides not to think about how
panicked her parents are going to be when she’s not here the next morning.

“…Where are you going?”
Ah.
“Um!” Sumire whirls around, and pastes on her best innocent expression, “Hi, dad.”
Her dad blinks, looking befuddled, “…Hi, Sumire.” He narrows his eyes, “Where are you
going?” He asks again.
Sumire chuckles to stall for time, and runs through her list of excuses.
Sudden training camp? No, that’s the kind of thing that Maruki would come up with, and
Sumire doesn’t have the reality-bending capabilities to back it up.
She’s running this bag over to a friend’s house? Not particularly convincing, and it kind of
sounds like she’s smuggling drugs.
A friend’s house, though“I- I wanted to stay at Haru-senpai’s place.” Sumire settles on, “I don’t know if I ever told

“You’ll be going to school tomorrow?” Her dad asks, as sternly as he can.
“Yep.”

“No, it’s-” That might be suspicious, “You can drive me to the train station?”
“I can do that.”
Her dad stands up, looking for his keys, and Sumire quietly puts on her shoes.

(Sometimes, Sumire wonders why she was chosen for this.
It’s an unbidden thought to have. So late in the game, too; but she can’t help but wonder.
Chosen is such a dramatic word. She isn’t sure she likes it, really. She’s sure that Goro and
Ren don’t, and they’ve always seemed far more chosen than she is. She doesn’t envy them
for it, nor does she begrudge their clear dislike of it.
It remains the question, then, of what she’s supposed to do.
She would say: stick to the plan. This has not worked out, historically, but it’s not though
everything is in shambles.
She thinks, that if she wished, she could take a step back. She has taken a step back. If in
battle she can meld seamlessly between offence and support, then she can certainly do so in
other situations as well.
But then why her?
Maybe it’s self-centred, to think that there is some grander reason for her role in this. Maybe
it’s a little spark of a desperate need, for a little more proof that it is Sumire that is worthy,
that is capable, and not anyone else.
She doesn’t really think that’s what’s going on here. But it’s a nice thought.
She reviews the future in her head.
Next up is convincing Sae Niijima to join them. Not really her specialty; Sumire’s only met
the woman once, at the Phantom Thieves’ new year’s party, and she definitely hasn’t met her
in this timeline.
She has, however, seen the inside of her heart. An uncomfortable degree of unbalanced
intimacy that Sumire will be sure to never mention to Niijima herself.
And then…

Sumire hopes that they can follow through on changing Doctor Maruki’s heart early. The
weight of it all sits square on her chest, and she wantsWell, that’s the question, isn’t it?
She wants everything to be okay, as vague and idealistic as it is. She wants to fulfill her and
Kasumi’s dream. She wants everyone to come out of this the other side alive and well. She

doesn’t think it’s anyone’s, really.
Someone has to do it. Some stubborn and rigid part of her mind declares.
Do they? Some other part counters.
If someone does have to play a role, how could it ever be her? And back around again, and
again, to the why of it all.
Maybe it doesn’t have to be anyone. Maybe they can justSumire always feels like she loses the thread when she gets to this station along her train of

been content to live in Maruki’s reality.
But she isn’t. That, at least, has been a constant since all of this began.
The train starts up again, and Sumire bites her lip.
Maybe, it’s all very simple. Maybe it’s what she’s been doing anyway. Halfway, at least.
You don’t have to do it alone, Ella finishes the thought, None of you do, and Sumire almost

Who’s doing the choosing, really?)
