Sumire lets her dad drive her to the train station, shoving her thoughts away after she opens
the car door. She takes the train to Shibuya, assuming that -even though it was never stated
outright- Goro would pick their main entrance to Mementos as a good place to camp.
She shakes off the wandering eyes of passers-by, and quietly slips into Mementos.
It occurs to her, as she trots down the steps, that she’s going to have to sleep in her Metaverse
outfit. She’s never considered it uncomfortable before, but coupled with the tiles littered with
stains of dubious origin, she wonders if she’s going to get much rest at all.
She walks down an extra layer, frowning as she doesn’t see Goro in the immediate entrance
of the tunnels.

There’s a sigh, as she steps onto the next floor.
“What,” Goro grits out, surrounded by accordion folders, a laptop, a backpack, and one
blanket, “Are you doing here, Violet?”
Sumire smiles sheepishly, and pats her own duffle bag, “Keeping you company?”
“I take it,” Goro continues, in the same clipped and exhausted voice, “That you have already
made up your mind about this?”
Well, at least he isn’t trying to fight it. “Yes!” Sumire confirms cheerfully, as she whips her
own blanket out of her bag, laying it down on the ground. She’ll have to wash it later. “It was
kind of scary, when you sent that message. I thought we’d have a little more time.”
“Didn’t we all?” Goro drawls. His mask is laying to the side, though the rest of his helmet
remains firmly in place. Sumire takes off her own mask, resting it on the ground beside her.
Sumire smiles, half-hearted, “I guess.” She wrings her hands together, “Did Shido call you in
for a meeting? Or did you… see someone, on your way home?”
“The former.” Goro responds simply, idly taking out some files from one of the folders, eyes
flicking across it disinterestedly, “I had been in the middle of my meeting with Sae-san when
it happened. I think she noticed something was wrong.”
“Oh…” Sumire grimaces, “She’s… going to think you died, huh?”
Goro freezes, like he hadn’t considered this, “…If all goes to plan,” He eventually says,
“Then that won’t be the case for long.”
Sumire guesses that’s true. She certainly hopes that it’s true.
“Is it normal, for Shido to call you in so suddenly?” Sumire asks.
“Of course.” Goro says, waving a dismissive hand, “But I knew he was going to call me in
today. Even if I hadn’t, outwardly, fucked up, he’d probably have wanted to gloat to himself
while I stood there.”
Oh.
“You could have said something.” Sumire tells him quietly.
Goro snorts, “Sure, I could have. But what would it have accomplished?”
Sumire sighs, and her past musings threaten to loop again, “Oh, I don’t know,” She taps her
fingers against the ground, rhythmic, “We could have helped you out?”
“Of course.” Goro says, agreeable in the way that means he actually doesn’t agree with you
at all, “You could have been my emotional support while I met with Shido. Oh, don’t mind
her, Shido-san! She’ll just stand in the corner while we chat. Do you mind if she pokes
through your filing cabinets?”

Sumire tries not to get knocked too off track by the absurdity of it all.
She swallows, “I- yeah. I guess we couldn’t have…” She trails off, and then laughs weakly,
“You still could have told us, though. Then we’d know, if…”
If something went wrong. Or, they could have been more prepared to plant a calling card.
“I had a feeling you would have all been insufferable about it, if I said I had to meet with
Shido.” Goro says bluntly, “And it’s not like it’s hard to figure out that I needed to see him, at
some point.”
Well now Sumire just feels stupid.
She decides to poke him with her pointer finger. “Did you not want us to worry? Or are you
just being mean for the sake of it?”
Goro frowns, his brow furrowing as he glares at the ground.
Sumire pokes him again.
He turns that glare on her, so affronted that Sumire has to laugh. She yelps when he pokes her
back, his gauntlets significantly sharper than her own gloved hands.
“I,” Goro starts, clipped and clearly enunciated, “Don’t know. I’ve just had a remarkably
similar conversation with the cat, so you’ll forgive me if I’m not in the mood.”
Sumire, unfortunately, does forgive him. She pokes him once more, both as revenge for his
retaliation, and to make her dissatisfaction clear.
“What are you, five?” Goro snaps, and Sumire dissolves into giggles.
“You poked back.” She points out.
“Eye for an eye.” Goro says with far more gravity than the statement really should have.
Sumire’s snickers die off, and she starts pulling the rest of what she packed out of her bag.
“You’re really sleeping here?” Goro asks, with some degree of incredulity, eyeing the ratty
sleeping bag that Sumire lays out over her blanket.
“Did you think I’d leave?” She asks, kicking out the fabric. Maybe she should have brought a
pillow.
“I had assumed that you would have thought better of it when you realised the conditions you
would have to suffer.” Goro drawls out, “Also, don’t you have school tomorrow?”
Sumire pats her bag, “I brought my uniform!”
Goro gestures around, “And you’re going to get changed where?”
Sumire pauses. She hadn’t thought about that. “…Up a floor?”

“Don’t. The twins will be able to see you.”
Sumire hadn’t thought much about the Velvet Room situation before, but now she has to
admit that a door and two girls she can’t see is a bit unnerving. “…A floor above that?”
Though, then she’d have to get changed in the open air, and that’s a bit disconcerting too,
even if there’s no one there, “A station bathroom, maybe.”
Goro shrugs, “That’d work, I suppose.”
Sumire suddenly realises that she isn’t going to have access to a shower until tomorrow
afternoon. She elects not to bring this up, if only to preserve her dignity and spare her from
another pointed look.
“This is kind of like another sleepover, isn’t it?” She says instead.
Goro snorts, “Is it better or worse than when we were all on death’s door?”
Sumire is already lamenting the lack of cushioning. She makes a face, and Goro seems to get
the gist. He huffs, and goes back to frowning at the paper in his hands.
Sumire tilts her head, “What’s that?”
Goro waves it in the air carelessly, “Evidence. Against Shido, that is. Some of this I managed
to grab years ago, so I hardly remember what’s on it.”
“You managed to get stuff like that?” Sumire asks, eyes widening.
Goro smirks joylessly, “It’s not nearly as impressive as it sounds. All of these are records that

“But there’s nothing about assassinations?” Sumire pushes. Or fraud, she thinks, or the
various election laws she’s sure Shido has broken.
“Not at all.” Goro says, crisply placing the paper back within its place in the folder, “He was
far more careful about my role in the conspiracy. If I were to go to the police, it would be my

half of them are in his pocket.”
Sumire bites her lip, “Then… if that’s… even when we do get a confession, is anyone going

“If Sae-san knows what’s good for her, she will.” Goro says, and it only half sounds like a
threat, “It will be difficult, though. There would have to be enough people willing to put
themselves in the line of fire in order to get a conviction to stick.”
Sumire thinks she sees the problem that is beginning to present itself.
She pulls her knees close to her chest, “You’re not going to do that, though.” She says,
decisive.

Goro’s face twists into something uncomfortable. “Last time, when Maruki brought me back,
I found myself standing in Shibuya station square with no recollection of how I got there or
how I survived, listening to Sae-san trying to convince Ren to testify against Shido. It seemed
like the only thing to do, to step in and take his place.”
Sumire looks at the ground.
“I would assume that in the true reality, Ren would have testified.” Goro continues,
“Considering I wouldn’t be there to step in.”
“But that’s not fair.” Sumire says in a small voice.
Goro snorts, “Which part?”
“All of it.” She shakes her head. “You said you wouldn’t…”
Sumire knows very well that Goro revealing his role in the conspiracy would not end well for
him.
Goro knits his hands together, “I had, perhaps foolishly, hoped that what I have collected over
the years would amount to something, but…” He gestures to the accordion folders, “There’s
not much.”
“All together, would it help?” Sumire tries.
Goro shrugs, “Possibly. Sae-san would have a better eye for the legality of it all. Paired with

she doesn’t haul me into the station the second she hears what exactly I am.”
Sumire grimaces, “…Maybe we should tell her that after we convince her to help us.”
“That might be for the best.” Goro says with a huff.
There is another option. If Niijima had initially thought that Ren’s testimony would be the
key to convicting Shido, then presumably that could work as well.
But Sumire doesn’t think that’s very fair, either. She’s sure Ren would do it, if he deemed it
necessary. She’s sure Goro would do it if he deemed it necessary too, and Sumire doesn’t
want any of it.
“What are you going to do, when all of this is over?” She blurts.
Goro gives her a look, “…In the event that I am a free man?”
“Pretend that isn’t a problem.” She says quickly, “Please.”
Goro raises his eyebrows, and leans back, sighing. After a moment, he says: “You go first.”
Sumire blinks, “Huh?”

“I need to think about it.” Goro explains, “Tell me what you’re going to do first.”
Sumire tilts her head, thinking about it. “Well… I’m only in my first year of high school, so I
guess I’ll finish that?”
Goro raises an eyebrow, “You guess?”
“I will!” Sumire corrects with a laugh, “Though that’s kind of a boring answer, isn’t it?”
“It is.” Goro says bluntly.
Sumire smiles, “Um… in that case…” She taps her chin, “Well, I really need to get back into
the swing of things with gymnastics, obviously.”
“Obviously.” Goro says, definitely mocking.
Sumire pauses, “I do need to.” She says, “This year has been… distracting.” Twice over.
Goro mirrors her pose, pulling his legs closer to his chest and resting his head on one of his
knees, “What are you going to do after gymnastics?”
Sumire frowns, “Hm?”
“Don’t play dumb.” Goro scowls, “You’ve told me before. Competing in gymnastics is
hardly a life-long career, so what about after? If you’re asking me about my goals for
something I never planned for, it’s only fair if you answer the same.”
Sumire laughs under her breath, “Well…”
She never did get around to thinking about it.
“I do love the sport.” She says, genuine, “And sports in general. Maybe I could stay in the
field?” Coach Hiraguchi is in her thirties, Sumire knows, so that job at least seems to have a
longer life expectancy, “I like cooking, too. And nutrition.” She lists.
Goro tilts his head to his other knee, looking her up and down, “Would you study something
like that, after high school?”
Sumire shrugs, feeling a bit exposed, “Maybe?”
Goro raises another eyebrow.
“How did this turn back around on me?” Sumire complains.
Goro snorts, “Would you like me to answer now?”
“Yes.” Sumire folds her arms, going for stern but probably hitting petulant, “You’re in your
last year of high school, so what are you going to do?”
Goro presses his lips together.

“I guess going to university doesn’t disgust me.” He eventually says. “Though, considering I
am either about to be declared missing or legally dead rather soon, I’m not sure how high my
prospects for graduating are.”
Right.
“If you do graduate.” Sumire amends, “What do you think you’ll study?”
Goro shrugs, “I have no idea. I’ve always said ‘Law’ whenever I’ve been asked in interviews,
but that’s just because it’s an obvious answer.”
Sumire taps her knees, “Do you think you’ll stay a detective?”
Goro makes a face, “Absolutely not. And I think I’ll be fired.”
“What if you went freelance?” Sumire asks with a grin.
“What, like Shirogane?” Goro’s eyebrows hike even higher, “Better, but opening a private

Sumire wilts a bit, “That’s true…” She considers it some more, “What about-”
“I think,” Goro interrupts her, “That this musing is rather pointless, when the future is so
uncertain.”
Sumire’s smile falls. “…Right.”
Goro frowns at the ground. He peels off his gauntlets, and says: “I’ll think about it some
more later, when more things are set in stone. Perhaps after we find out where we stand with
Sae-san.”
Sumire perks up, “Really?”
“Sure.”
She smiles, and lies down.

The morning after the school festival, Makoto still feels like she’s coming down from the
whirlwind of panic she felt, realising that time was much tighter than they had predicted. She
hadn’t been particularly involved in the aftermath- in either aftermath, she notices.
Failing to properly complete Okumura’s palace felt like a punch to the face. Makoto thinks
she’s been spiralling down ever since early October, when everyone’s lies were forced into
the open with all the grace of opening an airlock.
She had, foolishly, hoped that getting back on track would solve this. But they haven’t gotten
back on track. They missed the mark by a mile, and god, Makoto can’t stand this, she’s their
strategist, what the hell happened with Okumura? Why couldn’t she do anything-

“It’s been a while since we’ve had breakfast together.” Sae muses from across the table.
Makoto startles, and pastes on a shaky smile, “It has.” She agrees.
The next logical step for getting back on track is dealing with her sister.
Makoto doesn’t know what to do.
“There’s so much work to do.” Sae mutters. “Akechi-kun vanished halfway through helping
me last night; not that he was doing much to begin with.” She scoffs, but there’s a tight line
through her eyebrows that betrays her concern.
Makoto bites at her lips. “Hm.”
Sae huffs, “I’ll see if he’s free again today.” She looks towards the TV, “Let’s see if there’s
anything interesting on…” She hums under her breath.
Sae stands, coffee mug in hand, and moves to grab the remote off of one of the couch arms.
She fumbles for the on button, taking a sip of coffee as she does.
The screen flicks to life, displaying the news.
“Breaking news this morning, as Tokyo police releases a statement.” A woman recites, “It
has been revealed that Goro Akechi, often referred to as the second coming of the Detective
Prince, has been declared missing, and is presumed dead. A calling card was found in his
apartment, and the police have confirmed that-”
Sae drops her mug.
Makoto sucks in a breath. The only thought she can muster is that she’s probably going to
have to be the one to try and get those coffee stains out of the rug.
Sae’s shoulders are shaking.
Makoto swallows, “…Sis-”
“What, Makoto?” Sae snaps, eyes not leaving the TV as the news report continues.
“I-” She chokes, and clamps her mouth shut.
Here’s the thing:
Makoto knows, quite well, that Akechi isn’t dead. She didn’t expect the news to break so
quickly, but she did expect it to break. All of this is smoke and mirrors. The police statement,
the news report, all likely engineered by Shido to declare the message he wants.
It’s obvious- even though it’s not unreasonable to think that Akechi might be dead with the
information presented, the immediacy of the assumption and the fact that no one has
challenged it would ring alarm bells in Makoto’s head if she were not already in the know.

It doesn’t seem like her sister is hearing those alarms.
“Sis.” Makoto tries again, and what does she say, what can she say, she’s not grappling with
this news like Sae is and Makoto’s a terrible liar, “I’m so sorry.”
Sae breathes in sharply, “Don’t be.” She grits out. “We know who’s responsible for this.” She
picks up the mug, not shattered, but cracked along the side, “And I,” She slams the ceramic
on the kitchen counter, “Am going,” She marches to the table, grabbing her keys, “To find
them.”
Makoto keeps her mouth shut.
Sae freezes, halfway to the exit, choking on a laugh. “I don’t know what Akechi was playing
at.” She whispers.
Makoto steps forward, “What do you mean?”
Sae scoffs, still not looking at Makoto, “I swear he wanted me to gamble this case away.
Look where that got him.”
As far as Sae knows, dead in the ground, right under her nose.
Makoto clenches her jaw together.
“Make sure you go to school.” Sae says tightly from the doorway, pulling on her heels, “I
won’t be back tonight.”
“Okay.” Makoto says quietly.
“See you.” Sae calls, overlapping with the slam of the door.
And Makoto is alone.
She hesitantly pulls out her phone from her pocket, and taps on the Nav.
“Sae Niijima.” She says, clear, “Courthouse.”
And, her guess:
“Casino.” She whispers.
Candidate Found. The Nav chimes, Move closer to location to begin navigation.
“Of course.” Makoto says to the empty hallway.

When Ren trots down the stairs the next morning after a restless night of sleep, Morgana at
his heels, the first thing he sees is Sojiro with his head in his hands.

“…What’s up with the chief?” Morgana whispers, and Ren shrugs, inching forward a little
more.
Sojiro looks up, and the TV drones on. “Hey, kid.” He says, some small thread of accusation
pulled taught in his voice, “You seen the news?”
Ren frowns, and shakes his head.
Sojiro gestures carelessly towards the TV, rubbing at his eyes. “Might wanna sit down.” He
mutters.
Ren turns his head, confusion and dread slowly spooling in his gut. The report is
incomprehensible for a bit, Ren only having started listening in halfway through, but he
eventually gets the gist:
Goro Akechi, famed detective prince, has been declared missing and presumed dead after a
calling card from the Phantom Thieves was found in his home. Following both this and
Okumura’s psychotic breakdown, the manhunt for the Phantom Thieves has been declared a
top priority.
There is a small part of Ren that tenses and panics, even with the knowledge that this is all to
plan.
“That was quick.” Morgana comments, also looking a little shaken as a series of photos of
Akechi are displayed in some dramatic memorial.
Ren hums under his breath. The devil works fast, and Shido works faster, it seems.
“Kid…” Sojiro speaks up again, giving Ren a pitying look, and oh, right,
“He’s okay.” Ren blurts.
Sojiro takes a deep breath, apparently having missed the point, “Look, I know it’s hard when
stuff like this happens so suddenly, but-”
“No, I mean I know he’s okay.” Ren interrupts, and then realises that that still sounds like he’s
in denial, “We planned for this.” Mostly. “We left that calling card, to make it look like we
did something to him, but he’s camping out in the Metaverse right now.”
Sojiro blinks. “You…?”
“So everything’s fine.” Ren finishes, rubbing the back of his neck.
Sojiro pinches the bridge of his nose, “You’re actually serious. Kid, that news report gave me
a heart attack.”
Ren grimaces. He probably should have warned Sojiro in advance. “…Sorry?”
“I figured the calling card was a set up as soon as they mentioned it, but I thought that boy
actually died- …you’re sure he’s fine?” Sojiro interrupts himself.

Ren smiles, “He’ll be okay. It’s not like anyone can find him in the other world.”
“That you know.” Sojiro grouses, shuffling over to the coffee siphons with a huff, “But sure,
I’ll take your word for it.”
A pause.
“Why did you need to fake his death?” Sojiro snaps to the air.
Ah.
“Because Akechi’s stupid.” Morgana says helpfully.
“What did the cat say?”
“He called Akechi stupid.” Ren translates, because he might as well.
Sojiro snorts, like he doesn’t believe Ren for a second, “Sure. Now why does the detective
being stupid mean he needs to go into hiding?”
Ren had initially left faking Akechi’s death out of his explanation, because then he would
have been confronted with the why of it all, and that wasn’t a conversation he was ready to
have.
He doesn’t think it’s a conversation he’s ready to have now either.
Ren knits his fingers together, “Shido wants him dead.” He says, slowly, “And you said it
yourself: he’s not above killing teenagers.”
Sojiro releases a weary sigh, “How on earth did that kid piss off Shido?”
Ren shrugs, unhelpful, “Ask him yourself next time he shows up.”
“He’d better not be coming here.” Sojiro snaps, “Do you want to lead a trail to where we
live?”
Ren waves his hands, “Akechi’ll probably travel by Mementos, which means no one can
follow him.” And he sincerely doubts Akechi will be showing up to Leblanc voluntarily.
Sojiro rubs at his temples, “Whatever you say, kid.”
Ren tries to smile apologetically, and thinks he probably only gets halfway.

It's a little after Sumire leaves in a panic, realising she can’t tell the time in Mementos,
hoping that she isn’t too late for school, that Akechi realises that the Metaverse lacks several
amenities.
He knew this, obviously. It doesn’t take long to notice that cognitive food doesn’t actually fill
your stomach. In fact, getting hungry at all is a strange and nebulous thing in the other world,

not to mention other bodily functions, and Akechi isn’t sure he wants to know what several
days of existing in limbo catching up to him feels like.
So, he needs to leave. Discretely. Theft might be necessary, and Akechi has to supress a
groan at the irony. Using a card for money is a no-go, and going to a bank to withdraw cash
isn’t a great idea either. At the very least, he’s packed a nondescript hoodie and facemask;
he’ll have to do away with the gloves, but that should suffice as a disguise for the time being.
Akechi ducks into an alley on the surface of Mementos, having left most of his belongings
behind. It irks him, to leave it unattended, but shadows are the only potential dangers to it,
and they don’t wander this high.
By the looks of it, it’s mid-afternoon; droves of school children wander about station square
and central street, and Akechi makes sure to keep his head down as he ducks into the closest
Triple Seven.
He makes several laps of the store, taking note of where the security cameras are, as well as
the essentials he’s looking to swipe.
“Crow?” An incredulous voice hisses.
Akechi whirls around and claps a hand over Ann’s mouth.
She sputters, and pushes him away, “Hey! It’s not like I said your name!” She says, to her
credit, quite quietly.
“Don’t draw attention to me.” He snaps.
“I’m not!” She protests, “You’re the one who looks like you’re about to rob the place! What
are you doing here?!”
Akechi gives her an irritated look.
“…Are you about to rob the place?” She asks slowly, suspicion creeping into her voice.
“We need to leave.” He announces. It doesn’t look like anyone’s noticed them yet, but
paranoia leaves eyes burning in the back of his neck. He turns, and begins marching out of
the store.
Ann scrambles to follow him, “You didn’t say what you’re doing here!”
“I need food.” He snaps, taking a turn into the alley with the courtroom door burning blue at
its edges, “And water. I was going to make use of the station bathrooms, too. You realise they
don’t have those in Mementos?”
Ann’s eyes widen, “Ohhhh…” She drawls out, “Why didn’t you say so?”
“I just did.”
She laughs, “No, I mean yesterday. You slept in Mementos, right?”

“Better than the open air.” Akechi says, dry as the desert.
“But, not better than a proper house, right?” Ann says, a devious glint in her eyes.
Akechi wonders if she’s getting at something or if she’s just rubbing it in, “No.”
Ann beams, “You can stay over at mine, then!”
What.
“What?” He says, “No.”
Ann’s face falls, “Oh, come on! My parents are overseas! And staying in the Metaverse
clearly isn’t sustainable!”
“Absolutely not.” Akechi insists, with a little more fervour, “Are you trying to invite the
yakuza to come knocking at your door? Having me stay anywhere is a risk.”
“Not if you travel by Mementos, it’s not!” Ann declares, triumphantly putting her hands on
her hips like she had thought about this in advance and isn’t making a split-second decision,
“Y’know, I never thought about Mementos travel really, but it’s really convenient now that
we need it.”
“Mementos.” Akechi mutters into his phone, and Ann jumps as reality shifts. “It is quite
convenient.” He agrees, relaxing now that the nearby street is entirely empty, “Which is why
I don’t need to impose on your living space.”
Ann frowns, “I’m offering, though. Come on, Akechi-kun! My place is really big! We won’t
be stepping on each other’s toes, or anything.”
“I- all my stuff is here.” Akechi digs for some other excuses.
“And we’ll transport it through Mementos!” Ann counters, with all the flourish of someone
who has discovered a catch-all solution.
“I don’t particularly want to live with you.” Akechi grits out.
“But I’m a delight!”
“Are you being obstinate on purpose?” Akechi snaps.
Ann smiles sheepishly, “Yes?”
Akechi rolls his eyes, and strides towards the reflection of station square.
Ann jogs to keep up, “Please? At least living with me you wouldn’t have to keep ducking out
into public for like, basic necessities. I can buy everything!”
“That wouldn’t be a strain on your budget?” Akechi asks, already knowing the answer.
“Not at all!” Ann says cheerfully, “It’ll be fun, if anything- like having a roommate!”

Akechi gives her a look.
“…I’ll be gone most of the day, too? Because of school?” Ann tries, “And I have a guest
room, so you’ll have an actual bed.”
Akechi takes a deep breath.
“Please?” Ann asks, practically begging at this point, “You can’t deny it’s safer! And better
for your back, probably.”
Akechi grits his teeth, and cuts his losses, “Fine.”
Ann blinks, and then smiles, looking so much like her arcana’s namesake, “Great! Where’s
your stuff?”
And, of course, the Sun grows to rank four.

Chapter 67
Chapter Summary

Limbo, boredom, and a shift in plans.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Ren doesn’t think it’s unreasonable to call a meeting, just the day after everything seems to
have gone to hell. The time bomb has detonated, and now they can actually take stock of the
damage.
Through the group chat, everyone is quick to confirm that they’ll be at Leblanc shortly. He’s
not sure if Akechi has gotten the message, though, so he supposes he’ll ask Mona to grab him
should he be absent. Ann, strangely, messages back with a ‘we’ll be there!’, leaving Ren
frowning in confusion at his phone.
His silent question to the void is answered when both Ann and Akechi materialise out of thin
air in the middle of Leblanc’s attic.

“Oh, right! Get this!” Ann’s smile, impossibly, gets even brighter, “We’re roommates now!
Sort of.” She corrects, at Akechi’s withering glare.

“I’m right here.” Akechi grits.
“Well,” Ann drawls, plopping down on the couch, “I just pointed out how much better my
place is compared to the dirty floor of Mementos, and he agreed!”
“An oversimplification.” Akechi sneers, and takes a delicate seat next to her, “But I suppose
that is the gist of it, yes.”
“That’s… good.” Ren says slowly.

Ann nods, and Ren sees some of her cheer melt into smugness while Akechi pointedly looks
at the opposite wall. Ren rubs at his mouth to hide his smile.

explanation she gave Ren and Morgana with each new addition, to Akechi’s clear chagrin.
Sumire in particular responds with a relieved smile.
“Mementos is really uncomfortable.” She says by way of explanation, and Ren figures that’s
probably a sign to drop the subject.
Futaba is last to arrive, looking anywhere but at Akechi.
And, so,
Ren rolls his neck and takes a breath,
What now?

too long.

“Are we?” Futaba mutters.

Ren frowns, considering, “I would like to.” He says, “…But I think we should figure out

Sae has sworn off breaks.

She doesn’t have time, frankly. She’s wasted months, as far as she’s concerned, toiling at
leads and dead ends and frayed threads of nothing.
She’s known exactly who’s responsible for the mental shutdowns and psychotic breakdowns
for far longer than is reasonable, and dragging her feet has cost her far too much.
God knows the Director’s promise of a promotion is probably long rescinded. Too much
beating around the bush and not nearly enough results. Perhaps, the lack of tangible reward
would give Sae cause to slow down, but no,
Kobayakawa, though his death was initially ruled as a suicide, then a mental shutdown, and
only months later was a calling card unearthed in his office- Sae knew something was off
from the start. The fact that Kobayakawa was the principal of Shujin, of all places, certainly
did nothing to silence the alarm bells.
And then Okumura. Whatever grievous sins Sae is sure would have come spilling out in his
confession have been entirely overshadowed in her mind- The Phantom Thieves have
revealed their hand, and their little stunt with the CEO more than proves it.
And then, there’sHe’sNo.
Sae draws her attention back to the Okumura residence.
Several officers are milling about, questioning staff and combing the place for something,
anything. Okumura the younger -Haru, Sae believes her name is- sits stiffly on the living
room couch, hands drawn tightly together.
Time for an interrogation.
“Okumura-san.” Sae approaches her, and doesn’t sit down, “I’d like to ask you a few
questions.”
Okumura stiffens slightly, not quite meeting Sae’s eyes, before she nods. “Of course.” She
says, “And, please, call me Haru.”
“…Haru-san.” Sae amends. “If that’s what you want. I’ll start by offering my condolences,
first and foremost.”
Haru’s laugh is a tinkling, strained, thing, “Oh, there’s no need. It’s not as though my father is
dead.”
Sae supposes, that even without the psychotic breakdown to muddy things, she and Haru
have different definitions on what a change of heart entails.
“I suppose that’s true.” Sae concedes, nonetheless. “Now, you were the one to find the calling
card, yes?”

Haru nods, finally drawing herself up, “Yes. I found it in the mailbox. I’m sure some of the
house servants can confirm this, too.”
“Of course.” Sae hums, and notes this down, “Pardon my being so vague, but did you notice
anything off about your father, before and after receiving the calling card?”
Haru fidgets for a moment, “Well, he was certainly different after receiving it. But he was no
more different than I would expect after receiving a threat like that. In the following days,
I’m not quite so sure. I spent some time at a friend’s house.”
Sae nods slowly. She’ll have to question some of the staff herself. “And before?”
Haru hesitates.
“Haru-san.” Sae says, emphatic, “Any information you can provide could be instrumental in
this case.”
“I understand.” Haru presses her lips together, “Well- father had been… irritable, for quite a
few days before receiving the calling card. But, that’s because- um,” She grimaces, “A
business deal had fallen through.”
Sae’s eyes narrow, “A business deal?”
Haru nods, “You may have heard that my father was aiming to get into politics? He… found
a way to get a foot in the door, by having me engaged to the grandson of a rather renowned
politician.”
It is years of professionalism that keeps Sae from announcing her disgust.
“I see.” She says instead, “…And you said this deal fell through?”
Haru nods, “Yes- my ex-fiancé called it off.”
There is something about Haru’s posture, about her voice, that Sae wants to pry into. She
can’t meet Sae’s eyes for long, her voice is too flat, her hands are drawn white with how
tightly they’re pressed together.
But is it tension because of the topic at hand, or is it tension because of a lie?
What reason would Haru have to lie about this?
“Thank you, Haru-san.” Sae nods slowly, reviewing her notes, “This will be very helpful for
us.”
Haru smiles slightly, “I’m glad.” She fidgets, “Um, can I ask…?”
“Yes?”
“You asked me these questions for the Phantom Thieves case, right?” Haru asks, gracing Sae
with a rare bit of eye contact, “What about the case against my father? Is that being

prosecuted as well?”
Sae raises an eyebrow, “…Given his psychotic breakdown, his confession is being regarded
with scepticism at the moment. You don’t have to worry.”
“You misunderstand me.” Haru says firmly, “My father… has not been a good man, as of
late, Niijima-san.”
Sae gathered that. Revealing a bit more won’t hurt. “At the moment, the effects of the
psychotic breakdown… haven’t been subsiding as quickly as the ones we have documented
have in the past. Of course, it isn’t an identifiable medical condition, so no one can make a
claim as to what that means.”
Haru bites at her lip, glancing at the floor, “…And the change of heart?”
Sae hesitates, “…What he initially said during the press conference is still on record. But last
I heard he isn’t coherent enough to say much more. At the very least, he’ll likely be
prosecuted for assault.”
Sae can’t quite decipher the way Haru’s expression shifts, “I see…” She hums, “I- if it’s not
presumptuous- if you ever need someone to testify-”
“We’ll call on you.” Sae reassures her, “But, at the moment, the Phantom Thieves’ case is our
top priority.”
“Mm.” Is Haru’s only response, accompanied by a nod. She gives a short laugh under her
breath, humourless, “I suppose they are rather infamous these days.”
Sae doesn’t let her thoughts drift to“They are.” Sae says simply.
Haru shifts, “…If I may -sorry if this is personal- but, how are you, Niijima-san? The news
this morning; I know you and Goro-kun were rather close-”
Sae almost doesn’t recognise who she’s talking about, saying his given name rather than just
Akechi, “How do you know that?” She snaps.
Haru jumps, “Oh-! Well, Goro-kun and I are close friends.” She explains haltingly.
Present tense, Sae notes.
“He’s mentioned you before.” Haru continues, twisting her hands in her lap.
Sae has been doing her utmost to not think about Akechi.
She can’t, won’t, fall apart from this. Her reputation is already in tatters, she can’t afford to
take a few days off to do something as inconsequential as mourn.
Well,

That, and mourning implies that the subject in question is dead.
You don’t believe it either, A relieved and desperate part of Sae’s mind whispers as she eyes
Haru appraisingly, He can’t be dead, there’s no body, no chain that links it, even the calling
card was only mildly threatening at best,
Sae swallows.
“I’m doing fine.” Sae decides, snapping herself back to reality, “And I can promise you this,
Haru-san: I’ll bring the Phantom Thieves to justice. They won’t get away with what they’ve
done.”
Haru’s answering smile is hollow and disbelieving.

Akechi dislikes the waiting game.
He especially dislikes waiting for Makoto to act; as a simple point of pride, if nothing else.
He concedes that he can’t exactly be the one to organise a conversation with Sae, when
revealing his status as living to her could have unforeseen consequences if done indelicately.
Going through the logic of it all does little to solve the boredom, though.
Akechi has no desire to root around in Ann’s things. Or, rather, he already has, and has run
out of things to snoop on. Anything that he had thought might catch his attention is proving
fruitless. He swears TV used to be more entertaining when he was a child- and yet it only
takes five or so minutes before his mind begins to wander.
It’s a relief when the mid-afternoon dawns, and Ann returns with a cheerful “I’m back!”
from the front door.

Ann snorts, “I had school! You’re not that bored, are you? You can entertain yourself!”
As it turns out, such a task is easier said than done. When Akechi was, effectively, working
three full-time jobs, he would have killed for this kind of free time (And, technically, he had).
Now, with far too much time on his hands, he’s wondering if killing wasn’t his most
stimulating hobby.
“And, uh, anyway,” Ann continues, a bit sheepish, “I actually need to go. Right now.”

Makoto has a plan.
It’s not particularly defined, or smart, or, frankly, necessary, but it is a plan nonetheless.
Step one is sneaking out.
This isn’t a difficult step. Not in the slightest, considering her sister seems to have declared
the precinct and prosecutor’s office as her new home. Fine by Makoto- it just makes this
easier.
Step two is looking reasonably unsuspicious as a high schooler making their way to the
courthouse at night. A bit more of a hurdle, but she can pass as a bit older than she actually is
if she holds herself right and doesn’t look guilty, which should be enough to avoid scrutiny.
Step three is, well,
Take out her phone, take a deep breath, and whisper:
“Sae Niijima, Courthouse, Casino.”
And let the world shift around her.
The first thing she sees are the lights, neon and blinding. Overly colourful, pinks and reds and
greens and golds. Gaudy, far flashier than Makoto ever expected of something that resides in
her sister’s heart.
The second thing she sees is that her clothes haven’t changed. She can’t tell if that’s a good or
bad sign.

“And- it’s not like I don’t want it to be that easy,” Now she’s started, she can’t seem to make

success, and- look!” Makoto whirls, and points furiously at the towering casino, “Is this what
she thinks her job is? A gamble?”
A pause.
“No.” Akechi says. “The opposite.”
Makoto gives him a look.
Akechi shrugs, “She thinks justice is rigged. She thinks it’s the only path, making sure she
wins. Her shadow is the casino manager.” He explains.
“That’s worse.” Makoto grits out.
“I know.” Akechi says simply.
Another pause.
“And she still…” Makoto mumbles out, and then scoffs, “You wouldn’t get it.”
Akechi gives her a look of his own, “And what might that be?”
“You-” Makoto rolls her eyes, “You wouldn’t get it.” She repeats, “My sister loves you.
You’re everyone’s golden boy, while I have to sit, and-” She cuts herself off.
Akechi folds his arms, “…Whatever your grievances with Sae-san,” He begins, “Surely you
understand that she will hardly see me in the same light once she finds out what I’ve done.”
Makoto snorts, only half believing. Considering how unconcerned the thieves seem to be
with all that, Makoto could only throw her hands up in exasperated resignation if Sae did the
same thing.

“Sure.” Makoto says in acquiescence, “But that doesn’t mean anything’s changed. Sis could
hate you, and she’d still be the person who loved me less because I wasn’t useful to her.”
She wants to take the words back as soon as she says them. There’s a thread of I’m sorry, sis,
I didn’t mean it, I’m grateful for everything you do, I know it’s hard, I know you didn’t want
this to happen,
But, instead, she looks Akechi in the eye and dares him to refute her.
He doesn’t. He just nods, silently, and Makoto turns away.
“Do you want to change her heart?” Akechi asks.
“I-” Makoto chokes, “I don’t know.”
Akechi raises his eyebrows again.
“I don’t…” She swallows, “I don’t want to-”
She probably should have thought this through a little more.
“Changing a heart is a large undertaking.” Akechi says, cutting off her stuttering, “Not just in
the work required to accomplish it, but also in what it does to the recipient.”
Which is why Makoto doesn’t know.
“A benefit, however, to how much effort it takes to complete a palace infiltration,” Akechi
continues, voice deceptively light, “Is that you don’t have to make a decision right away. Or
at all, in fact.”
Makoto narrows her eyes, “What are you suggesting?”
“Am I correct in thinking that you don’t want the others to hear about this?” Akechi turns and
raises an eyebrow, and Makoto frowns as she tentatively nods, “Then how about this? You
and I explore this palace together, in secret. There needn’t be a particular end goal, but I
assume that you’ll be stalling a talk with Sae-san until you’re either satisfied, or your hand is
forced.”
Is she really so obvious? Makoto hopes that this uncomfortable insight is a result of a
conversation she and Akechi had in the last timeline. Still weird, but far better than the
possibility that Akechi just understands things about her.
Oddly, she feels like he isn’t that thrilled by the prospect, either.
“You’d be correct.” Makoto admits, “But- it’s not like I’m trying to stall, it’s just-” She looks
up, again at the lights, flashing rhythmically, “She’s my sister.”
“So she is.” Akechi hums. He folds his arms, “Well? Yes or no?”
Makoto opens her mouth.

AndDamnit.
“Let me think about it.” She decides, which isn’t much of a decision at all, she knows, but
still.
“If you’re concerned about our safety,” Akechi continues, and it’s a small comfort that he
seems to have missed the mark on what’s causing Makoto to hesitate, “Then don’t be. You’re
perfectly adequate in healing and support, and I can cover navigation and any need for
damage.”
It’s about the closest thing to a compliment Makoto thinks she’ll ever get from Akechi. “I
know.” She says, finally managing to scrape together some composure, “I just feel off, lying
about what we’re doing.” She smooths her hands over her skirt, “But I’m not opposed. That’s
why I need to think about it.”
Akechi shrugs. “Don’t take too long.”
It’s always the timer, isn’t it?
(In Akechi’s mind, the High Priestess grows to its fourth rank.)
***
Ren isn’t sure how long Makoto needs, really, to organise everything with Niijima, but he
appreciates the semblance of a break.
Not that the stress has abated. No palace infiltration only means that Ren has more time for
the other things he's put off. The list is so long and so ambiguous that Ren doesn’t quite know
where to start.
Everything, as ever, still feels too hasty.
Spending time on the roof during breaks at school ranges emotionally from a quiet place to
think when Ren manages to get there on his own, to utter chaos when joined by some of the
other thieves.
There was a time, last time, to be precise, that the roof was also a place ofIt still is, Ren is reminded abruptly, a place of simple labour, as he sees fluffy auburn locks
peeking out from under a sunhat across the roof as he opens the door.
Haru turns, blinking with surprise, “Oh! Ren-kun!”
Ren waves, “Hi, Haru. Uh- I hope I’m not interrupting?”
She shakes her head, “Not at all. You can join me, if you’d like? You said you helped me out
in the garden a lot, last time.”

“I did.” Ren reconfirms. “I can help.” He squats next to the planters, and rolls up his sleeves.
Haru smiles, as bright as she’s ever been, “Thank you! Is Mona-chan not with you today?”
Ren is starting to get déjà vu. He shakes his head, “No, he went to hang out with Ann.” He
idly picks a weed out of the soil, “You’re calling him Mona-chan again?” He says without
thinking.
Haru blinks, “Again?”
“Oh- you called him Mona-chan last timeline,” Ren explains, “You were pretty close, since
you joined us by finding Morgana when he ran away.”
Haru laughs under her breath, “I suppose even if circumstances are different, we are
fundamentally the same people.”
Ren isn’t sure how much he can refute that.
Haru is different, from what he remembers. But that’s just the thing- Ren doesn’t know if
she’s actually different, or if he’s just seeing her from a different angle. All the gratitude and
the sparks of a first friend are directed elsewhere, the dynamic shifted entirely.
All there is to be done is gardening, it seems.
“Did I hate him, last time?”
Ren nearly falls over at the question. He turns and gives Haru an alarmed look.
He knows who she’s talking about.
Haru smiles, “I’m sorry, that was a bit out of nowhere, wasn’t it?”
“A bit.” Ren agrees.
“I’d ask Goro-kun himself, but I’m unlikely to get a straight answer.” She explains, “And I
wouldn’t want to upset him, asking something like that. I doubt Sumi-chan really knows
either- and I think the question would upset her even more.”
A good point.
“Why do you want to know?” Ren asks slowly.
“A passing curiosity, I suppose.” Haru hums, “Goro-kun told me, ahead of time, that he was
in a position to assassinate my father. And then, when he got his memories of last time back,
that he is the person who once killed my father.” She frowns, “It didn’t really matter to me. It
still doesn’t, if I’m being honest. Goro-kun might be the same person who did those things,
but the consequences have effectively been erased.”
Ren nods, tentative, “…I know Akechi sees things differently.”

Haru laughs, “Of course! Sometimes I can’t help but be shocked at how similar we are, and
then with things like this we’re entirely opposites.” She looks down, back at the soil, “I even
told him that if it came down to him or my father, given the circumstances of his employment,
shall we say, that he shouldn’t make the choice for my sake.”
Ren smiles, and thinks that Haru really is the same as ever. “If you’re asking about how you
felt about Akechi, last time…” He trails off, and trues to think of how to word it, “I don’t
know for sure, really. But I don’t think you hated him. You were pretty nice to him, all things
considered.”
“I suppose I expected that.” Haru says lightly, “I asked you only because I know my
perception of it is… coloured. Goro-kun and Sumi-chan were my first real friends. I can’t
ever imagine hating either of them.”
Ren ignores the hollow ring of another thing so different. “…Beyond curiosity,” He
continues, pulling out another weed, “Was there any other reason you wanted to know?”
Haru doesn’t look up, tilling the dirt a little more.
Ren waits.
“Niijima-san -the elder one, that is,” Haru eventually says, “She came over to my apartment,
for questioning, along with some other officers. She implied that the effects of the psychotic
breakdown haven’t seemed to have quite worn off yet.”
Ah.
Haru pushes the soil around, inspecting one of the plant leaves with gloved hands, “I don’t
think I’ll ever be getting my father back.” She says, detached.
“I don’t think you ever were.” Ren says, not unkindly.
Haru smiles, unhappy, “I know. I never could quite seem to get it through my head.”
Back to the planters. Ren picks a ripe tomato off the stem, setting it to the side.
“I could never hate him.” Haru says quietly, and Ren isn’t quite sure who she’s referring to.

Chapter Summary

Deals, casinos, and dodging concequences.

Another timer to the pile is hardly new.
Akechi wishes that he had given Makoto a deadline to make her decision. He’s not entirely
sure what that deadline would be, but another nebulous limbo is hardly what anyone needs
right now.
He’s also stuck in the unfortunate position of not having a reliable means of communication
with anyone except for Ann. He bought a burner phone on the way back from Sae’s palace,
but he didn’t link a new number to it. He simply waited for the Nav to appear on the
homepage, and returned Ann’s phone.
Hopefully Makoto will have the foresight to try and contact Akechi in a way that is distinctly
unsuspicious.
For now, though, Ann kicks her legs back and forth on the couch, frowning at her phone.
“Um…” She mumbles, and Akechi looks up, “So… I think Futaba wants to talk to you?”
That isn’t what Akechi wanted to hear.
“And how does she intend to do that?” Akechi asks, stalling.
Ann nearly drops her phone as it starts ringing.
“Uh.” Ann gives him an apologetic look, “Like that?”
Akechi rolls his eyes, and holds out his hand. Ann passes him the phone, mouthing sorry as
she does.
“Hello?” Akechi says, flat.
“What happened to your phone?” Is the snappy response.
“I left it to rot in the collective unconscious.” Akechi explains tiredly.
“Oooh.” Futaba drawls out, “That makes sense I guess.”

“I bought a burner.” Akechi continues, glaring at Ann and hoping she’ll get the message to
leave the room, “I don’t have a number attached to it, though. I assumed that would be illadvised.”
“Ah…” Futaba hums, and Akechi still can’t quite get a read on her, “Well, so long as it’s a
completely new number you should be good. And you don’t spread it around to people who
shouldn’t have it.”
“I see…” He says, and tries to figure out how to shoo Ann away without insulting her
gracious hospitality too much. She pointedly ignores him.
“Yep.” Futaba says with a pop, “We could get that done pretty quick, actually. I could make
sure all the money stuff is linked back to me, which won’t look out of place with all the other
shit I’ve bought.”
“As opposed to a strange man in a face mask and hoodie demanding to by a new sim card.”
Akechi follows the thread of logic. He raises an eyebrow, “We?”
“Yeah.” Is the simple response, followed by a pause. “You’re coming to Akihabara with me,
by the way.”
Akechi was afraid of this, “Is that so?”
“You’d better come with!” Some fire flashes in her voice, “I know where you live!”
Ann must hear that, as she frowns and her brows furrow. Akechi glares at her again.
“Do the words on the run mean nothing to you?” Akechi snarks with the least amount of
venom he can manage.
“Uh, yeah,” Futaba scoffs, “It means you get to play the role of my nameless and mysterious
bodyguard as we wander the streets. It comes with a tragic backstory and everything.”
“Have you actually thought this through?” Akechi asks lowly.
“Of course I have.” Futaba snaps, “You were willing to live the highlife of Mementos real
estate until Ann saved your ass, and you would have had to walk around town like a normal
person then.”
Apparently, Ann can hear everything, as she chimes in: “She’s kinda right…”
“Is that Ann? Thanks for backing me up!”
Akechi can feel a migraine coming on.
“Alright.” He mutters, “It’s your funeral. Or, more accurately, mine.”
“Yeah, yeah.” Futaba blows a raspberry, “You’ll be fine. I’m a great navigator. Akihabara is
no problem for us.”

Akechi grits his teeth, “I’ll meet you in the laundromat near Leblanc.”
“Be quick!”
And the line goes dead.
“So, uh…” Ann twirls her hair around a finger as she takes her phone back, “Are you two
going to be okay, or…?”
Akechi thinks his glare might be losing some of its effect, but he turns it on her again
anyway, “Weren’t you the one backing her up in this?”
Ann waves her hands, “I was just saying that one point was kinda true! I didn’t mean that
going outside is a good idea!”
“Then where were you during that part of the argument?” Akechi hisses, pulling his hoodie
over his head and rummaging around for his facemask.
“Well, maybe it’ll be good!” Ann says, flustered, “Like, good that you won’t have to use my
phone all the time. And, uh…” She grimaces, “I dunno what’s going on with you and Futaba,
but maybe you can sort something out…?”
“What’s going on is that I murdered her mother.”
Ann’s grimace gets even more strained, “Uh, yeah, right. …If she’s willing to talk to you,
then…?”
“Stop trying to give advice on things you know nothing about.” Akechi snaps, “I’ll be back
later. Or I won’t. Don’t bother looking for my body.”
“Alright, jeez!” Ann rolls her eyes and flops back on the couch, “Maybe get in a better mood
before Futaba has to deal with you.” She mutters.
Akechi says nothing, and melts into Mementos.

As it turns out, Futaba is the one that’s late.
“Sorry!” She yelps, barrelling into the laundromat, “I got distracted. And I had to get Ren and
Mona off my back.”
Akechi raises an eyebrow, “They don’t know where you’re going?”
“If they did, then they’d insist on coming along.” She says, not quite meeting his eyes, “And
you want that even less than I do.”
Point. “Right. Shall we go, then?”
“Yeah.” She kicks at the floor, then narrows her eyes. “Wait. Your disguise kinda sucks.”

Akechi blinks. He gestures to how his hair and most of his face is entirely covered, “It’s

Akechi sincerely doubts that’s the case. “How would you suggest I fix that, then?”
Futaba whips off her glasses, and shoves them on Akechi’s face.
“There.” She says, triumphant, as Akechi tries to recalibrate from shock. “You and Ren have

Akechi does not gape like a fish, “…Ah.”
Futaba squints, “I can’t see properly.”

The trip to Akihabara is mercifully short, and predictably uncomfortable. The heavy

“Screens ruin your eyesight, you know.” Akechi snipes.
Futaba sticks out her tongue, “Usually I have a key item to fix that. It’s not supposed to leave

Akechi understood about half of that. “You can take it back, if you wish.”

Akechi clenches his fists in his pockets, “Of course.”

Futaba groans, “See! You’re even doing it now! I’m not stupid!”
“I don’t believe you are.” Akechi says truthfully. “You’d need at least a modicum of

Futaba angrily takes a package off the wall to get a closer look at it, “Not gonna happen. You

She waves the package in her hand, “I’m gonna go buy this. Then we’re gonna go

“Thanks.” She mumbles, and tilts her head, “I guess… you’re gonna keep being cagey no

“Promise.” She insists, “You’ll help me.”
“Of course.”
“And you’ll help fill the gaps.”
“Not the deal.” Akechi snaps.

Futaba scowls, “We’ll workshop it.”
“We won’t.” Akechi promises, and takes the box out of her hands to finally march up to the
register.
And, of course, the Death reaches rank five.

It's a familiar turn of events, when Sumire finds herself window shopping in Kichijoji on a
Monday afternoon. More familiar still, when she nearly walks straight into Ren, who seems
to be doing much the same.
“Ren-senpai!” Sumire yelps in apology, “Oh- sorry, I wasn’t looking where I was going-”
“Neither was I.” Ren says sheepishly, “Don’t worry about it.”
Sumire laughs, feeling a bit relieved, “Well, okay then.” She tilts her head, eyeing the bag at
Ren’s side, “Is Morgana-senpai not with you today?”
Ren shrugs, “Nah. He ran off to hang out with Ryuji and Ann. I was just killing time.” He
rubs the back of his neck, “What about you?”
“Oh, well,” Sumire smiles awkwardly, “To be honest- do you remember how I dragged you
along to help me pick out a birthday gift for my dad, last time? I, uh, sort of forgot, this year.”
Ren snorts, “I know the feeling.”
“Right.” Sumire laughs, “I remembered this morning. I guess I’ll just buy the same thing I
did last time?”
Ren nods, “He liked them, didn’t he?”
“He did.” Sumire hums, “I got a bit distracted along the way. Some of these store fronts are
so flashy.”
Ren readjusts the bag over his shoulder, “I’ll come with.” He smiles, “Maybe you can buy
those gag glasses this time.”
Sumire snickers, “Maybe I will. Remind me when your birthday is, Ren-senpai?”
“That’s cold.” Ren pouts, performative.
Sumire shrugs, “You’re the one that suggested it.” She teases.
Ren laughs, and they fall into silence as they wander down the streets of Kichijoji, towards
the other main road.
“You know,” Sumire starts, as they enter the store selling a wide array of glasses frames, “It’s
strange. I worked myself up so much trying to figure out what my dad would like last time.”

Even though she wasn’t her at the time, it was still a very Sumire thing to do, she thinks
wryly. “And now it’s just… one and done. The second I find where the frames are I can leave
the store.”
Ren hums, distant, “That’s good.”
Sumire readjusts her ponytail, for want of something to do with her hands, “I guess. It felt the
most… off-putting, around April and May. I got used to it, I think. Or things changed enough
that it stopped feeling like I’ve been doing everything twice.” She skips over her languishing
gymnastics career in her head. Later.
“I get that, a bit.” Ren mumbles. “Things started changing even before I remembered
everything, but it was still… disorienting. And there’s a lot of stuff that hasn’t changed. And
a lot that has.”
Sumire frowns, “Yeah…” She turns, directing her attention back to the wall of glasses, “…
Did something happen?”
Ren shrugs, “Not really. It’s been happening for a while now.” He tugs at his fringe, “Just… I
talked with Haru, the other day. We used to be pretty close, you know? And I still remember
all that, but she doesn’t. And it’s never going to be the same, because the circumstances are
too different.”
Ah.
Now that was something Sumire only ever experienced in bits and pieces.
In the beginning, when she was so furious with Ren she could barely stand to look at him, she
had been conflicted. What right did she have, to project her anger and sorrow onto someone
who, for all intents and purposes, was a different person entirely?
Their relationship could never be the same, but that was a choice Sumire made. And,
ultimately, it all resolved quite well for her. She’s had her cake and eaten it too. She never had
much to lose to begin with, really- for all that it was odd speaking to the thieves while they
had no recollection of her, she never knew them that well to begin with.
Even with Goro, who Sumire will tentatively claim she was closest to aside from Ren in the
January prior; she made far more progress with him in the span of a few months than she
probably would have in a lifetime, if only because she knew where to look.
(And, a ghost could hardly have spilled secrets and friendship once the puppet it possessed
was tossed to the wayside upon the collapse of the reality that created it. Sumire doesn’t
much like thinking about that, though.)
“Even the things that aren’t different.” Ren continues, “Ann and Ryuji invited me along today
too, not just Mona. But they wanted to go to the arcade to play this new game that I
remember coming out, and I already played it with them when it released.”

Sumire skims the wall in front of her for a familiar set of red frames, and comes up empty.
“Too much, huh?”
Ren tugs at his fringe again, more fiercely this time, “Yeah. I didn’t want to ruin their fun or
anything, so I just… said I was busy.” He huffs, “It’s the same with so many people I know.
They’re not different, since they don’t really have much stake in all the stuff we’re doing, so
it just feels like I’m having the same conversations over and over.”
“I feel that with my coach, sometimes.” Sumire admits, “I kind of… sped things up a bit, but
she gave me the same word-for-word speech about needing to figure out who I am after my
last competition.”
Ren gives a wry snort, “Really? Even though you’re not… y’know?”
Sumire shrugs helplessly, “Yeah. I think she can tell I’m distracted, is all.”
“Right.” Ren mumbles, and scoffs, “It’s like all the stuff I want to be the same has changed,
and all the stuff I want to be different is stuck in place.”
Sumire laughs, “Inconvenient, isn’t it?” She swallows, “I’m really glad I’m not alone in this,
though.”
“You were for a while.” Ren points out, quiet, “Sorry I took so long.”
“It’s okay.” Sumire says, and finds that she means it.
Ren’s eyes flick down to the floor, and he says nothing else.
Sumire frowns at the selection before her, “I can’t find it…” She mumbles.
Ren tilts his head, and he points to a gap between some of the frames, “Isn’t that where it
was, last time?”
Sumire furrows her brows, trying to recall, “I think so…” She laughs, “Guess I was too late,
then.”
Ren smiles, awkward and laden with irony, “Want to pick something else?”
Sumire sighs, “I have to, don’t I?”

Apparently, Makoto is far more punctual than Akechi gave her credit for.

“Well, look at that. I knew you weren’t dead.”
Ah.
Akechi sighs, and turns.

Sae strides forward, all her distortion in place; wide-brimmed hat decorated with yellow roses

He didn’tIt’s uncomfortably familiar, to be met with his own face.

There’s a nervousness, to lying that everything is okay.
Sumire had joked, fantasised, played pretend- all of it, hoping for some truth that everyone
might have a future.

She’s always had a future. By some definition, at least. Even when it changed, even when her
image of it shattered with the oncoming force of a truck, she twisted and leaped and dodged
and found herself back at square one.
The fragility of the concept only hit her on a cold morning in early February, listening to her
closest friend choke out his sorrows and excuses. And still, the understanding didn’t stick.
Being forced to face it again etches it into her mind a little deeper.
Sumire hates that there has to be someone, anyone, put up for slaughter in order to get
Shido’s conviction to be permanent. Hate in general isn’t something she really experiences
often- it’s rather novel, she thinks, above the dread and the taste of bile in the back of her
throat every time her train of thought passes it by.
There has to be a way out.
On Tuesday afternoon, she pads up the stairs to Leblanc’s attic, throwing an apologetic smile
over her shoulder at Sojiro, who just sighs and waves her off.
“Ren-senpai?” She calls up the stairs as she crests over the top.
Ren, who is lying back on his bed and scrolling idly through his phone, Morgana off who
knows where, sits up abruptly, “Sumire? What’s up?”
She gives half a smile, “I just wanted to talk a bit about our plan. Or, um, what’s left of it.”
Ren snorts, and stands, shoving his hands in his pockets. “If you’ve got a solution to all our
problems, I’d love to hear it. I’ve been fresh out of ideas for a month.”
Sumire’s smile becomes a little more genuine, “I wish. But, no,” She sucks in a breath, “I
think we need to rethink how we’re dealing with Shido.”
Ren’s eyes narrow, and the levity leaves his face, “Yeah?”
“Niijima-san, the older one, that is,” Sumire starts, “You said she asked you to testify against
Shido, as the leader of the Phantom Thieves, right? And that thanks to Doctor Maruki it was
Goro that took your place.”
Some understanding creeps into Ren’s expression, “That’s right.”
“Well, that can’t happen, obviously.” Sumire blurts, “That’s not fair- to either of you.”
Ren bites at his lips, “Don’t I know it.” He mutters. He strides over to the moth-bitten couch,
and collapses onto it, patting the spot next to him. Sumire takes the offered seat.
“Goro said that the evidence he has on hand isn’t enough.” She continues, “That it’s the kind
of thing that could supplement a testimony, maybe, but not be enough on its own.”
All her words stumble to a stop, as she runs out of things to spill.

After a moment, Ren hums, and leans back. “…Niijima needed me or Akechi because we
know about the Metaverse, I think. For the testimony.”
Sumire picks at the skin around her fingers, “I didn’t realise they’d believe that in court.”
Ren shrugs, “Who knows if they would have? I didn’t get to the station, and Akechi said all
that happened to him was getting questioned before being released come new year’s.”
Sumire frowns, “So… maybe if we got someone else who knows about the Metaverse to
testify?”
“In a way that doesn’t implicate themselves?” Ren points out, “Or Akechi?”
“What if we didn’t care about them?” Sumire blurts, then grimaces, “Um, I mean, what if
they were a person who… also needs to kind of go to court.”
“Someone in on the conspiracy?” Ren concludes, “I guess… we’d have to change their heart,
or something. We could persuade them to not out Akechi while we’re at it, maybe.”
Sumire nods eagerly, “Yes! Something like that!”
Ren looks as accomplished as Sumire feels for a minute, before his eyes flick to the side in
thought, “But… we wouldn’t be able to do it too early.”
Sumire slumps, “Right… it would have to be after Shido’s change of heart, probably, or he’d
just, uh,” Murder whoever it is that is suddenly running to the media to confess their sins.
Ren grabs his chin in a familiar gesture, and Sumire almost smiles, “Not just that.” He adds,
“Even if Shido is down for the count, there are still a lot of people who stand to lose
something from one of their own testifying. We have to worry about the entire conspiracy.”
“Everyone?” Sumire clarifies, feeling a bit overwhelmed, “…Not just the people on top?”
“Maybe just the people on top.” Ren amends, “The people who would have the knowledge to
notice something is wrong, and the power to do something about it.”
“So, what?” Sumire readjusts her glasses nervously, “We have to change all their hearts?
How many of them even are there?”
This is starting to look like a far bigger task than Sumire bargained for.
“At least five.” Ren digs his palms into his eyes, stretching out his legs, “Give or take. Six,
probably, if we also need to nab someone who has more specific knowledge on cognitive
psience. Shido probably still has at least one researcher lying around that he hasn’t killed.”
Sumire laughs, half-hearted, “Hopefully.”
Ren puffs out his cheeks, and mutters, “Names, names, we need names. And time. Shit.”

“How long do you think it would take to track all the people we need in Mementos?” Sumire
asks cautiously.
“They might not be in Mementos.” Ren points out, “Some of them might be, but even more
of them might have palaces.”
“Shoot…” Sumire mumbles, “So, that’s-”
“If we’re lucky? A day run of six Mementos targets.” Ren finishes, “If we’re unlucky, and we
usually are, that’s six palaces. Plus Shido.”
Six palaces. Seven. Sumire hopes to anything that it’s less, but potentially six palaces that
they need to clear in a narrow window after they deal with Shido, but before the Metaverse
disappears entirely.
She swallows, “Can we secure the routes beforehand?”
“Before Shido?” Ren tilts his head, “I guess… yeah. Yeah, that’s- something.” He leans
forward, “We need names, obviously. I know some, thanks to Shido’s palace last time. We
can check which ones have palaces, and do them… I guess while we’re waiting for Makoto
with Sae?”
“That could be a day from now.” Sumire points out with a weak laugh.
Ren returns it, weary grin directed at the wall, “We’ll stick to last timeline’s schedule, then.
Our deadline for Shido is just before the election, so we have…about a month and a half.”
That’s…
Tight. No time, and all the time in the world simultaneously. Sumire thinks they could clear a
palace in a day if they really put their minds to it, but that’s working under the assumption
that each palace is easy, and that no cognitive roadblocks present themselves.
If history has anything to show for it, it’s that roadblocks will certainly present themselves.
“…Names.” Sumire eventually says, “Let’s get those first.”
Ren huffs a laugh, “So we’re doing this?”
“Of course.” Sumire smiles, genuine, “Would you rather go to jail?”
“No,” Ren says tiredly, “No, I really wouldn’t.”

Chapter 69
Chapter Summary

A ship, a customary change of plans, and a casino.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

It is unrealistic, to wish to be free from other’s perceptions of oneself.
Isolation and humanity simply don’t mix. Nor is it feasibly possible to be scrubbed from
minds on which you have already made an impression. It could be argued that the solution is
simply never making an impression at all, but, well,
It’s far too late for that, Akechi thinks.
If the version of him that toils idly on a cruiser that splits a bloody sea is downright insulting,
then the echo of him that gambles in gaudy lounges, odds stacked against him in favour of
the house, isAn enigma, and nothing more. There’s simply nothing to go on, if Akechi wishes to construct
an accurate picture of how Sae truly feels about him.
A cognition of a cognition. It’s funny, really. Hilarious.
If Akechi ends up forming a bond with that one, too, he’s holding Makoto solely responsible.
He gets the feeling that might not be a problem, as the Tower, ever unsteady, sways this way
and that in its unbalance, as if in laughter. He can never be sure what that thing finds
amusement in, but he certainly doesn’t appreciate it.
Slipping away from Ann’s sights isn’t particularly difficult. It’s tradition by now to take an
evening walk. She honestly might have been more suspicious if Akechi abstained a night.
Her narrowed eyes and pursed lips tell Akechi that this is not the case. Alas, there isn’t much
she can do.
He doesn’t have much of a destination in mind. It’s refreshing, to take a walk with the
express purpose of actually clearing his head, rather than marching towards the red-tinted
reflection of the courthouse.
Getting lost in his head leads him to the Diet Building instead.

Of course.
Where else?
He internally prods at the Tower, wondering again if these things have some kind of
subconscious influence on him. How infuriating, that his most annoying bond is the one
immune to traditional death.
He may as well stop by.
(It’s stupid- it’s always stupid, saying hello to that thing.
Shido’s ship is a deathtrap, and his cognition is the blade there to sever his neck. A blade that
once succeeded, Akechi is loath to remind himself, tapping idly at his throat in lieu of
memory of where the bullet hit.
He doesn’t know why he makes these excuses to drop by- god forbid that the true reason is
something as simple as curiosity. He has his answers.
So why does he keep coming back?
The bricklaying isn’t complete, the foundations unsteady.
Always more work to be done.)
He shifts- barely to the left. Shido’s distortion is so large that Akechi wonders if he even
really needs the Nav, or if he could just stumble and find himself in a red sea beneath a
permanent sunset.
But, today, he finds himself on the deck.
“You’re back.”
Akechi turns, and sees the cognition leaning against the railing, hair and blazer entirely
soaked through, dripping seawater against the ground.
Ah. A change.
“I’m back.” Akechi agrees.
He supposes the state of the cognition isn’t all that surprising. Akechi is a proper traitor to
Shido’s cause now, after all. There’s no reason to tolerate his presence as a pseudo-guest on
the ship any longer.
He wonders if the cognition resents him.
“Here to kill me again?” It smiles, “Or maybe I’ll get you, this time.”
Akechi tilts his head, and sneers, “Have you turned this into a game?”
The cognition shrugs, “What else is there to do?”

“Did they throw you overboard?” Akechi doesn’t deign it with a response.
The cognition rolls its eyes, “What does it look like? No, I just decided to go for a swim
instead,” It mocks, “Very refreshing. You should try it.”
“I’ll pass.” Akechi drawls.
“Your loss.” Is the airy response.
Akechi snorts, and turns towards the double doors leading to the lobby of the cruiser,
narrowing his eyes, “I wonder.” He starts, “How do you feel about the captain, these days?”
The cognition gives him a blank stare. “Well. Aren’t you hopeful?”
Akechi turns to glare at it, “Excuse me?”
“I see what you’re asking.” It continues, “You want to know if the captain still sees you as his
unfailing puppet, no? How I feel is an exact reflection of whether the captain truly respects
you or not. Supposedly.” It tacks on.
Akechi scoffs, “Of course not.”
“You want to know if you’re free.”
“I don’t.” Akechi spits, “I hardly care what that man thinks of me anymore, and the feeling is
clearly mutual.”
“So you admit that you did care?” The cognition asks, unassuming smile in place.
“Are you done?” Akechi snarls, “What are you getting out of being a nuisance?”
The cognition shrugs, “Call it curiosity.”
And, well, isn’t that hilarious. “Find something better to do.”
The cognition gestures, bemused, towards the rest of the ship, and towards itself, “I’m not
entirely sure if you’ve noticed, but setting foot back inside is a surefire way to find myself
thrown over the edge again. I guess the cleaner is only paid to -ha- clean interiors.”
Akechi rolls his eyes, “So you’ve decided that your only alternative is to bother me, is that
it?”
“You’re the one that came here.” The cognition points out, “From my perspective, you’re
bothering me.”
“Aren’t you satisfying your curiosity?” Akechi levels another glare in its direction, “I could
just leave. Leave you to your boredom.”
The cognition tilts its head, “Then why aren’t you?”

A better question would be why Akechi came here to begin with, but that’s not something
he’s ever been able to answer.
Akechi folds his arms, “You’re never quite what I expect you to be.” He observes.
The cognition raises an eyebrow at the change in topic, “Is that so?”
“Mm.”
“In what way?”
Akechi huffs, “It’s hard to describe.” He says, truthfully.
To describe, would be to recall a gun, and the smell of iron, of blood, of steam, and desperate
voices and a siren and“To be honest,” The cognition slices through his thoughts, “I’m never quite what I expect to
be, either.”
Akechi narrows his eyes, “Aren’t you supposed to be one note?”
The cognition snorts, “Supposedly. I was, I believe. I had a role, a purpose, an end point.” It
levels a pointed look at Akechi, “I suppose I only have you to blame for the rug being pulled
from under me.”
“You’re welcome.” Akechi intones dryly.
The cognition laughs, “It’s funny; you are, by design, the bane of my existence. Everything
you do has unintended consequences forced onto my psyche- the way I think, and act, and
even talk.” It spits, “And yet, the thought of trying to kill you unprompted isn’t as appealing
anymore, because of you, if only because I’m no longer inclined to do such a gracious favour
for the captain.”
Akechi stares, considering, “…Does that make you free?”
“Of course not.” The cognition says simply, “I’m tied here so tightly that even throwing me
overboard can’t get rid of me.”
A moth to a flame, or a stone to the bottom of the ocean floor. Akechi thinks how he keeps
returning here with no rhyme or reason, and grits his teeth.
“Maybe that’s your fault too, though.” The cognition continues airily. “Being tied between
two points is awfully novel.”
Akechi furrows his brow, “What do you mean?”
“This.” The cognition sighs, and Akechi feels the Tower in his chest strum dissonantly, “I’ve
no idea what it is, but it is connected to you, yes?”
That’s new.

Akechi knows that shadows can feel the arcana. His short encounter with Sae in Mementos
months ago revealed that. Beings such as José, or the twins, can feel them too; even beyond
their own designation.
Cognitions, Akechi reasons, are made of the Metaverse. It isn’t entirely absurd to think that
they could feel these threads too.
Except it is absurd, because the thing before him isn’t real. Just an ever-changing jumble of
perceptions and unwanted opinions. It’s barely any different from a wall, and it seems as
though becoming aware of the arcana is a new development(Can a wall, if scrubbed clean, hide a mirror beneath?)
“I think the captain knows what it is.” The cognition mutters, “Has one of his own. Not that
he ever told me anything- and he certainly won’t now.”
“Right.” Akechi murmurs, barely listening, trying to make sense of it all.
It’s tied to fate, no? Robin supplies, If the bond becomes stronger-IT STRETCHES ON ALL SIDES. Loki continues, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHTSOMETIMES IT ISN’T FIGURATIVE AT ALL.
How helpful.
The cognition is giving him an odd look.
“What?” Akechi snaps.
“I can…” It mumbles, “You’re talking to them, aren’t you?”
A thread of panic lances through Akechi’s chest, “You-”
“I don’t know what they’re like.” The cognition says in a rush, speaking over him, “I only
know that I have them, since the captain knows it.”
“Another curiosity of yours?” Akechi asks warily.
The cognition smiles a TV smile, more slanted than ever, “Indulge me. I’m you, so it stands
to reason that they’re just as much mine as yours.”
“You’re still on that?” Akechi hisses, “I would have assumed that you were riling me up for
Shido’s sake. What happened to not doing favours for him?”
The cognition chuckles, “I thought I’d say it for old times’ sake.”
Something about the words ring false. Akechi doesn’t care to push.
“Whatever.” He mutters, and decides playing along is harmless, “Loki.”

Loki dutifully unfurls, Akechi’s mask burning away. The cognition’s eyes widen in
something that might be wonder, before it tilts its head, and frowns.
“You have two, right?” It asks.
More, technically, but Akechi internally concedes that the Atropos and Lilim that have made
themselves at home within his soul are hardly him in the same way Robin and Loki are. “You
want to see him?”
The cognition nods, eyes narrowed in- something.
“Robin Hood,” Akechi calls, guarded, aware of the shortcomings of his less-experienced
persona.
The cognition’s eyes narrow even further as Robin stands to his full height, taking in the bow
and cape.
“It’s…” The cognition mumbles, “Not quite right.”
Akechi raises an eyebrow.
“Neither of them are- full.” The cognition explains haltingly, “They’re not me.”
“Of course they’re not.” Akechi says, unexpected relief spreading in his chest, “They’re me.”
“Are they?”
Akechi sneers, “That’s enough, isn’t it? You got to look.”
The cognition’s frown doesn’t abate, looking almost confused.
(If you were not a wildcard, Akechi remembers Justine’s voice, unbidden, then your
awakening likely would have killed you.
And yet, he is a wildcard.
His soul is volatile, fractured, half-shattered- whatever. All he needs is balance, and he has it.
Robin and Loki bicker as they always have, but they are his to control.
There’s nothing else to find, is there?)
This cognition has no idea what it’s talking about.
“I think that’s enough for today.” Akechi declares, turning on his heel, “Enjoy your
boredom.”
The frustrated expression on the cognition vanishes, melting into that amused neutrality it’s
so fond of, “Sure.”
Akechi takes out his phone, calling Robin back, typing in Mementos.

“Come back soon.” The cognition calls as the world warps, and the Tower reaches its seventh
rank.

Ann kicks him, “I clean! I’d be living in a pigsty if I didn’t. Akechi-kun just cleans even
more.”

Haru giggles, “It sounds like everything is alright, then.”
“Sure is!” Ann says, maybe a bit too loud.
Because, quite frankly, she isn’t sure if everything is alright. Akechi himself is- fine. It’s nice,

Maybe she’s overreacting. Akechi says that he’s going for walks to clear his head. Ann can’t

Maybe she’ll just… push a little harder? She thinks she can say that she and Akechi are

The last few weeks have been a blow to Makoto’s pride.
Everything, from the lead up, to the misunderstandings, to the need to wait, to being forced to
work with Akechi of all people, all compounds to- this. she wishes she could catch a break.
And it is a matter of force, with regard to her most recent issue. She hardly wants to work
with Akechi, and she’s sure Akechi doesn’t want to work with her, either.
But she’s not an idiot. Exploring her sister’s palace on her own, with her current skill and
lack of navigational abilities, is practically suicide. Akechi is her only ticket to getting
something done.
Which, given their… altercation, last they met, means that Makoto is once again in the
position of having to suck it up. A task far easier over text, she finds.
Queen: Meet again tonight at the usual spot.
Crow: Gotten over yourself, have you?
Makoto desperately wants to punch him.
Queen: Have you?
Crow: Have I ever?
At least he’s self-aware. Makoto might refrain from punching him.
Crow: That aside, enough that I’m sure we can coexist. I’ll be there.
She might just take out her frustrations on Akechi’s cognitive double. She thinks that Akechi
himself will be doing that already.
But- Good. Good, she hasn’t pissed Akechi off so horribly that she has to beg him to do her a
favour. By the sounds of it, he’s just going to be making unprompted jabs at her
intermittently. He does that anyway, so no skin off her back.
Making her way back to the courthouse and slipping into the casino is a practiced art, at this
point. Waiting is, too, and Makoto makes it a point not to fidget in anxiousness, ignoring the
indignant envy that bubbles up her throat at the sight of the palace.
She came here to know, to understand. She can’t run the second she doesn’t like what she
sees.

The thought doesn’t make this any easier.

Damn.
