There’s a ping at the Diet Building.
If Takahashi is to be believed, there was a breach of a manifestation within the last few hours.
As ever: no way to identify it’s owner, nor who infiltrated it, nor how many, nor even exactly
when, but there was, definitively, something that pierced the veil at the Diet Building.
Alarming, to say the least.
Masayoshi Shido is not a fool.
The two notable cognitive world entries of the past few days, following Akechi’s arrest and
everything that was botched with it, are not subtle in their locations. The SatoTech

headquarters could only reasonably house one man’s distortion, and the TV studio that
Akechi himself made trips to so often has a limited list of suspects as well.
The courthouse and the defunct laboratory in Odaiba (last he heard, they were turning the
place into a stadium) remain dormant. Perhaps the thieves decided making trips back there
was too risky. Or, perhaps, their business there was simply complete.
How unfortunate for them, that the steel trap snapped on their leg at just the wrong time in
that case. Though, Shido has far more than one steel trap lining the veins of this city.
If the owners of the manifestations that the thieves are poking their noses into are obvious
based on location alone, then the Diet Building does not need a second consideration. What it
does need, is fortification.
Shido has neglected to tell Sato, nor any of the potential candidates for the TV studio, that
they ought to be on their guard. He never studied psychology, exactly; but even he knows that
how the men in question would react, and, by extension, how that would affect their
manifestations, is unpredictable. No sense in potentially weakening their defences.
Given the thieves’ near infallible success rate, he supposes he ought to be concerned for their
impending changes of heart. Or their potential mental shutdowns, if Akechi is going rogue.
They won’t get far, if they all go running to the press. What Shido does know is that Akechi
has always needed a name. The Cleaner has no name that anyone could possibly know.
With any luck, the thieves will perish via some pitfall in his associates’ heads.
With any extra luck, the thieves will perish via some pitfall in his head. And wouldn’t that be
a stroke of poeticism?
But, first,
Well, Wakaba didn’t send him monthly reports of her findings for nothing. Some defences are
in order.

If they’re lucky, there won’t be a barrier to access. Noir knows that this will not be the case.
She, and the Phantom Thieves at large, have markedly terrible luck.
The final room of the palace is a long and grand corridor, closer to a great hall. There is a
semblance of a stage at the end of the room, surrounded by the final roll of red carpet and
housing their shimmering immaterial target. Ooe’s shadow stands on the steps that lead up to
the the raised segment of floor, laughing haughtily with some cognitions that chatter
mindlessly.
“You know,” Mona speaks up as they exit the safe room, “Isn’t this palace supposed to be an
award ceremony?”
“That’s what it says on the pamphlet.” Joker agrees, dry.
Mona rolls his eyes, but continues on, “It doesn’t look much like a ceremony, is all.” He
narrows his eyes, “More just a… party.”
Barring the red carpet splitting the room, and the broad podium at the end of it, Noir has to
agree with the assessment. There haven’t been any presentations in any of the sections
they’ve trampled through, and now none here, where they should expect it most.
“Award ceremonies are usually one-time events.” Violet points out, “…So maybe it needs a
trigger for it to actually happen?”
“But palaces don’t have to follow that kind of logic.” Mona shakes his head, “For all Ooe
cares, the TV station could be an eternal loop of him getting more and more awards, and
everyone giving a standing ovation every two minutes.”

Noir is a bit surprised the palace isn’t that.
“But it’s not.” Joker counters, “So, maybe there is a trigger of some kind.”
“In here?” Noir asks, “Or out there?”
“Out there, most likely.” Mona folds his arms.
“Or it could be when anyone makes an attempt to take his treasure?” Violet suggests.
Noir hums, then jolts, “His interviews.”
Joker blinks, “Huh? Oh.”
“That would make sense.” Mona nods eagerly, “Every time he goes off to give an interview
in the real world, all the festivities pause and he gets presented an award here. Everything
else is just the pre-party.”
“I wonder if anyone else gets any awards, in that case?” Violet hums. “There are a lot of oneoff and returning guests in the real world, so I’m curious if Ooe acknowledges them at all.”
“Think we’ll find Goro in here?” Ren asks abruptly.
Haru thinks that she has had quite enough of cognitions of her friends. “I hope not.”
“Right.” Joker coughs.
Mona sighs, “If we’re done… should we get back to securing our route? All we have to do is
check if the treasure is accessible.”
Noir internally reiterates that the Phantom Thieves are never lucky. She is not so much a fool
to hope otherwise, to quash what little universal leeway they are granted thanks to something
as irritating as jinxing herself.
“Get ready for a fight once we test this.” Joker warns them, as they weave between cliques
and clumps, “Is the security level still rising permanently, Mona?”
“Not right now.” Mona says, sniffing at the air as he does, “I think since we’re in a proper
area again, the palace isn’t freaking out.”
“It probably helps that we didn’t break through the ceiling to get here, this time.” Violet says,
and adds as an afterthought: “Twice.”
“Something like that, probably.” Joker agrees, eyes narrowing as they approach the steps. He
freezes, and they all startle and freeze with him. “Wait.”
“What is it?” Noir asks, urgent.
Joker looks alarmed at her tone, like he didn’t give them all a heart attack, “Oh- I just want to
check something here. We’re still clueless about the Cleaner’s name, but there might be

something in here since Ooe is of a similar standing to Shido, so…” He rubs the back of his
neck sheepishly, “I thought that might be good to do before we piss everyone off.”
Everyone visibly deflates.
“Are we looking for anything in particular?” Noir asks, “Or are we just going to poke around
and see if anything sticks?”
“The latter, mostly.” Joker admits.
Violet hums, contemplative, “Would a cognition of the Cleaner even be allowed in this part
of the palace?”
Mona shrugs, “Dunno. Ooe’s got a serious case of being cryptic about his rules. For all we
know, the Cleaner isn’t allowed to set foot in here. Or maybe Ooe doesn’t know he exists.”
“We also might find something big, if only we check.” Ren counters.
“Then let’s check.” Noir agrees. They have nothing to lose from trying, aside from
potentially provoking a fight.
None of them move.
Mona coughs.
Violet laughs uncomfortably, “…So? Where do we start?”
“We could split up.” Noir offers.
The all hum. Still, no one moves.
Joker sighs. “Okay, maybe I should have thought of a plan ahead of time.”
“Do you know what he looks like?” Mona asks.
Joker grimaces, “Vaguely?”
“…Enough to identify him in a crowd?” Violet pushes.
“If he’s shirtless?” Joker clicks his tongue, “Probably.”
Noir scans the room to check if there’s anyone obviously shirtless walking around. There
isn’t.
“You know,” She starts, “These kind of events are often used for networking.”
Joker turns to her, “Yeah?”
“They’re beds of flattery. Alcohol loosens lips and gets people to see others in a marginally
more appealing light.” She elaborates, “It’s all quite convenient for laying the soil of
negotiation, not to mention information gathering.”

Violet blinks, “You think people will just be gossiping about the yakuza like it’s nothing?”
“Not necessarily.” Noir shakes her head, “But the point is, you can make them gossip.”
“Huh.” Joker turns back to the room, “Well, we’ve done info gathering before.”
Mona very suddenly gives him a dubious look, “Sure.”
“I didn’t say we did it well.”
“…I think cognitions are more liable to be easily tricked, so you might be in luck.” Noir says.
“What about Ooe’s shadow, then?” Violet’s eyes flicker in the man’s direction, “He’d be
sharper, but he’d also have more information, wouldn’t he? No weird rules about who’s
allowed to know what in his head.”
“True.” Joker nods, and pauses. “…You seem pretty good at all this, Noir.”
That is an impression that she seems to keep giving, yes. “Are you asking me to try my luck
with Ooe?”
Joker shrugs, “You’ve talked your way through this palace before. Successfully.” He adds,
and Violet winces, “And you’re pretty experienced at this in general.”
“I’m not.” Noir blurts.
He blinks, “Oh.”
“I mean,” She doesn’t know why she admitted that, “I’ve been at these types of events
before, of course, but I didn’t really speak.” Her job was to stand and look pretty, she
supposes. “I mostly just watched my father try and ingratiate himself with potential business
partners.”
There’s an awkward pause.
“Did he ever start gossiping about the yakuza like it was nothing?” Violet asks.
Haru’s lips twitch up, “Believe it or not, he didn’t.”
Sumire almost looks disappointed.
“So you can’t talk to Ooe?” Joker ventures awkwardly.
Noir tugs a bit at her hat, “I can try.”
“Then go for it.” He says, and that’s that.
So she shall.

Noir doesn’t make a straight shot for Ooe.
She makes a show of mingling, first. There’s a shadow with a plate of drinks, and she sweeps
off a champagne flute to try and fit in.
She takes a sip. It’s pretty good. Though perhaps now is not the time for a psientific
investigation on whether one can become intoxicated off of cognitive alcohol in a cognitive
space. Maybe Goro already knows.
She shuffles further towards the podium, toeing along the edge of the red carpet and smiling
blithely at blurry-faced strangers as she does.
She hits a wall.
Not a literal wall- nor really a metaphorical one. She simply approaches the edge of the semicircular podium, less than half a metre away from the carpet that encircles it, and can
progress no further. Ooe stands behind the block, tittering a grating laugh to some cognitions
that Noir is sure she’d recognise if she paid more attention at the parties she’s been dragged
to.
Barriers ought to have some more elegance than just that, she thinks. No barrier at all would
be preferable, of course, but it is what it is.
The conversation between the shadow and cognitions trails off, leaving Ooe to stand alone on
the steps, eyeing his treasure every so often.
Nothing to be done, then.
“Ooe-san.” Noir pulls a smile together, and does a small curtsy, “I wanted to formally
introduce myself.”
If the shadow is startled at being so suddenly addressed by a strange woman in a mask and a
feathered hat, he doesn’t show it, “Ah,” He exclaims performative, “And who might you
be?”
“Haru Okumura,” She tips her hat slightly, passing her drink to her other hand. She’s glad he
at least doesn’t seem to recognise her from the thieves’ short encounter with him on their first
proper infiltration here.
“Okumura?” Ooe’s shadow narrows his eyes at her suspiciously, “I am… surprised that you
were granted access here.”
It’s awfully convenient that he’s too proper to call her out immediately. “Yes, well,” Noir
tucks her hair behind her ear, “My accomplishments have caught some eyes, these days.”
“Have they?” Ooe still sounds dubious. “I suppose you are awfully young to be the head of a
business. Though you just inherited it.” He says with some disdain, before smoothing himself
over. “Well, nonetheless, it’s good to see you here, Okumura-chan. How are you enjoying the
festivities?”

Noir smiles, thin-lipped, “They’re quite impressive, Ooe-san,” They’re even blander than
Shido’s parties, “And of course, the opportunity to speak with the guest of honour is the
highlight.”
Ooe chuckles, “You flatter me. If you ever need any advice, do get in contact. Business and
politics are similar, in many ways.”
Noir gets that impression, yes. “I’ll keep that in mind, Ooe-san.” She swirls her flute of
champagne, affecting a thoughtful expression, “I did have some questions, actually, if you
have the time.”
The shadow’s expression tightens, but he still smiles, “Of course! Ask away.”
“Thank you,” Noir smiles again. “You and Shido-san have something of a working
relationship, correct?”
Ooe freezes. “Ah,” He stutters, “Indeed. He should be somewhere around here, actually.”
Noir thinks that while Shido certainly fits the definition of someone who belongs here, that
Ooe likely twists the narrative of those circumstances as much as possible. “You get special
access to his services, don’t you? It’s quite the accomplishment to be in his good graces like
that.”
The shadow coughs, “ Ah, you’ve,” he clears his throat, “You’ve heard about that, have
you?”
“Of course.”
“Yes- well.” Ooe’s jaw grinds, “Colour me surprised, Okumura-chan.”
“Surely you noticed my father’s -ah- business aspirations?” Noir reaches for a mask, and
lands on someone else’s. She’s sure he won’t mind her borrowing it. “His trigger-happiness
very nearly brought the whole thing down, so I must apologise for that.”
Ooe’s gaze turns apprising, “Yes, well. It would be improper to judge you for your father’s
actions.”
“Thank you.” Haru doesn’t smile. “Of course, I would never wish to destabilise Shido-san in
any way before we have yet to build a rapport. I don’t think I’ll be resorting to the same
methods as my father.”
The shadow’s brief look of consideration turns uncomfortable again. “That’s… good to
hear.”
“I’m glad.” Noir looks to the ground, “Though, that doesn’t mean I may need some…
external assistance when dealing with any issues I may face. …You wouldn’t happen to know
any alternatives, would you?”
Golden eyes flit about nervously. “Not by name.”

“But you know where to find them?”
“No.” The shadow laughs, strained, “When Shido-san and I became partners in the political
world-” Haru almost makes a face, “-I went to him for any… requests. This was before he
found his discreet methods, mind you. After that, I doubt he’d made much use of alternatives
at all.”
Where does a shadow’s knowledge begin and end, Noir wonders? Shadows are inherently
more self-aware than cognitions, as she’s seen, even partially aware of their half existence;
and yet they can get wrapped up in the play of their delusions with just a short push down a
path of conversation that cancels that out.
A shadow cannot draw conclusions about the real world, she decides.
Well, that isn’t particularly important, she supposes. The only problem is that if Ooe truly has
no knowledge of the Cleaner’s identity, talking it out with his shadow isn’t going to get her
any closer.
“That’s a shame.” Noir says, “Perhaps I will have to rely on Shido-san’s services after all.”
She sighs, and takes a sip of the flute still in her hands, “He did offer more than just discreet
solutions to begin with.”
“That’s quite true.” Ooe agrees, “Your father favoured Shido-san’s unique services, from
what I saw.”
“Do you know how many he commissioned?” Haru asks.
Ooe coughs, “What?”
“Do you know how many psychotic breakdowns my father commissioned.” She says again.
The shadow sniffs, “How should I know that, Okumura-chan? A fair few, I’d wager. It
certainly speaks to your father’s lack of business sense.”
Perhaps. Though Haru thinks it may be less to do with business sense and more to do with
unsubtlety.
“Of course, my apologies for asking.” She takes a sip of her glass, “But how about you?”
The shadow’s eyes sharpen further, “What about me?”
“How many have you ordered?”
The pulsing red ever-present at the corners of Noir’s vision bleeds a little brighter. She
ignores it. She already knew this was a dangerous topic to tread.
Gold flashes, “What are you looking for, Okumura-san?”
Good question.

She can’t call it curiosity. The term seems too innocent, for what she is asking. She could
tack ‘morbid’ on the front and call it a day, and yet that doesn’t seem quite it either. Too
detached, too uninvolved. Too ignorant of where she stands, as a thief, as an Okumura.
So perhaps the true answer is somewhere closer to“Have you ever been curious as to what a psychotic breakdown feels like, Ooe-san?”
Gold dims, replaced with dull confusion, too baffled to be outraged, “I certainly have not.”
Haru swirls her glass, “Ah, of course not.”
Ah, now there’s the outrage, “Are you threatening me-”
“No, what would that accomplish?” Haru lies, “It was truly just a curiosity.”
It’s not really a threat. She has neither the intention nor capability to enact such a thing
anyway. Though, if it isn’t a threat, then what was the point of the comment at all?
Perhaps the topic has her on edge. Perhaps she’s curious herself, her father permanently
scarred and her friend bringing them on himself with little regard and nought in the way of
consequences. Or maybe there are, and she just can’t see.
Curiosity still doesn’t feel right.
(Haru does not like this man. Yes, a threat is far closer to the truth.)
“I am astounded you have not deigned to learn acceptable topics for polite conversation.”
The shadow snaps.
“Please excuse me.” Noir hums, “I did not mean to offend.” No sense in kicking off a fight
when the treasure is neither accessible or corporeal.
That red pulses brighter.
(That feeling again, that you don’t belong, you need to leave, you need to get out, you don’t
belong here, you don’t-)
Perhaps she pushed too hard.
(What for?)
Noir bows, “I think I’ll be taking my leave for now, Ooe-san. Congratulations on your
awards.”
“Yes.” The shadow blurs at the edges, “I think that would be for the best.”

“Agreed.” Joker cracks his neck, “We’ll account for timing once we get there.”
Noir smiles a bit at everyone’s eagerness to leave. She’s feeling the sentiment rather strongly

Joker flashes one last look at the expanse of the palace, before smirking, and whipping out
his phone with a flourish, “Let’s head home, shall we?”

The high of both teams finishing their respective palace runs (barring the calling card and
final curtain call) dies very quickly and with little ceremony, when Sumire realises exactly
what day it is.
November eighteenth should be, by all rights, a day like any other. Maybe it should have had
a ticket to being remarkable by virtue of being a break from the Metaverse, but no, no, it can
still be associated by proxy.
Sumire doesn’t need to listen to Maruki’s farewell speech, because she remembers it very
well. Not that she would have put much effort into listening anyway, but now she just has the
misfortune of knowing what he’s saying even while she does her best to squeeze her eyes
shut and ignore him.
She didn’t get the chance to slip into the bathroom and wait it out this time around, so now
she’s stuck.
Her mind wanders, because she can’t keep it on a leash like she’d prefer.
Last time, Maruki had gotten up on his soapbox and told them all how proud he was, how
grateful he was to have taught here and met them all, of their growth and their progress,

And, most importantly, how they could always run.
Kasumi Yoshizawa, or her corpse, had taken to her own internal soapbox and thought that
this particular sentiment was perhaps not the most healthy thing to internalise. Sumire
Yoshizawa, a year and the end of the world removed, can appreciate the irony in this. She
can’t seem to muster the will to see much humour in it though.
She wonders if Ren, nestled somewhere else in the school hall, is feeling much the same.
Maybe he is able to find it funny. Sumire isn’t sure if he should.
Sumire wonders, as Maruki goes on, if the man has ever heard the words coming out of his
mouth. She supposes most of them are relatively innocuous, or even the notoriously ignorant
Shujin staff would have heard the alarm bells. Or maybe they wouldn’t have. They did let
Kamoshida run around unchecked, after all.
But Maruki is just a washed up researcher, not an Olympic medallist. So maybe they would.
Maruki finishes his speech, managing to smack his head on the microphone as he bows,
causing the entire student body to jump, and then chuckle, as the sound reverberates through
the hall.
“Thank you all.” Maruki finishes with a sheepish grin and an embarrassed flush, and walks
offstage.
And he’s gone.
At least Sumire won’t have to avoid him at school, anymore.
(Where did he even go, in these intermittent months? Skulk around his probably-bad
apartment, wallowing in unemployment? Get all his affairs in order before tripping headfirst
into godhood? Sumire knows he didn’t plan it, his palace told them all that much. The red
rain and spires of bone erupting from the ground took him by surprise as much as they did
her.
He did have a counselling practice outside of his work at Shujin, so maybe he just went back
to that. Though Sumire doesn’t recall if he even kept it open- she had her own sessions
transferred to the school nurse’s office for convenience.
What difference does it make, in the end? It’s set to be discarded come Christmas eve either
way. Barely a stepping stone towards the Doctor’s true ambitions.)
She’s going to have to see him again, eventually.
The new year heralds poor tidings, a month and a half in advance. Will she be plunged back
into her delusions? Will she be able to resist it at all, even now that she so vehemently
doesn’t want it? She was so desperate to be Sumire that something let her try again, claw
blindly at things she hadn’t even begun to understand to try and pave the way for a different
fate.
But maybe she was just a convenient target.

She hopes, and vows to never say to anyone, that Goro and Ren will wake her up first when
the time comes.

And the world would be all the better for it. If only Ren did this the first time around.

Morgana hisses a warning from the bag.

“Hm?” Maruki blinks, “Oh, well… it’s not one place, really. I have a lot of,” he pauses,

“Don’t tempt fate!” Morgana despairs, which is an excellent point.
Ren sighs, running a hand through his bird’s nest of hair. Maybe he really is just as bad as
Goro.

“Haven’t you made the point that you’re me?” Not that Sae can really believe it, “You should

“Stuck in the same house as all your biggest problems.” The shadow remarks. “And yet

Aside from her chat with Makoto today, of course. “Akechi keeps to himself.” Sae points out,

Sae goes to say the latter, but that would be a blatant lie. The former doesn’t fit, either.
“There’s been nothing to discuss.” She says simply.
The slots finish spinning. A cherry, gold, and a seven. The shadow clicks her tongue.

“I get it.” Sae snaps before the shadow can say something condescending, “I’m avoiding

“And why shouldn’t you?” The shadow cuts a glance to her, “They’re both fuckups that

The only thing worse than when this thing is disagreeing with her, Sae comes to a realisation,

“I’ve been working with Akechi.” Sae protests weakly, “On Oracle’s data.”
She doesn’t need the shadow to tell her that hardly counts. When they get to work, it’s easy to

Apparently old habits for Sae and Makoto involve“Not speaking to each other.” The shadow finishes the thought with a sly smile.

Talking to Akechi was work. Talking to him was a convenience, and Sae wasn’t looking to

“You rarely got any done at dinner. You even admitted it to him what dinner was about.”
Fine, Sae could always tell when Akechi hadn’t eaten, because he always looked thoroughly

“And what about Makoto?”
Must it always come back to Makoto?
“Of course it-”
“Because I can hardly stand to be in the same room as her sometimes!” Sae snaps, “All she

Her shadow stares.
“They’re so similar.” Sae hisses, “All I had to do with him is shove food at him and he’d be

Her shadow keeps staring.
“I think,” her shadow eventually says, “That we might be downsizing the casino soon.”
“Good for you.” Sae snarls.
Gold flashes with amusement, “Still not all there, are we? Well, I think you got what you
came here for.”
And then some.
Her shadow clicks, and the room alights again. The clumps of cognitions pay them no mind,
as the sounds of the casino bustle along unbothered.
“I’m going home.” Sae announces to no one.
Her shadow waves a hand in response anyway, “By all means. I have better things to be
doing than entertaining you. Or this place’s collapse.”
Could that happen, if Sae stays here too long? She doesn’t want to know.
She turns on her heel, and starts the long march back.

Hearing Sae and Makoto shouting isn’t Akechi’s business. Hearing doors slam also isn’t his

But they aren’t, so it’s not.
(He did catch his name a couple of times, but what does he care what the Niijimas’ opinions

Akechi doesn’t want to talk to her, so go figure. Why did he come out here, again?

Well, that tracks.

Patently untrue. Robin sniffs.
SPEAK FOR YOURSELF.

Clearly.

The problem with a deadline being in the next month over, Sojiro has mused at many points
in his life, is that it always feels further away than it actually is.
Sojiro hasn’t had patience for politics in years, and whatever remaining thread he has is worn
especially thin by the constant chatter about the upcoming election that his myriad regulars
have taken to gossiping about in his shop. It threatens to snap entirely when Shido is brought
up; as he is often, given he’s one of the main contenders.
But, patient or not, the election is less than a month away. As is whatever deadline the kids
mentioned. Ren and Futaba asked for his help, and he’s not one to backtrack on a promise.
No guarantees whether the promise is accomplished successfully, but he tries.
It’s the early morning of the twentieth when Ren stumbles down the stairs, looking for all the
world like he hasn’t slept in three years. “Hey, kid.”
Ren blinks, looking up, “Yeah?”
“I’m not gonna open the store today.” He jerks a hand to gesture around, “You still need that
name, yeah?”
The kid looks slightly more awake now, and the cat trots down the stairs, “You’re going to
start digging, chief?”
Christ, talking to a cat is weird. “I am.” He nods as the cat hops up on one of the bar stools.
He’d normally protest, but now that Morgana has proven alarmingly sapient, he feels weird
kicking him off surfaces.
“Do you need anything?” Ren asks.
“A bit.” Sojiro nods, giving the bench a quick wipe down. Just because he’s not opening
today doesn’t mean the place can be anything less than spotless. “You said you were working
with some other folks, didn’t you?”
Ren nods quickly, “Iwai and Ohya. You want to talk to them?”

“Just to compare notes.” Sojiro waves a hand.
“And gossip about Ren?” The cat chimes in.
Sojiro snorts. “That too.”

find them here. Iwai’s pretty consistent, but you might have less luck with Ohya.”
Sojiro picks up the paper and squints down at it, “…One of these is in the red light district-”

“What are we doing?” Morgana asks, tail flicking.
“Mementos!” Ren calls as he dashes back up the stairs to escape scrutiny.
“Finally!”

It’s exceedingly rare that Ann’s living room is empty in the middle of the day. In the middle
of a Sunday, no less, where Ann herself has nothing better to do than laze about her own
apartment.
Akechi makes sure to take advantage of this. If boredom was slowly killing him before the
apartment gained two extra occupants, then it’s taken to beating him over the head since.
Makoto’s olive branch and he and Sae’s joint project notwithstanding, Akechi isn’t rushing to
spend time with any of these people.
Which, naturally, is why he genuinely considers dipping back into his murderous hobbies
when Sakamoto bursts into the living room out of thin air with a boisterous “Yo!”
He freezes when he sees Akechi on the couch.
Akechi makes sure to give him his best withering glare.
“Dude.” Sakamoto says in response, “Chill.”
“Why are you here.”
“Didn’t you ask that last time?” Sakamoto scratches at his neck. Akechi can’t remember.
Probably.
“The question still stands.” He says.
“Oh.” Sakamoto shoves his hands in his pockets, scuffing his shoe against the floor, “M’here

The thing is, the twentieth simply doesn’t hold significance. Ren wonders if it would have in

As it turns out, being stuck in the back seat also means being stuck in reserve.
It also means being squished against the side of the van while Noir and Queen stare off into
the middle distance, not making conversation. Sumire wishes she hadn’t been so quick to
give up her spot in the middle row.
At the very least, from what she can see, Crow seems to be having fun. Every now and again
Joker will waste their time by crashing into a wayward shadow, and Crow will leap from the
van cackling for violence and blood, ignoring most of Joker’s orders all the while.
Most of is a step up from none, so Sumire supposes that if Joker has any sense he’ll take what
he can get.
“It’s almost relaxing,” Noir eventually speaks up, her voice nearly drowned by whatever
argument Oracle and Panther have roped Skull into, Fox interjecting with increasing
frequency, “Being here and not having to do anything.”

“…I think you and I have different definitions of relaxing.” Queen says weakly.
Sumire eyes the walls of Mementos through the van window, “It isn’t so bad.”
Queen mutters something else that is likely also contesting that claim.
Noir laughs under her breath. “I think Mementos just doesn’t faze me by this point.”
“…To a certain point.” Queen acquiesces, “But I think the blood, flesh, and veins will always
rub me the wrong way.”
That’s fair. Sumire had been filtering them out, honestly.
“José is down here somewhere.” She points out, “But I guess that’s a blip in the-” blood,
flesh, and veins. And- are those spinal vertebrae? “-everything.”
Queen hums, eyes fixed on the floor of the van. The conversation peters out.
…And, back to relative silence.
Noir is first to break again. “It’s good we’re getting all this done at once.”
“I hadn’t really been thinking about it,” Sumire admits, “But I agree. We were really letting it
pile up.”
“…You know, I had thought about using my position as student council president to collect
requests from the student body. Discretely, of course.” Queen says, pushing her mask up,
“But that isn’t really possible any more.”
Sumire grimaces, “I- right. It was a nice thought, though.”
“Mm.”
“…I can keep an ear out, if you’d like?” Noir offers.
Queen quickly shakes her head, “We’re all busy enough as is. Who knows? This might be our
last major Mementos trip before- you know.”
Now that’s something uncomfortable to think about. “We’ll probably go again in January, at
least.” Sumire says, remembering the particularly dire requests that had slipped through the
cracks of Maruki’s reality.
Noir blinks, tilting her head, “I didn’t realise that would be necessary. But it’s nice that this
place won’t be completely gone. Not until we deal with Doctor Maruki, at least…”
Queen grumbles something, some variation of different definitions of nice.
Noir catches it, and chuckles, “We’ll get there when we get there.”
Sumire has to privately admit that mindset has had diminishing returns of late.

Time, as it happens, despite it’s insistence on bending for her, moves at a fixed rate. The days
will slip by far too quickly and far too slowly to get anything done within a reasonable time
frame, and all Sumire has been able to do is play support.
She doesn’t have connections. She’s a gymnastics prodigy of dubious talent. She can’t track
down the yakuza, or dodge politicians, or kill gods. The minute the situation with Yaldabaoth
is sorted and the Velvet Room is all back to -admittedly, questionable- normality, Sumire is
going to beg Crow to beg someone for answers, because the question of why the hell this
happened to her is beginning to surface in her mind once again.
Don’t dwell, don’t dwell,
But there’s nothing to do but dwell when that’s all she has.
Her problem, the problem she was prepared for, the problem she was the most afraid of, was
changing the heart of one Doctor Takuto Maruki.
She can help with that. She can. Crow and Joker can only be in so many places at once and

But Doctor Maruki isn’t going to be an issue until Christmas. Holiday cheer all around. Far

So: later it is.
Yaldabaoth is a can of worms that can’t be cracked until Shido is ruined, and they can’t risk

But, she shouldn’t diminish their progress. They’ve gone the full mile with Ooe and Sato’s

They’re halfway done with goal one of three, except each goal has subsections and

“Do you think we’ll find anything about the Cleaner in Mementos?” Sumire asks broadly,

It certainly does. And Shido’s palace, to Sumire’s knowledge, is big. Not the kind of place

In the row ahead, Panther loudly boasts a counterargument to Skull’s borderline monologue

“Shido’s palace.”

“Right.” Sumire prompts.
“I’m more concerned about what else might be waiting there.” Noir says, “Crow died there,
and he’s historically hard to kill.”
Queen opens her mouth, closes it, “…Did either of them mention exactly what it was
that…?”
“It was Goro-kun’s cognition inside the ship.” Noir responds, a bit distant. She quickly adds,
“He mentioned it when I asked.”
Cognitions are always a bit of a toss-up with regard to their place in a palace. Sumire prefers
the fodder, the faceless masses; no matter how unnerving they are, they’re at least easy to
kill. Cognitions that wear distinct faces, girls in leotards that whisper names that aren’t hers,
flowers that sing and wail until they’re made to shut up, automatons in pink and blue and
neon that sacrifice themself at a word.
And, mirrors of teenaged hitmen that can get the better of their counterpart. Sumire isn’t
looking forward to it.
“Well, we’re ready for it now.” Queen points out, though she also sounds unnerved. “We’re
not going to be blindsided by anything.”
“Unless the palace has changed.” Sumire points out, and immediately regrets it. The laws of
the universe dictate that acknowledging their terrible luck means that something even worse
will happen.
That said, they have terrible luck . The even worse thing was probably going to happen
anyway.
“…The foundation will likely be the same.” Queen corrects herself.
“Most likely.” Noir agrees, “Though, perhaps we should stop discussing it.”
Sumire refrains from mentioning that she was the one to bring it up in the first place. Noir’s
anxiety is understandable, if not slightly uncharacteristic. Shido, Sumire would assume, holds
less presence in Noir’s life than her father or Sugimura. Though, what does she know? She’s
certainly anxious herself.

Anxious, and impatient. She used to have far better self control. Not where it counted, of
course.
She’d like a distraction.
“Joker.” Sumire shouts over everyone’s voices, and the van abruptly goes silent. “Can we
swap the front lines?”
A pause. “Sure.” He says, “Fox, Panther, Cr-” Crow makes a low sound that very much
resembles a growl, “ Just Fox and Panther, swap with… Queen and Violet. That all good?”

Sumire breathes a sigh of relief. Just something to do is enough.

Sojiro figured he’d have to wander around for a while, but it turns out the Crossroads bar
opens its doors relatively early in the day.
He had, for all of five seconds, assumed he’d get to do his waiting inside the bar. No such
waiting turned out to be necessary, with a woman matching Ichiko Ohya’s description already
trying to drown her sorrows sitting perched on a stool.
The woman who he assumes owns the bar eyes him suspiciously, “Welcome.” She says, a bit
gruff, “I haven’t seen you before, honey. Looking to try a new bar?”
“Not quite.” Sojiro says carefully, “Though I wouldn’t be opposed to sampling your drinks.”
Ohya lifts her head up slightly at that, eyes narrowed in matching suspicion to the bartender.
“Well, that’s lovely to hear.” The bartender says, “Call me Lala-chan. What are you here for,
if not quite drinks?”
“The pretzels are good.” Ohya interjects.
“They are.” Lala nods, passably nonchalant.
Sojiro chuckles, “I might order some of them, then. But I’m actually here to chat her.” He
nods towards Ohya, “Ohya-san, yeah?”
There’s a flash of alarm in her eyes, “That’s me.” She says, slow, “Whadd’ya want?”
“You know a Ren Amamiya?”
Lala stiffens, and Ohya can’t quite mask her anger. “Never heard of ‘im.”
Sojiro probably should have seen this coming. Striking up conversation with Iwai wasn’t
exactly smooth sailing, but at least things never got actively hostile. He supposes it should be
comforting, that Ren inspires such loyalty. Fixing all their problems with magic probably
does the trick.
“Relax.” He scoffs, “Ren’s the one who told me where to find you. I’m his guardian.”

Lala untenses, peering at him curiously. Ohya doesn’t look entirely convinced.
“Is there trouble?” Lala asks, picking up a glass to wipe it down.
“No, no,” Sojiro quickly waves off her concerns. There really is no smooth way to introduce
this topic without potentially hitting fifty rocks along the way. He nods towards Ohya, “We
have a common goal, is all, related to Ren and his activities.”
“Oh.” Ohya’s eyes widen, and some of that drunken flair swoops back onto her face as she
grins, “Oh! Well why didn’t’cha say so?”
The aforementioned rocks, mostly. “Hard to say.” Sojiro tells her bluntly.
Ohya waves a hand, “Oh, fair enough. Lala-chan! Can we borrow the seats in the back?”
Lala snorts. “Do you see anyone else here? Take ‘em.” She gives Sojiro one final look, “You
sure you’ll both be alright?”
“We’re just swell.” Ohya drawls, seemingly genuine. “C’mon, old man. What’s your name
again?”
“Sojiro Sakura.” He offers, finally taking off his hat, “Forgive my manners.”
“I’m not really a manners gal, so you’re forgiven.” Ohya unpeels herself from the bar, “Just
back here.”
Sojiro makes to follow her, before Lala clears her throat, “Anything I can get for you while
you talk business, honey?”
Sojiro considers it, “…Some of those pretzels, if they’re as good as you say.”
“Oh, they’re fine. Store-bought, but you’ll end up eating fifty if you go for five.”
“I’ll take ‘em.” Sojiro laughs under his breath, “And your favourite non-alcoholic. This is a
conversation better had sober, pretty sure.”
Lala snorts, “Tell that to Ichiko-chan. Anyway, coming right up. You go sit down.”
“Thank you.” He says with a short bow.
“Your kid’s a sweetheart, so you get fancier service.” She winks, and laughs, “Don’t let
Ichiko-chan rile you up.”
“I won’t, I won’t,” He chuckles in return, and goes off to sit across from Ohya.
Her head whips up, “You ordered those pretzels to share, yeah?”
He didn’t, but he’s not looking to hold them hostage either. “Sure.”
“Score.” Ohya looks mighty pleased, “So!” She leans back, “A common goal, huh?”

“I hear you’re on the hunt for someone especially slippery.” Sojiro remembers business. He
remembers how to talk it. He’s a bit rusty, but business feels a more appropriate mask for
Ohya than it did Iwai, so out of storage it comes. “I’ve got connections of my own, but I
wanted to check with you and Ren’s other contact to make sure I’m not treading old ground.”
“Other contact? What, you mean the old guy at the gun store?” Ohya scoffs, “Sorry, model
gun store?”
Maybe business isn’t her forte. “Yeah.” Sojiro grunts, “That guy.”
“S’ been a few days since we’ve talked.” Ohya drums her fingers against the table, “You
already spoken to him?”
“I have.”
“Anythin’ interesting come up?”
“Aside from narrowing the field of search, not much.” Sojiro admits, “We’re all at a loss.”
“Figures.” Ohya mutters, “Hunting Kaneshiro and Kayo was way easier than this, and some
of that was a nightmare.” She pauses, “Wait- you the ex-fed Amamiya mentioned?”
Ren has to find a better way to introduce people he knows. “One and the same.” Sojiro
confirms tiredly.
Ohya cackles with something to the left of awe, “Would ya look at that? It’s not too much to
hope that all your shady government buddies have lists of all the yakuza assassins they know

And wouldn’t that make his life easier? “I’m afraid it is.” Sojiro tells her, “The best lead I’ve
got is to go digging for politicians who might use the same service that are less careful than
Shido.”
“Sounds like you already think that’s a dead end.”
So much for optimism. Sojiro grimaces, “Well… not exactly. I’m not confident, but I’m not
hopeless.”
“That’s something.” Ohya sighs, “What’s Mr. Model Guns lookin’ for?”
“Same thing I am. But he’s attacking it from the provider side of things.” Sojiro explains,
“Only so many families dabble in politics, and even fewer dabble successfully.”
“Don’t I know it.” Ohya mutters absent-mindedly, “Kaneshiro wasn’t a family, but his funds
were being funnelled somewhere, right into someone’s pockets. …It’s an interesting line of
attack, I’ll give you. Might have to dig into it myself, if I can.” She sighs, “Problem is, the
people who tend to have this information also tend to have their living rights revoked pretty
quick.”
Yeah. That is a problem. “Hence my caution.” Sojiro says wearily.

“Caution away.” Ohya says dismissively, “You’re no help if you’re dead.”
“No one is, traditionally.” Sojiro deadpans, “That aside, I take all that to mean your progress
has been slow?”
Ohya scowls, “Yeah. Snail pace. My boss is still breathing down my neck, and I’ve got
deadlines to meet. Everything has to be as discreet as I can muster.”
“You’re not throwing yourself off cliffs, are you?”
“Aw, are you worried about little ‘ol me?” Ohya says with enough sarcasm that she almost
loops back around to sounding genuine, “I see where Amamiya picked up his charms.”
The kid damn well better have charm, else Sojiro has failed as a pseudo-parent. “Call it
professional concern.”
Ohya drops the theatrics and rolls her eyes, “I’m not chasing thugs down back alleys if that’s
what you’re wondering. All the risks I’m taking are the same as the ones I took in my
personal projects. Don’t get your knickers in a twist.”
“All going well, here?” Lala chimes in with two drinks in hand and a bowl balanced in the
crook of her elbow.
“Yeah, yeah, don’t worry Lala-chan.” Ohya waves her off. She pouts as she picks up her
glass, “Lala,” she whines, “This is just water!”
“You’ve had enough for today.” Lala says with no remorse.
“It’s four PM!”
“And you’ve had enough.” Lala flicks her shoulder, “Sorry for the interruption.”
“No worries.” Sojiro says, trying not to smirk into his glass at the display. Lala laughs, and
shuffles back off.
Sojiro takes a sip of his drink. It’s pretty damn good. He hopes it isn’t going to break his
wallet.
Ohya, still scowling, shoves a handful of pretzels in her mouth, “Anyway. What were we
sayin’?”
“You jumping off cliffs.” Sojiro recalls. “But moving on, you got anything else to report?”
Ohya glares at the table, “Not really. I’ve been making some more progress on tracking down
Kayo, but that’s about it.” She elaborates after Sojiro’s vaguely confused look, “She was my
partner. In journalism, mostly. She vanished at one point chasing a lead. Kid told me she had
a mental shutdown.”
Is that knowledge granted to Ren by Akechi or the time travel, Sojiro wonders?

He tosses a pretzel in his mouth. It’s passable. “My best friend had a mental shutdown.”
“That sucks.” Ohya says, so fast it must be instinct, “That really sucks.” She taps her nail
against her glass, “That why you’re in this?”
Sojiro snorts. “Nah. I’ve got kids to take care of.”
Revenge sounds less appealing when you’re old. It also sounds less appealing when the face
of half the targets you ought to be after is a scrawny kid with a black eye and a defensive
scowl.
Taking Shido down a peg or twenty is a pretty nice bonus, though.
“Well, good for you.” Ohya says, bitter. “I’d say I’m in it for Amamiya, but I don’t really
owe him anything.” She huffs, “Not yet, anyway. He kinda implied my boss would be taken
care of at some point.”
“Does he have to make it sound like he’s braining people in back alleys?” Sojiro grouses.
Ohya snickers, “Oh, no, he only asked for my boss’s full name. Very sly, very smooth.” She
frowns, “I guess I owe him for what he told me about Kayo. I still haven’t found her, but. It’s
good to know what happened. And that she’s out there.”
“She’s still alive?” Sojiro blurts, incredulous.
Ohya throws up her hands, “That’s what I said! Mental shutdown kinda implies it, yeah? But
apparently they’re not one-hundred-percent fatal.”
Isn’t that something?
All told, he only found out Wakaba had a mental shutdown relatively recently. Suspicions
were just suspicions, and he didn’t have the time nor energy to fight what the cops told him.
Suicide, right in front of Futaba. He knew something wasn’t right, but, he was tired.
And now, assassination, shady dealings, Wakaba’s nervous laughter and “I think someone has
it out for me” . The conclusion feels obvious, when it’s all laid out like this, but Sojiro was
never a detective. He doesn’t have the stomach for it.
That aside, it still wasn’t the mental shutdown itself that killed her, was it? Her mind got
axed, and she fell onto the road. Blunt force trauma, spine snapped, skull crushed- whatever,
Sojiro didn’t read the damn autopsy.
(So if it didn’t happen there, then, could Wakaba have lived?
A stupid, fleeting thought. By the sounds of it all, there isn’t much living to be done even if
the body persists after the mind has been killed.)
“I’d ask Amamiya more about it,” Ohya’s voice snaps him back to attention, “But he’s real
cagey about how it all works. Stealing hearts, I mean.”

Sojiro scoffs lightly under his breath, “Trust me,” he says, “it’s more trouble than it’s worth.”
Ohya’s eyes alight, “So you know?”
“Not at all.” Sojiro half-lies, “He tried to explain it to me, and I got lost about a minute in.”
Ohya slumps back, “I hate being out of the loop.”
“Join the club.” Sojiro raises his glass.
“No, seriously.” She snaps, eyeing his drink with annoyance, “I don’t owe Amamiya
anything, but I still want to help with this. Preferably snag the guy’s name myself. I’m doing
this for me, kind of for him, definitely for Kayo, but all I’ve done is turn up a whole lotta
nothing.”
Sojiro snatches another pretzel. “Join the club.” He repeats, “None of us have made
progress.”
Ohya presses her lips together, too irritated to be classified as a pout. “I,” she begins, “Am
the best damn journalist the office has. And yet here I am, and I can’t do shit.”
Maybe Lala had the right idea, cutting her off the alcohol. Sojiro doubts she’d be spilling this
to a relative stranger if she were entirely sober, though she puts up a good show of complete
lucidity.
Or maybe there’s some solidarity, between those who are trapped between the walls of
blissful ignorance and not being able to do anything. God knows it seems to have gotten
Niijima to take the stick out of her ass.
“When all is said and done,” Sojiro says, “You’ll get to write some damn good articles
dragging Shido through the mud.”
“I can’t wait.” Ohya drawls, “I’d like to drag his stupid assassin through the mud, too, but we
can’t all get what we want.”
“No.” Sojiro grimaces, “We can’t.”

Ren will stand by the fact that Mementos is an excellent distraction. If Goro weren’t so
insistent on being endlessly contrarian, he’d probably agree. He would have agreed,
begrudgingly, during January, but that sounds like a topic that is equivalent to waving a neon
sign saying Punch Me, so Ren keeps it to himself.
The rest of the thieves definitely agree, at least. All in all, Mementos and their veritable
mountain of requests they’ve been ignoring is all smooth sailing. Mishima will probably cry
tears of joy when Ren finally texts the poor guy back.
When they reach the top floor once again, Morgana wastes no time in bursting back into his
cat-ish form.

“Finally!” He says, like he’s endured a hundred years of hardship, “Freedom!”

Sumire looks very thoughtful, “…Do your organs turn into machinery?” She wonders aloud,

Goro smirks, “Well, now I’m curious.”

Ren finally takes pity, though the twins also look vaguely curious, staring from either side of

“Some of those guys really grossed me out.” Ann shudders, “And why didn’t you mention

When Ren initially started the Phantom Thieves alongside Ann, Ryuji, and Morgana, he was
under no illusions that their jobs would be risk-free.
His first experience with the Metaverse was nearly getting impaled in his shitty gym
teacher’s cognitive sex dungeon. Anything that might have screamed ‘your safety is
guaranteed in the coming year’ was unceremoniously tossed out the window, with a side of
blood and masks and fire.
And that was fine. Thrilling, even.
It very suddenly wasn’t, when there was a corpse on the other side of steel shutters, and all
Joker could do about it was pound his fists into the metal and try to carve a path.
He couldn’t. How could he have?
Very suddenly, he couldn’t be so blasé. Very suddenly, the thought of putting anyone on the
front lines made ice-cold terror clench around his chest. Very suddenly, Ren was infinitely
glad that there were no important cognitions to be found in Maruki’s laboratory.
Shadows aplenty, to be sure; but Ren doesn’t care for reminders of his failings, even when
the universe is forever insistent on dredging them up again, and again, usually in the form of
some snide remark from one Goro Akechi.
He can’t dwell on it. He hasn’t dwelt on it. It would be wildly impractical, and just a bit
absurd. All his thieves range from highly competent fighters to downright terrifying, and
trying to keep them from throwing themselves into the fray with blood and blades would be a
fool’s errand at best.
But, that doesn’t exactly apply in the real world.
If any of them had access to their personas in reality, they could raze the city if they so chose.
Alas, they cannot. They certainly can’t fight off one, or a gathering of people intent on killing
them. If they toe the line that Shido has set, they’re dead.
Ren will not stand for anyone dying on his watch.
(But, if they do, there’s always-)

Ren will not stand for anyone dying on his watch.
But inaction will be their death sentence, too. A certain one, at that. Risk is all there is.

Well, that’s the question, isn’t it? Ren keeps his expression flat, “Cast a wide net. Boss, Iwai,

It is. It barely sounds better than letting Iwai, Ohya, and Sojiro do their work at their pace.
Another little time waster to make them feel accomplished.
( God, Ren misses feeling on top of the world. He misses tripping down hills and mountains

The thing is, there isn’t much other than trash to fish up.
Sumire tries, she really does. She looks, and looks, and looks, and she is frankly sick of
staring at Shido’s face and listening to Shido’s voice. A myriad bodyguards and potential
subordinates appear in his speeches that have made it to the internet, and she doesn’t know
where to begin.
None of their names appear anywhere. She checks Ooe’s speeches -the one’s that don’t
happen at the TV studio- and can’t seem to recognise any familiar faces. She, and she’s sure
the other thieves as well, are essentially throwing darts into the void and hoping to find a
dartboard somewhere further down the pit, let alone the bullseye.
Only one night of digging through all of this is enough to convince Sumire that this is a lost
cause. Perhaps it’s too early to throw in the towel, but she’s been agonising long enough to
know what a dead end looks like.
She can only hope that the thread of the Cleaner at large isn’t one of them.
(He isn’t necessary, they all know that. And yet letting him run around unchecked is a risk
they can ill afford, when their own lives are the ones ultimately at stake. She would happily not quite, but close enough- run herself into the ground trying to hunt this man if it means
Goro and Ren and Haru and everyone else will be safe.

The trouble is, running herself into the ground isn’t accomplishing anything.)
Sumire Yoshizawa is, perhaps, the worst equipped person to track down a yakuza assassin.
Second only to the rest of the Shujin student body, several of whom she is uncomfortably
listening to chatter away during their lunch break.
“I’m telling you,” One of the girls -Yamada, she thinks- says, “Something’s happened to
Niijima-senpai.”
Technically, something has. Though nothing so dramatic as to what Yamada is probably
thinking. “I’m sure she’s fine.” Sumire interjects quietly.
Another girl, Kimura, scoffs, “Sure she is, Yoshizawa-chan. She’s totally fine, and that’s why
she’s vanished without a trace. She’s left the student council scrambling, you know.”
Yamada flicks her on the arm, “You don’t get to talk! You’re a first year, you barely do
anything on the student council.”
“Well, I do now!” Kimura complains, “They keep trying to swamp me with stuff. Which isn’t
cool! I have finals to study for!”
Right, exams. Sumire worries for her grades, since they’ll be taking place in the days that
they’ll also be clearing out the palaces and Mementos-bound shadows of Shido’s associates.
“We all do.” Yamada reminds her. “Especially Niijima-senpai, if she keeps missing school.”
“I’m sure she’s fine.” Sumire repeats, “And it’s not really our business, anyway.”
Kimura groans, “I guess.”
These girls almost certainly do not have information about the yakuza. The very notion is

“I wish they would- I dunno, make the exams easier this year.” Yamada sighs, “We’re

“Wouldn’t they have to do that every few years, then?” Sumire points out, mildly confused,

Oh. It’s easy to forget their impact when Sumire is one of them. She’s so wrapped up in their
own problems that she hasn’t stopped to consider public opinion for a while.
“Ugh.” Kimura clicks her tongue, “Them.”
“You love them!” Yamada accuses.

“That was before they killed the Detective Prince!” Kimura waves her arms emphatically,
“They were cool when they were dealing with that creep Kamoshida, but murder is a line I
don’t wanna cross.”
It’s a line the Phantom Thieves (Bar one. Or two. Three, if Sumire sucks it up and counts her
inaction with regard to Kobayakawa) aren’t particularly fond of crossing, either.
“How quickly your loyalties change.” Yamada sighs.
Kimura waves her arms even more violently, “And what about that Okumura guy!”
“He was a CEO.” Yamada points out with a sniff.
“So you’re on their side, then.”
“I didn’t say that.” Yamada quickly corrects.
Sumire stifles her sigh. So much for their fans. Though their affections were fickle to start;
she probably should have expected this, and not just from the precedent set by last timeline.
“I know he was probably shitty.” Kimura inspects her nails with an air of I’m about to make
some political commentary, “But that was messed up. And on live TV, too. And, again!
Akechi-kun!”
“I hope he’s alright.” Sumire offers quietly, “His death isn’t confirmed.”
“Oh, right.” Yamada blinks, her eyes widening, “Yoshizawa-chan, I heard a rumour that you
were friends with him?”
Sumire tries to remember when that started circling around. The school clean-up, maybe?
She vaguely recalls the fact being pried from her. “I- um. Yes.”
“Lucky.” Kimura mutters.
“Not so lucky if he’s hurt.” Yamada smacks her arm.
Kimura sighs, “True, I guess. It’s kinda strange that we haven’t heard anything about what’s
been going on, though.”
“Are you kidding?” Yamada gapes, “There was that whole thing just the other day! They
caught the leader and everything!”
“And then he escaped!” Kimura protests, “Guess their whole shtick is being Phantom
Thieves. I wonder if he’s a ghost?”
Sumire almost snorts. Considering Goro’s laundry list of situations, ‘Ghost’ is hardly the
most inaccurate moniker he could be granted. She isn’t sure if he’d appreciate it. Depends on
his mood, she supposes.

“Get real.” Yamada scoffs. “But, I guess. I wonder if we’re not hearing anything much
because there’s nothing to tell or if it’s because it’s all classified?”
“Ooo, that could be it.” Kimura nods eagerly, “I mean, Akechi-kun was in charge of the
Phantom Thieves case and the mental shutdowns and psychotic breakdowns. Maybe they
don’t want anyone else to be targeted because of that.”
That could be an angle. Shido might not be eager to paint any targets on his subordinates.
That, and the thieves have yet to make any public moves of late. Still, it’s something to
consider.
She isn’t so hopeful as to think that Shido is simply at a loss for how to spin this to the
public. He’s had plenty of time to think. She supposes all that’s left is to wait for the axe fall.
“I feel like something big is going to happen, soon.” Sumire voices with some dread.
Kimura hums with forceful agreement, “Right? There’s this foreboding…”
“Foreboding, which doesn’t get us out of exams.” Yamada reminds her.
Kimura buries her palms into her eyes and groans, “Don’t remind me, please.”
Sumire chuckles, indulging them.
They don’t know anything about the Yakuza, she reminds herself. Sumire has, historically,
been uniquely terrible at fishing for information, and she isn’t about to ask about assassins
outright.
But surely she can get something out of this. A new insight she hadn’t considered, perhaps.
“I wonder if they’re making any progress on the mental shutdowns and psychotic breakdown
cases lately.” Sumire muses aloud.
Yamada blinks, “Aren’t the Phantom Thieves behind that, though? The cases must’ve been
merged by now.”
“Not necessarily.” Sumire pokes at her bento, “There’s no definitive proof that the thieves are
actually behind them. That we know of, at least.”
“It’s bad to make assumptions.” Kimura agrees slowly.
Sumire hums, “Right. I’m just curious, I guess.”
Yamada sighs, “I can’t tell if I’ll laugh or stop listening to the news if the thieves turn out to
be innocent.”
“It’d be nice if they are.” Kimura frowns, “But I doubt it.”
“Y’know, the mental shutdowns kinda remind me of something though.” Yamada leans
forward conspiratorially.

Sumire jerks forward, “Yeah?”
“Just- they’re targeted, right? And they’re being done by someone.” Yamada explains, “Back
when my sister was in high school -she’s way older than me- she said there was this rumour
about a revenge website-”
“What?” Kimura interrupts, “No way.”
Yamada rolls her eyes, “Yeah, I know it sounds stupid, but it’s just what my sister told me,
okay? It was just a rumour, anyway.”
Sumire’s seen stranger. A website where you can get revenge, whatever that is attempting to
imply (Sumire vaguely acknowledges the neon signs blaring in her head that it was probably
murder), is hardly on the scale of ridiculous that she’s used to. Though, it is still rather
bizarre.
It also sounds like the kind of thing that would need assassins to run it. Maybe not their
assassin, but, possibly…?
Sumire sighs through her nose. On second thought, digging for something like that sounds
like she’d be signing up for a one way ticket to get murdered herself. And a computer virus,
to boot.
“When did your sister go to high school again?” Kimura asks suspiciously.
Yamada frowns, “Like, 2009? 2010? I can’t remember.”
“So, forever ago.” Kimura smooshes her cheek into her hand, “That website’s probably long
gone.”
“Not if you look on the dark web.” Yamada says breezily. “And- hey! I thought you didn’t
believe me!”
“I don’t!”
“You’ve been on the dark web?” Sumire blurts, incredulous.
Yamada flushes, “No! I’m just saying, if a website like that still exists, it’d be on the dark
web.”
“That’s fair.” Kimura concedes, “You’ve gotta work on your phrasing, though.”
Yamada groans, “You’re the ones who took it the wrong way.”
“Sorry.” Sumire offers.
“It’s fine.” She dismisses, “Anyway, I’m sure the dark web was, like, the first place the cops
checked. I don’t think it’s actually related to the mental shutdowns. But they do kinda seem
like assassinations, right?”

“They do, a bit.” Kimura looks contemplative, “And, I mean, what else are you gonna call
what happened to Akechi-kun? And everyone else. Does that mean the psychotic breakdowns
are targeted, too?”
“Probably.” Sumire taps her fingers against her desk.
“Okumura definitely was.” Yamada points out, “And if they aren’t, then what? Why else
would someone do all this, if not for a purpose?”
“Random chaos?” Kimura suggests.
“Only half the time, though?”
If the general public were this sceptical and insightful, even if only once in a while, then
perhaps the Phantom Thieves would not be in this problem to begin with. Perhaps, the public
wouldn’t be tripping over themselves to vote for a tyrant.
She isn’t sure if she can blame them for Maruki. She wanted it, too. And they hardly wished
for Maruki exactly.
(They only have themselves to blame for that. Them, and the man himself. Unintentionally
manipulative and omniscient as he is. He brings promises and sweet lies to his lips like it’s
second nature. He’s only so dangerous because he had the power to melt them into truths.
…
How quickly and efficiently could Maruki dig for information to use as ammunition,
anyway?)
“I’m sure we’ll hear more soon.” Sumire says, her thoughts miles away.
She isn’t- will not, consider it.
(Ah, but they are desperate.)

Chapter 92
Chapter Summary

Digging graves, twice over.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

There is something about having business at the Takamaki residence that always feels a bit
off-kilter to Haru.
She and Ann, she will admit, are not particularly close. Nor is she to the Niijimas. She and
Goro certainly are, which is her primary reason for making the unfortunate trip via
Mementos, but she still feels the need to smile and make nice with the others despite their
presence being all together irrelevant to her needs. Ignoring them is far ruder than they
deserve, and far more awkward than she can handle.
(And it’s not like she has any reason to ignore them. Haru thinks Ann and Makoto are quite
lovely, the former near constantly, the latter when she wants to be. She’s just tired, and will
continue to be tired. She ought to bridge the gap, but she’s never known how.
She decides, on the spot, that she will be dragging Goro and Sumire on a long and relaxing
vacation once all of this is over.)
All this to say, that she intends to materialise in the living room rather than directly into what
has become Goro’s bedroom. Maybe she’ll stay for tea. She saw all the thieves just yesterday,
but perhaps someone has made progress already in their collective search. She doubts it, but
building bridges and all that.
Sae Niijima is the only one present in the living room when she arrives, stiffly flipping
through a book, spine rigid and muscles tense. Haru wonders if she shouldn’t have just
skipped the pleasantries anyway.
Niijima’s head snaps up at the sound of shuffling feet, “Haru-san.”
“Niijima-san.” Haru bows her head slightly, “Hello. How are you?”
She snaps her book shut. “I’m well.”
Haru hums.
“And you?” is added as an afterthought.

“I’m quite alright.” Haru lies. She’s awful, actually. She’d like to speak to Goro as soon as
possible about their myriad foolish decisions, but, alas, she’s trapped herself here. She should
have saved this for her way out.
“That’s good.” Niijima says.
“Mm.”
A cough.
“Well.” Haru starts, “I’m here for- well, I should-”
“Are you and Makoto close?” Niijima blurts.
Haru wonders what on earth she’s just stumbled into. “…We’re friends.” She decides,
tentatively. She can never tell if Makoto likes her all that much. And Haru herself; well, she
isn’t bitter about being attacked in Mementos all those months ago, but she certainly
remembers that it happened.
“I see.” Niijima says stiltedly. She swallows, “So- close enough, you would say?”
“…Not as close as you and her, surely.”
A bitter laugh. Haru really isn’t sure what’s being assessed here.
“Have you ever gotten into an argument with her?” Niijima asks, enigmatic.
Mementos once again flashes to the forefront of Haru’s mind. “I… suppose.” She settles on,
“Born of a misunderstanding, and ultimately resolved.”
“Right.” Another pause, “How did you resolve it?”
“By clearing up the misunderstanding, mostly.” And a close shave with the Reaper.
“Wonderful.” Niijima voices, dry.
Haru is beginning to see what information Niijima is trying to extract from her. She supposes
this comes under the purview of building bridges, but she thinks she might be unqualified for
such a sharp leap so soon.
She threads her hands together, “…I find that simply addressing the issue as quickly as
possible is the best course of action.”
“That won’t work.”
She raises an eyebrow delicately, “…Why not?”
Niijima sighs, frustrated, “It just- won’t.”
Haru is hardly an expert on the subject, so she’ll have to take her word for it.

“Why am I asking you, anyway?” Niijima mutters, dragging a hand down her face, “You’re a
child.”
It is a childish urge to insist that she’s not a child, so Haru buries it. “Why not ask Ann-chan,
or Goro-kun?” She offers, “They might have more… actionable advice, with whatever it is
you’re struggling with.”
“Akechi’s half the problem.” Niijima spits, and sighs, “But… maybe Takamaki.”
Goro being the source of this problem is hardly surprising. And Ann might be inclined to be
on Makoto’s side on principal, if this is the kind of argument that requires as such. Haru
elects not to voice this. Niijima seems like she’s agonising enough already.
“Sorry to- sorry.” Niijima says haltingly, “I shouldn’t have sprung this on you.”
Instinct and desperation are two things Haru is quite familiar with. She’s asked stranger
questions. “It’s alright.”
“If you say so.” She picks up the neglected book off the coffee table, “…You’re here to see
Akechi, aren’t you? I won’t keep you.”
“I am. Thank you.” Haru hovers for a moment, despite having been dismissed, before starting
off down the hall.
She doesn’t bother knocking before opening the door. She isn’t sure if it’s because she knows
she’ll be welcome, or if she doesn’t want to bother with the formality. Either way, Goro
startles from where he’s sitting.
“…Come in.” He deadpans.
Maybe not as welcome as she thought. She can’t help the upward quirk of her lips. “Hello to
you, as well.”
He rolls his eyes. “Sit down, if you must.”
Haru takes the offer, tucking her skirt beneath her legs as she hops up on the bed. “…I had
thought you’d be in a better mood, after yesterday.”
Goro scowls, “Didn’t we all.”
“I tend to find destroying shadows quite cathartic.”
He barks a laugh, “I can tell.”
“Are you not the same?” Haru raises an eyebrow.
Goro sighs, “Oh, certainly.” He threads his fingers together, “But catharsis is only effective
for so long. And we’re in a veritable swamp of problems, aren’t we?”

So spending the entire Sunday systematically lowering the shadow population of Mementos
didn’t quite dent the scales for the selection of issues they’ve both stumbled upon and created
for themselves. Haru supposes she can relate.
“And which of these problems are you brooding over today?” She asks lightly.
Another scowl. “I’m not brooding.”
Haru very pointedly looks around the dark room, curtains permanently drawn, lights off, and
not a single piece of entertainment in sight.
“I think you’re brooding.” She tells him.
“I am not.” He insists. “I’m contemplating the shitshow we’ve made for ourselves.”
Haru thinks that the line between brooding and contemplating is rather thin. She also thinks it
doesn’t need to be thin to place Goro very solidly on the brooding side.
She’ll let him win this round. “And what has your contemplation reaped?”
Goro huffs, “Only that the Cleaner is more of an ass than I gave him credit for. And that I
ought to have tracked him down years ago.”
“…His elusiveness is more reprehensible to you than the assassination?” Haru questions.
“I’m an assassin.” He reminds her, “It would be hypocritical.”
Point. But, then again, Goro has had no qualms being hypocritical in the past. Haru has also
had minimal qualms with murder in the past, so she supposes anyone in this situation
attempting to claim the moral high ground would border on ridiculous.
“His phantom-like nature is rather irritating.” She settles on saying.
“Joker ought to sue.” Goro mutters.
She giggles, “If only. Maybe someone would tell us his name if we dragged him to court.”
Goro snorts, and Haru smiles wider.
“Well.” He says, after the moment has passed, “I take you didn’t come here to simply join in
on my pity party.”
“I did, a bit.” She protests, “But there is more, yes.”
He sighs, “Hit me, then.”
Haru bites at her lip, “You remember what Futaba-chan said, yes?”
Goro sighs, extremely weary, “How,” he snips out, “Could I possibly forget?”

Yes, how could they? The knowledge had been tossed out with little fanfare, something that
wasn’t an active threat and nothing that could be acted upon. Haru had been so taken aback
by Goro’s demand to rush off to Shido’s palace to confront his cognition, that any memory
pertaining to the information had simply vacated her mind; a thread not pulled upon by the
situation at hand.
Presumably, the act was equally impulsive for Goro.
Neither such negligence solves their problem.
“They’re going to find out.” Haru says.
“Who?” Goro raises an eyebrow, “Shido? Or the thieves?”
“Shido already knows.” She points out, “He just can’t do anything about it.”
“I suppose not.” He drags a hand down his face.
“Unless he can?”
“No.” Goro shakes his head, “I don’t think so. Nothing points to it. We were just supremely
unlucky, being kicked out of Sae’s palace when we were. Shido was probably counting on us
having to exit the Metaverse at some point, but he either doesn’t know or hasn’t considered
Mementos as a way to sidestep that.”
Haru narrows her eyes, “You’re not sure if he knows?”
“I haven’t told him.” He clarifies, “But that doesn’t mean Wakaba didn’t.”
Ah.
“He has her research.” He adds.
“I know.” She says, “But either way, we’re likely safe from him?”
“Likely so.” Goro confirms. “Probably.”
How reassuring. “At least we haven’t ruined everything.” Haru says, tugging at the sheets.
He snorts, “I wouldn’t count us out yet. Shido might not know how to touch us out here, but
that doesn’t mean his palace won’t be a nightmare. Especially now that we’ve done him the
courtesy of tripping the alarms.”
Haru supposes she should prepare herself for very abruptly falling out of Ren’s good graces.
And everyone else’s, for that matter. She’ll have Goro on her side, at least. Maybe Sumire
will pity her. Or maybe not, since they left her out of the ill-advised excursion.
“Maybe he’ll diminish the threat after we don’t act for several weeks.” Haru suggests, with a
tad too much hope.

“Unlikely.” Goro dashes those hopes very quickly, “He’ll probably just grow more paranoid.
Or overconfident, which is arguably worse in a cognitive space.”
True. It wouldn’t do for the man to suddenly delude himself into thinking he’s invincible. At
least brute force tends to shatter such illusions where necessary.
“Should we tell them?” Haru asks.
“Hm?”
“The thieves.” She clarifies. “Ren-kun. Waiting until we set foot in Shido’s palace will only
dig our graves deeper.”
“Unless,” Goro counters, “We’ve been blowing this out of proportion, and Shido’s palace
will be exactly as it should be in a few weeks time.”
“Do you really want to take that gamble?” Haru asks, halfway exasperated.
“I’m a gambling man.” Goro says darkly.
She hums, “Meaning…?”
“Meaning I have no idea.”
“Wonderful.” Haru slumps.
She understands Goro’s hesitance. She understands it very well, in fact. She does not want to
face this in the slightest— she had assumed any consequences for their sojourn would be
immediate in nature, wrought by bullets or knives or spells.
The last time anyone kept secrets in their band of thieves, it ended very poorly. They have an
opportunity to nip it in the bud.
Haru dearly wishes she was in on the time travel crowd. And that she could bend it to erase
far pettier mistakes.
“We should tell them.” She decides, with appropriate gravity and dread.
“Ah.” Goro eyes her, “Are you certain?”
“Are you?”
“Clearly not.”
“Then I’ll be certain for the both of us.” She draws herself up, “We should tell them. Before
this gets any worse than it needs to.”
Goro makes a pained face, “You’re right.” He grits, “Of course you are.”
Haru smiles.

“I do hate you for it.”
She frowns.
“Not really.” He amends. “Well, a little bit.”
Haru laughs, “Can I assume you’re dreading this confrontation as much as I am?”
“It doesn’t have to be a confrontation.” He corrects.
It likely will be, once Ren catches wind of it. “We’ll be as delicate as we can.”
“We?”
Haru frowns again, “Were you thinking of leaving me to explain alone?”
Goro blinks. “No.” His eyebrows draw together slightly, “I thought I was going to have to
explain on my own.”
“Well, you won’t.” She says primly, “I should have tried harder to stop you, anyway.”
“You didn’t try very hard at all.”
“I remember.”
Goro smirks, like this is all suddenly very amusing, “I suppose we’ve dug our graves
together, then.”
Haru laughs, because they certainly have.
“When are we going to get this done, then?” She asks.
“Well.” He begins, “The longer we leave it, the more likely one of us will end up getting
stabbed.”
“By who?”
“Ren.” He answers immediately, “Or Sumire.”
“Sumi-chan wouldn’t.” Haru insists.
“She might.”
She might. Haru sincerely doubts she would literally stab either of them, or anyone, for that
matter, but that’s nothing to say of the other categories of response they may receive.
Turnabout is fair play, but there’s still a measure of cruelty in it. Haru knows she’s a
hypocrite.
Goro presses his lips together, tense, or irritated, “Tomorrow, I suppose.”

Haru sighs, defeated. “Tomorrow.”
“Oh.” He pauses, “By the way. Makoto already knows.”
Haru stares, “She…?”
“She noticed I was missing, the night we went out.” Goro explains, surprisingly calm. “She
called me on it.”
“I am astounded,” Haru says slowly, “That the rest of the thieves have not also been made
aware of this fact.”
Goro shrugs, “She can’t take the high ground here, so she won’t.”
Haru had assumed her aforementioned hypocrisy would be a trait shared amongst myriad
other thieves. Perhaps the blatant tattle-tale nature of the act swayed Makoto to keep her
mouth shut.
“She doesn’t seem the type to have forgotten Futaba’s discovery.” Haru comments.
“Neither are we.” Goro points out. Alas, and yet. “Besides, I didn’t tell her where we went.
Just that we went.”
Haru presumes that Makoto will not be happy to hear that the situation is likely worse than
she assumed. So much for building bridges. Perhaps Sae will have more luck. Or not, if she
was turning to Haru for advice.
“Tomorrow.” Haru repeats.
Goro clicks his tongue, and looks to be planning his funeral. “Should you summon everyone,
or should I?”
“You still don’t have a phone, no?” Haru points out, “It’s my turn to be cryptic, then.”
Goro snorts, “That it is.”

As little as Akechi wants to reveal what can only be classified as a joint misdemeanour, the
bracing conversation has at least reminded him that he’s still lacking in a way to
communicate with those outside of this apartment.
He is, of course, now allowed to leave. Still requiring outside assistance to do so rubs him the
wrong way for a multitude of reasons.
The tense atmosphere in the apartment has yet to dissipate, with both Sae and Makoto
predictably dragging their feet in reconciling.
Perhaps he’s being unfair. It’s only been two days. Then again, Ann has clearly picked up on
it, and her awkward laughter when caught between frigid stares has done little to help the

situation. The air only grows more oppressive as Haru leaves for the day, the two of them
solemnly resigning themselves to their fate come tomorrow.
He still needs his damn phone. He can stomach the living room long enough to demand that.
Sae looks especially unhappy, when Akechi catches her in the midst of not reading the book
in her hands.
“You still have my phone, yes?” He asks without preamble.
Sae looks unimpressed by his cutting to the chase, though the intimidation factor is nullified
somewhat by the deep circles under her eyes. “I do.”
Akechi holds out a hand expectantly.
“Do you know,” Sae says, very dry, very disdainful, “That there is a wonderful magic word
called-”
“Are you serious?”
“If you don’t believe me, I’m sure Takamaki-san has a dictionary lying about somewhere.”
She says smugly.
“She does.” Akechi had taken to reading it in a particularly dour fit of boredom.
“Well, look at that.” Sae mutters, turning back to her book.
Akechi stares, and waits. “…Are you holding my phone hostage?”
“Why do you need it?” She questions.
He rolls his eyes, “Because the only reason you’ve been hanging onto it is so I can’t run off
into the Metaverse.”
“As you tend to do, so I hear.”
He glares, “It’s well within my right to do so. And I’m not injured anymore, if that happened
to be among your main concerns.”
Sae freezes, before tapping at the page she’s opened to absently, “…I suppose it was.”
Akechi raises an eyebrow. He would have thought Sae would be more wary of handing a
known killer his favourite weapon. Not that he particularly intends to use it as such, but she
doesn’t know that.
“…Can I have it back?” He asks again when the silence drags a bit too long.
Sae cuts him a suspicious look, “You’re more eager than usual.”
Akechi pastes on his very best TV smile, just for her, “I’ve acted similarly in the past.”

“Let me rephrase.” Sae looks vaguely disgusted, which is rude. “You’re more demanding
than usual.”
He can’t really refute that, so he won’t. “Is it so hard to believe I’m sick of being caged in
here?”
“I’m stuck here, too.”
“How terrible for you.” Akechi deadpans, “You’re still holding my ticket out.”
Sae slowly removes his phone from her pocket, but doesn’t hand it over. “Do you have a
destination in mind?”
“A walk around the block.”
She looks surprised, “That’s it?”
“Yes.” He answers truthfully.
Something passes over Sae’s face as she snorts. “Didn’t you take a trip out of the house just
yesterday?”
“And?” Akechi sneers, “I’d like to do it again.”
“Don’t we all?” Sae mutters. She shoots him another searching look, “Is there a reason you’re
so desperate to have this today, and not tomorrow?”
Maybe he should have come at this with a gentler hand. Or maybe that would have just made
her equally suspicious, and he just can’t win.
Akechi drops his hand to his side. “I fucked up.” He admits.
Sae looks alarmed, “You—?”
“It’s nothing as dramatic as you’re envisioning.” He says breezily, “But I imagine there will
be objections to my free reign in the Metaverse after tomorrow, and I’d like to secure my way
in before that happens.”
“You realise you aren’t convincing me in the slightest?”
“I wasn’t doing that before, either.” He points out.
She ignores him, “It sounds like giving you free reign, as you put it, is just giving you another
avenue to fuck up some more.”
How blunt. “I won’t.” He says, more out of obligation than anything else, “But If I’m trapped
here for any longer, I’ll go crazy. I just want to take a damn walk.”
Sae stares him down, before she huffs.

“Even when you are saying quite possibly the most suspicious things you’ve ever said,” She
grouses, “You’re remarkably convincing.”
“Surely I’ve been more suspicious in the past.”
“I never quite picked up on any of the I’m secretly an assassin hints you’ve dropped in the
past,” Sae says drily, “So, no.”
In hindsight, he had genuinely —if accidentally— been dropping some such hints. Sae likely
wont appreciate this fact.
He tilts his head, “…And?”
Sae grits her teeth. “You want to go outside now?”
“Preferably.”
She stands abruptly, “Fine.” She snaps, “I’ll give your phone back. But take me with you.”
Akechi scowls, “Is this your stipulation? You hover and keep an eye on me?”
“No.” Sae says, “But if I stay cooped up in here much longer, I’ll go crazy too.”
Well, Akechi thinks as Sae finally drops his phone into his hand, he can hardly say no to that.
