It’s been two days since Sojiro pulled up his bootstraps and decided to contact Ohya and
Iwai, and he’s been dragging his feet ever since.
Back in the days when he had a job that actually netted him an income, this would not have
disturbed him. He had a multitude of odds and ends to attend to, and even the most important
of assignments could be pushed back a few days at a time.
Unless, of course, Shido or Wakaba were involved. God help him if he tried to shirk their
respective demands and requests.
Shido is definitely involved in this project of his. Wakaba technically is, a few times removed
and beyond a veil or two, but Sojiro will still count it.
Their presence (ghostly or otherwise) is exactly why he’s avoiding his task, however.
He isn’t afraid of them. Not really. He used to be, for a time— he could probably say it’s why
he quit. Shido’s eyes were just a bit too sharp and Wakaba’s words just a bit too evasive and
Sojiro had enough. Distance does wonders for dulling the knives of each.
Distance does nothing for dulling the distinctly more literal knives he may encounter if he
fucks this up.

He’s old. He doesn’t mind danger so much anymore— hey, he’d even go so far as to say he
misses it. But he’s got two kids and a cat to take care of (and, a whole wealth of extra kids if
he dabbles in honesty) and he’s not going to pull on strings recklessly at the risk of sending
something toppling down on top of them.
But he does need to pull strings. Just: delicately.
Eventually.
Sojiro sighs, and wonders if calling up the Niijima lady for not-advice would count as
progress. The shop’s main regulars passed through hours ago and he’s sick of polishing the
same glass five times over.
The bell chimes. Sojiro quirks a brow as someone enters, a built man in a rather impressive
suit; crisp, a bit too fancy for what could very well be hired muscle.
“Welcome.” Sojiro grunts, nonetheless, “Bit late for coffee.”
The man chuckles, “Good thing you serve curry.”
“Yeah.” Sojiro deadpans, setting down the now-pristine mug on the counter with a clink,
“Great.”
The man takes a leisurely seat at the bar (the detective kid’s old chair, funnily enough). “Just
one plate, Boss.”
Is this a new intimidation tactic? Asking politely to be served? Sojiro can’t decide if it’s
working, but he at least hopes that he’ll be paid for his troubles before this gets ugly.
“Coming right up.” He says after a beat, and tries not to turn his back as he shuffles off to the
kitchen, pot of curry simmering away.
One shoddily arranged plate of rice and curry slid carelessly to the correct seat later, the man
forgoes taking a bite, and instead steeples his fingers. “So tell me, Boss. How’ve ya been?”
“Have we met?” Sojiro asks, fumbling in his pocket for a cigarette. He’s tried and somewhat
failed to kick the habit when he took in Futaba, and again when he took in Ren, but he thinks
this situation warrants a smoke. He doesn’t get not-quite-threatened very often, anyway.
The man grins, “You wound me, Boss.”
“I’ll take that as a no.”
“Sharp.” Is the flat response.
“You gonna give me a name to work with, here?”
“Oh, sure.” The man makes a show of patting himself down for a business card, and shrugs
when he turns up nothing. “Tanaka will work just fine.”

“Uh huh.” Sojiro digs around in his apron for a lighter after successfully fishing out a loose
cigarette. “Do you mind?” He gestures vaguely, not waiting for a response as he lights it up
anyway.
Tanaka has a general air of amusement, “No, I don’t.” He picks up his spoon, “But I’d think
your kids do.”
There it is. Sojiro tries very hard not to bite down on the cigarette in his mouth.
“This is good.” Tanaka comments mildly around a mouthful of curry.
“Thanks.” Sojiro snaps.
“No, really.” Tanaka pushes, “This whole place is lovely.”
Sojiro rolls his eyes. “By all means, burn it to the ground. The insurance payout is worth
more than if I tried to sell it off.”
“And when did I even imply such a thing?” Tanaka looks hurt, “I just said this place was
lovely.”
“Mm.”
“Despite the fact it reeks of smoke.” He continues, “Your kids-”
“You know.” Sojiro interrupts, “Usually, when I threatened someone, I’d tell them what the
hell I’m asking for.”
Tanaka chuckles, “You have no flair for dramatics, Boss. Let a man set the stage.”
“I’m not a fan of method acting.”
“As I said.” Tanaka makes an mm sound around another mouthful of curry, “I implied no
such thing.”
“Should I play a guessing game on who you work for?” Sojiro grits.
Tanaka flashes a knife grin, “I think you’re already well aware, Boss.”
Shido really was far too reliant on a teenager if this is how his lackeys conduct business these
days. Sojiro really misses a good old-fashioned Nice place you got, shame if something
happened to it. Here’s an itemised list of my demands.
“I am aware.” Sojiro says, and takes another drag, “You should head off and tell your boss
that I terminated my employment nearly three years ago. Not sure if he forgot.”
Tanaka chuckles, “I’d love to, Boss. Small problem.”
“Which would be?”

“That’s not what I’m here for.” Tanaka looks him up and down, “Even if he wanted you back
in action, you’re hardly in your prime anymore.”
It’s only been three years. Though he concedes said years have not been particularly kind to
his knees. Or his back. Or his nerves.
Sojiro sighs, and douses his cigarette in the ash tray he keeps behind the counter, “Then what
the hell are you here for?”
“See, the boss was real vague.” Tanaka drawls.
“Never a good sign.”
“Yeah.” Another spoonful of curry, “Terrible sign, usually. Means my job is a pain in the ass.
And probably means the guy on the other end is about to have a terrible time, too.”
(Sojiro wonders, in a moment of frustrated clarity, if this guy is the Cleaner.
It’s possible. Certainly so if Sojiro is enough of an annoyance, which he usually is when it
comes to Shido. Though he thinks he’s been doing an excellent job of keeping his head down
these past years.
But, even if he is, that knowledge is supremely unhelpful. If this guy’s name is actually
Tanaka, Sojiro will light Leblanc on fire himself.)
“How awful for you.” Sojiro intones, flat.
Tanaka hums, “I know.”
“Has your stage been thoroughly set yet?”
He chuckles, “I’m getting there. Right now, actually.” He leans forward, “See, the boss is real
curious about that Isshiki lady’s old work.”
Ah.
Sojiro isn’t sure if he ought to be relived or not. Maybe he will be, the day people stop
coming to him of all people to try and dig up ghosts.
“That’s too bad.” He says, and wishes he hadn’t put out that cigarette. “I’ve got nothin’ for
him.”
“Really.” Tanaka says.
“Yep.”
“The boss seems to think otherwise.”
“The boss can think all he likes.” Sojiro scoffs, “Doesn’t change the fact that I know nothing.
Anything Wakaba said to me flew right over my head.”

“But she did say things to you.” Tanaka points out.
“Sure.” Sojiro shrugs, “But she said a lot of things. Nothing I can remember in the specifics.”
Tanaka stares.
“Didn’t Shido have copies of all her stuff anyway?” Sojiro points out, “What the hell does he
need me for?”
“No idea.” Tanaka leans back in the stool, “But he’s been… antsy, ever since that business
with the Phantom Thieves.”
“The business with the Phantom Thieves is still happening.”
“That it is!” Tanaka laughs, “I suppose I can’t complain. I’ve been getting more work lately.”
Presumably because Shido’s favourite assassin defected just the other week. “Well,
congratulations.”
“Yeah.” Another piercing stare. “You know anything about all that?”
(Is he curious, or did Shido ask? Did he notice how Sojiro tensed, or did he just find a
convenient segue?)
“Not a clue.” Sojiro says evenly, “I’ve been avoiding the news, lately.”
“A man like you, not even staying up-to-date?”
“I’m sick of looking at Shido’s face.”
Tanaka cackles, “Aren’t we all! I have to work with the guy, I don’t need to see him on my
TV, either.”
A sentiment Sojiro surely would have shared if he kept up the government work. Sojiro
might also be dead if he kept up the government work, so he abandons the train of thought.
Tanaka pulls out a wallet, rifling though some bills, “Boss’s gonna be real disappointed you
had nothing to say to him.”
Sojiro snorts, “What does he want? A postcard?”
“A postcard of this place would look nice.” Tanaka comments mildly. “Might last longer.
How much do I owe you?”
Sojiro levels a glare at him for that particularly unsubtle insinuation, and taps the hanging
sign above his head.
“Right, gotcha.” Tanaka drawls, sliding the requisite money over. He stands, the stool
screeching so loudly that it must have scuffed the floors. Sojiro will have to fix that,
assuming the place lasts that long. “I’ll be seeing you, Boss.”

“I’m sure you will.”
“Who knows? Maybe I’ll be back with better questions.”
“One can only hope.” Sojiro deadpans.
Tanaka chuckles, and throws up a hand in farewell, the bell clanging loudly as he shuts the
door none too gently.
Well then.
Sojiro slowly picks up the scraped-clean plate and dumps it in the sink. That’ll be Ren’s
problem for later.
Or maybe it’ll be no one’s problem, depending on what Sojiro decides to do next.
There are two paths to take here.
As far as he knows, Shido has no knowledge of Leblanc’s connection to the thieves. If he did,
surely it would have already been raided five times over, scouring for both the members and
any information relating to the cognitive world he can get his mitts on.
A passing suspicion, then? Even if that were the case, Shido isn’t really at the point where he
needs an excuse to act on a hunch. Either he really is just fishing for any last thing that
Wakaba left behind, or he’s just testing the waters.
And, thus, what to do next?
Sojiro does not want to be caught unawares the next time Shido sends someone his way. He
certainly doesn’t want Ren, or worse, Futaba, to be present while it happens either.
So he can either push his luck, or get the hell out of dodge on a passing fear.
Sojiro sighs, giving the shop a once-over.
Well, maybe they’ll leave the place alone if it’s half abandoned, anyway.
There’s a buzz in his pocket. He scowls, and takes it out.
Futaba: soooo
Futaba: should i pack my stuff
Sojiro sighs again, louder and more obvious this time. He forgot she likes to keep her ears on
everything she can. He texts back an affirmative, and wonders what the hell he can
reasonably rescue from the shop before it presumably gets torn apart.

Ren comes home to a mess.

This is business as usual for the attic. He kept it relatively spotless last timeline, but
something about consistent misery and stress has led him into a series of bad habits,
including leaving his dirty laundry and thieving materials strewn about on the floor. Morgana
has complained about this on many occasions.
This mess is not contained to the attic.
“What the…?” Morgana pokes his head out of the bag as the bell above the door tinkles to a
stop.
“Hey.” Sojiro says, frowning at several textbooks and trying to pile them into a dufflebag.
“Sup.” Futaba says, in the middle of… dismantling a computer?
“Uh.” Ren blinks.
“Leblanc’s compromised.” Futaba explains, “Maybe. So you gotta pack your stuff.”
“What?” Morgana yowls, sounding as panicked as Ren feels.
“Some shady guy showed up.” Futaba continues.
“Mighta been your guy.” Sojiro adds.
“Might’ve been.” Futaba nods, “But it’s not like we got his name, so we’re still square one
there.”
“Okay.” Ren says, slowly, “And…?”
“He just asked for more information about Wakaba.” Sojiro waves a hand, “But if he comes
looking for more, I’m not risking it.”
Morgana leaps out of the bag, “That’s fair.”
“Sure is.” Futaba unscrews something else from the desktop casing.
“…So should I…?” Ren gestures to the attic.
“Quickly, if you can.” Sojiro grunts.
“I’ll help.” Futaba abandons her PC, “How much stuff do you have, anyway?”
“Two cardboard boxes’ worth.” Ren guesses, jogging up the stairs, Morgana on his heels.
Ren frowns as he crests the top of the stairs and surveys the attic.
“Wow.” Futaba exclaims, “Its messy in here.”
“That’s what I’ve been saying.” Morgana chimes in.

“Not important.” Ren cuts them both off, scooping a pile of dirty shirts out from one of the
myriad corners.
Morgana paces the room in a circle, his lack of opposable thumbs getting him out of packing
duty. “You should probably take down the Phantom Thieves’ banner.”
Ren had, for a second timeline in a row, thought it was a hilarious purchase. “Probably.”
“D’you think all this junk can somehow link you back to all your friends?” Futaba asks,
pointing to the shelves with Ren’s various knick-knacks.
“They’re not junk.” He protests, “But, maybe. Dump it in the box. Carefully.”
“Will do.” Futaba starts tossing stuff in.
“That’s not very carefully.”
“We gotta go quick.”
“Is it really that bad?” Morgana asks worriedly.
Futaba pauses in her scooping, “Well, they’re probably not coming here now.” She concedes.
“But I don’t want to risk it, if they are.”
“Where are we even going?” Morgana pushes.
“Dunno.” Futaba shrugs, “Sojiro might have a place lined up.”
Ren doubts it, if this truly was so sudden. “…Haru texted the group chat that she wanted to
meet up today.”
Futaba frowns, “She did.” She whips out her phone, “I’ll text everyone to make sure they’re
not on their way here already.”
“They won’t get a text if they’re in Mementos.” Morgana points out.
“True.” Futaba says, “But that’s a whoever’s-in-Mementos problem.”
“Us, shortly.” Ren quips.
Futaba hums, “But, again, where?”
Ren mulls it over. “…I don’t know how urgent Haru’s thing is. Hopefully it’s nothing, but we
should probably address it just in case it isn’t.”
“It can be a double meeting, then.” Morgana leaps up on the couch, “We talk about getting
evicted, Haru talks about whatever she needs to.”
“Our last meeting that wasn’t in the Metaverse was in Leblanc.” Futaba frowns.

“Well, half our group is already at Lady Ann’s.” Morgana says, tail flicking, “Even if we’re
not staying there, it’s good to make a pitstop. Plus, that means we can loop Niijima in
immediately as well.”
“True.” Ren nods, “Ann’s it is.”
Futaba suddenly groans, “Are we gonna have to walk all the way there?”
“You have me, remember?” Morgana interjects drily, “It’ll even be comfortable, without nine
people trying to cram in.”
Ren pauses in his haphazard packing, and frowns. Sojiro will probably be grossed out by the
very concept of the Monabus. At the same time, the alternative is showing off his piss-poor
driving and possibly getting a lecture out of it.
Ren sighs. He’ll live.
“Almost done.” He announces, tearing the Phantom Thieves banner off the wall and tossing it
on top of his box of clothes.
“Yep!” Futaba agrees, very awkwardly trying to lay a massive shogi piece on top of all of
Ren’s other trinkets. She scoops up the box, “Downstairs-ho!”
Morgana leaps up to take residence on Ren’s shoulders as they all trot back down the stairs,
back to the sight of Sojiro still scowling over some books.
“Why bother with the textbooks?” Ren asks dubiously.
“They were Wakaba’s.” Sojiro explains. “She didn’t write them, but I don’t know if she wrote
annotations, and I’m not gonna look through all of these to check. I don’t want anything
getting back to Shido if I can help it.”
“Makes sense.” Futaba says vaguely, eyeing the books almost hungrily.
Sojiro regards her for a moment, before waving a hand, “You can take a look if you like, once
we settle down somewhere.”
“Thank you.” She says, quickly enough that it sounds like one word, as she gets back to
dismantling her computer.
“How long is that gonna take?” Morgana asks.
“Not long.” Futaba doesn’t look up, “It’s kinda like a puzzle set, see? It all fits in real neat.”
She pauses, groaning as she has to grab the screwdriver again, “’Cept the parts I went
overboard with.”
“How could you not have foreseen that you’d be on the run from the government some day?”
Ren deadpans, “For shame.”

Futaba sticks out her tongue, “This thing is my baby.” She declares, “I’m not leaving it
behind, or risking anything getting jumbled or cracked while still in the case.”
“Fair enough.” Sojiro interjects. “You kids know where we’re headed?”
“Ann’s.” Ren says, and takes out his phone, “Via Mementos.”
Sojiro’s expression says more than enough about how exactly he feels about that. He eyes all
their luggage, “Can we take stuff with us?”
“So long as we have a hand on it, I think.” Futaba says, followed by a triumphant cry as the
last piece of her PC comes loose. She delicately lays it in a cardboard box of her own,
shoving the case in another. “Done!”
Sojiro gives up on tetris-ing his own belongings, tossing the rest of the books in a bag with
little fanfare. “We ready, then?”
Ren walks over to flick off the lights, and then shoves both of his boxes together, and grabs
the touching edges with one hand. “This might be unpleasant.” He warns.
Sojiro grunts something that’s probably adjacent to a dismissal.
Ren shrugs, glancing around to check the blinds are all drawn and that no one is peering in.
“Mementos.”
Beginning Navigation.
The transition is as smooth as its ever been. Which is to say, as unpleasant as Ren predicted.
There’s an imbalance to go with the usual disorientation, the swirling reds and blacks. The
leap between realities apparently considers Ren’s luggage and extension of him, his centre of
gravity suddenly too far to the right. He can imagine Futaba has it the worst, her own luggage
more than Ren’s and Sojiro’s combined.
“Hate that.” Sojiro grouches as everything settles.
“You’ll hate this even more!” Futaba says cheerily, swinging the door open with a muffled
chime.
“Don’t forget your stuff.” Ren calls. He’s not carrying it for her.
Futaba bursts back in the door, “Yeah, yeah. But first: Mona! Do your thing!”
“Now?” Morgana complains, now standing on two legs.
“We need a place to put our stuff!”
“Ugh.” Morgana rolls his eyes, hopping out onto the street, “Make it cool.” He says under his
breath.
Ren smirks, “Look away, Sojiro.” He says with the utmost seriousness, “It’s not decent.”

“Don’t make it weird!” Morgana yowls, scandalised.
Sojiro just looks vaguely baffled, “What’s happening?”
“We’re getting our ride.” Futaba says by way of explanation.
“Right…”
Before Sojiro can ask any further questions, there’s a bang, and a puff of smoke, leaving a
giant van where Morgana once stood.
“What.”
“Alrighty.” Ren swings open one of the doors, “Get your stuff.”
“Make it quick!” Morgana demands over the radio, “Just sitting here like this is weird!”
“I-” Sojiro cuts himself off, and rubs at his temples. “Okay. I shouldn’t be surprised, really.”
“I knew he wouldn’t be impressed…” Morgana mutters dejectedly.
Ren pats the hood of the van, “You’ll get ‘em next time, Mona.”
“Were Haru, Yoshizawa, and Akechi impressed last time?”
Hm. “Haru was.”
There’s a defeated groan, and Ren supposes he ought to start grabbing his boxes.
It takes ten minutes, give or take, to pile everything in the back seats. Futaba claims shotgun
immediately, keeping the box with all her computer parts securely in her lap. Ren shares a
look with Sojiro, waiting to see who will back down first.
“You don’t have a license.” Sojiro eventually says.
“Good thing there aren’t any cops around.” Ren counters. “And do you want to drive the
cat?”
“Hey!”
“Well, when you put it that way…” Sojiro grumbles as he pulls open the door for the second
row of seats. He pauses, one foot in the van, “If I see any reckless driving, I’m taking over.”
“You got it, Boss.” Ren says, hopping into the driver’s seat. He’ll abstain from vehicular
shadow-slaughter today. Not that there are any on the surface to begin with.
“You know the way?” Sojiro asks.
Futaba snickers, as there’s a green glow, and the outline of her mask flickers and vanishes in
blue fire, “He does now!” She holds out her arm, pointing straight ahead, “That way.”

“Thank you, Oracle-GPS.” Ren salutes her.
“I accept cash as payment.”
Maybe Ren should run over some shadows, in that case.

Chapter Summary

Lessons thoroughly not learned, and searching for shelter

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Sumire can’t help the shroud of dread that hangs over her after Ren’s text to meet at Ann’s
apartment. Perhaps it’s the different location that throws her off.
All told, it’s a reasonable place to meet. A majority of their group takes residence there
anyway, and yet she can’t help but feel something is off. A loose pane of glass, ready to take
the rest of the window with it.
She’s probably wrong. It’s probably paranoia. She’s spinning a web out of nothing, and this
will just be a completely normal, standard meeting, wherein Haru’s cryptic text the day prior
was simply poor phrasing and isn’t all that pressing.
This fleeting hope is dashed once she arrives in Ann’s apartment, nearly tripping over the
Sakura’s luggage as she materialises out from the Metaverse.
“Hi, Sumire.” Ren says, not commenting on the mess, “That’s everyone, then.”
Goro hums vaguely. He looks a bit like a man marching to the gallows, and Haru’s
expression isn’t much cheerier.
A simple scan of the room tells Sumire that no one is dead, so that’s something at least.
“Is there any reason Niijima and I need to be here?” Sojiro comments, looking a bit awkward.
“Well, it’d be weird if you left.” Ryuji points out.
“And you may as well sit in.” Haru adds.
“If you insist.” Sojiro grumbles.
“So…” Ann looks between Haru and the pile of belongings currently littering her kitchen,
“Who wants to go first?”
“Guess we’ll start.” Futaba tucks her knees to her chest and shuffles forward, “So, uh,
someone real shady showed up at Leblanc this afternoon.”

There are a few grunts of alarm, and Sumire feels her gut clench. “Define shady.” Yusuke
says warily.
“As in, maybe-the-Cleaner shady.” Ren chimes in.
“He certainly gave off a distinct impression.” Sojiro sighs, “I’m not one-hundred percent sure
that Leblanc and our house is fully compromised, but…”
“Better not to risk it.” Sae finishes. “Understandable. You have direct ties to the conspiracy, if
once or twice removed. You’re a person of interest from several angles.”
“I remember.” Sojiro cuts her a pointed look. “But, yeah. I don’t think Shido’s linked any of
you kids to the thieves, but I don’t want to give him the chance to get any closer.”
“If he knew,” Goro says flatly, “He would have sent more than just someone to threaten you.”
“My line of thinking exactly.” Sojiro leans back in his corner of Ann’s couch.
“So where will you be staying, then?” Makoto pipes up.
“Haven’t figured that out yet.” Morgana sighs.
“This place is -uh- getting kind of crowded.” Ann admits, “I’d offer, but…”
Ren waves a hand, “You’re doing plenty already, Ann.”
“We’ll sort somethin’ out.” Ryuji says, “But, I’m kinda curious. Like- why now?”
Sae frowns, “What do you mean?”
“Like- if Shido still doesn’t know who we are, why go after Boss and Leblanc?” He
elaborates.
“Tanaka gave the excuse of hunting for Wakaba’s research.” Sojiro says, “I would’ve figured
he had it all already, but maybe there’s something in particular he’s looking for.”
Haru and Goro share a look. Sumire tilts her head at them, and they both tense.
“…He may be getting paranoid.” Haru offers after a beat.
“Well, we haven’t made any public moves since Akechi-kun’s jailbreak.” Yusuke comments,
“Perhaps he’s getting antsy.”
“Could be.” Ren agrees.
“Or.” Goro grits, “There could be a more direct cause and effect.”
Makoto raises an eyebrow, “Such as?”
There’s another pause, as Goro presses his lips together.

“…Is this related to what you wanted to talk about, Haru-senpai?” Sumire guesses, rather lost

Sae gives Goro a sharp look, “What did you do?”
“Oh, don’t give me that.” He snaps.
“Shido’s paranoia may be linked to recent activity in his palace.” Haru announces primly,

Ann immediately buries her head in her hands, “Oh my god.”

Sumire thinks this is probably worse than anything she could have cooked up in her anxietyriddled brain. Aside from the lack of deaths, of course.
Ren is eerily quiet.
“So you’re saying you went to Shido’s palace.” Futaba says flatly. “After we said-”

“How long ago was this?!” Morgana demands, leaping up onto the back of the couch, tail

“And why,” Ren says, “Do you know?”

know you went to Shido’s palace!”
“That’s because I didn’t tell you.” Goro deadpans. “What, would you have snitched if you

“Yes!”
Sumire…
…Isn’t actually sure if she’s allowed to be angry. Though, it isn’t as though hypocrisy isn’t
already rampant among their number.

She can’t quite muster anger, when she tries. She gets about as far as frustration before

“…Fill me in.” Sojiro says over the increasingly angry mutterings and accusations being

“No way you’re on their side.” Ryuji stares at her, incredulous.
Sumire offers a very small shrug.
“Sorry, Sumi-chan.” Haru says quietly.
“You’re sorry to her?” Makoto glares, “What about the rest of us!?”
“This meeting wasn’t for apologies.” Goro sneers, “We’re just letting you know.”
Ren takes a sharp breath, and pinches the bridge of his nose, shoving up his glasses in the
process. “Just-” he takes a second, “Why. Start there.”
“Hm.” Goro looks paler, somehow. “You aren’t going to like this.”
“No, I don’t think anyone will.” Haru mutters.
Sumire vaguely recalls the last time Goro confessed to running off to Shido’s palace, shortly
after the mess of he and Ren regaining their memories. She doesn’t want to jump the gun,
but…
Goro makes a short, frustrated growl before speaking, “Shido has a rather chatty cognition of
me wandering his ship.”
Ah, there it is.
“You’re not serious.” Ren says.
“It hasn’t tried to kill me in a while.” Goro says, like that makes it better.
“It was rather rude.” Haru counters.
“Rude, but at least it never reached for its gun.”
“Yes.” Ren says, voice like ice, “That would be awful, wouldn’t it? You, being shot by
Shido’s cognition of you in a place where no one can find you.”
Goro scowls, “Haru was there.”

“You realise that you two nearly getting yourselves killed is the least of our problems, right?”
Futaba snaps.
“Uh, pretty sure it’s a big problem.” Ann cuts in.
Sumire locks eyes with Yusuke, who gives a helpless shrug. In a moment of clarity, Sumire
suddenly understands exactly how Haru felt after everyone else went running off into palaces
of their own. Somehow, being made to watch the aftermath without being at fault feels worse.
She can’t even hide behind the confidence of conviction this time, with no such conviction
being her own.
It also would have been nice if they thought to bring her along.
“We’re well aware of what we’ve done.” Haru interjects, voice cold, but still miles warmer
than Ren’s. “Had we recalled the developments regarding Shido’s knowledge, we wouldn’t
have gone.”
“You forgot.” Futaba says, disbelieving.
“I was having a bad day.” Goro says.
“Implying you usually go to Shido’s palace on bad days?” Ren says, and it almost sounds like
he’s joking.
“That’s the sum of it, yes.”
“I cannot fucking believe you.”
“Alright.” Sojiro holds up his hands, and the fire temporarily dispels, “Tearing into each other
isn’t going to help.”
“Well!” Morgana still looks like he’s been kicked, “What will help?”
A pause.
“Time travel?” Makoto offers. A laugh bursts out of Sumire before she can shove it down,
and she quickly clamps a hand over her mouth.
“Seriously...” Ryuji mutters.
“It’s not as bad as it could be.” Goro says, still oddly calm, “My cognition is a far cry from
what it was last timeline.”
“Meaning?” Ren grits.
“Meaning, that it isn’t capable of running off to report every mishap to its dear Captain.”
Goro explains, “Unless it feels like taking a trip overboard.”
Ren throws up his hands. Sumire feels a bit like doing the same.

“You know,” Futaba speaks up, with the utmost sarcasm, “That makes me feel so much
better.”
Haru sighs, frustration clearly getting the better of her, “You’ll live.”
“Will we?!”
“Boss is right.” Yusuke says, “What’s done is done. Arguing will get us nowhere.”
“It’s getting us somewhere.” Morgana protests, “And, seriously, what are we going to do?”
Hm.
“…Can we do anything?” Sumire uncomfortably raises her hand to catch the others’
attention, “If Shido is already just… more paranoid, then I think that ship’s sailed.” She kicks
herself for the accidental pun.
Ann frowns, and tugs at one of her pigtails, “That’s it?”
“Really.” Sae says drily, stone-faced.
“Better we know now, then finding out later, right?” Sumire points out, fiddling with her
glasses.
“That’s what we were thinking.” Haru chimes in.
“And you couldn’t have said this seven days ago.” Futaba’s glare reignites.
Goro sniffs, “If you’ll recall, the potential aftermath slipped our minds. And the exact
potential consequences were only brought up two days ago.”
“And you’re otherwise unrepentant.” Ren finishes.
That isn’t entirely fair, Sumire supposes, when she’s fairly sure no one else ever felt
particularly sorry for their own duo and trio palace excursions. Sumire herself can only
source her regret to the fact that she accomplished nothing from the risk.
Of course, she should have known she wasn’t going to get anything from the start. But,
hindsight and whatnot.
“Did you get what you were looking for, at least?” Sumire asks.
Haru shrugs. Goro tilts his head, “Conversation, and a series of pointed insults?” He
summarises, “I got what I should have expected, if not what I was looking for.”
Well, they’re all on the same page then.
Ryuji digs his palms into his eyes, and mumbles, “We’re all stupid.”
“So there’s really nothing we can do.” Futaba says, fists clenched, “You fucked things up and
you can’t even fix it.”

“You ran off to Maruki’s palace.” Goro snaps at her.
Futaba’s scowl morphs into a sneer, as she flexes and clenches her hands before tossing them
up with a furious “Ugh!”
“None of this was our intention.” Haru says after a moment of silence.
“We kinda already knew that.” Ann shuffles on her feet.
“Is that all this meeting was for?” Morgana asks sullenly.
“No.” Ren interjects, “We were in the middle of trying to sort out our sudden lack of place to
live.” He smiles brightly, “Great that we know why, now.”
“Would you like to blame us for any other problems while you’re at it?” Goro spits.
“Where should I start?”
“Okay.” Sojiro cuts them off again, “No one’s happy.”
That doesn’t really need to be said, Sumire thinks.
“But even if you kids have no way to solve that problem,” he continues, “There are other
things to discuss. Without the potshots, preferably.”
“Can’t be my place.” Ryuji says immediately.
“Nor mine.” Yusuke chimes in.
Sumire coughs, “Um, I think my parents would ask too many questions.”
“Well, who doesn’t have parents?” Morgana asks.
Half the group raises their hands.
Futaba frowns at Ren. “You have parents.”
Ren shrugs, “I assumed the question was who doesn’t have parents who live with them right
now.”
“That’s what I meant.” Morgana agrees.
Ann makes a face, “…So that’s still everyone who either doesn’t have a place to go or is
already living here.”
“I don’t have parents.” Yusuke points out.
“You live in a dorm, dude.” Ryuji thwacks him on the arm.
A pause, and everyone looks at Haru.

“…We did rule out your place last time we were shuffling people around.” Sumire points out.
“Based on paranoia.” Haru points out, “If things are urgent, then it’s a risk we may have to
take.”
“Then I suppose the question is whether it’s better or worse than if you had just stayed in
your own home.” Sae nods to Sakura.
“We could just stay in Mementos.” Futaba mumbles.
“It’s not very comfortable.” Sumire warns.
“And the Chief doesn’t have a persona.” Morgana adds, “I don’t wanna know what staying in
the Metaverse overnight does to him.”
“It has varying effects.” Goro offers.
“Oh, wonderful.” Futaba scoffs.
“The police haven’t been near my home in a few weeks.” Haru thankfully says before that
can escalate, “And if Sakura-san goes hunting for a safehouse of some kind, then it only has
to be for a few nights anyway.”
“Boss.” Sojiro corrects, “And, yeah, I was planning on it.”
“That sounds like it’s settled, then.” Yusuke hums.
So it does.
Ren shoves his hands in his pockets. “Then we’re done here.”
Sumire winces at the barely restrained fury. Goro just stares him down.
Sojiro sighs, and stands, back and knees audibly cracking as he does. “Another car ride,
then?”
Some of the other thieves that had snagged a seat begin to stand as well, muttering amongst
themselves as the meeting comes to a definitive close. Haru takes a moment to move from
where she’s standing next to Goro, a vague gesture from Sojiro apparently reminding her she
needs to move with them.
Sumire should probably go home too.
Probably.
(But, being stuck in an apartment with three people who are somewhere between livid and
generally upset with you can hardly be pleasant.)
She’ll let her parents know where she is. Or, adjacent.
“Mind if I stay over?” Sumire whispers to Goro, taking Haru’s place at his side.

He raises an eyebrow at her. “Whatever for?”
Sumire shrugs.
He raises his other eyebrow.
Sumire shrugs again.
He snorts. “Sure. But don’t you have school tomorrow?”
“I’ll leave early.” She decides.
Goro sighs. “I can’t stop you.”
He could, if he wanted. Sumire takes the comment as a thank you.
***
Sleepovers in the midst of everything else going to hell are a bubble of near-normality that
Sumire has grown to appreciate.
Perhaps her anxiety truly was unfounded. Argument aside, it’s all as resolved as it can be.
(But will it stay that way?
One of the stipulations they discussed not two days ago was that prolonged inaction could
contribute to Shido’s potential paranoia even more. Damned if they do and damned if they
don’t: the point is, they’re on a clock.
They need to deal with the Cleaner, fast, but they just don’t have the means to. They’re no
closer to discovering his identity, let alone making progress on what -with their luck- will
likely be a palace.
What can you do?
Another desperate thought creeps into Sumire’s mind. A vague notion that she had
smothered, when last faced with no other options.
She wouldn’t be making a deal. No, certainly not. And she was never the target of said deal,
anyway. Her acceptance or denial never really meant anything in the end.
But if she asked for help…
Could he even help?
Would he hold it over her?
No, she decides. Not in a traditional sense, at least, and she supposes that’s the dangerous
part.)
“So.” Goro says into the dark, clearly sensing she’s still awake, “Any grievances to air?”

Sumire sits up, tugging awkwardly on her borrowed clothes. She can kind of spot the glint of
Goro’s eyes at the opposite end of the bed. “I think Haru-senpai covered my bases, last time.”
Goro snorts. “Next time I do something foolish, would you like to come with me instead?”
“Next time?” She says, making a token effort to sound disappointed.
“It’s bound to happen again.”
Sumire can’t help a burst of giggles. “It might be nice. Let Haru-senpai come with us, too.
Make a trip out of it.”
Goro hums, sounding amused.
“Or.” She says, “You should bring Ren-senpai, so he can’t be mad at you this time.”
Goro grunts something unflattering.
“Or maybe he’d just try to stop you.” Sumire muses.
“Please.” Goro scoffs, “If he’s in on it, suddenly it’d be a necessary detour.”
Sumire supposes that sentiment would fly with the lot of them. She wondered when they
stopped being good at teamwork.
“…Do you really go to Shido’s palace so often?” She asks quietly.
A pause.
“Not often.” He protests.
“Often enough.”
“I suppose.”
Sumire sighs, “The Metaverse being gone once this is all over will stop that, if nothing else.”
“I’ll probably end up just being reckless in reality instead.”
“Please, don’t.”
Another pause.
“If I must.” Goro sighs.
Sumire smiles at the begrudging concession, unsure as to its honesty, “Thank you.”
“Don’t mention it.”
Sumire hums, and lies back down. With the curtains drawn and the lights off, it really is
nearly pitch-black in here.

“Good night.” She says.
“Night.” Is the tired response.
***
It’s been eight days.
Hardly a worrying stretch of time. But, a lot can happen in eight days, and the Phantom
Thieves have moved quickly in the past.
Goro Akechi has moved quicker. Masayoshi Shido supposes that if his son was gunning for
his head, it would already be rolling on the floor.
The thought isn’t comforting.
Perhaps there truly is another manifestation at the Diet Building? Kasukabe, the younger, was
always too much of an obvious puppet for Shido to ever bother sending Akechi after him, but
it wouldn’t surprise him if perhaps he had some hotspot of delusion centred on his place of
work. Could be his father, too.
Or not.
Shido clenches his jaw, casting an eye out the window. He stands, folding his arms.
He’s scoured all Wakaba’s journals. He’s beginning to feel he jumped the gun, in sending
Akechi to kill her off. Who knows? Maybe a month or more and she would have cracked the
veil to the cognitive world wide open.
Or maybe not. Her results were dwindling, in the sunset of her life. Shido could never tell if it
was greed, cold feet, or if she had truly discovered all there was to find. Her death was
inevitable, nonetheless.
And, still, the cognitive world remains stubbornly inaccessible, save for a few blips of data
on a chart. That particular discovery felt like the jackpot, snapping up his wayward son right
out of thin air.
And then he vanished, right out of his cell. The Cleaner hadn’t been thrilled to find his mark
missing. Understandable; Shido himself had wondered if the whole situation was a joke in ill
taste.
And even now, with pings appearing in pointed locations (and again at the Courthouse, for
some unknown reason) Akechi and the thieves themselves simply aren’t appearing. Wakaba
had written about some place— Mementos? —that wasn’t quite a palace, that couldn’t be
tracked via the same methods palaces could, spread far too thin. Perhaps they’re using that to
get away.
The question then remains as to why they didn’t just use that at the courthouse. A
coincidence? Bad luck? So much for the infallible iron jaws lining the ground where the
thieves may tread, if the one instance of them setting it off was simple clumsiness.

Shido scowls down again at the blinking lights of Tokyo.
He considers himself a calm man. As much as he can be, in his position. Stresses can be
smoothed over, urges alleviated in a myriad ways. He can keep his composure.
These thieves are putting his patience to the test.
He dutifully practices the tactics Wakaba devised to make a manifestation as obstructive as
possible. He reminds himself constantly of the mechanics of the Metaverse, hoping to
entrench his corner of it in so many unpredictable layers that any intruders can barely get past
the front door.
Then again, Wakaba likely tried to fortify her palace too. Only half out of suspicion, he’s
sure. Wakaba was ever-so-eager to turn herself into a maze for her lab rat. He wonders if she
thought that put her and Akechi on equal footing, somehow.
The point remains: her methods are not infallible.
Shido cuts a glance over to his liquor cabinet. It’s late enough in the evening that he doesn’t
feel the need to hold himself back from taking off the edge. He swiftly pours himself a glass
—whiskey, why not— and moves back to the window.
He ought to redouble his efforts in tracking down the thieves’ identities. They’re only
phantoms when they’re playing pretend. In the real world, bones are bones and flesh is flesh.
If Akechi tracked them down, Shido can too.
There’s that nagging feeling that Sakura knows something. Sakura didn’t quite retire while he
and Shido were on amicable terms; Shido’s sure that Sakura immediately suspected him of
having a hand in Wakaba’s death. Though, perhaps not. He made no move to act after the
fact, other than to take custody of the girl. Self preservation, or ignorance?
Any semblance of good graces that remained between them was surely dashed when Shido
sent the Cleaner off to have a chat with the man.
He takes a sip from his glass.
Not that he regrets the order, of course. If Wakaba squirrelled away anything of hers, she
would have left it with him. He’ll have to ransack his home and that café later. No stone left
unturned.
What can be done?
He should have cut these threads years ago. They’ve all become a royal thorn in his side. It’s
what he gets, he supposes, for making assumptions. That Wakaba had expended her use, that
the thieves were skittish cowards, that Sakura was going to stay out of his way, that Akechi
wouldn’t be swayed by the romanticism of thievery over some damn loyalty.
All far too much trouble than it’s worth.

Well, if those threads are more like chains, he ought to shatter the weak links while he has the
time.
He slips his phone out from his pocket, and types in a number not saved in his contacts. The
line goes through on the second ring.
“You want me to rough up Sakura properly this time, Boss?”
So eager. Shido appreciates such a simple monetary relationship. “Maybe later.” He says. “I
have a proper job for you, first.”
The Cleaner snickers, “Music to my ears.”
Shido wonders if he missed the business, in the years that Akechi was his favoured assassin.
It really is too bad. Shido had fun parading the kid around at meetings. It was downright
hilarious to see people slowly realise his mysterious attack dog was the skinny brat with a
plastic smile. Not that all of them had the brains to figure it out.
“You remember our mutual friend?” Shido asks.
“Gonna have to be more specific.”
His kingdom for some instinctive understanding from his subordinates. “The SIU director.”
“Ahh.” The Cleaner hums, “What, he piss you off?”
“He’s a nuisance.” Shido says, truthfully. The man was always plagued by delusions that they
were equals in any sense of the word.
“Whatever you say, Boss.” The Cleaner chuckles, “What’s the deadline?”
“As soon as you’re able.”
“If I must.” A sigh, “That’s gonna cost you more.”
Shido suddenly appreciates monetary relationships far less. “If I must.” He echoes.
“Good to hear, good to hear.” The Cleaner drawls, “You’ll be seeing the news by the
morning.”
The Cleaner did always have a faster turnaround than Akechi tended too, for the larger
targets. Bones are bones and flesh is flesh, he supposes.
“See to it.” He says, “You’ll be hearing from me soon.”
“Best thing I’ve heard all year.”
The line goes dead.
What can be done? He asks himself again.

Even the strongest of links can be cracked under the right pressure. All he has to do is apply
it.

The meeting yesterday was, Sojiro can say with confidence, the worst meeting he’s ever sat
through. He used to work for Shido, so he can recognise that’s saying something.
The whole thing was fairly innocuous until it wasn’t. He was stuck in the middle, for a
meeting that wasn’t even about him, flying furies and icy stares on all sides.
He had been under the apparently false assumption that the Okumura girl was the most
responsible of the group. His impression of the littler Niijima and even Yoshizawa too tainted
by tales of reckless missions into the cognitive world with little regard for the consequences,
not to mention panicked and messy attempts at timeline fixing that he doesn’t care to think on
for more than five minutes at a time.
Turns out Okumura is just as guilty of being a foolish teenager as the rest of them. Go figure.
Sojiro couldn’t muster up the will to be particularly angry. Sure, it’s apparently backfired on
him and his home, but he gets the feeling that was a ticking time bomb to start. His kids, on
the other hand, looked ready to commit murder.
He sensed they were more angry at Akechi, who seems to have a penchant for getting himself
and others killed, than Okumura, but the trip through Mementos to her fancy penthouse was
far from comfortable. Okumura’s request to drive was shut down with a stony I’m driving,
without so much as a glance her way. She had sniffed, and hadn’t bothered asking for
shotgun.
“I’ve had my staff on paid leave for the past few weeks.” Okumura had explained quietly
when they arrived. “And there are no security cameras inside the house- only pointed at the
front door and post box. So feel free to wander. I can set up the guest rooms.”
Sojiro had raised an eyebrow, “You have three guest rooms?”
Okumura had smiled faintly, “Two, technically. But you can take over my father’s room.”
Sojiro’s back decides that attempting to graciously demand he sleep on the couch instead
would be foolish. Hopefully, he’ll only be imposing for a day or two at most.
The frigid atmosphere hasn’t thawed in the slightest come the morning.
“We’ll stagger our arrival at school.” Ren says, over a breakfast of toast. Okumura’s kitchen
isn’t stocked enough at present for the usual curry, and Futaba’s been pouting about it all
morning. Morgana had happily accepted the canned tuna in the pantry, though he had turned
up his nose at first.
“Of course.” Okumura says primly. “When do you usually arrive?”
“Right before homeroom.” Morgana chimes in.

“Ah.” Her eyebrows twitch up, “We won’t have a problem arriving separately, then.”
“…We’ll hold down the fort.” Sojiro adds.
Okumura smiles, “Please do. Help yourself to anything you might need.”
Ren’s chewing gets pointedly louder. Sojiro would tell him to spit it out if he wasn’t
concerned it’ll be an insult thrown at their gracious host.
He doesn’t have to, in the end. “How dangerous was Shido’s palace, while you were there?”
Ren asks stiffly.
Okumura gives him a flat stare, “Well, we didn’t get past the deck.”
“Not even the front doors?”
“No.”
“Crow’s cognition was just hanging out there?” Futaba speaks up with a frown.
Sojiro fails to see the significance, but judging from Ren, Futaba, and the cat’s matching
confusion, he assumes it isn’t normal cognition behaviour. Or, maybe, it isn’t normal Akechi
cognition behaviour.
“He was right there, just as we entered.” Okumura confirms. “Where was he last time?”
“Bowels of the ship.” Ren explains, clipped. “Engine room.”
“Ah.” She tilts her head, “He was also drenched to the bone.”
“That’s new.” Ren comments.
“I gathered.” Okumura says, “He’d been tossed overboard, at some point. Multiple times,
apparently.”
Futaba snickers. Sojiro personally thinks the image is rather grim. Ren must think the same,
as his expression darkens further.
Okumura casts a glance at her phone, and stands, “It’s about time I start getting ready, I
think.”
Ren checks his phone as well, raising his eyebrows, “You could push it for an hour.”
“I arrive half an hour before homeroom.” Okumura says, “And I have to walk.”
“Oh.”
Okumura says nothing more to that, and strides off to get herself ready for school.
Sojiro sighs, and picks up his plate, “I’m gonna get to work.”

***
Getting to work involves a lot of stalling.
Stalling, meaning: thinking. Thinking about what angle to pursue, thinking about the risks of
each. Snapping up a safehouse isn’t the most difficult thing in the world, but the surrounding
irritation and dangers bloom given that he needs it quick and he needs it effective.
If he still worked for the government, and Shido by extension, getting one would barely be an
issue. Problem is that Shido would then know the location of said safehouse, which would
put a bit of a damper on his triumph.
Similarly, tugging on his old colleagues to lend a hand is an awful lot like playing roulette.
Not all of them worked for or around Shido, but it’s been two years. Any confidence Sojiro
had in them then is meaningless now. Getting sent a card at Christmas and new years doesn’t
mean they wouldn’t throw him to the wolves if required.
Asking won’t hurt, though. Mostly.
He should try a different tact, first.
Iwai and Ohya are options. He’s not convinced they’d be any help, but he’s reasonably
confident they’d be tight lipped. It’s something to consider.
The issue is, he can’t just buy a house. That would be absurd. He needs an already existing
space that someone has for express purposes such as hiding from people that want you dead
or want to burn down your café to prove a point. Things government workers have in spades,
and that journalists and model-gun-store owners are far poorer in.
Though, what does he know? Ohya’s been hunting dangerous leads, and Iwai’s ex-yakuza.
They could have contingency plans for when things go south.
Asking won’t hurt. He’s a little more convinced about the thought this time.
He isn’t quite sure what either of their work schedules are, but it’s just past noon. Perhaps
Ohya will already be drowning herself in beer and spirits at this hour. Iwai’s shop doesn’t
seem like he gets much business, but he’ll hold off for now.
He almost calls directly from his phone, before he decides that perhaps he should avoid
unnecessary risks. He’s useless with technology, so he isn’t really entirely sure if this is a
danger. Futaba won’t begrudge his questions, he hopes.
He knocks on the door to the room she’s claimed, “…Futaba?”
There’s a muffled: “Yeah?”
“Can I borrow your expertise?”
The door swings open, and Futaba is looking at him with a raised eyebrow, “…Whaddya
need?”

Sojiro almost laughs at how much she sounds like a shady vendor. “Is there any way you can
make a phone call… not traceable? Untrackable?”
“Oh.” Futaba shoves her glasses up her nose, “Easily. It’ll look real suspicious to whoever
you’re calling though.”
He can work with that. “That’ll do.”
Futaba snags his arm and drags him into her room, “Or, you could just get a burner. But I’m
guessing you don’t wanna deal with that?”
It’s been a while since Sojiro has been in need of burner phones. He wishes he had thought to
snap one up. “Well, I definitely don’t want to go outside.”
“We could take a trip through Mementos.” Futaba says, plopping down on a pillow on the
floor, next to her computer and a monitor she must have borrowed from Okumura, “Butlater. This is easier right now. You’ll have to use my computer though.”
“That’s fine.” Sojiro says, even as he internally holds a funeral for his knees for when he’ll
have to sit on the floor.
“Great!” Futaba says with some fanfare, typing away at a rapid fire pace, “What number are
you try’na dial? Or would you rather text?”
“Calling would be better.” Sojiro says, pulling out his phone. “And I’ve got her contact here.”
Futaba eyes the number, typing some more, “Cool. Here, sit down.” He does, with some
effort, “Press here to call, and here to hang up. Oh, and if you want to talk to someone else,
type in the number here, country code and all. All this is doing is basically making a call
from a number that doesn’t exist. Here are some headphones…” She snaps them over his ears
before he can protest. “And good. You need me to scram?”
“…You don’t have to.” Sojiro says, a bit lost, “But you might be bored just listening to me
talk.”
Futaba sticks out her tongue, “I’m gonna hang out in the living room.” She says, snapping up
her laptop, “Try not to blow anything up, Sojiro!”
He chuckles as she dashes out of the room, “I’ll try.”
He’s very grateful Futaba made the whole setup so simple, else he probably would blow
something up somehow. He readjusts the headphones, and presses the call button.
It only rings once before it declares that the number couldn’t be reached. Sojiro isn’t that
surprised- if this is dialling from an unknown number, it probably looks like a scam call or
worse. He tries again, twice, before it finally goes through.
“Who is this?” Ohya’s suspicious voice filters through.
“Hey.” He says, awkwardly, “It’s Sakura. Mind if I ask a favour?”

There’s a pause. “Ohhh.” Ohya eventually drawls, “It’s you! You pick up a burner or
something?”
“Something like that.” Sojiro agrees.
“Mm. What’s up?”
“You have anything resembling a safehouse waiting to be put to use?”
Another pause. “Jeez. The hell did you do?”
“Exist in Shido’s general vicinity for a portion of my life.”
Ohya snorts, “Rookie mistake. What happened?”
“Nothing. Yet.” Sojiro says with emphasis, “I’m not sticking around to let something happen,
specially with the kids.”
“Right.” Ohya’s tone sobers, “Amamiya all good?”
“He’s fine.” If not cursing the stars and all his friends, “Again, preventative measures.”
“Gotcha.” Ohya sucks in a breath through her teeth, “I’m not a stranger to needing a place
to camp out, exactly, but I’m usually the couch-surfing type. When I’m tracking a scoop far
from home, y’know? Even when I’m looking for safety, none of my go-to places are exactly
the height of security.”
“I see.” Sojiro frowns.
“Lala-chan might be able to hook you up, though.” Ohya continues, contemplative, “She’s
set up some places for some of the girls in the area, y’know? Nothing too fancy, but just a
place to get away. That’s if you’re willing to set up shop in Shinjuku, of course.”
“It doesn’t need to be fancy.” Sojiro assures her, “Just a place Shido won’t know about, or

Just when everything felt like it might have been finally settling into a new normal, Makoto
feels knocked off her axis once again.
Shows what she gets for feeling hopeful. Or for ever giving Akechi an inch of grace.
Shido’s palace, of all the places! She isn’t entirely sure what she assumed when Akechi had
been dodgy about where he ran off to, the night she caught him coming back. Mementos
would have been her first thought, but he would have just told her that.

She really should have expected this, in hindsight. It doesn’t help that she’s trapped in the
same damn house as him, so long as neither of them storms off to Mementos in a huff.
She’s trapped in the same house as Sae, too. What fun.
Makoto chews furiously on her lip, glaring daggers into Ann’s TV, not paying much attention
to the news. One of the few days she can snap up the living room in solitude and all she can
seem to do is stew.
You could give him a piece of your mind. Johanna comments, sounding almost amused of all
things, Her, too.
Oh, and Makoto wants to.
But she can see the writing on the wall. Any argument with Akechi is bound to go in circles
with accusations of hypocrisy quickly snuffing Makoto’s extremely valid complaints, and
they’ll both get nowhere.
(Any argument with Sae is bound to go the same way it did a few days prior. Makoto will
refrain.)
And it isn’t hypocrisy, really, when Makoto’s main complaint is that Akechi somehow
managed to make a right mess for everyone else. Even if the Sakuras’ being uprooted cannot
be attributed to a direct cause and effect, the fact remains that Shido’s palace, the palace
they’ve all been dreading, will now likely be markedly more difficult upon entry. Not to
mention the ever-present danger of being tracked down in reality that has now been
exacerbated.
But, a needling little voice hums, Your own excursion resulted in him tossing himself to the
wolves so you could get away.
Oh, fine, maybe it is hypocritical. That concession doesn’t change the fact that what Akechi
did was irrecoverably stupid. There’s no reason he couldn’t have been content terrorising the
shadows in the upper layers of Mementos.
There’s a part of her that dearly wishes she had just ratted him out days ago when she caught
him coming back, but she wonders if that really would have changed anything. Sumire was,
infuriatingly, right when she pointed out that there really isn’t much to be done but go
forward.
Spilt milk, under-bridge water, cold tea, et cetera. The TV continues to drone on, and Makoto
is still furious.
Maybe she should just punch him and be done with it. She’s been itching to for months at this
point. Assuming Ren doesn’t beat her to it.
“Some breaking news.” The news anchor announces with a grim expression, “The Tokyo
police have just announced the death of the director of the Special Investigations Unit-”
Makoto snaps back to attention.

“-Was found in the early hours of the morning in his office, shot to death. The police have
opened an investigation into the murder, and are offering a thirty-thousand yen reward for
anyone with information regarding-”
The SIU director was one of Shido’s. This, she remembers amidst the swirl of information
being dumped in batches. A small revelation, one that had surprised her for all of three
minutes, if only because that was her sister’s boss.
One of Shido’s, but clearly not important enough to warrant being named a part of his inner
circle. Certainly not important enough for Akechi to name him a part of Shido’s inner circle,
and thus not someone they had to concern themselves with.
And now he’s dead. In an entirely mundane way, as well. Bullets are certainly faster than
killing the manifestation of someone’s psyche, she supposes, even if Shido had the option
still available to him.
Makoto knows three things:
One: That it is almost certainly Shido that arranged this murder. She can hardly fathom
considering an alternative.
Two: With Akechi having long since turned traitor, the most likely culprit for the dirty work
of this operation would have to be Shido’s next favourite assassin. The Cleaner is brutally
efficient, it seems.
Three: With the above in mind, the trail may not yet have gone cold.
A lead.
A lead, and nothing more. Makoto’s spark of triumph is slightly doused at the sudden brick
wall. It’s not as though she can waltz onto the crime scene with a cardboard detective’s badge
and demand to investigate. And even then, what would she do? Employ forensics? With what
data to compare to?
Ah, right. She does know one more thing, as well:
This case will undeniably go cold in the hands of the police. Even without the late SIU
director’s fingers in the investigation, by way of his being the corpse in the equation, Makoto
has seen the list that Sae and Akechi have been filling out of the myriad confirmed
conspiracy members in the force. It would not be difficult for Shido to have those he wishes
assigned to the investigation, and that thirty-thousand yen reward is likely just for show.
So she supposes she can’t hope for the Cleaner’s name and face to be blared across the TV
screen with the announcement he’s been caught anytime soon, either. Nothing’s ever easy.
No forensics, no investigation, no convenience.
You have more than just that. Johanna points out.
That’s true.

If the Phantom Thieves will not be granted access to the physical, then the mental will have
to suffice. A trail is a trail, a path a path, and Makoto is as sick of sitting around as everyone
else.
She stands in a hurry, grabbing the first pen and wayward receipt she can get her hands on,
collapsing on the floor in front of the TV and coffee table in a huff, ready to take notes like
her life depends on it.
***
If there is a lesson that has been beaten into Sae’s head the last weeks, over and over, it is that
leaving things to fester and rot will always leave a stench of something foul.
She used to be rather good at ignoring it. Weigh the pros and cons: Makoto hates her, forever
bitter and resentful, and, yet, food will be on the table, bills paid, and Sae lauded as a rising
star in her career. She barely saw Makoto enough for it to even matter anyway. The answer to
her problems was to simply dig a deeper grave.
But now she’s been forced to breathe cleaner air, and the rotting smell is overpowering each
time it wafts her way.
Waiting for the perfect moment is a fool’s errand. The memory of golden lights set in her
own face, a mockery of her features, tsks and gives her a shove.
Don’t.
Makoto is probably busy. Sae shouldn’t bother her while things have so recently been turned
on their head yet againShe’s the one who reached out first. A stubborn memory hums.
—And all Sae had done in response was spit in the face of her grievances. The perfect
moment doesn’t exist, and Sae would wager that the moment grows steadily worse the longer
she leaves it be.
She stands from her bed with a huff.
Well, then.
She strides into the living room, and freezes in the entryway at the sight of Makoto furiously
scribbling on the back of a receipt, glaring craters into the TV.
Maybe the perfect moment doesn’t exist, but surely some are better than others. She sighs
internally. Too late now. If she turns back around she’ll end up losing her nerve for another
month at least. Possibly several. Likely several.
Sae clears her throat uncomfortably, still not daring to take another step forward.
Makoto’s head whips around, eyes narrowed and ready to unleash her fury on any
unfortunate soul fool enough to interrupt her. They flare wide after a beat, surprise dulling

anger, before they sharpen again.
“Sis.” She says, pointedly turning back to the TV. “I’m busy.”
Oh, the irony.
Sae stiffly moves to stand next to the couch, “What are you working on?”
“Cleaning up Akechi’s mess.”
Sae raises an eyebrow. She’s unsurprised at the venom, but, “I thought the general consensus
was that it was a mess that couldn’t be cleaned up?”
Makoto rolls her eyes, “All of this is his mess if you look hard enough.”
Arguably true, if fiercely uncharitable. Not like Sae can talk.
(With regard to the aforementioned mess, Sae can only muster up the energy to feel tired. She
can only really feel tired, in the days following her encounter with her shadow, but she
supposes that’s better than nothing.)
Sae isn’t really sure what to do with that, regardless. It’s not her job to bear the strain
between whatever the hell her sister and Akechi’s problem with each other is, despite the
nagging voice that tells her it is.
She presses her lips together, “…Do you have a moment?”
“I’m busy.” Makoto repeats.
Sae finally registers what’s on TV, “Watching the news?”
“The SIU Director was found dead this morning.” Makoto delivers the blow primly, clipped,
“I’m certain the Cleaner did it.”
Sae stares, then blinks, “He’s what?”
Makoto doesn’t dignify that with a response, her attention solely fixed on the droning of the
news host, firing off facts about the murder that she diligently records in a hasty scrawl.
Sae takes this as her cue to finally take a seat, a tad dazed.
“I thought you hated your boss.” Makoto comments.
“A bit.” Sae admits. She says nothing more.
Makoto shrugs, and lets it go.
Sae steels herself, and swallows, “We should talk, Makoto.”
“Should we.”

“Don’t be like that.”
Makoto inhales sharply, her knuckles turning white where she grips her pen, “I have things to
do.”
“How much information is that report really giving you?” Sae asks, eyeing the TV as it pans
over some vigil being held at the precinct.
Makoto tosses her pen down on the coffee table, crossing her arms with sharp frustration,
“Barely anything.”
Sae hums.
Makoto silently picks up the remote with resignation, powering off the TV with a click. She
turns to look at Sae fully, “What do you want, Sis?”
Ball’s in her court.
“I should apologise.” Sae begins, haltingly. She has to pry the words from her mouth, a bitter
aftertaste left in their wake.
“Should you.”
Sae remains unenthused at the confirmation that yes, this conversation is going to be grating
the whole way through. She takes another steadying breath, “Yes.”
Makoto stares, “And?”
“I went to see my shadow the other day.” Sae should probably get that out of the way.
Makoto gapes at her.
Maybe she shouldn’t have said anything. She decides in advance to not make the mistake of
ever mentioning it to Akechi.
“You—” Makoto stutters. After a beat of looking a bit like a fish, she throws up her hands
and shouts, “Ugh!”
Sae grimaces.
“Why?” Makoto demands.
Sae takes care to sidestep Akechi’s favoured batch of excuses. “…After we argued, I got in
my own head.” She pauses, “Literally, I suppose.”
Makoto rolls her eyes.
Sae’s grimace widens, “And… that’s about the sum of it.”
“Really.” Is the deadpan reply, pure exasperation overriding and shock that may have
lingered.

“Really.” Sae echoes.
Makoto crosses her arms, “And, what, that’s all you came here to say? And you couldn’t say
this when Akechi and Haru-san were fessing up?”
“No, I—” She pauses, willing herself not to snap. “I wanted to say that you were right.”
Makoto blinks. “Oh.”
Another pause.
“About everything?” She asks suspiciously.
“Most things.” Sae corrects.
“You were avoiding me.” Makoto accuses.
Sae breathes in sharply. No use in denying it- such things have long since served their
purpose. “Yes.”
“You admit you were obsessed with your work.” Makoto pushes.
Sae clenches her jaw, a defence on the tip of her tongue, ready to lash forward. She forces it
back down. “It’s not that simple, but… yes.”
Makoto scoffs, but continues, “You cared more about him than you did me.”
“No.” Not that.
Makoto throws up her hands, “Then, what? Why are you like this?”
A broad demand. “It wasn’t about…”
It wasn’t about Akechi, but that isn’t very true at all. Sae could twist it, say it wasn’t about
Makoto, but that isn’t true either.
There will never be a time where Sae is not in over her head.
“It was about both of you.” She finally says. “And me.”
Makoto scoffs, “No shit, sis.”
“Language.” Sae says reflexively.
Makoto glares at her.
Sae rolls her eyes, but backs down. “Nevermind. What I mean is that— well—” god, what
the hell does she mean? “How I feel about the both of you is complicated.”
“I could have told you that.” Makoto mutters.

“Sure,” Sae waves a hand sharply, “But I wouldn’t have listened. Not to you.”
Makoto eyes her, appraising, “…But you listened to yourself, I take it.”
Sae snorts, “I’m not convinced that thing was me.”
“Believe it.”
She’d rather do anything else. “Well, either way, I’m not going back, so it doesn’t really
matter.” She holds back the urge to fidget, “You’re right that I listened to it, though.”
A flash of curiosity sparks in Makoto’s eyes, “And what did it say?”
Sae presses her lips together. She roots through her confrontation with her shadow in her
memory, trying to find the words.
Words come easy. Words that she’s willing to share, however, are a different beast.
She sighs. “I don’t think I’ll ever be what you want me to be, Makoto.”
Makoto turns away sharply. “I just want my sister.”
She makes it sound so simple. “Well, I’m not very good at that.” Sae dearly wishes she was.
“And besides, you needed me to be a guardian too, and I’m downright bad at that.”
Makoto whips back around to glare at her. “I don’t need a guardian.”
Sae shoots her a look. “You’re a child. Of course you do.”
Makoto barrels on, ignoring that. “You were just fine at being my sister before Dad died.”
“Was I? Really?” Sae scoffs. “I didn’t have a job, then. Dad was always busy too, and you
don’t resent him for it.”
“That’s not—” Makoto stutters, her eyes going wide.
“You remember that time very differently than I do.” Sae grits out.
Makoto sneers, “Don’t turn this back around on me.”
Sae wants to argue. She feels venom creeping up her throat like bile, knives sitting at the
edge of her tongue. She holds it in.
She swallows, and takes a breath. “You’re right.”
Makoto scoffs, “Great.”
“This is what I mean, Makoto.”
“What?” Is the unhappy and petulant response, “That we’re doomed to never get along ever
again?”

“I didn’t mean that.” Sae mutters.
Makoto gestures violently, “Then, what? You can’t be my sister, I don’t want you to mother
me—”
“Then who will end up putting food on the table?” Sae demands, “Pay the bills?”
Makoto makes a frustrated sound between clenched teeth, “If it was really so much, then you
could have asked me to help.”
“You’re a child.” Sae repeats, “I can’t ask that.”
“And you resented me for it anyway.” Makoto says, cold.
Well. Sae can’t argue that.
Makoto looks away again, “Is that why you spend so much more time with Akechi? Because
he was doing something?” She laughs bitterly, “Had a fulltime job while juggling school and
TV appearances while I’m just a measly honours student?”
“…More like two fulltime jobs, I suppose.” Sae says, for lack of anything better to say.
“Oh, brilliant.”
Sae ignores the biting sass. “He was… easier to deal with.”
“Really.” Makoto deadpans.
“Comparatively.” Sae amends, “Back then, at least. But I barely even know how to be in the
same room as you anymore.”
Makoto is silent, her head tilting down.
“I think I want to get my own place after high school.” She eventually says.
Something in Sae’s gut twists. Well, that’s that then. She’s screwed all this up so badly that
her sister will be ditching her for greener pastures at the first opportunity. A rift too wide, the
bridge long since burned to ash.
“I don’t—” Makoto cuts off her spiral, clicking her tongue, “I don’t mean that…” She tries
again, “I think we’d get along better if we didn’t live together.”
Sae gives her a long look, knocked off kilter, “You think so?”
Makoto shrugs weakly, “Maybe. Half the problem is that you have to take care of me, right? I
can take care of myself. You don’t have to worry about me.”
“You shouldn’t rush.” She barely thinks before the words are out of her mouth, “You’re
young, and getting your own place while you’re still completing your studies is
complicated.”

Makoto rolls her eyes, “It all comes back to studying, doesn’t it?”
“It’s important.” Sae retorts, feeling a bit chastised.
Half a smile flickers at the edges of Makoto’s lips, “I know. But it’s not like I’m struggling.”
“University’s different.”
“I know that too.” Makoto sighs, “But I think I should try. Besides, it’s not like you’ll be
locking the door behind me after I leave, right?”
“Of course not.”
“Then it’s worth a shot.” She knits her fingers together, “It’s better than you hating me for
being another thing on your plate.”
Sae winces, “I never hated you, Makoto.” She never could.
“It sure felt like it.”
Another failure for the pile, then. She wonders how many other misconceptions she’s let stew
between those who are most important to her.
“It’ll be a while before that happens, anyway.” Makoto says, and Sae hates that she feels
she’s being comforted, “I might have to repeat my third year.”
For everyone’s sake, Sae hopes not. “You’ve been a near perfect student thus far. And you’ve
been keeping up with the school work even while you’re not in class.”
“Well, Shujin isn’t exactly the height of rationality, so.” Makoto huffs.
That’s true. There’s a part of Sae that wishes she had picked a different school, when
hurriedly scouting for a place after their father died and Makoto was set to graduate middle
school barely a few months after. That ship has long since sailed, unfortunately.
“…If you’re sure.” She finally concedes.
“I’m not.” Makoto admits, “But I want to. And I’ve been planning on it for a while, anyway.”
And what more can Sae ask for? A twenty-step plan for how she plans to navigate this
change in her life? It wouldn’t be remiss, she supposes, but even she can acknowledge what
constitutes a step too far.
Makoto eyes the abandoned note-taking receipt still sitting on the coffee table. She clears her
throat. “If that’s everything?”
It doesn’t feel like it should be all. The win scenario in Sae’s head involved a full
reconciliation, a complete sisterly re-bonding for everything they’ve missed, everything
they’ve left behind. Complete with hugs, joyful tears, and a family dinner to boot.

It was never going to be quite right. It wouldn’t have felt right if it was.
Sae can still try and go for the half mile. “What do you want for dinner tonight?”
Makoto stares, “Huh?”
“You heard me.”
The stare turns suspicious. “Right…” A pause, “…What’s in the fridge?”
“Don’t mind that.” Sae instructs, “Whatever you want, I’ll make.”
“You can’t get groceries.” Makoto points out.
“I’ll ask Takamaki.” Sae deflects. It does feel a bit in poor taste, to demand their gracious
host fulfill such a request, but surely she’ll understand.
Makoto must be thinking the same thing, by the look on her face, but she doesn’t comment.
“…Stirfry.” She says eventually.
“Just stirfry?”
Makoto shrugs, “I like the way you make it.”
Sae tries not to feel too proud. It’s hardly appropriate, when she hasn’t made it in over a year.
She nods, and stands, “Stirfry it is.”

Chapter Summary

Bold plays and mystery solving
