Sumire cannot for the life of her tell how many of her thoughts are catastrophising and how
much is rationalisation.
Her plan is, by definition, extremely foolish. But she also has an inkling that it might be
something resembling clever, and that the consequences are not as destructive as one might
immediately assume. Besides, while the thieves traipse down a path filled with endless
roadblocks, what other choice does she have than to be a bit reckless?
That sounds like something Ren would say. That sounds like something Goro would say.
Sumire starts wondering if this is a terrible idea after all.
Too late to back down. Or rather, she’s already come all this way, and turning back now
would leave a sour taste of defeat in her mouth.
Now she really sounds like Goro.
Well, in for a penny.
Sumire knocks quickly, thirteen times in rapid succession, on the door to Doctor Maruki’s old
practice. She isn’t sure if he still offers sessions, but she’s pretty sure he also lives here, which
is both a bit funny and kind of sad.
She’s about to go for knock number fourteen before the door swings open, revealing one
harried looking and vaguely panicked Takuto Maruki.
Sumire is struck by the sudden and certain revelation that this is definitely a bad idea. But
now that the Doctor has seen her, she also knows that all she can do is lie down in the grave
she’s dug.
Why him? Ella asks with some distaste, like she doesn’t already know, and like Sumire isn’t
asking herself the same question despite it all.
The three following things are true:

One, while Maruki had access to the depths of Mementos as its newly crowned god; he, his
persona, and the unique implements within his palace were able to scour the depths for
knowledge about its residents. Its residents, Sumire assumes, including anyone who has ever
had a connection to the collective unconscious. Which is to say: everyone.
Two, Maruki is the type to be helpful to a fault. A martyr. Sumire doesn’t plan on asking for
anything so dramatic, but she feels she can be certain he will help her if she asks.
Three, is that he’d damn well better help her, because Maruki certainly owes her.
Sumire adds an addendum to her knowledge of three things.
Four, she has no idea how much this version of Takuto Maruki knows about Mementos and
the Metaverse in general.
That might be problematic.
Clearly he knows something, if he’s already awakened to his persona enough to use it. Not to
mention his shadow, which knows far too much. Though Sumire isn’t sure if she wants to
poke the sleeping bear in that regard.
Though surely said bear is going to wake up at some point no matter what she does, right?
Given recent events, though, she certainly doesn’t want to be the one to wake it up early.
“Yoshizawa-san?” Maruki gapes at her.
Right, yes. The grave she dug. She should probably get comfortable.
“Um.” Bad start. “Hello, Doctor.”
Maruki blinks, quickly rubbing at his eyes underneath his glasses, like he thinks he’s seeing
things. “Uh.” Bad start for him, too. “Yes. I— it’s been a while?”
Sumire thinks of when he came to speak to Haru on the roof. “Not that long.”
“Well,” Maruki stumbles over his words again, “I meant— since you’ve been here.”
That’s true. Sumire in this timeline only had about three sessions before the weight of a year
lost came crashing on her mind. She’s been doing moderately well at avoiding the man ever
since, though her track record at avoiding his private practice and the nurse's office is far
more successful.
“It has.” She comments, wringing her hands. “…Can I come in?”
Maruki nearly falls over, leaping back from the door. “Of course! Um— it’s a bit messy— I
haven’t reopened since I left Shujin, actually-”
Sumire tunes him out, taking in the sight of the cramped lobby. It’s familiar, but not too
familiar. Even in the original 2016, she only came here about two extra times before moving
most of her sessions to Shujin’s nurses’ office for convenience.

“—Sort of between jobs. I’ve been trying to finish my paper still, actually…” Maruki
suddenly trails off with a nervous laugh, “…But you don’t need me dumping all that on you.
My apologies.”
All told, that small faux pas is probably at the bottom of Sumire’s list of grievances.
“…I’m technically not open.” Maruki adds, when Sumire stays silent. “But, if you came all
this way for a session, then I’d be happy to—”
“No.” Sumire blurts. “No, I’d really rather not.”
Maruki gapes, before mumbling, “I… sort of expected that.”
So he does notice when he’s getting the cold shoulder.
“I don’t need therapy.” Sumire declares, and she tries not to begrudge Maruki’s poorly
concealed dubious look, “But I do need your help.”
Maruki blinks, “I see…” he coughs, “Well, I’d be happy to help you, of course, Yoshizawasan. Just… if you aren’t here for counselling, then I’m really not sure what I’d be helping you
with?”
“You have other skills.” Sumire points out, a bit confused.
“None that your friends don’t also share, I’d think?” Maruki clarifies, looking sheepish.
Technically, he’s correct. On a broad level, at the very least. With some tedium, the thieves
could scour Mementos for answers, interrogating shadows to pry for their knowledge. But
given that they don’t even know where to begin, and that Maruki’s particular skill set is far
more targeted, this is the best option.
…It really does still feel like rationalisation.
Can Maruki even do this stuff consciously? Now, before his persona is fully formed?
“…There’s something you can do that no one else can.” Sumire toes the waters carefully.
Maruki looks taken aback, laughing uncomfortably, “News to me!”
Sumire realises yet another problem in her plan.
Goodness, they’re piling up.
The snark is unnecessary. Nevertheless, the problem is that this conversation is most certainly
going to be a dance of the two of them trying to figure out how much the other knows.
Sumire presses her lips together, “…Ren-senpai mentioned your research to me once.”
Maruki’s eyes widen, “He did? Well!” A slightly baffled laugh, “He did seem interested, um,
months ago— before he started avoiding me.” He trails off.

Sumire coughs politely into her hand.
“…Or maybe I’m overthinking it.” Maruki adds.
“Probably.” Sumire says, avoiding eye contact.
“Yes, probably.” He agrees, not sounding particularly convinced, “Um, what did he say?”
Sumire doesn’t have a clue what Maruki has told Ren in the past. “Oh…” She hums, “Stuff.”
“Stuff?”
“Mhm.”
Maruki waits for her to elaborate. Sumire physically can’t, so she doesn’t.
Does he already know who the thieves are? Sumire can’t remember. Surely Ren wouldn’t
have told him, this time around. But making assumptions has bitten her before, so.
“The election’s soon.” She blurts.
Maruki’s expression darkens, “It is.”
“I can’t vote, but…” Sumire curses herself for stating the obvious, “Um, what are you
thinking?”
He laughs tightly, “Well, it’s how it always is, you know? No one ever looks particularly
appealing.”
Sumire barely knows who the other candidates are. Someone named Kasukabe seems Shido’s
biggest contender, from memory. “Everyone seems pretty thrilled about Shido.”
“Ah.” Maruki fidgets, “How do you feel about him?”
“I really don’t like him.” Sumire says frankly.
He looks relieved, “Me neither, honestly. We’ve never met, but…”
“Similar circles?” Sumire offers. She’d be surprised, if she didn’t already know.
“Yes!” Maruki nods, “That.”
Sumire hums.
After a moment, Maruki looks baffled again, “Uh… so, is the election relevant, or…?”
Well, if she doesn’t give him anything to work with, then this won’t go anywhere.
“A bit.” She admits.
Some shock. “Oh?”

“Well, more relevant to Shido, specifically.” Sumire tugs at her ponytail.
The shock melts into something that might be dread, “…Oh?”
Sumire quickly folds her hands together when she accidentally snaps a strand of hair. “I need
information.”
Maruki stares, “And… you think I can get it for you?”
“Well you’re good at…” hm. “Swaying people’s hearts. So I wondered if you were any good
at reading them, too.”
Maruki suddenly looks very pale. “Um.”
Sumire waits.
Maruki coughs. “Uh— yes. Right. So. …You?”
She picks at her nails.
“…Did Amamiya-kun tell you this?”
“Personal experience.” Sumire says tightly.
Maruki puffs out his cheeks, “Okay. Yes —ha— I was wondering if you… noticed? I mean, I
would have sounded crazy if I asked if you remembered what your name is, and just plain
rude if I pretended I didn’t remember, and it was pretty clear you were going by Sumire,
rather than—”
“Yes,” Sumire snaps, “I noticed.”
“Yes.” Maruki echoes. “That makes sense.”
This is a mess. Sumire suddenly wishes she had dragged Haru or Goro into this, if only for
their sharp tongues. They probably would have turned such a blade on her, if she told them
her plan, though, so it’s really for the best she’s left them in the dark.
For now. The cat will come out of the bag eventually. Preferably when Sumire can come to
them with a side of results to soften the blow.
Do not pull the punches of your conviction.
Ah.
Sumire has a moment of clarity.
There is no way to reason with a man like Takuto Maruki. His ideals are too solidified in
grief and folly, no cracks to wedge things like logic and opposing pathos inside. He will
always stand at the thieves opposition come the day where he gains the power to do so.

But, at least for now, their goals align. And while their goals align, the doctor cannot be so
easily swayed. Sumire doesn’t think she’s wrong to seek his help when all other options are
exhausted.
Perhaps she’s just as foolish as she’s ever been, just as foolish as Goro and Haru for their
most recent sojourn into enemy territory, but she’ll scrape something out of this whether
Maruki wants her to or not.
Ren will surely be furious, but he’ll live. Sumire finds that she doesn’t care much.
“Since we’re on the same page.” She straightens her back, making an effort to look Maruki in
the eye, “I want your help.”
Maruki goes to say something, and Sumire cuts him off.
“You won’t be turning any of your abilities in my direction.” She ought to get this out of the
way, “Whatever you think is best for me.”
Maruki stutters, “I— that was never my—”
Yes, his intent was more than pure. There was a time when Sumire had found it within herself
to be genuinely grateful, even just a day before everything had turned on its head. That time
has long past, and she no longer has the space beyond the knots in her chest.
“That’s my first condition.” Sumire interrupts. “The next is that this stays between us.”
“Well, if it’s dangerous, then—”
“You’ll understand why this has to stay private in a second.” She brushes him off, and he
shuts up. Her hands are shaking, “Do you agree?”
Maruki gives her a long look. He chuckles, “You really don’t like me very much.” He
comments, “You must be desperate, to come to me then.”
Sumire gives no affirmative.
Maruki nods, solemn, “I agree to your terms.” He blanches, “Um— unless you’re asking me
to harm someone? I think that’s a good line to draw.”
“Do you mind indirectly harming Shido?” Sumire asks blithely.
“Well indirectly isn’t so bad.” Maruki says immediately, ever the master of the loophole.
“Great. Because you’ll be doing that.”
“Right.” He coughs. “Uh, more specifically, what exactly do you want me to do?”
“I really just need information.” Sumire tries not to fidget, “A name. Someone Shido hires to
do jobs for him.”

Maruki blinks, looking a bit in over his head, “And— you think I can get this information?
And— why do you need it?”
“I know you can get this information.” Sumire insists. She’ll let him draw his own
conclusions about the second question. The solution to being a terrible liar is to just not
speak.
Maruki gives her a dubious look, “…Something to do with,” he falters, “Ah, what I did to
you?”
“That’s the one.” Sumire says dully.
“Right.” Maruki presses his lips together, “Yoshizawa-san, I’ll be honest, I really don’t know
how to help you.”
“You can.” She tells him, finally injecting some determination into her voice, “What you do
to people— it’s different, but in the same… realm.”
“And… you know this.”
Sumire nods furiously.
He must sense some truth to her words, given he hasn’t dismissed her entirely just yet. “If
you’re certain…” He mutters, “But, before that. Can I ask, are you a member of the Phantom
Thieves?”
Hm. Sumire presses her lips together.
Maruki seems spurred on by her silence. Maybe she should have tried for a lie after all. “And,
are Amamiya-kun, Sakamoto-kun, and Takamaki-san also members?”
Sumire grimaces.
Maruki lets out a breathless chuckle, “I thought so! Ah— sorry, you’re probably wondering
how I knew, yes?”
Well, yes. “A bit.”
“I saw the three of them— well, I think they must have been exiting a cognitive manifestation
of some kind. They just,” He makes a poof sound, “Out of thin air! And if you’re a member
too, I can probably guess who else is…”
Sumire would really rather he didn’t, but she supposes she can’t exactly stop him. Doesn’t
mean she has to sit through it, though. “Back to the matter at hand?”
Maruki nearly chokes, “Ah- yes. Sorry. It’s just nice to get confirmation. I wasn’t sure if I
was going crazy.”
Sumire can understand that at least. “So you will help me?”

“I said I would.” Maruki nods, “But, again, it might not be a matter of want.”
“You can figure it out.” He has before.
Maruki still looks a bit sceptical. “Right… I’m sure. Though, um, are you able to be a bit
more specific? I think I’m being set up for failure if I don’t know who to look for alongside
not knowing how.”
Sumire blinks. Right, whoops. “A yakuza assassin.”
“A what?!”

There’s a sense of serenity that comes with having nothing better to do.
If life were not so turned on its head, Akechi thinks he would have been in prime position to
do something about their little problem with the Cleaner. Such as potentially meeting him
face to face, if luck were on his side.
Which it rarely is, so perhaps the thought is moot.
The SIU director is dead now, of course, and the knowledge should probably bring Akechi
some vague sense of unease. He can’t really bring himself to feel anything about it now, and
all he offered the news as he saw it was a dubious raised eyebrow. Funny, that Shido was so
desperate to get rid of the man that he resorted to far messier methods for lack of a mental
shutdown. Maybe that should have been Akechi’s route to tracking down the Cleaner.
Hypotheticals are hardly ever useful, though, and Akechi remains with nothing better to do.
Nothing better to do beyond wandering the surface layer of Mementos, that is.
There’s a certain serenity to this place, too. A commodity which he is rarely granted, even if
it comes with a veneer of falsehood he is all too happy to ignore.
Limbo has bled into hell, and Akechi deserves to take a damn walk.
“Your pose was better five steps ago.”
Akechi closes his eyes.
Yusuke Kitagawa was not the person he expected to run into here, but he supposes he should
have expected it, if only because he really ought to start expecting the unexpected. So much
for serenity.
The man in question is sitting dead centre in the scramble crossing, an easel and palette stood
in front of him.
What are you doing here dies on Akechi’s tongue. The answer should be obvious even
without the visual cue.

“How long have you been painting me?” He demands instead.
“I haven’t started.” Kitagawa admits. “I was painting the city, but your presence adds
something to the composition I quite enjoy.”
Of course. “I’m not going to pose for you.”
Kitagawa frowns, “Can you not be convinced?”
“No.”
“A shame.” He sighs, “Well, unless you have other business, you are welcome to join me.”
Akechi raises an eyebrow, “In painting?”
“If you wish, but simply your company will suffice if not.” Kitagawa turns back to the
skyscraper landscape, haloed in red, and dabs some more paint onto his brush.
You do have nothing better to do. Robin points out.
An irritatingly correct statement. Surely even wandering aimlessly would be a better use of
his time?
It wouldn’t, Akechi answers himself before one of his personas gets the chance to quip
something snarky, rolling his eyes as he wanders over to stand behind Kitagawa.
Kitagawa smiles at him briefly, before refocusing on his canvas. The painting is as
technically skilled as Akechi expected, depicting the cityscape in effortless detail, all bathed
in that dull red of Mementos.
What really draws his eye, though, is the sky. Kitagawa has brushed it in swirling reds and
blacks, a spillage of a silvery miasma in its centre; a distant star absent from the true scene
before them.
“I have painted Mementos before.” Kitagawa comments as Akechi takes in his work,
“Though it was in the tunnels, as Ren escorted me. Just a sketch, lest shadows and the reaper
accost us.”
“No such trouble up here.” Akechi hums.
“Exactly.” Kitagawa nods, “And I admit I feel I limited myself in fixating on the
underground. I had dismissed the upper level as an exact reflection of reality, and not worth
my time.”
“I take you changed your mind.”
“Obviously, yes.” Kitagawa huffs a laugh, “I haven’t yet managed to extrapolate a
meaningful difference in the buildings, but the sky does captivate me.”

Akechi looks up, tilting his head. When he first stumbled into Mementos, all those years ago,
the sky had made him dizzy with vertigo from its constant movement. Learning that he had
not yet escaped the hell he had assumed was limited to the tunnels until he figured out that
his phone was the source may have contributed, as well.
“It’s certainly different.” He comments.
“And yet you find no meaning in it?”
“No.” Akechi admits, “If meaning is not immediately obvious in the Metaverse, it’s rarely
there at all.”
“I didn’t take you for someone to only examine things on the surface level.” Kitagawa tears
his eyes away from his work to instead study Akechi.
Akechi scowls, “You apply observations on a broader scale than you should.”
Kitagawa’s face scrunches, looking chastised. “Ah… that is a habit of mine.” He picks up a
palate knife, mixing acrylics together, “I have dragged Ren out on a fair few adventures in the
past. Every time I thought I was coming close to understanding some universal truth of
beauty, I was soundly proven wrong.”
Akechi raises an eyebrow, “You believe art’s foremost purpose is to be beautiful?” It isn’t a
philosophy he expected from Kitagawa.
“In a sense.” Kitagawa nods, “But that beauty can be found in many things is something I’ve
learnt as well.”
So, a nothing statement. Typical of an artist, Akechi supposes.
“The Sayuri was my muse for a very long time.” Kitagawa continues. “When I thought it
painted by Madarame, I tended to forgive him for a lot of things. No man who created
something so beautiful could be entirely awful.”
“A foolish thought.”
Kitagawa huffs, a grimace twisting his lips. “Apparently so. And it turns out Madarame never
even painted it to start.”
“Who did?”
“My mother.”
Ah. Akechi swallows.
Kitagawa shoots him a look, though not one Akechi can read, “I did try to tell you we had
much in common, once.”
Akechi scoffs, “What? By virtue of having mothers?”

Kitagawa frowns, “Well, if you insist on putting it like that.”
This remains a discussion Akechi doesn’t care to have.
“Anyway.” He deflects, and eyes the scenery again, “…You find this place beautiful?”
“I often find the human heart a beautiful thing.” Kitagawa smiles, “Why would the
combination of many of them not also be beautiful?”
“Because usually the culmination of human hearts results in a shitty subway.” Akechi
deadpans.
Kitagawa sighs, “I admit I had a rather… flat view of this place, at first.” He adds another
stroke, “I found human desire to be fascinatingly ugly. Tainted and impure, while the Sayuri
stood as a paragon of virtues.”
“Even more idiotic than your last folly.” Akechi drawls.
“I wouldn’t say that.” Kitagawa hums lightly, “I was still wrong, of course.”
“And are you right, now?”
“Perhaps not.” Kitagawa shrugs, “But maybe I am.”
“So you don’t know.”
“I suspect I never will.” Kitagawa sighs, “The time I’m most confident in any given truth is
often when there is something lurking around a corner to prove it false.”
Akechi is sick of standing. He lowers himself to the ground, cross-legged, leaning his chin
against his hand. “And so you come here, to hunt for universal truths.”
“Something like that.” Kitagawa dismisses.
Akechi rolls his eyes.
Kitagawa busies himself spreading some more paint, brightening the added star in the sky of
his canvas, before he speaks again. “Tell me, what did Maruki’s reality look like?”
Akechi blinks, back straightening in surprise.
“I’m curious.” Kitagawa adds, when Akechi takes too long to respond.
Well, that erases Akechi’s first question of why the hell do you want to know. “…Like
Tokyo.”
“Obviously.” Kitagawa scoffs, “He did not manufacture a complete fantasy land. The
specifics, please.”
“Well, it was January.” Akechi intones flatly, “So it snowed, every so often.”

Kitagawa shoots him an exasperated look. “Specifics.”
Akechi drags a hand down his face, wondering why he’s even bothering indulging this.
Kitagawa is strange and incomprehensible on the best of days; meeting his wavelength for
even a short chat should be cause for alarm, frankly. “Everyone smiled too much. It was the
dead of winter, but the sun always shone a bit too bright.”
Kitagawa whips a hand out to snatch a sketchbook that had been resting on his easel, nodding
vigorously as he pulls a pencil from behind his ear. “Continue.”
Akechi sighs, “I said it snowed- and it did -but never like it should. It was too…” he clicks
his tongue, “Gentle. Never any ice to slip on under the piles of it.”
“I see.” Kitagawa mutters, furiously making marks across the page.
“His palace was mostly white.” Akechi continues, “Excluding Eden at the top.” And the
thrice-damned light puzzles.
Kitagawa blinks, “Eden? Is that a moniker you’ve granted the place, or one inherent?”
“Inherent.” Akechi snaps. “The whole palace was exceedingly biblical.”
“Fascinating.” Kitagawa murmurs, “Maruki’s psyche is a wealth of inspiration, it seems. I
look forward to seeing it in person.”
Theoretically, there’s nothing saying Maruki will become a problem in the future. Though,
who is Akechi kidding with that. “I don’t.”
“A pity.” Kitagawa remarks, “But I suppose you’ve seen it before.”
Died there, too. “More than I care to recall.”
Kitagawa hums, narrowing his eyes at his hasty sketch. Akechi hauls himself to his feet to
take a look. It’s about as abstract and inscrutable as he expected.
“So.” Akechi says, leaning back so he isn’t looming, “Are you here on a break, or is this your
way of hunting down the Cleaner?”
“A break.” Kitagawa says shortly, “Do you truly believe I of all people am capable of
tracking this man down?”
Akechi remembers stalking the thieves in the finals stretch of Shido’s palace, so he knows
that Kitagawa is, at the very least, capable of distracting the Cleaner, cognitive double aside.
Actually tracking him is another matter, and he does have to admit that Kitagawa is on his list
of least likely candidates to get them out of this bind. “No, I suppose not.”
“Exactly.” Kitagawa sniffs, and adds a halfhearted dab of paint to his canvas, “I’m surprised
you’re here, though.”

Akechi sincerely doubts that, given how unbothered the man was upon their meeting. “I have
nothing better to do.”
“Then we’re all out of ideas, it seems.”
Now that is an unfortunate truth. Akechi is half tempted to declare they all just give up on the
Cleaner, just to get Shido’s palace finished and out of his damn mind, but, well,
There’s so much risk. So much hinging on luck, that if there’s even the possibility they’re
saving themselves by doing the heavy lifting now, then it might just be worth it.
“What are you thinking?” Kitagawa asks without turning around.
“That I’m starting to think like Ren.” Akechi replies bitterly. Too much caution, and an
unfortunate bundle of hope that’s lodged itself in his chest. It would be far less work if he
didn’t care what happened at the end of it all.
He’d like to say he doesn’t, but dammit, dammit, he does.
Kitagawa chuckles, “For better or worse, perhaps.”
Akechi snorts. “Definitely for worse.”
(The Hanged Man hums a pleased melody, neglected for so long, and grows to its fifth rank.
Akechi weaves it in with everything else he’s tried to ignore, and wonders when this will all
pay off.)
***
Despite feeling marginally less scattered, Ren still isn’t entirely sure where to go from here.
He’d say the unfamiliarity of Haru’s penthouse apartment isn’t helping, but he knows that’d
be grasping for excuses.
Maybe combing Mementos is really their only option. It’s not impossible, per se, just tedious.
His phone rings.
He half expects Futaba to be calling him, despite her being in just the room over, or, hell,
even Goro, but he cocks his head in surprise as he sees Makoto’s name flash on his screen.
“Hello, Ren.” Makoto says crisply as soon as Ren picks up the phone.
“Hey.” Ren flops back on his bed, “This a social call or something else?”
“Something else.” A pause. “I… might have an idea for a lead.”
Ren sits up. “Oh?”
“Well, it’s nothing so solid.” Makoto admits, “Just an idea, but it is a start. I figured since
the SIU director was murdered, we-”

“He was what?”
Another pause, more pointed this time. “Do you… not watch the news?”
“Not often.” Ren mutters.
“I suppose that explains why you haven’t heard.” Makoto clicks her tongue, distracted,
“Well, I suppose you’ll hear it from me: The SIU director was found dead in his office
yesterday, and the police are supposedly investigating it.”
“The Cleaner killed him.” Ren clocks immediately.
“That’s the assumption I’m working with.” Makoto agrees. “The people on the investigation
are probably Shido’s too, so I was thinking,” she sighs, “Oh, I don’t know- maybe that they’ll
know something, or they’d have interacted with the Cleaner’s subordinates, and that we
could start chasing a lead that way.”
It’s a good lead. Which, of course, is relative, as it’s better than the nothing Ren had before.
It does still boil down to combing through Mementos, though. Ren’s nerves have not been
saved by Makoto’s timely intervention.
“If it’s all we have, we may as well chase it.” Ren declares, “I’ll get Futaba on getting the
names of the people on the investigation, and we can start hunting them in Mementos.”
“Great.” Makoto sounds relieved, “I’m glad we can finally start doing something. I think I’m
going stir crazy.”
Ren snorts, “You aren’t the only one, I hear.”
“I noticed.” She says drily. “See you.”
“Bye.” He responds, and the line goes dead.
Ren sighs as he shuffles with little dignity out of his bed, opening the door to the hall to track
down Futaba.
On the way to the living room, Morgana spots him and starts trotting next to his feet. “What’s
up?”
“Trying to find Futaba.” Ren explains.
“I think she’s in the living room.” Morgana rolls his shoulders slightly, “Haru’s there too.”
Ren tries not to grimace. He’s reached a truce with Goro, though he doesn’t care to have a
repeat of the conversation with Haru for a multitude of reasons. He figures dropping the cold
shoulder might be enough to settle the matter, though he isn’t entirely confident.
His pondering is cut short as he enters the living room, giving an awkward nod to Haru and
Futaba as he does, despite the latter’s nose being buried in her laptop. Morgana leaps into

Haru’s lap, and she giggles slightly, giving him a scratch behind the ears.
She meets Ren’s eyes, and her mirth cools, “Ren-kun, is there something you need?”
Makes sense he has to work harder than that. Nothing in life is easy. “From Futaba, mostly.
But—uh—hi.”
Haru looks vaguely bemused. Ren misses when he was smooth.
…Were you ever smooth? Metatron asks dubiously. Arsène snorts somewhere in Ren’s mind,
clearly eager to respond, and Ren pushes the both of them down.
Futaba whistles, “O-kay, moving on, whaddya need?”
“Makoto has an idea.” Ren says.
Haru tilts her head, “For tracking down the Cleaner?”
Ren nods, and Morgana narrows his eyes, “What’s she thinking?”
“Well.” Ren shoves his hands in his pockets, “Apparently the SIU director got murdered.”
Futaba hums, and types away at something, “Yeah, I did see the news on that. Probably the
Cleaner, right?” She types some more, before freezing over her keyboard. “Ooo! Does Queen
want me to track down the goons that are supposed to be investigating?”
“Bingo.” Ren snaps his fingers at her, “Can you do it?”
“Can I do it, he says.” Futaba mocks. “Of course I can.”
Haru looks between them, eyes wide and rapt with attention, “You think we can track him
down with just that?”
“No.” Ren says, and Haru frowns, “We’ll have to go subway diving with whatever Futaba

Haru sighs, slumping slightly, “I see…”
“Shido can’t toss us a freebie, huh?” Morgana complains, eyes squeezing shut as he yawns.
“Not in his dictionary, I don’t think.” Ren quips. Like father like son, he thinks for a beat
before crushing the thought somewhere it’ll never see the light of day again.
“It’s no fun if it’s free.” Futaba says; which is a blatant lie, but Ren appreciates the attempt at
enthusiasm. “I’ll get started on that.”
“How long will it take?” Morgana hops out of Haru’s lap to squint at Futaba’s laptop.
Futaba shrugs, “A day, if I’m lucky? Maybe more.”
Ren presses his lips together, but nods anyway.

They have less than a month, by now. It’s doable, but only if they start doing sooner rather
than later. It might be the time to stop acting like they have days to spare.
More to the point: it might be time for riskier plays.
Like what?
Ren doesn’t know. He doesn’t want to know, so he doesn’t have to consider playing them.
The thought of it unwinds a spool of dread in his gut, razor sharp and entirely convinced that
nothing is going to go their way.
“Make all this your top priority.” He tells Futaba. “The sooner we find something, the sooner
we can finally get this palace cleared.”
“Or, he’ll be a scrub in Mementos.” Futaba says, already typing away.
Haru snorts in blatant disbelief.
***
Perhaps it’s time to start making moves.
No one has ever accused Shido of being an idle man, but it’s difficult to act against a target
one cannot see. If the thieves are not going to make a move, then Shido will simply have to
do so himself. He’s not so arrogant to lay claim to a throne without checking if there are
assassins lurking at its back.
There’s a question that should have been solved months ago. That being: who are the
Phantom Thieves?
Children, to start. Akechi is one of them too, so that’s one down and who-knows to go.
Perhaps he’d have a more accurate look at how much work he’s setting himself up to do this
evening if anyone in his employ was even the slightest bit competent. A number would have
been nice.
Something he and anyone with a brain deduced months ago is that they’re Shujin students,
almost certainly. Some of them, at the very least; there would be no reason for their first
target to be Kamoshida otherwise. Why would they know of him, or care, if they weren’t the
victims themselves?
And thus, the first dead end. He recalls the SIU director had the principal of that school
conduct investigations into the student body, which predictably turned up nothing. And
naturally now they’re both dead, Shido can’t ask anything in the way of clarifying questions.
Shido clicks his tongue, and spins in his chair to face the window. God forbid children be
easy to catch.
He swipes open his phone, typing in a number, and waiting for the line to click through.
Only one ring. Must be a slow day. “Something up, Boss?”

Sasaki sounds worried. For himself, most likely. It isn’t often Shido rings him out of the blue.
“I need a favour. How far did your lot get in investigating Shujin with regard to the Phantom
Thieves?”
There’s a pause. “Not… that far.” Sasaki starts, placating.
“I don’t care.” Shido cuts him off, “All I need is the reports.”
“Then you’ll get them.” Sasaki catches on. “Only be a moment, Boss.”
“Good.” Shido snips, and hangs up.
To Sasaki’s credit, it does only take a moment for an email from a burner address to appear in
his inbox. Lists and summaries of the ongoing and thoroughly stalled investigation, all
complied for perusal.
Efficient, yet not enough to make this less tedious. A shame, but expected.
And so he reads,
And reads,
And reads.
Shido can conclude three things:
The first: the one that jumped out at him, the one that intrigues him most, is that Makoto
Niijima has been absent from class ever since the chaos with Akechi’s arrest and subsequent
escape. Sae Niijima, notably, was the last person to see Akechi in his cell while still in
custody, and was quick to vanish off the face of the map in the aftermath. Perhaps the state of
the kid made her pity him, or dredged up some compassion for criminals that was
conspicuously absent beforehand, or hell, Akechi just changed her heart.
If her younger sister was not aware of the thieves and their activities beforehand, she
certainly is now.
The second: There are at least three students that stick out like a sore thumb when
considering Kamoshida as a first target. Ryuji Sakamoto, Ren Amamiya, and Yuuki Mishima
were all slated to be expelled by the man before his change of heart, and miraculously
escaped unscathed thanks to the sudden confession.
The former two, notably, have spent a considerable amount of time hovering in circles
alongside the missing student council president.
The third: something absent from the notes, but something Shido recalls himself, is that Haru
Okumura has been awfully friendly with Akechi in the past. Lurking in the corners of parties
they both obviously hate, apparently too stupid to not notice how obvious their little
partnership was.

Shido isn’t sure whether to consider Okumura senior’s psychotic breakdown a point for or
against the younger Okumura’s involvement with the thieves. Perhaps Akechi’s blunder was
simply a favour for the girl.
Something to consider.
Makoto Niijima, Ryuji Sakamoto, Ren Amamiya, and Haru Okumura. All prime candidates,
but nothing solid. Even in the case of Niijima, knowing who she is is meaningless when she’s
missing.
Hm?
How curious. Shido almost laughs. Amamiya is under the care of Sakura of all people. Even
the name seems strangely familiar, though he’s no idea from where. All circumstantial, of
course, the kind of evidence that would only fly in a court of law if Shido had his grip on it.
But he does have his grip on it. Who knows? Maybe Wakaba’s girl is in on the whole thing
too.
It’s a start. Quite the compelling start. This work could have been done months ago.
He scoffs to himself. Akechi clearly did do this work months ago. It’s a shame his loyalty
was dashed before he handed over the damn names.
No matter. Half his ducks are in a row. Now all that remains is what to do with them.

Futaba thinks she’s allowed to be angry.
Considering how angry everyone else was, she doesn’t even think she’s particularly out of
place. One with the mob mentality! What a novelty.
The problem is that her friends have trouble staying angry, so she’s gonna be the odd one out
again pretty soon, she figures. One by one they’ll all be won back over to Akechi’s lone wolf
bullshit somehow. It’s not like he’s even trying; what, does he just have some latent charisma,
or something?
Logically Futaba knows that Haru is probably equally to blame for this mess, but Akechi has
a habit of taking things from her, and this is just another point on the list. And besides, who
can stay mad at Haru for long? She’s got latent charisma.
…Is that the thought process Ren uses to forgive Akechi so easily? Gross. Futaba sticks her
tongue out at the air.
Point: She’s mad. Point: She’s allowed to be mad. Point: Akechi is annoying and there should
always be at least one person mad at him at all times, lest the universe collapse, and Futaba is
more than happy to volunteer as tribute.
Futaba doesn’t like sleeping in Haru’s house. She wants to go home.
She scoffs, forcefully enough to blow the hair out of her eyes, and dispels the thought from
her mind. Ren asked her yesterday to hunt down Makoto’s lead, and it’s runaway thoughts
like these that have kept her from making as much progress as she would have liked.
The thought remains. Of course it does.
There is a way to solve this, though it’s only had about a fifty-percent success rate in the past.
Futaba thinks on it some more. She bumps the estimate down to about thirty-six. Still, it can’t
hurt to try.

She sighs, thunking her head against her computer’s casing and powering it off. It’s a
Saturday, so Ren, Mona, and Haru should only be at school for a little while longer, but she
still doesn’t really feel like tracking Sojiro down to explain why she’s leaving the house. She
rummages through her things, whipping out a scrap piece of paper and scribbles down gone
to Ann’s, tossing it on the bed as she fumbles for her phone.
She feels a bit like the eye of the Metanav is judging her as she whispers in Mementos, and
she resolutely ignores it.

Getting to Ann’s house without the far superior transportation of a Cat Van is, Futaba finds

the price, as those who choose endurance as a dump stat often do.
This had better be worth it. She’ll be blaming Akechi for her sore feet if it isn’t.
She almost knocks on the door before she remembers that would be entirely pointless, and

…She could hop over to the right side of reality and knock. Or, she could freak him out and
materialise directly inside his room. She wrinkles her nose, thinking of all the ways that
could backfire on her specifically, and deactivates the Nav in the hallway like a normal
person.
She injects as much fury as she can into her knock.
“I’m busy.” Is the muffled curt response.
Futaba narrows her eyes, “Are you really?”
There’s a thud, some stomping, and the door swings open. “What are you doing here?”
Akechi snaps.
While Futaba stewed in her anger a fair distance away from the subject of it, she apparently

Akechi’s expression darkens further, somehow. “Do we?”
Futaba makes a frustrated noise, barely retraining herself from stomping her foot, “Just let me

“Fine.” Akechi scoffs, rolling his eyes. He mockingly sweeps an arm in a bow as he steps

Futaba kicks him in the shin. He doesn’t flinch. Damn. She dumped strength, too.

Futaba’s opinion of Goro Akechi tends to come in waves.

Chapter 97
Chapter Summary

Dinner made with love, and the antiquated art of dragging one's self over the coals

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Ann thinks that once all this is over, she’s going to take a nice long holiday.
Her parents can probably set her up. They get to go overseas all the time, so why not her?
Hell, maybe she can make it an extended trip and study abroad, or something. There are
plenty of modelling opportunities in the west besides.
But, first, interfering in politics. And the collective unconscious. And the state of reality, but
if Ann keeps listing all the stuff she has to do, she’s gonna collapse.
Well, that they all have to do. Ann has found that she as an individual hasn’t actually been
that helpful, to her chagrin.
She wants to. Badly. Makoto had been a whirlwind of ideas just yesterday on how they could
stalk Mementos for answers, following the death of the SIU director. Ann had mostly nodded
along, not really following.
Beyond going along with whatever Ren and the others decide to do, Ann thinks the only
other thing she could probably contribute is to waltz into some Yakuza family’s house to bat
her eyelashes, and hope they let something spill.
She shudders. Yeah, no. Not doing that.
The next best thing she can do, though, is making sure everyone doesn’t fall apart. Which, if
she does say so herself, she isn’t bad at. Living with Akechi and the Niijimas for —nearly a
month, god— has definitely been good practice.
Practice that exclusively prepares her for dealing with the exact same problem, but it’s a
pretty big problem to start, so she won’t complain.
Ann isn’t an idiot; she can tell when the air is tense in her own house. There was a few days
where even she couldn’t handle being in the same room as both the Niijima sisters, and lately
Akechi has been leaving thunder in his wake, to say nothing of the aborted shouting match he
and Futaba were having when she snuck into the house.

Ann didn’t hear much of what was said, and she isn’t stupid enough to ask. Makoto seemed
curious, too, though she also possesses a modicum of wisdom, and isn’t going to go poke the
literal assassin for answers, especially while they seem not happy with each other.
An understatement, Hecate snickers, which she can only get away with because neither
Makoto nor Akechi are capable of hearing her commentary.
With that in mind, though, Ann returns to her list of things-she-has-to-do.
Interfering in politics by finding the Cleaner? Decidedly impossible! For her, anyway.
Stumbling her way through seducing(?) Yakuza goons is a last resort.
Interfere with the collective unconscious? A later problem! Interfere with the state of reality?
A later problem!
Interfere with the interpersonal relationships of her housemates? Extremely doable!
Step one is to bang on Akechi’s door and hope he doesn’t murder her.
He opens the door on the first knock, surprisingly.
“What?” He snaps, which is less surprising.
Ann beams, trying to deflect his death glare, “You’re going to help me with dinner.”
“What?” He says, more baffled than angry this time, “I’ll burn your kitchen down.”
Ann can’t tell if that’s a threat or a prophecy.
“Well,” She drawls in a sing-song voice, “It’s just stirfry, so it won’t be too bad.”
Akechi’s glare gets darker.
“We usually just get takeout.” He says, sounding more petulant than Ann thinks he means to.
“Today I feel like cooking!”
“Can’t you ask Makoto?” Akechi pinches the bridge of his nose.
That is an unfortunate hurdle of logic that Ann doesn’t quite know how to leap. She settles
for ignoring him. “C’mon! Unless we wanna have dinner at, like, 10, then we should get
started.”
She starts striding towards the kitchen, and he automatically follows her to continue
protesting. Ann tries not to pump her fist in triumph.
“I’m not helping you.” He insists, “If you need something from me, try doing something less
convoluted.”
“I do need something actually,” Ann says cheerily, “And that’s for you to chop this
capsicum.”

She shoves the offending vegetable into his hands, and Akechi scowls. Maybe she shouldn’t
give him a knife, actually.
Akechi cuts off her sudden dilemma by just grabbing a knife and chopping board himself,
and beginning to violently hack the vegetable in half.
…Or is it a fruit? Oh, whatever.
Ann rummages around for wherever she last dumped the pots, (hm, dusty. She gives it a
rinse.) getting some rice going. Even with Akechi’s prophecy of a ruined kitchen, Ann can
admit she isn’t great at cooking herself. But, she has a recipe, so it should be fine.
Akechi’s scowl deepens, like he can hear her thoughts even as he tortures the capsicum she
gave him.
“Did Makoto tell you about her idea?” Ann asks breezily.
“Makoto isn’t talking to me.” Akechi says, flat.
Ann should have seen that one coming. “Well, she has this idea of where to start when we go
to Mementos. Since, y’know, the SIU director died, and all the people investigating would
have to cover up what really happened.” She waves a hand, “She’d explain it better.”
Akechi sighs. “I’m sure.”
“Do you not like it?”
“It’s no worse than going in blind.” Akechi says. “But it still sounds extremely tedious.”
“Fair enough.” Ann peeks over her shoulder to assess the damage. “You’re, uh, supposed to
be dicing it, not… pasting it?”
“I am dicing it.” Akechi snaps over his butchered capsicum.
Ann supposes it’ll all get mixed together once it hits stomach acid, anyway. Her own attempts
at rice aren’t much better, though at least the rice won’t be paste.
“I kinda thought you and Makoto were… getting along lately.” Ann says, slyly as she can.
Akechi turns around to give her an incredulous look. “Were you paying attention at all?”
Rude. “I am!” Ann protests.
Akechi rolls his eyes, “Then you’ll notice that Haru-san and I aren’t anyone’s favourite
people at the moment.” Ann snorts dubiously. “I’m surprised you aren’t giving me a repeat
lecture right now.” He adds pointedly.
Ann shrugs, “Like you said, it’d just be a repeat. And I can’t exactly talk, right?”
“Didn’t stop Makoto.” Akechi mutters, “Or Futaba, for that matter.”

“Riiight,” Ann draws out with a nervous laugh, “What were you two talking about yesterday,
anyway?”
“Not your business.” Akechi says while brutalising the last of the un-mashed capsicum.
Maybe not, but the curiosity is going to eat at her. “Whatever you say…”
Akechi scoffs, and focuses all his attention on the cutting board.
The silence persists as Ann warily hands him another vegetable. And another. And another.
And as she swears loudly when the rice starts to spill over the pot and onto the stove.
Akechi is still, to her great surprise, the first to crack.
“She told me about Sato’s palace.” Akechi snips.
Ann freezes, body halfway into the lower cupboards as she tries to drag the wok out from its
designated corner. “What did she say?” She asks carefully.
Akechi rolls his eyes so forcefully that Ann can see it even from her awkward position on the
floor, “She told me what you saw.”
Which can only mean one thing, really.
“Oh.” Ann coughs, trying to busy herself with shuffling the wok into her arms, “Uh— sorry
for not telling you.”
“Well, it’s hardly my business what happens in that man’s palace.” Akechi says, managing to
sound sarcastic even without the right inflections in his voice.
“Well, it was your mom.” Ann says, nearly falling over as she heaves the wok onto the stove.
“None of us really…”
None of them really know what happened there. Nothing good, to be sure. Ren definitely
knows. Haru and Sumire probably know, now that she thinks about it. Futaba… maybe?
“Wanted to put yourself in the line of fire?” Akechi assumes, incorrectly, (though now that
Ann thinks about it, that definitely was a pretty big reason) “Fair enough, I suppose.”
“We probably should have said something.” She admits in a mutter.
“I might have killed you.”
Ann laughs disbelievingly, “Futaba seems alive to me!”
“Yes, well.” Akechi’s expression is grim, “I’m not confined to your apartment anymore.”
That didn’t really stop him from leaving before, Ann barely restrains herself from saying.
“Enjoying your freedom?” She offers instead.
“I suppose.” He sniffs.

Ann pours a generous dollop of oil into the wok as she turns on the burner, tipping in the
capsicum and halfheartedly pushing it around with a wooden spoon.
Does she need meat for this? Meat goes in stirfry. She probably should have gotten that going
before she tipped the capsicum in. She awkwardly turns the heat down very low, shuffling off
to the fridge to hunt for whatever she can find.
Chicken! That’ll do.
“Sorry that you’ve been bored.” Ann says as she quickly joins Akechi with another cutting
board on the kitchen island and hacks the meat into strips.
Akechi scoffs, still chopping away. “Technically, all you’ve done is enable me.”
Ann shrugs, “I think the boredom’s getting to me too.”
“I didn’t think it could.”
Ann isn’t sure how much of that can be interpreted as a backhanded insult. She opts to ignore
the possibility. “Well, you thought wrong.”
Akechi snorts. “I’m surprised, what with the front row seats to the Niijima drama you’ve
been getting.”
Ann turns back to the wok and tips the chicken in, surreptitiously making a triumphant face
at the wall for the perfect segue Akechi’s granted her. “You say that like you aren’t a part of
it.”
Akechi throws his head back, and makes a much meaner face at the ceiling. “I am most
certainly not.”
Ann puffs out her cheeks, “Debatable.”
Akechi waves a hand, not turning around. “It’s not my problem.”
Ann isn’t sure if Akechi is being obstinate because he’s talking to her, specifically, or if he’s
genuinely deluding himself. Both options pose a problem for her Solve the Household Drama
plan.
“Fine!” Ann declares dramatically, “Don’t tell me. But if Makoto kills you after you neglect
accepting my wisdom, then don’t come crying to me.”
“That will hardly be a problem, if I’m dead.” He pauses. “And what wisdom?”
Rude. “Well I’m glad you asked.” She sniffs.
Akechi raises an eyebrow, glaring at her expectantly.
Ann thinks maybe she should have planned all this out a bit beyond step one. Step two,
tragically, remains a mystery, as she’s hit with the sudden realisation that she’s just as clueless

on how to solve this as Akechi is.
Ann coughs, puffing up her chest, “Are you listening, o student?”
“What.”
“The way to anyone’s heart,” She says, “Is food.”
“I’m not sure that’s the original saying.”
“Which is why we’re making this.” Ann says loudly over top of him, gesturing broadly to
their… attempts. The chicken sizzles encouragingly. “With love.”
“Love.” Akechi deadpans, eyeing his butchered vegetables. At least he can admit he did a
bad job.
“Yes, love.” Ann scoffs dramatically, “If you don’t care about the food, how can you show
you care about the people you’re giving it too?”
Akechi’s look turns even flatter.
Ann drops her arms to her sides. “You do care, don’t you?”
“Do I?” Is the dry response.
Ann looks at him incredulously.
“What?” He snaps.
“You literally let yourself get arrested for us.” Ann tells him, slowly, “You knew what was
going to happen with that.”
Akechi rolls his eyes, “And?”
Ann supposes they have been over this. For all Akechi’s bluster, his insistence that such a
thing was strategic is the unquestionable truth. Debates over pain tolerance aside, they were
most likely to let Akechi live long enough for the rest of the thieves to cook up a rescue plan.
And they did. It worked, somehow, miraculously, and Ann is still reeling from it weeks later.
But, still, really?
Ann crosses her arms, shooting Akechi a look, “Why can’t you admit you care about the rest
of us like you do Haru-san and Sumire-chan?” And Ren, but bringing that up is likely to
bring an onslaught of fervent denials that she doesn’t want to deal with.
Akechi blinks. “Excuse me?”
“Sure, maybe you don’t like us.” Ann says airily, “But you obviously care.”
“I think you’re fine.” Akechi admits like it’s physically painful.

Ann resists pumping her fist, but she does beam. “See! That wasn’t so bad.”
Another deadpan stare. “Makoto and I have never gotten along.” He says.
Ann shrugs, “And? Ryuji and I don’t get along half the time, and I still care.” She pauses,
“And bull! You were getting along for a little bit!” A very short while, on two separate
occasions, but it still counts.
Akechi rolls his eyes, “Yes, and now we’re right back to where we started.”
“The point stands!” Ann insists. “It’s not like admitting it changes anything.”
“Well, since you’re so knowledgeable about how I feel about things, then admitting such a
thing is redundant.” Akechi sneers.
Ann scoffs, “Uh huh.”
She supposes, in a way, there is something that changes by admitting it.
“I think.” She declares, a smug smile creeping up her lips. She gets it. Not so enigmatic now.
“That you don’t want to have to try.”
Akechi scowls, and Ann considers that she shouldn’t provoke him while he’s still holding a
knife. “Excuse you.”
Well, too late now.
“I’m serious.” She waves a hand, “You try with Haru and Sumire, sure, but you like them.”
Ren, once again, is an outlier and shouldn’t be counted. “But Makoto? Sae-san? Too much
work for you, I guess.”
“I’ve been trying very hard to stay alive.” Akechi snaps, “I don’t have much time left over to
play nice.”
“Felled at the first hurdle.” Ann sighs.
Akechi sneer turns genuinely venomous, and Ann suppresses a flinch. “Unfortunately,” he
snarls, “Not everyone can be as air-headed and cheerful as you. Some of us have better things
to worry about than making friends.”
Ann ignores the slight. She’s heard it all before. Instead, she scoffs, marching up and shoving
a finger against his chest, “You’re trying hard to survive. But what’re you gonna do after?”
Akechi glares.
“Well?”
“I don’t know.” He says coldly.

Ann smirks, “Mope around with nothing to do? Maybe catch up with Haru-san and Sumirechan every so often? Avoid Ren until the end of time?”
“I’m not pathetic.”
“Uh huh.” Ann hums, “Sure. I get that you like to keep yourself so busy that you don’t have
to think about how miserable you are, but what about when you can’t?”
“Try me.” Akechi growls.
“You’re practically throwing yourself against the walls now that you have nothing to do.”
Ann barrels forward, “The only thing you seem even vaguely entertained by is throwing
yourself into danger and getting into shouting matches.”
“Are you finished?”
“No.” Ann pokes him forcefully again. “Think about it. Are you trying to live just so your
life can suck?”
The stove still burns, fire crackling and oil spitting. Akechi stares her down, his back pressed
against the kitchen island. Ann pointedly folds her arms, glaring up at him.
“I take your suggestion,” Akechi finally says, slowly, like she’s stupid, “Is to replace my time
sink of murder with friendship.”
Ann sniffs, “You should try it.”
“I have tried it.”
“Then I don’t know why you’re so sceptical.” Ann puts her hands on her hips, “If you went
all in, maybe you’d learn to be less of a dick.”
“Unlikely.” Akechi says.
Yeah, that one might be a lost cause. “Well lucky for you, you’re charming enough as you
are.” Ann tosses her hair, “Now you just need to learn to not be an asshole.”
“I was unaware there’s a difference.”
“Well there’s your first problem.” Ann pointedly turns back to the stove, and hurriedly turns
off the burner as she sees the stirfry in the wok burning. “So: dinner.”
“Dinner.” Akechi repeats.
“Apology dinner.”
“What am I apologising for?” Akechi snaps.
Ann figures that would be self-explanatory, but she supposes that kind of thing would
probably be better served as a mutual apology when it comes to the Niijimas. “Peace-making

dinner.” She corrects.
“Made with love.” Akechi adds, dryer than the desert.
Ann turns to shoot him a smile, “Exactly!”
“Do I get a choice at all?” Akechi grits.
“You haven’t left yet.” Ann points out. “I couldn’t physically keep you here if I tried.”
Akechi scowls, like he hadn’t realised that. Ann tries very hard not to snicker.
“We’re almost done, anyway.” Ann gestures vaguely to the kitchen at large, “May as well see
it through, right?
“There’s a fallacy in that.” Akechi mutters, but he doesn’t leave.
Ann smiles to herself.
I know you. She thinks, and she gets it, gets him, and feels a thrill of triumph at very likely
being person number four for whom it’s clicked for. Maybe this’ll finally be enough to
convince him to add her to his closely-guarded list of actual friends, for all her prior attempts
with varying degrees of success.
She hums a cheerful tune, and thinks the apartment might be a bit sunnier after this.
(Though she misjudges it’s source, the Sun does indeed grow to its ninth rank. In his mind,
Akechi scoffs, thoroughly sick of the timing of such things. For all his lack of trying, he
seems to be bundled in a fair few near-blood-oaths.
The arcana have never once implied they have to mean good things, though. Several of them
are direct evidence to the contrary. The burden of making lemonade, so to speak, rests solely
on him.
Wonderful.
The food isn’t disgusting. A solid rung above edible. Makoto pokes at it like she suspects it’s
poisoned, Sae thanks the two of them for making it, and dinner isn’t terrible. What a novelty.
He really hates it when other people are right.)

In retrospect, it’s excellent timing that Sumire pushed for a Tuesday meeting rather than a
Monday one. Ren frowns down at his phone.
Ohya: yooooo
Ohya: Lala-chan got your place ready
Amamiya: today?

Ohya: yeah today
Ohya: chop chop
Ohya: come to crossroads and we can go from there. it’s closed for today so don’t worry
about that
Amamiya: are you gonna be there too?
Ohya: sure am
Ren shrugs to no one, and accepts that the extra hands could be helpful. He makes a
halfhearted effort at cramming his clothes in his bag, before realising he should probably tell
everyone else to start packing up.
“Today?” Futaba complains when he swings by her room. “Why do we even need to leave?”
“Because.” Ren starts picking up her disaster zone of a floor to spur her to action, “You never
know when someone might knock on Haru’s door, and then what are we gonna do?”
“Persona.” Futaba mutters in a mockery of a battle cry, before angrily powering off her
computer and dismantling the relevant parts.
“You’re leaving today, then?” Haru comments, when Ren finds her in the living room.
Ren scratches the back of his neck uncomfortably, “Uh. Yeah.”
“Finally!” Morgana cheers, leaping off the pillow he’s made a nest of. He freezes, “Not— uh,
your house is great, Haru.”
Haru giggles, “No, I understand that you’d be anxious to get going, Mona-chan.”
“M’not anxious.” The cat mutters, and proceeds to curl back into a loaf, because he’s a cat
and thus has no material possessions.
“The journalist texted you back, huh?” Sojiro asks, once Ren finds him pointedly avoiding
Okumura senior’s old bedroom. “’Bout time.”
“Lala-chan worked as quick as she could.” Ren shrugs.
Sojiro waves a hand, “I know, I know. We going right now?”
“Right now.” Ren replies for the third time in fifteen minutes.
Sojiro sighs, “Well, not like any of us had much luggage to begin with.”
Tell that to Futaba, Ren thinks, before begrudgingly realising he ought to help her with her
stuff if they want to move out sometime this century.

They do, in fact, get out the door within the century.
Out the inter-dimensional veil, rather. And within the hour, to boot. Haru opts not to come
along, if only to avoid the irritating back-and-forth through the Metaverse that would inspire.
And, perhaps, to avoid awkward close quarters.
“So,” Futaba chimes in from the front of the van, having stolen shotgun from under Ren’s
nose. “Are we gonna materialise in the middle of Crossroads?”
Ah. Ren hadn’t considered that. “…I could get out at the place I usually do, and then ask for
the address?”
“Could work.” Sojiro says from the driver’s seat, taking more caution along an empty road
than is probably necessary. “I think the main issue is whether you’re gonna reveal this,” He
gestures out the window, “Or the concept of it, to your reporter friend and our generous
benefactor.”
Ren sighs. Ohya already knows something about cognitive psience, though it’s highly
unlikely she’s made the connection to physical cognitive space. Lala is good at pretending
she’s never heard anything, so Ren doesn’t doubt she can keep a secret, at least.
“They probably won’t question it.” Ohya will. Ohya definitely will, but Ren dealt with her
shitty boss just the other day. She owes him one. “Trying to come up with a cover story
would just be weird.”
“Fair enough!” Futaba chirps, “I trust that your friends haven’t been sent to steal all our
secrets and kill us in our sleep.”
Arguably, Goro had fit that definition. “They haven’t.”
“Good.” Sojiro grunts, “’Cause we’re here.”
Ren nods and quickly ducks out of the van, walking into Crossroads and finding it pleasantly
intact. He supposes it’s enough of a hub for people that it’s able to stamp its impression on
cognitive space. If this were something he could figure out how to explain as a compliment
for Lala’s business, he would certainly tell her.
He taps at his phone to drag himself out of Mementos, and tries not to laugh at how Ohya
nearly tumbles out of her bar stool.
“Wh- you-?!” Ohya gapes at him, “Lala-chan, am I drunk?”
“You usually are, honey.” Lala says matter-of-factly from behind the bar.
“Yeah, but am I drunk right now?”
“You haven’t had anything to drink.”
“Well, shit.” Ohya clicks her tongue, and points an accusing finger at Ren, “Did you just
teleport?”

Ren shrugs, finding this is pretty funny, actually, “No. Don’t worry about it.”
Ohya splutters, “Oh I’m gonna worry about it alright-”
“Is your family here as well?” Lala interrupts, turning to Ren, “Or nearby?”
“Yeah.” He nods, “Is our place nearby? It’s easier to, uh, show up closer.”
The phrasing is all off, but Lala seems to get the gist as she nods. “It’s a few houses back,
actually. Off the main road, but not so far back you’ll get lost.”
“You’re right near where Lala-chan lives, too!” Ohya says cheerily, seemingly having
forgotten her irritated bafflement at Ren’s apparent teleportation, “So if you need help, go
bother her.”
“Or you could let yourself be bothered, Ichiko-chan.”
Ohya blows a raspberry, raising an eyebrow in Ren’s direction, “If you’re desperate.”
Ren shrugs, “We should be fine. If we play our cards right, no one will know anyone lives
there to begin with.”
“What? ‘Cause no one’ll ever see you entering or leaving?” Ohya says, glaring as Ren just
smiles enigmatically. She sighs, “Oh, whatever. I’ll drag an answer out of you someday.
Place’s this way. Follow me.”
Ohya and Lala both lead him out the back of the bar, down a dingy alley and to an equally
dingy building, with a set of rickety stairs leading up to a door on the second floor.
“It’s just you in the whole building, first floor’s empty.” Lala explains as she walks up the
stairs, and unlocks the door. “Power and water are all good, I checked. Ichiko-chan and I are
more than willing to help you unpack, too.”
Ohya sighs, “oh sure.” She waves a hand at Ren, “Go do your… magic.”
Ren snorts, and does just that.

There’s a veneer of angry curiosity from Ohya and a general aura of not my business from
Lala when Sojiro, Futaba, and Morgana all materialise in the middle of the apartment.
Unpacking is relatively quick (except, as is custom, for Futaba) and everyone is left scattered
about. Sojiro and Lala chat in a corner, presumably gossip; Futaba talks at Morgana, and Ren
is left to deflect Ohya’s probing stares.
Ohya eventually groans in defeat, “Mark my words, kid…”
If Christmas eve goes as it did last time, Ohya may indeed get the answers (or close enough)
that she wants. Ren decides not to dangle hope, squatting down to properly fold a cardboard
box.

“Is it something to do with the cat? I bet it’s something to do with the cat.” She mumbles.
“How’s your yakuza-hunting going?” Ren interrupts.
Ohya blinks, and lets out another groan, even more defeated than the last. “Like shit,
Amamiya.”
“Yeah.” Ren says with the utmost sympathy. “Me too.”
“Running low on time.” She comments.
“I’m aware.”
Ohya sighs, “Got any magic up your sleeve? Cognitive psience not helping you on this one?”
“We’re working on it.” Ren shrugs. Some magic might finally be coming to help them out,
should Sumire’s gamble pay off.
Ren is trying not to be too optimistic. They have a backup plan in Mementos. Or a plan A?
Asking Maruki for help, of all people, reads to Ren like a last resort. Then again, should the
man whip out a name with ease, Ren is going to be left fuming that they didn’t go to him
weeks ago.
Ren knows they can’t afford to wait on Maruki to start, so the tedium and potential dead end
of dragging themselves through an unpleasant subway seems an inevitability.
They’ll have to rely on both plans. Can they even trust Maruki to do this on his own? Will
they have to help him along, in discovering his abilities? They’ll practically be tying the
noose to hang themselves with, at this rate.
Can they afford to keep putting off Shido’s palace in favour of the Cleaner? The longer Ren
thinks about, the more he’s certain the Cleaner is a loose end that can’t be left unattended.
“You look like you’re working yourself in a fit, kid.” Ohya says.
Ren thunks his head against the cardboard box in his hand, “I am.”
Ohya whistles, “Well, at least you’re honest.”
“Talk me through it.” Ren looks up at her, “Exactly how like shit is your search going?”
“Well!” Ohya says with the drama of a storyteller, “The problem is that your man knows how
to clean up after himself. No loose lips, no whistle blowers, nothing. Anyone who knows a
lick of anything isn’t willing to chat, and they definitely wouldn’t be willing to chat to you,
before you get any funny ideas.”
Unless, of course, Ren goes rummaging through their subconscious. He ignores the pointed
look. “Figures.”

“Wonder what it’s gonna look like once you change the guy’s heart.” Ohya muses. “That’s
what you’re planning, right?”
“Yep.” Ren says with a pop, “…His subordinates might kill him before he ever gets the
chance to confess anything.” Not that the confession was the end goal, in this instance.
Ohya raises an eyebrow, “And you’re cool with that?”
Ha.
“Yeah.” Ren says easily, “It’s us or them, and I’m kinda tired of sacrificing us.”
Ohya gives him a stilted pat on the shoulder. “Fair enough, kid. Just don’t want it to weigh on
your conscience.”
“It’s not like changes of heart are much better than death. For what it does to the people
suffering them, at least.” Ann and Goro would probably argue that they’re even worse. Ren
feels like he doesn’t get an opinion, on this one.
“Mm.” Ohya hums with pseudo wisdom. “Philosophy. Not my thing.”
Ren snorts. “Whether we think about it too hard or not, we’ve gotta do what we’ve gotta do.”
And they’d better do it quick.

Sumire wonders if she should have spent Monday planning her funeral. Getting her affairs in
order, giving her teary apologies to her parents, making peace with her mortality, et cetera.
She acknowledges that most of the thieves probably won’t even be that upset with her. Ren
wasn’t that upset with her, so that’s one major hurdle already leapt.
The hurdle that is convincing-Goro-Akechi-that-working-with-Maruki-is-fine-actually is far
more daunting. Sumire privately admits she may be screwed.
(Pragmatism should surely sway him to her side. Surely. If not that, then their friendship
ought to shield her from the worst of his usual ire. She isn’t afraid of him, not really, hasn’t
been for a very long time, but, still—
Goro isn’t the forgiving type, even if he’s forgiven her for various slights before. He still

Akechi surveys the stadium fence with a dispassionate air.
The last time he was here, he didn’t pay it much mind. A lifetime removed from its
significance. The time before that, he was far too focused on the braided metal that towered
up, up, and that he was determined to make his tomb.
He can still see flickers of Maruki’s palace even here, beneath the twisting scarlet vortex of
Mementos’s sky. Shimmering silver and reflected rainbows, a hearth for the torch he
glimpsed at the centre.
The sight is unpleasant. He feels the urge to spit on the ground. He refrains.
He doesn’t feel betrayed, per se.
It’s not like Sumire has done anything, beyond being the first to break their deadlock. He
should be thanking her, technically. All this business of doing things the hard way is for his
benefit. And Ren’s, he supposes.
But she still went to Maruki, of all people. She stillTold Ren first. It’s just like old times. Akechi supposes he hasn’t given her any reason to have
expected a positive reaction. Perhaps that’s why she ran to Ren first, as the only other fool to
give an inch for Maruki’s madness.
Cold.
BUT NOT WRONG.
No. No, he’s not wrong at all.
There is a marked difference, naturally, between Ren caving to Maruki’s ultimatum and
Sumire strong-arming the man into helping them while he’s not busy tearing the world apart
and disturbing the dead.

But a lifetime ago, Sumire was first to cave, wasn’t she? She may be happy to lay her sister’s
mask to rest now, but what happens when Maruki offers her a better deal? Maybe he’ll bring
the whole puppet out of storage, next time.
(She wouldn’t. She wouldn’t be swayed. She’s- She wouldn’t.

“Crow.”

“I suppose not.” She says, tapping the tip of her shoe against the ground. She blends in with

Sumire clears her throat. “I suppose not. Ready, then?”
Ren, still flushed from running and vague embarrassment, nods. “Ready.”

It’s difficult for Mementos to get more red, so it doesn’t. Instead, everything flashes white.

Each half of a shattered attendant can feel it, plain as day. Not nearly as catastrophic as the

Takuto Maruki sits at his desk, frowning at his notes and decidedly not taking the hint that his
ventures are unwelcome.
(There isn’t much of a hint to take, technically. Shattered attendants are not in the business of
lowering themselves to human methods of communication for anyone that isn’t a wildcard,
and consider a locked door enough of a deterrent.
Probing humans, fools that they are, are unable to interpret a metaphysical locked door for
what it is, and tend to try breaking open the window. Deeply unfortunate, (and out of
anyone’s control) that this particular human is actually capable of doing so.)
Takuto has been trying for days since his first attempt to inch past the barrier that Shido’s
mind poses. He’s gotten quite well-versed in making the leap between Ren’s thoughts to
Shido’s, but that wall just won’t budge.
Each time he tries, he’s met with a click of the tongue from an unseen dissenter. No help or
further explanation to be found.

A ticket.

Shido has a terrible headache.
This is not particularly uncommon. It’s usually something he soothes with liquor, when he
gets the chance. He would pay it no more mind than it’s making itself known. But,
But, the most recent report from Takahashi still burns a hole in his desk, and headaches could
portend something far more sinister.
He’d be a fool to ignore it.
He also can’t do anything about it.
It’s been days since there was any activity at the Diet Building, and now there’s a spotlight on
Odaiba. Whatever is there is apparently relevant once again.
Headaches, and nothing at the Diet Building. Headaches, and something in Odaiba.
Was there something in Odaiba of any importance? He can’t recall. The Kirijo
conglomerate’s headquarters, perhaps? He certainly can’t complain, if the thieves are
bothering Kirijo rather than him. He doubts it, somehow.
“What.” Shido mutters, thinking of treachery and wayward sons, “Are you up to?”

Takuto has a terrible headache. He can’t quite decide if it’s a side effect from diving through
a rather literal manifestation of someone’s mind, or if it’s a direct consequence of the sight
before him.
Goro Akechi, half drowned and smiling pleasantly, stares him down. “You know,” he
comments, “I don’t believe we’ve met.”
“Well,” Takuto laughs nervously, “We’ve been having conversations.” And they have met.
The visage is not real.

He looks real enough.
“Barely.” Akechi dismisses. “I mean that I almost expected you to be someone I know.”
“You don’t remember me?” Takuto questions, cautious.
Akechi’s smile grows sharper, “Ah, you’ve met my counterpart, then?”
Takuto is very lost.
“Goodness, you are clueless.” Akechi sneers, “Use that head of yours. In a place like this,
what would a constructed perception of another person take form as?”
Takuto’s eyes widen as understanding dawns, “Oh, of course— then you’re—? Shido’s

Not-Akechi raises an eyebrow at the barrage of questions. “If you’re curious as to the internal
logic, there’s more than you’d think, and less than makes sense. The ship functions as it

A non-answer for a non-person. “Right.” Takuto coughs. It really does reek out here. “So, do

Another pristine smile. “But you just got here.”
Takuto really doesn’t like the sound of that. Does this— cognition, he supposes, act

to want him dead, or can he just… exist so long as he doesn’t touch anything?
The cognition snickers. “My, you look like I’ve just threatened to throw you overboard. You
just found your footing, I wouldn’t do that so soon.”
…Or it’s just messing with him.
Can cognitions do that?
Dolls cannot have a mind of their own, no matter how their strings are pulled.
Takuto is still pretty sure it’s messing with him.

“…This is probably rude,” He says, wondering how to breach the topic of are you sapient,

The time.
Right, he doesn’t have all day.

He’s distinct from Shido, and he can recognise the person he’s based on as separate from

“No thievery? No murder threats? You don’t want me to do something in the real world?”
Takuto blinks, “Oh, were the Phantom Thieves here?”
Sato snorts, “They’re a joke. A gaggle of children. They can’t hurt me.”
“…But Akechi can?” Takuto clarifies.
“Well, he didn’t.” Sato says, seeming to calm himself down, “So maybe he was all bluster.
Maybe He wouldn’t let him.” He shoots another look from across the room, “But you’re new.
It’s never good when He shakes things up.”
Fair enough. Takuto would love to ask the cognition waiting in Shido’s head some questions,
but he doesn’t even remember what he did. Or, not him, technically.
There would be little confusion if you separated the doll from the soul.
But the cognition really is rather lifelike. It would be rude to think of him only as inanimate.
“I promise, I just want to know about the Cleaner.” Takuto bows, parallel to the ground, “On
my word.”
“That doesn’t mean much.” Sato points out, “But I don’t have much of a choice.”
“Exactly!” May as well play into it. “So, uh, what do you know?”
“Not his name.” Sato sighs, “I’m the best there is, but there’s nothing I can do if there’s no
digital footprint to start. This guy was probably born into the business, or he’s so thoroughly
cut himself off from his past life that he may as well have been.”
Well, that’s unfortunate, if not expected. “What about him as a person?” Takuto pushes,
“Have you met him?”
“Once.” Sato admits, “But He likes to record their meetings for me to scour through, on the
order that I thoroughly destroy them once they’ve served their purpose. All I can say is that
he’s an unsettling type. Akechi knew his place, in front of Him at least, but this guy likes to
laugh it up. Pretend like he owns Him, rather than the other way around.”
Judging by the circumstances, Takuto isn’t sure if anyone owns anyone here. “Do you know
anything more specific?”

Sato’s head tilts, “He never seems desperate. He stopped giving the Cleaner so many jobs
after Akechi came on the scene, but he never even batted an eye. I can’t tell if that means he
has more clients than we think, or he’s a great actor.”
Definitely unnerving, Takuto has to agree.
“And…” Sato continues, “He’s yakuza, definitely. He’s got the tattoos to prove it, but I swear
the goons are for show.”
“Goons?” Takuto blinks.
“Yeah.” Sato nods fiercely, “Whenever he meets Him in person, he’ll have a couple of guys
with him to sneer and laugh with him, but it doesn’t look like he actually works with them,
you know? They’re just there. Maybe he’s the only one who actually does any work in the
whole clan.”
Takuto doesn’t know, actually, but it’s another piece to a very enigmatic puzzle. Even if that
part is just speculation.
Gold flicks to the side, “That’s all I’ve got.”
“That’s more than enough.” Takuto reassures him. It isn’t, but he isn’t going to get anymore
by trying to be threatening. “Though, one more thing?”
Sato sits up straight, “What?”
“Do you know how he takes his coffee?”
Sato stares at him.
“It might be important.” Takuto says sheepishly.
“…He prefers tea, actually.”
It’s something!
But, it seems he’s done all he can here—
—it’s with that thought that he smells blood and the sea once more.
“Hm. You’ve lost your footing again.” Akechi comments.
“Uh, thank you!” Takuto quickly shouts out to Sato, “You’ve been a big help!”
“Or maybe you’re just finding it?” He muses. “Hard to tell, honestly.”
“No wonder I haven’t heard of you.” Sato eyes him with disdain, “Whatever you’ve got
going on is obviously alarmingly experimental.”
Oh, it sure is an experiment.

“There you are.”
Takuto doesn’t get the chance to retort to Sato’s comment, before his back is hitting the steel
deck of Shido’s cruiser once again.

Ren doesn’t like what’s happening with Maruki’s palace.
Granted, he never liked the place. But the fact that something is so blatantly wrong, and the
fact that it’s Maruki is cause for alarm.
He also fell through a door, so he’s still trying to shake that off.
It also smells like blood and seawater, which beyond the general embarrassment of falling for
trapdoors is setting off a whole new set of stress reactions that Ren didn’t even know he had.
“…Is there something bad about this smell?” Sumire asks, looking worriedly between Ren
and Goro.
“I suppose it’s not unique.” Goro says, clipped. “But it’s the same stench that permeates
Shido’s palace.”
“Oh.” Sumire looks unsettled, “Um, maybe we should go back to the hall…?”
They could. They’d risk trapdoors again, (Ren was the only one stupid enough to stand
directly on the doors, he knows) but they could.
But this is also the only place that’s smelled of progress, unpleasant as it is.
“I wanna know why this place smells like Shido’s palace.” Ren shoves his hands in his
pockets, clenching them tight. “I say we keep going here.”
Goro inclines his head slightly, “Agreed.”
Sumire nods, “Here it is, then.”
…Despite the smell, here is still a whole lot of white void.

Ren picks a direction, and starts walking like he knows the way to go. “We’ll probably hit
something eventually.”
“Sometime this century.” Goro sneers.
“I’ll do you one better.” Ren says, with no idea if he can actually meet the century deadline.
Sumire idly clasps her hands behind her back, looking around as if there’s actually anything
interesting to look at. “…Can you hear that?”
“Hear what?” Goro snaps, and there’s a vindictive part of Ren that feels a lance of
satisfaction at Sumire getting the same cold shoulder he’s been getting for month. He tries to
bury it. He’s only half successful.
Sumire tilts her head like she’s trying to strain her ears. “It… kind of sounds like waves?”
All at once, the white cracks. A chasm falls, something else jammed in its place, like a
window carved out of the void.
Or, not quite a window. More a cross section of a stage, if a stage were embedded perfectly in
the ground and brought with it a chunk of the sky and scenery. The scenery being a perfect
recreation of the deck of the Cruiser of Pride, the crumbling remains of Shido’s vision of
Tokyo laid beyond it.
Ren hasn’t seen this place in over a year. He can’t say he’s thrilled to be reintroduced.
Goro folds his arms. “Whose fault do you think this is?”
Sumire, who had jumped about a metre in the air when the ship cracked into existence, turns
to give him a truly incredulous look.
Goro gestures sharply, “That Shido and Maruki’s cognitions are colliding would not be my
first assumption.”
Oh. “So either Maruki’s in the middle of something, or we’re affecting the space here.” Ren
concludes.
“Um, I’ve never seen Shido’s palace before, so.” Sumire offers, pointedly absolving herself
of all possible guilt.
Goro turns to stare at Ren.
Ren splutters, “This is more likely to be your fault than mine!”
“Oh, is it?”
“Actually, this one happens to be on me.”

Maybe Ren should have brought some playing cards with him, or something.

Noir really does wish Mementos was a little more exclusive.
There’s always been things trying to kill her and her friends. That part is non-negotiable. But

of the tunnels, too, but she supposes that’s a later problem.
Right now, she could do without the tense silence in the van. Then again, that might be her
own fault.
So much for building bridges. She considers that perhaps the demeanour she’s allowed

Or maybe that’s uncharitable. Prim aloofness and barely restrained violence hasn’t put off the
thieves coming from anyone else. Everyone’s tired. Now isn’t the best time to be forging
better bonds.

Besides, she’s pretty sure she’s friends with Mona. She just cant have a whispered

Noir tends to prefer her axe, but she also wouldn’t mind throwing a few kicks once they have
