The tunnels are a fair bit easier to navigate the second time around.
Of course, the first time around, Takuto didn’t even realise there were tunnels. He still hasn’t
got a great grasp on vision, yet, but it’s improving!
His progress is also a little haphazard. It’s surprisingly hard to backtrack to minds he’s
already been to if he hits a dead end; excluding Shido’s cruiser, and he’s been avoiding
making a return trip. He doesn’t want to test the limits of that cognition’s indifference.
(That overwhelming flood of knowledgeunderstandingyouknowhowtodothis has yet to make
its return, too. Takuto is glad for its absence, though he kind of wishes he was able to do what
he did in Ooe’s palace on his own. …Though he’d like to be less destructive about it.)
The mind he’s currently picking through feels like a brick wall. Someone entrenched in the
conspiracy purely in a monetary way. Clearly important, but not remotely trustworthy enough
for Shido to tell him anything of value. A far cry from Sato’s role.
A whole conspiracy! Takuto’s still a bit caught up on that slip of information he’s come by in
his search. It’s not as surprising as it could be, but even so, just the inkling of it was only
something Takuto ever considered at his most bitter.
Focus. This one lies close to the centre.
Yes, yes, he’ll try and find something to springboard from.
Hideo Matsui’s mind is an unfortunate stream of women riches shido important valuable
riches security attack dog cleaner shido riches women necessary rewards patience tense
women shido ooe fujimoto cleaner attack dog okumura—
Okumura?
Well, he supposes Okumura would have had to have been somewhat relevant, given what
happened to him. (Another thing to retroactively attribute to Akechi, Takuto thinks) But is his
mind even accessible? He’s not dead, last Takuto remembers, so—

Stars, nebulae, and a stunning view of earth, all frozen still in greyscale.
Perhaps he jumped the gun.
The space station is silent.
Takuto hits the ground with an unceremonious oof, spilling against the floor of a giant domed
amphitheatre. Half the dome is cracked, segments breaking off into the vacuum of space.
Apparently things like air don’t matter in the cognitive world, as Takuto can breath just fine.
Or it’s a side effect of whatever happened here. Giant appendages of something look like they
had burst from the metal floor, supporting the structure and tearing it apart in one action.
He’ll take it, either way.
In the centre of the room, the only thing in colour sobs messily.
“Hello?” Takuto tries, dusting himself off, “…Okumura-san…?”
The figure looks up, and gold flashes first. Gold first, and then everything else at once; from
his fishbowl helmet to his blue skin, and knock-off sci-fi attire to boot. A red glow clings to
him, shadowy wisps coming off him like steam.
“It’s gone.” Okumura says.
“Uh.” Actually, psychotic breakdown aside, hadn’t the Phantom Thieves supposedly done
something to Okumura too? Takuto is starting to lose the thread on who did what as he learns
more.
“Are you a messenger?” The shadow begs, “It was here! It was! Tell it to give it back to
me!”
Takuto really jumped the gun. “Sure…” he starts, “Give what back…?”
“The final piece for my utopia! It was the foundation, and those rats took it!” The shadow
points up to the ceiling.
Takuto obliges, and looks. At the highest point of the dome, an indent is carved out. From it,
matter ripples and shifts and bleeds, an afterimage of black, white, and a bloody grin that
cracks and laughs.
Well. No wonder this place is a mess.
“…And you want me to talk to who about that…?”
“There was a god here.” The shadow states, “Crawling through the pipes. It fortified my
station beyond imagining, and then it left. Tell it to come back!”
A god? Takuto does remember Okumura rambling some similar nonsense when he had the
misfortune to catch his psychotic breakdown live when it happened. Figures that it would go
back to the source in his mind, even if what exactly the source means is unintelligible

There is nothing here. Leave, but lay the foundation. Once the false idol is ousted, we
may fix what was ruined.
Can he? That would be nice. Something here has thoroughly been broken.
“I’ll… do that,” Takuto says to the shadow, “I’ll be back soon?”
“Hurry. You have to hurry! It’s all wrong, wrong, you have to fix it, it’s—!”
Takuto leaves the shadow to his rambling, and tears himself back to the blood and railway
tracks.

“But good enough of an answer, for now.” Justine raps her fingers against her clipboard with
finality. “I hope you will consider what we’ve said, defendant.”
“I’ll consider it.” Akechi forces past his teeth.
Justine nods. “Good.” She looks past him. “The Justice and Magician look impatient.”
Akechi turns, and catches Ren’s eye. Sure enough, he does look rather bored. Sumire, though
unable to perceive the Velvet Room enough to quite spot him, looks similarly aimless.
Ren cocks his head, raising an eyebrow in something that might be concern. Akechi looks
away.
“Have fun standing around.” He says to the twins.
Justine looks unimpressed. Caroline sticks out her tongue, “Trying to undermine your
minimal effort already, defendant?”
Akechi doesn’t dignify that with a response, and instead marches back towards the others.
“Anything interesting happen?” Ren asks, as Sumire blinks, and offers a wave.
“Nothing.” Akechi brushes past him. He pauses, and turns back around, “You weren’t
listening, were you?”
Ren raises his hands in surrender, “Nope.”
“I wasn’t either.” Sumire says, then turns a bit pink, “Um, not that I could.”
“Whatever.” Akechi interrupts. “Let’s just go.”
Finally, they leave, the gaze of the cameras nestled within the tangled steel trailing along their
backs.

Are they just going to read the file at him? “None.”
“Good grades, too. Nice job on cleaning up, kid.”
Ren had good grades back home, as well. “Mm.”

with Sojiro Sakura in Yongen-jaya as part of your probation?”
“Leblanc.” Ren corrects. They’ve all whisked themselves away to somewhere else, but
there’s still that hissing reminder in his mind, distance yourself, “His café. So— Sakura-san
wanted me to have my own space, so I’ve been living in the attic.”
“I see.” The detective chuckles, “Sounds like you’re living the dream.”
Ren clasps his hands together in his lap, digging his nails into his knuckles. He nods.
He can’t remember what the cops who questioned him like this last time looked like. He can’t
remember what the cops who interrogated him looked like. They wouldn’t remember him,
either. He wonders if that would be true even if time hadn’t folded on itself.
“Yeah.” Ren remembers to respond, belatedly. “It’s nice.”
It was, though it took time to appreciate.

Ren feels Morgana’s tail brushing up his leg, in— warning? Commiseration? He doesn’t feel
much comforted.
He needs to leave. Leave this room, leave the school. Beyond the pressing requirement to get
out get out get out he understands that he’s been compromised either way. If these cops
wanted to, they could arrest him right here. Shujin isn’t a safe place to be.
“Well, thank you for your time, Amamiya-kun.” The detective says, after marking a couple
things down. “You’ll be escorted back to your classroom.”
The cop at the door steps out of the way, gesturing for Ren to stand up. Ren obliges, quickly
hefting up his bag while trying to not make it looks like there’s a cat in there. The trip back to
2-D’s classroom is simultaneously twice as long and over in an instant, and Ren lowers
himself back into his chair, amazed his legs don’t shake, as the cop calls in the next student.
Ann whips around to raise her eyebrows at him. Ren shrugs. He can get his shoulders to
move a bit easier now.
“Ren!” Morgana hisses, leaping back into the underdesk. “I don’t think…”
“I know.” Ren whispers.
“Are we gonna be okay?” Ann leans further back.
“I don’t know.”
“I think we should leave.” Morgana says. Ren scratches him behind the ears. “I don’t know.
It’s just a feeling.”
“You think they’re out to arrest people today?” Ann bites down on her nails.
“I don’t know!” Morgana’s tail lashes anxiously. Ren’s leg starts to bounce.
Ren shoots his hand up.
Kawakami pauses in her half-hearted lecture. “…Yes? Amamiya-kun?”
“Can I be excused.” He says. “To the bathroom.” He clarifies.
Kawakami sighs, “Sure, go for it.” Her concern is well-masked, if it’s there at all, but usually
she would at the very least let out an exasperated can’t you wait till the break?
As Ren gathers his things, acting like that’s something entirely normal to do when taking a
trip to the bathroom, Ann catches him by the sleeve, “Should I be getting out of here, too?”
Ren doesn’t know if that’s what he’s doing. “I don’t know.” He says, holding open his back
for Morgana to leap into, “Depends.”
Ann is actually starting to look nervous, now. She’s done a good job of keeping it together,
Ren can acknowledge through his own nausea. “Well… I’ll text you after they question me, I

guess.”
“Okay.” Ren mutters back, and strides across the room as fast as he can, giving Kawakami a
stiff nod on the way out.
At the first opportunity, he ducks into the bathroom, locking himself in one of the stalls and
half-collapsing on the toilet with the lid closed.

Ren runs a hand through his hair. It snags on the knots. “I don’t know.”
“What if something happens, though!?”

room, where two cops of dubious familiarity stare at him for a living.
Ren tries to take a deep breath. He still feels like there are ants on his neck. “If we leave now
it’s obvious I’m running.”
“So?” Morgana demands, “They won’t be able to find you!”
“What about after, though?” Will it matter? Once the Metaverse is gone and the existence of
the Phantom Thieves is hopefully reduced to a dubious urban legend, even past Shido’s
eventual trial, will anyone care enough to hunt down the leader?
He didn’t have to turn himself in last time, but that was thanks to Maruki. Who’s to say an
easy switch like that will stick in the real world? They don’t know who he is now, and Ren
wants to keep it that way.
But they do know.
But they don’t know for sure.
Would it matter either way at all?
Ren doesn’t want to be some level of on the run for the rest of his life. He doesn’t want to be
the guy on a list who needs to have twenty eyes turned his way to make sure he never acts
out.
(Then what does he want?
The world keeps turning. Arsène muses, nonsensically. Ren takes that to mean he doesn’t
know either. Or he’s not self aware enough.)
Caution, or expediency?
They’ll know anyway.

“Let’s go.” Ren decides quietly, tugging his phone from his pocket.
Morgana nods. “Good. We’ll tell everyone else that we aren’t going back to school.”
No, no they aren’t. Some things never change.
“Mementos.” Ren whispers into the receiver.

Haru has spoken with police a fair few times over the past few months, following her father’s
breakdown. She must say, she much preferred when it wasn’t obvious how suspicious of her
they were.
“Haru Okumura.” The detective greets, as she’s escorted to the student council room. “A
pleasure to meet you.”
Haru hums. It isn’t much of a pleasure to meet him, in turn. She pulls back the chair, and
smooths down her skirt as she takes a seat.
The detective’s smile strains as the silence stretches a bit too long. “Right.” He says, “We’ll
just be asking you a few questions, if that’s alright?”
Well she hardly has any choice. “Of course.”
“Great.” The detective leans back, “How close would you say you were to the incident
involving Suguru Kamoshida at the start of this year?”
“Not at all.” Haru answers easily. “I wasn’t a student of his, nor was I close to any of the
victims.”
“I see.” The detective nods, “How about a few times removed? Do you know anyone who
was particularly angry about the incident?”
As far as questioning goes, it’s rather clumsy. Haru assumes they already have a list of
suspects printed out ready to arrest the second they act a little too suspicious. She assumes
she very well may be on that list. It all depends on how sharp a man Masayoshi Shido is, and
that’s not a bet she would like to take.
“I’m not very close with anyone at this school.” She says, as her first lie, “Anyone I’ve
spoken too hasn’t had much to say on the matter, especially months after the fact.”
“You believe the situation is resolved?”
“So long as Kamoshida is prosecuted successfully, then yes.” Haru says, a bit pointed.
“Of course.” The detective agrees easily. “Now, forgive me for bringing up your father, but
I’ll be asking a few questions about him as well.”
Haru nods. She expected as much.

“Were you ever the target of harassment at school due to your family?” The detective asks,
his tact shifting. Haru muses that if they wanted to play up the we just want to bring those
who’ve hurt you to justice angle, they ought to have led with that.
“No.” Haru tells him, “As I said, I’m not close with many people, and I avoid introducing
myself by my family name when I can.”
“Huh, clever.” The detective hums, “Is there anyone who you’ve heard expressing any anger
or discontent towards your father, broadly?”
Haru gives him a delicate shrug. “My father angered a lot of people. I suspect anyone who
works for Big Bang Burger would have reason to have grievances.”
“Did he anger you?”
Well, there goes the sympathy angle. “He was my father.” Haru says, and that part is honest.
“I’ve forgiven him for a lot of things even before…”
She trails off, hoping they’ll interpret her silence as a quiet grief, rather than the unknowable
bundle of something she still struggles to examine in full. Perhaps she’ll get the chance, when
the police aren’t breathing down her neck.
“My condolences, Okumura-san.” The detective says.
Haru shifts in her seat. “Is that all?”
“Ah, just one more thing.” He says, “Makoto Niijima, your student council president, has
been missing for several days.”
Haru widens her eyes, “I did notice she was absent.”
“Right.” The detective says, “You said you weren’t close with many people at this school, but
did you have any conversations with her? Anything to indicate her whereabouts?”
“None.” Haru answers, “We rarely spoke. I hope she’s alright, though…”
“As do we.” The detective hums, clicking his pen with finality. “Well, that’s all for today.
You’ve been very helpful, Okumura-san.”
Not even a passing mention of the Phantom Thieves, is it? Perhaps she should have brought it
up herself. She imagines her more gossipy peers would turn the tables on who it is that’s
being interrogated quickly, given the chance.
It’s a bit late to tack on. Instead, she stands, smoothing her skirt again. She gives a short bow
to both the detective and the officer at the door as she’s escorted out.
It’s good the Sakuras have already left her apartment. Perhaps she should consider re-hiring
some of her father’s favoured muscle. If she’s to be in danger even while she’s giving her
pretence of playing by the rules, she thinks now is the time to make a stand on Shido’s level.

“Therapy?”

That wasn’t the point Ren was trying to make, but he can’t quite tell if that’s supposed to

An interlude, from a time indeterminate:
There is a man who sits at the top of a tree, and crafts paper dolls.
He makes them from reference. Life-like, perfect mirrors of reality. He folds the paper just so,
creases it with precision, and not a soul can distinguish them.
Often, his reference will have jagged edges. Razor blades extended to slash and cut, to make
paper ribbons or to spill blood and crack bone. He tucks the edges away, carefully, to let his
dolls fit in. No one will mind, he thinks. It’s better this way.
His dolls are perfect. He sets them down among the clay people, smiling as they slide right
back in. No one ever realises that the original was gone for even a moment.
The first doll he made sliced open his hand.
It was a small thing, barely a papercut. But as he tried again to fold in the edges, the doll
leapt out of his hands, smeared with clay, and was lost.

Well, there wasn’t much he could do about that. A first draft, there’s a learning curve for
everything. The next doll he made did no such thing, and none thereafter.
He tried to put it out of his mind. An impossible task; he made that doll for someone special,
after all. He saw the doll dash past the base of his tree, the clay boy he made it for grinning
with delight, and frowned. It’s good he likes it, of course, but he worries about those jagged
edges.
He’ll smooth them down later. He’ll pick out the kiln-fired shards from the boy too, while he’s
at it. They’ll both be happier for it.
One day, the first doll comes to kill him.
The man isn’t entirely sure how to react. He could simply crush the paper in his hands and be
done with it, but it feels cruel to damage something he made with such care. He folds it in
half instead, and tucks it in his pocket. He’ll fix it later— he has so many more dolls to craft.
The man at the top of his tree—
There is no tree.
But there is snow. The kind one finds on a crisp February morning.
But there is steel. The kind one finds twisted in knots.
But there are nerves, and veins, and wires, all pulsing and beating in mockery of a heart.
There is a tree.
And there is a torch,
Takuto wakes up.
What a strange dream, he thinks, and goes back to sleep.
The tree keeps growing.

It turns out, camping out behind a dumpster is a really shitty place to be.
Ohya supposes misery loves company. Misery loves company slightly less when it’s shared
with a gruff gun weirdo that she barely knows even in a professional context. Misery loves
company slightly more when it’s shared with someone who also has a vested interest in
helping out a certain kid in over his head.
“So…” Ohya says, fiddling with her camera lens.
“Quiet.” Iwai grunts, doing an admittedly excellent job of peering inconspicuously over the
dumpster every once in a while.
Being inconspicuous is, in many respects, the foundation of Ohya’s job. Doesn’t mean she’s
great at it, unfortunately. Her best strengths come with her myriad connections and being
more persistent than the average dog gunning for a bone. She’ll still stick around for the
inconspicuous part, though.
Her other greatest strength is talking someone’s ear off until they cough up something
interesting.
“Talked with the kid much?” Ohya asks, conversational.
“You’re the one who had to contact me, what do you think?” Iwai snaps back, apparently
forgetting his own vow of silence.
“Hey, the kid looked rough.” Ohya waves a hand. “Besides, he’s a wanted man. You want
him to risk trekking all the way to your dingy back-alley shop? Weirdo teleporting aside.”
Iwai turns to give her a look, “Weirdo what now?”
Oh. Oops. Tight lips are only selectively one of her great strengths. She guesses Amamiya
hasn’t shown that particular stunt to Iwai just yet. Ohya shrugs, trying to play it off, “They
call him a Phantom Thief, but he’s more like a ninja if you ask me. Just showing up places
and scaring the living daylights out of everyone.”

“Guess he’s pretty light on his feet.” Iwai comments, losing interest.
After a moment, he adds, “Did get a call from the ex-fed, though.”
Ohya is glad that the two of them have independently decided to refer to Sakura near
exclusively as such. “Oh ho! And what did he spill?”
“Nothin’ that helps us, before you get excited.” Iwai grunts. “Just to ask if I had a place for
some other kid and his mom to set up shop.”
Ohya grimaces, “Apparently the cops are startin’ to get antsy, so I’m not surprised that a
couple of the other kids need to get outta there.”
“Yeah.” Iwai agrees. “It’s a good place, so they’ll be fine. I might have to do grocery
shopping for them or some shit, which I’m less thrilled about.”
“Oh, you’ll live.” Ohya rolls her eyes.
Iwai rolls his right back. “The more I go back and forth the more chances someone has to
connect the place to me.”
Oh. That too. “Maybe Amamiya or whatever kid you’re setting up can help you out there.”
She says, vague. Their whacky teleportation really does have infinite uses.
“Shut up.” Iwai hisses suddenly, and Ohya does just that.
She hears the sound of two sets of footprints walking past the alley they’re camped in. Two
men, chatting.
“—s her name?”
“You think I write that shit down?”
“Ah, you’re no help.”
“You tryna steal her from me?”
Some laughter. “Yours? She’s paid to like you! Don’t let the boss hear how you’re wastin’
your paycheck.”
“It ain’t his business after…” the voices fade as they wander past.
The two of them sit in silence for a few tense beats. Ohya fiddles again with the settings on
her camera, for want of something to do.
Photography was never her exact speciality. She’s the writer, the interviewer, she doesn’t
really have an eye for this stuff, even if she can get by. This camera isn’t even hers.
There’s some unresolved righteous fury that causes her fingers to tighten in their grip. She
could probably find Kayo right now, if she wanted. Whatever it was that Amamiya did, it got

the chief off her ass and solidly in her pocket.
She’s been busy. Busy doing fuck all, that is. There’s about nothing she’s been able to
contribute to the thieves search, and even now she’s just playing along with Mister Gun
Weirdo’s own leads. If she wants to be entirely honest with herself, she’s had all the time in
the world.
She’s just a coward.
What does it even look like when someone survives a mental shutdown?
“If you’ve got your head in the clouds, you might miss something.” Iwai grumbles.
Ohya snorts, “Miss what?”
Iwai shrugs, “Tattoos, maybe. You never know.”
Ohya begrudgingly fixes the settings she was fiddling with. Even if they’re only camping
outside Iwai’s old haunts for someone who might be willing to spill info, it’s a fair enough
point.
“…How’s the shop going?” She fishes for more small talk as she joins Iwai in standing. She
kinda forgot how bad she is at letting silence sit. A blessing and a curse, in most cases.
“Same way it always is.” Iwai mutters, keeping his voice low, “Got a couple a’ repeat
customers. Enthusiast types. The occasional dumbass that I have to kick out. The occasional
cop that I also have to kick out, but nicer.”
Ohya snickers. It’s a good image.
“Kid hasn’t swung by in a while, except to fill me in on all this mess, so I guess he’s got all
the stuff he needs.” Iwai adds.
“Huh.” Ohya hums. “…What the hell can he even do with fake guns?”
“Beats me.”
Privately, Ohya decides to file this under Magic Bullshit. Seems like a good call.
“So,” She says, “Are we just gonna stand behind the dumpster all day or are you gonna work
your magic?”
“I’m lookin’ for a mark.” Iwai snaps back.
“Well you’ve been lookin’ for three hours.”
“Yeah, yeah.” Iwai mutters. He suddenly holds up a hand, “Hold on.”
“Found someone?” Ohya doesn’t dare peek over the top of their hiding place.
“Maybe.” Iwai whispers back. “Probably. Saw someone I remember.”

Ohya raises an eyebrow. “That a good or a bad thing?”
“Let’s find out.” He cracks his neck, and steps out past the dumpster and out of the alley.
“Well, look who it is? You’re a sight for sore eyes.”
Whoever it is Iwai’s spotted, they sound a bit younger than the usual fare of yakuza goons.
Twenty-something, Ohya guesses. “Iwai? Hey, it is you! The hell’re you doing here?”
“Just in the area.” Iwai says, and Ohya scrambles to whip a notepad and pen out of her
pockets.
“Thought you quit the business?”
“Thought you were too young to be in it.”
“Hey now, I’m a grown man!”
Iwai’s disbelieving snort is audible even from Ohya’s hiding spot. Maybe she should learn to
mimic it. Seems like the sort of thing that would win any argument immediately. “Everyone
under thirty looks like babies when you're my age.”
“You aren’t even fifty yet.”
“I’m gettin’ there.”
Ohya has to clamp a hand over her mouth. She didn’t foresee unwanted laughter to be one of
the hurdles she’d have to leap, but apparently the gun weirdo can be funny when he wants to.
“Yeah, yeah.” The twenty-something says. “Anyway, you got business with the boss or
somethin’?”
“Nah, course not.” Iwai brushes him off, “Parted amicably.”
“Whatever you say…”
“I do like to keep an ear to the ground, though.” He continues. “Hear what’s what. Some
folks haven’t got the message that I’m not in the business anymore, and I like to know who’s
knocking at my door.”
“If there’s other families bothering you, I’m sure the boss can—”
“None of that.” Iwai interrupts, “I’m really just lookin’ for a lead. I can clean up my own
mess.”
“Someone mentioned you and Tsuda were getting into it.”
“Tsuda learned to back off.”
“Alright, alright.” The twenty-something says, placating. “Not a fan a’ gossip.”
“Never have been.”

“Fair enough. Well, what can I do ya for?”
It’s a good thing the kid-kind-of-too-old-to-be-a-kid is stupid enough to let this conversation
happen right out here in the open, Ohya muses. Nice to have her ears trained in on the whole
thing.
“Know anything about the Shiraishi family?” Iwai finally asks.
“Shiraishi…” the twenty-something mutters.
“Ever heard of ‘em at all?”
“…I have.” Is the eventual answer. “They keep to themselves, enough that I only really
started hearing about them recently.”
“Been making waves, have they?” Iwai asks.
“Eh, nah. Just makin’ themselves known. Word is their boss is getting bored sticking to the
shadows.”
“Probably something like that.” Iwai agrees.
“So they’ve been bothering you?”
“Not really.” Iwai dismisses. “Just nosing where it ain’t their business. You know where I can
chat with ‘em?”
There’s a pause. Ohya hovers her hand over her notepad with her pen expectantly.
“…You sure you wanna talk to ‘em alone? I’ve heard they only start shit with people who get
in their way.”
“Well,” Iwai says, “I just wanna make it clear exactly how not in their way I am.”
“…I’ll ask around.”
“Thanks, kid. Be in touch.”
Well, isn’t that something?

Things Ryuji assumed he was getting into, joining the Phantom Thieves:
One: Kicking ass, taking names. Shredding through Kamoshida’s palace was awesome in
every sense of the word, minus the parts where Kamoshida himself sucked.
Two: Maybe dodging the cops. Ryuji was pretty sure what they were doing wasn’t technically
legal, and that became extra obvious when Akechi stood up on live TV and gave his whole
spiel.

Three: Probably hiding this from his mom, forever.
Things Ryuji did not assume he was getting into, joining the Phantom thieves.
One: Time travel.
Two: Dodging the cops, badly.
Three: Definitely not hiding this from his mom. He’s going to have to stop hiding it from her
right now, in fact.
He’s actually already packed up his room. Crammed everything in boxes and bags. He was
gonna have to do it anyway, so why not sooner rather than later?
He’s also using it as a way to avoid talking to his mom. Sue him. Or, don’t, since that’s how
Ren got into this mess, and as much as Ryuji’s life kinda sucks right now, he still doesn’t
envy Ren’s.
“Ryuji!” His mom shouts from the other room, “Dinner!”
“Yeah, got it!” He shouts back, voice crack and all. It feels like it’s probably a bad omen.
He should bring it up over dinner. Right? It’ll be fine. …Right? Yes. Yes it will. His mom is,
without question, the best person ever, which really only adds to the pressure of Ryuji
absolutely not wanting to tell her about how his stupid vigilante stunts have uprooted their
life. Or will uproot their life. Definitely will, as quickly as they can be packed and ready to
go.
He scoots out of his room, with the same amount of dignity as a man marching to his absurd
and easily avoidable death, and takes his usual seat at the table.
“Okonomiyaki.” His mom declares, shifting the food onto his plate. It looks damn good, as
normal.
Ryuji shoves some into his mouth before his mom even gets the chance to sit down, just to
postpone his demise a little longer. The vaguely more responsibility-oriented part of his brain
internally thwacks him over the head for this.
“You didn’t go to school yesterday.” His mom says, as soon as she sits opposite him.
Ryuji chokes on his food. Oh, shit.
“And the school phoned me to say you skipped your afternoon classes on Friday.” She
continues.
There’s probably a lesson to be learned here about putting off important things. Ryuji will not
internalise it.
They actually almost already had this conversation, yesterday, when his mom told him he
was going to be late if he didn’t get his ass in gear, and Ryuji had replied “not goin’” with a

poor excuse for finality.
His mom must have heard something in his voice, because she let it go. Sucks that isn’t going
to work for more than one day.
“Um.” Ryuji coughs.
“I just—” his mom sighs, “I thought things were going better at school. You said you and that
girl Ann were getting along again, and— what was your new friend’s name?”
“Ren.”
“Ren. And that other boy? The one that came around for dinner once?”
“Yusuke.”
“Him! And didn’t you even say you were friends with the student council president?”
“Uh. Yeah.” Ryuji debates shovelling some more food into his mouth.
“That’s great!” His mom exclaims, the way she did the first time she heard this information.
“So what’s happening?
“I’m a Phantom Thief.” He blurts.
His mom stares at him.
Well, she did give him the perfect setup.

It’s not too weird for Ann to get a call from Ryuji, but it is pretty weird for him to start it with
“I think it went fine?” with no build-up or lead-in.
“Uh.” Is all she can think to say in response. On the floor, sitting on her futon, Makoto gives
her a strange look.
“Wrong number?” Makoto guesses, face serious in the way that probably means she’s
somehow twisted wrong number into a series of highly specific circumstances that mean the
apartment is compromised and the world is ending.
“No.” Ann says. Makoto’s expression darkens further. “It’s Ryuji.” Her expression
immediately un-darkens, into something resembling disappointment.
“Oh, hey, is that Makoto? Sick.”
“Yup.” Ann turns her attention back to the phone. After a second, she scrambles to put it on
speakerphone. “Uhhhh what’s up?”
“The sky.” Ryuji says.

Ann waits. Makoto also waits.
“Tough crowd.”
“Bad joke.” Ann counters. “But seriously, you gonna spill, or…?”

“Well…”
“It went… pretty okay…?”
“Yeah, let’s go with that.”

already know.”

Makoto pouts, which is a rare enough sight that Ann almost bursts out laughing.

“Metaverse.”
Ann whistles. “That’d do it.”
“Almost gave her a heart attack, I think.”
“That’d also do it.” Makoto agrees. “Are you ready to move out?”
There’s a sigh, “Yeah, I guess. Mom’s been packing. I should probably help her out,

“Probably.” Ann agrees.
“Mm.”
There’s a distinct lack of movement or hanging-up sounds on the other end of the line.

“I know it sucks.” Ann says, commiserating.

anyone yesterday, but they were still around.”

A pause.

It’s a rare occasion that Sumire feels she’s slipped under the radar. Whether it be the spotlight
or the regular gossip mills, she’s found herself the unfortunate centre of attention these past
two-one years.

But the police stalking the Shujin perimeter and its student council room hardly seem to care
she exists at all. She hasn’t even been called in for questioning, as many of her distinctly
unsuspicious classmates have.
“I heard Sakamoto and Amamiya weren’t at school on Saturday!” She hears one student
whisper.
“Really?! Are they here today…?”
“Haven’t seen ‘em!”
Sumire really wishes they would stop talking. If not for Ren and Ryuji’s sake, then for the
sake of not drawing any more attention from the prying ears of officers, their exact pool of
knowledge unclear.
Sumire certainly doesn’t want to draw any more attention to herself, either. She doesn’t know
what she’d do if she had to pack up and run. Hide in Mementos, maybe? But she’s got two
parents, a scholarship, and a gymnastics career she ought to be thinking about, sputtering its
last breaths or no.
A little dramatic. Ella chides. Sumire supposes she agrees. Once the year is gone she can
always regain her momentum. Maybe. Potentially.
It’s always the second priority.
She should find something to pass the school day that isn’t just wallowing.
Speaking with Haru tends to make her feel better. This was closer to an absolute truth earlier
in the year, but it’s hardly Haru’s fault that everything to do with the thieves is so turbulent
that it seeps into what remains of their normal lives, too.
Well, usually it’s not her fault.
That aside, Sumire begins climbing the stairs to the roof to track her down. If there’s anything
about Haru that will never change, she thinks, it’s that little garden of hers.
(It would have changed, had they not been caught in a year long stasis. Sumire suspects that
Haru will find some other small garden to dote on once she graduates, though, if not a larger
one.)
Sumire has her hand on the doorknob to the roof when she jumps about three feet in the air as
someone calls out to her.
“Are you allowed to go up there?”
Sumire does not shriek, “Um!” She whirls around, and sees a— detective? He’s got the
police badge, but no uniform— standing, lackadaisical below her on the stairs. “I’m part of
gardening club.”
He just looks confused at that.

“The garden’s on the roof.” She stumbles over herself to elaborate.
“Ah, gotcha.” The detective clicks his tongue. “Might I ask for your name? I don’t believe
I’ve had the pleasure of interviewing you yet.”
“Oh, no I, um.” Sumire swallows. She’s bad at this. Why is she bad at this? “I haven’t been
called in yet. I’m Yoshizawa.”
“Yoshizawa…” The detective mutters, and smiles with recognition, “The gymnastics honours
student, right?”
“Mm.”
“Hey, good luck with that.”
“Thank you.” Sumire says tightly.
“And sorry, for your loss.”
Oh. Sumire feels her chest spasm with sudden tightness, before she can’t really decide what
to feel at all. She can’t really decide what to say, either.
Are police allowed to know that? To bring that up? Who is she kidding, of course they’re
allowed. The conspicuously crossed-out row above her name on the class roll is apparently
enough to make an impression.
“I’ll let you get back to gardening.” The detective gives a wave, “Don’t stress too hard when
you get called in for questioning, hey? It’ll just be a short chat.”
Sumire nods numbly, and waits for him to disappear completely out of sight before spinning
on her heel to rip the door to the roof open. She slams it shut behind her, collapsing against it
and sliding to the ground.
“…Sumi-chan?” Haru’s voice wafts from the direction of the planters.
“Mmpf.” Sumire grunts into her knees. She can’t find the willpower to look up before she
hears Haru’s shoes gently tapping towards her, taking her own seat against the door.
“I think I heard some talking.” She says mildly. “Was someone bothering you?”
“One of the police officers. The detective, I think.” Sumire admits, peeling her face off of her
legs.
Haru hums, in a way that suggests that explains it all. Sumire feels her chest loosen slightly.
“They are a bit unsettling, aren’t they? Did he say anything in particular?”
Did he. “Not related to the thieves.”
“Well, that’s good then.” Haru leverages herself off the ground, dusting off her skirt and
stockings. “Do you want to help me? I’ve got some weeding to do. I’ve been neglecting the

poor seedlings of late, I’m afraid.”
“That’s what I came here for.” Sumire laughs weakly, taking Haru’s offered hand to haul
herself up.
Haru tosses her some gloves, and gestures to the growing pile of weeds on the concrete that
she’s already excavated as the toss pile, and they get to work.
Sumire doesn’t mind silence too much. But right now, she’d prefer some chatter. “I don’t
know why they scare me so much.” She says.
“They are rather dangerous.” Haru says in a low voice. “It’s not just the threat of arrest that’s
looming, either.”
No, the threat is far worse. Though maybe that’s always been the case, and it’s only now,
tangled in the heart of it all, that Sumire gets a front row seat to exactly what that means.
“They don’t even seem that suspicious of me.” She grumbles to herself, ripping out a weed
with extra force, “I’m painting a target on my back acting like this.”
“If they don’t consider you a suspect, then you’ll seem like any other nervous teen.” Haru
smoothly counters, “They don’t have any other frame of reference to compare you to.”
“He knew me by name.” Sumire says.
“Well, you are an honours student.” Haru points out, “I suspect they’d know Makoto-san’s
name too, even if she wasn’t an active person of interest.”
Haru really is very calm about all this. Annoyingly so. Sumire knows better than most that
she isn’t as put-together as she appears, but the facade is an excellent one, she has to concede.
“I’m surprised you haven’t decided to follow in Ren-senpai and Ryuji-senpai’s footsteps.”
Sumire comments, idly tugging another weed out of the soil.
Haru hums, her attention focused on the planters. “I considered it.” She says after a moment.
“But even though I admit my interview was somewhat concerning, I believe I’d be
significantly harder to get rid of than most of our friends.”
A fair point. Sumire tilts her head, “I guess you have…” she pauses. “Bodyguards?”
Haru giggles, “I suppose I could hire some, yes. But I’m mostly referring to the optics. My
father has just gone insane.” She says, conversationally, “If I were to mysteriously vanish so
soon after, it would raise some questions. I suppose they could just murder me in the way that
was done to the SIU director, but I’m of the belief it might be more trouble than it’s worth.”
Sumire dearly hopes her belief is correct, because this seems like a dangerous game to play.
All of this is dangerous, though. It didn’t stop Sumire when this started and she’s not going to
let it stop her now, either.

It would be rather sad to give up, so close to the end. Ella muses in agreement, and Sumire
can hear the hum of bells and ticking clocks ringing in her ear.
She hesitates to call this close to the end, but she couldn’t agree more.

One of these days, Akechi is going to properly assess the potential obstacles they may
encounter in the future and deal with them in advance, before they’re all stuck with the
waiting game once again.
He used to be quite good at doing that. He’d gotten into the rhythm of what Shido would
want when, and would clear requests in large batches, do schoolwork ahead of time, come to
interviews with his makeup already done, the works. An infinite shame that it’s so much
harder to work against Shido than for him.
The grass is always greener. Robin comments. Akechi ignores him, as he usually does.
Mementos remains as a wonderful place to clear his head. He could never tell if this place
made things better or worse, months ago, but that was before he had the free time to
aimlessly wander the surface. Tokyo minus the entire population is quite the place to be.
“I suppose you did imply you come here recreationally.” Kitagawa says.
Akechi supposes he should have expected Kitagawa to do the same, after their last encounter.
His lip still curls with annoyance. His kingdom for people to leave him alone.
“I get bored.” Akechi tells him, not turning to look. “Unless I feel like bothering any of my
current housemates, or like provoking Shido and the police into trying to arrest me again, this
is the only place to go.”
“I’m more surprised you don’t spend your time down in the tunnels.” Kitagawa comments,
not sounding particularly judgemental. Akechi still bristles.
Though— damn, he could be doing that, couldn’t he? Has he seriously conditioned himself

“Existing.”

COWARD.

Annoyingly, it is.

Maybe Akechi should have just rotted away on his bed and stared at the ceiling all day.

Ridiculous.

WITH WHAT WEAPON?

pace a little more. “Make your point.”

Nothing ever feels like just a conversation. Everything feels like knives running over his skin
looking for the best place to stab into his ego or his trust.
“Do I seem like I have a point?” Yusuke prods.
“No.” Akechi lies.
“Hm.”
“Let’s just go.” Akechi turns on his heel. “I think I’ve had enough wandering for today.”
“Oh.” Yusuke jogs to keep up, “Then I believe I’ll stay here. I’ve barely taken a look
around.”
“Apologies for distracting you.”

“Not at all.” Yusuke already seems to be losing interest in Akechi and is redirecting it to the
scenery, “Goodbye. If you wish to see the painting when it’s done, please do let me know.”
Maybe he will. Or maybe he won’t, to prove a point of his own.
You’re tangled in knots. Eurydice comments, voice wafting from a deeper recess in his soul.
Picking at the thread is getting nowhere. It’s hard to tell if it’s pulled looser or tighter as the
Hanged Man grows to rank six.

Ann isn’t a big fan of the cops calling her in for questioning again.
It’s pretty much the same as the first time, which is the only thing keeping her from dashing
into the Metaverse and sprinting all the way home. The questions are a little more probing, a

expression bored enough for plausible deniability.

“You look like shit.” Akechi tells her when she gets home.
It’s Ann’s first instinct to be supremely offended, because it is quite literally her job to look

It had become remarkably apparent, exactly what ordeal they would all have to tolerate when

Given the general state of things, (that being, cutting it as close to the wire as they dare)

He doesn’t think anyone got the last laugh there. Even Shiraishi seemed unsatisfied, which is
as much a recipe for future success as it is great pain and complication.
The thieves had parted with a smattering of expression, ranging from dour to irate. Ann had

so.”
He also doesn’t see a version of Makoto who would ever surrender herself to complete
humility. One caught in the throes of developing a complex, however, he thinks is extremely
likely. Has already happened, in fact.
“Seemed par for the course, to me,” Akechi says.
Makoto’s nose wrinkles further. She says nothing.
Maybe Akechi should give up and retire to his room, if this is how it’s going to be. He still
doesn’t want to leave the living room.
“If you were so unsatisfied with how things were going, surely Joker wouldn’t begrudge a
small mutiny?” Akechi says drily.
Makoto snorts, “And put myself in charge instead? We’ve all seen how that tends to turn
out.”
Akechi hasn’t seen Makoto’s leadership firsthand, actually. He also thinks he may have
stumbled upon the root of the complex. The urge to leave strengthens.
“Doubtless Shiraishi would fail to be satisfied by the outcome of a rigged shooting game,”
Akechi says.
Was there not some resolve to try harder? Robin comments.
Yes, but not with Makoto.
Loki laughs. Akechi isn’t sure whether to take that as at least half his soul being on his side
or not.
“Don’t try to make me feel better.” Makoto snaps.
Akechi wasn’t trying to do that, exactly. “Would you rather I tell you how much of a terrible
shot you are?”
Makoto looks angrier. Akechi rolls his eyes.

“I don’t need to listen to you,” Makoto decides.
“You don’t,” Akechi agrees.
Makoto stares at him like she’s just remembered he’s there at all. Akechi stares back.
Makoto’s stare narrows.
“Why are you so good at everything?” She blurts.
Akechi thinks that perhaps he really should have left, a few minutes ago.
“You exaggerate,” He says mildly.
“Top of your class,” Makoto lists.
“I’m technically a dropout,” Akechi says. They both are.
“Celebrity.”
“I think I’m last week’s news, at this point.”
“Physical strength, apparently.”
Akechi frowns down at himself, “You’re surprised?”
Makoto glares at him, “You look like a twig.”
Akechi, very slowly, very pointedly, flexes an arm.
“You look less like a twig,” She concedes, with what must be great difficulty. “But you still
look like you’d fold with one punch.”
“I don’t,” Akechi informs her.
“I’m aware.”
Makoto’s jealousy has been a point of contention between them for as long as they’ve known
each other. First, and then again, over and over, about Sae. About grades. About everything
under the sun, apparently.
Akechi had found it amusing, had sometimes needled this fact directly. Other times, he hardly
cared at all. These days, he finds himself wishing to be removed from the situation entirely,
whether trapped between the Niijimas or caught against Makoto’s expectations for herself
and him.
He has been trying. Surely no one can accuse him of apathy, in the face of whatever the hell
Makoto wants from him.
Ah, Eurydice deigns to comment, But you have certainly been masking it as such.
Akechi doesn’t think those things should be so intertwined.

“Whatever,” Makoto says. “It doesn’t matter.”
“It doesn’t,” Akechi agrees.
“That’s easy for you to say.”
“It shouldn’t be particularly difficult for you to say, either.”
Makoto doesn’t seem to have a response for that one. Akechi takes the short reprieve to stare
up at the ceiling.
“…Do you seriously want my life?” Akechi says, after a belated burst of absolute incredulity.
“I’d probably put it to better use than you do,” Makoto hisses.
“Alright, Miss hindsight.” Akechi says with venom, “By all means. Dying and then having
your corpse strung up like a puppet is sure to be a delight for you.”
“That isn’t.” Makoto’s face spasms. “That isn’t what I meant.”
“Really.”
“Really,” She spits. “I don’t get you.”
“You’ve shared similar sentiments before.”
“And you haven’t changed.”
He isn’t sure if he trusts her opinion to be unbiased, but he finds can’t really tell either way.
Haven’t the thieves’ personas evolved after they achieved personal growth, or something
equally saccharine? Robin and Loki remain in their jagged pieces, unable or unwilling to fit
together.
Makoto’s persona hasn’t changed yet, either. Akechi recalls Anat, and Agnes, and has only
seen Johanna for months.
“Neither have you,” He says.
Makoto’s hands flex.
“I have changed,” She insists after a moment.
“Really?”
“The me from the start of the year wouldn’t have been able to do this,” She says. “Any of
this. I would have been— I don’t know. Too scared, maybe.”
Akechi thinks Makoto had been at a tipping point for a long time. He also thinks there’s a
difference between fear and cowardice.
Uncharitable.

Perhaps. But then again, he doesn’t quite believe it of her now. He supposes she really must
have changed.
“Then what the hell does any of that have to do with me?” He snaps.
Makoto blinks, then looks annoyed, “It doesn’t.”
“Which is what I’ve been trying to—”
“Except it does, too,” She immediately amends.
“Make up your mind,” Akechi hisses.
“Only after you do,” Makoto immediately fires back, which is so childish and nonsensical
that Akechi can’t find an easy way to refute it.
***
Makoto doesn’t think she’s won, exactly, when all Akechi gives her is an unimpressed look,
but she does appreciate the moment of him not talking.
It’s always all about him, somehow. And what’s worse is that he only makes it so
intentionally about half the time. She wonders, often, if she’s the only one who feels like this.
The only one stuck in a one-sided rivalry with someone who has deemed that he has better
things to think about than how he’s a wrench in the gears of her life.
When she joined the thieves, she felt more assured than she’d ever been her whole life.
A goal, a purpose, and a righteous one to boot. It was easy to take charge with strategy, to
offer her thoughts; she’s student council president, she knows how to manage a group
meeting.
But she wasn’t the leader. Ren is. Was. Still is.
She didn’t mind being support. She filled her own irreplaceable niche, and that was enough
for her, really. Then Futaba joined, and she was clever, and smart, and a prodigy, and Makoto
had no idea how to talk to her. Which was fine, she was still important,
Then Ren started having visions and dreams, and it was another puzzle to solve. A mystery to
crack. Who is the black mask? Surely the girl with crimson red hair and not the boy who
called her a pushover.
Then, another domino along the line, she figured she could tolerate Akechi’s sudden presence
if he was willing to play nice. It felt charitable, like she was being the bigger person. Like all
of her strained smiles and the twitches in his expression meant winning. Like trying to save
him could mean—
Could mean,
(What, that he owed her? That he could never possibly win again, with an outstanding debt.)

And then,
The boy who called her a pushover was instead the man who’s killed and driven others mad,
and her short-lived spark of pure vindication was quickly smothered with no one else caring
nearly as much as she did. Her bone-deep certainty of being right was shattered twice in as
many days, and it didn’t really feel like they had any leader at all, anymore.
It certainly wasn’t her. She’s always liked the idea of leading. Holding authority where she
used to have none. Dad was a leader.
She can’t do anything right, never could, never will. Akechi can’t, either, but he has the
audacity to fail upward.
She fails, and trips down, down,
Within the wellspring of your own mind.
She thinks it’s a little more literal than that.
You envision a pit, a ditch, a cliff face, and forget that it could not possibly matter less if
your grip upon fictional handholds is firm.
It’s not so simple, though. Makoto knows she’s prone to spiral. She also knows she’s—
Justified?
Well, when put like that.
The fact remains that pitfall or no, some things are unsalvageable. Some twists of fate leave
things permanently out of her grasp and she doesn’t know what she’s doing wrong.
You had such conviction, when you were swatting flies. Her persona laments.
Things change.
Not everything must. The ground will shift, but you can choose to stand firm, or adapt.
Hm.
Metaphorically.
She gathered. But she still—
She,
She’s not contrarian.
You aren’t.
The last time she was ever so cornered that she nearly brought everyone down with her, she
felt her blood burn so hot that she cracked the floor and blazed a path with fire and engine

exhaust. It had been electric, pure sensation and conviction that she wasn’t going to let
anyone—
Anyone,
There is not much point to an obstacle that you can simply walk around.
She’s starting to see that, yes.
It’s not as electrifying. Not as burning, or even as strong a force of will that overcomes her.
More a swoop, a drop, and a pleasant warmth that spreads outward to the tips of her fingers
and toes.
And, a name that bubbles up to her lips.
“Anat,” Makoto shares with the ceiling.
The obstacle gets to hear it too. “Goodness.”
Makoto looks back down, and narrows her eyes, “Don’t tell me you recognise her.”
“Whatever epiphany you just had, you must have had last time, too,” Akechi comments, dry
as ever.
Makoto snorts, “Good for me.”
Akechi tilts his head, “I suppose.”
Well.
A moment of silence, where Makoto finds that the ceiling is rather good company, actually.
“…Is that all?” Akechi asks.
“You can leave.” So can Makoto, but she really doesn’t want to.
Akechi sniffs. “I don’t want to.”
Worse than an obstacle, the implication that they’re in any way similar makes her skin crawl.
She stands quickly, “Have it your way.”
Akechi raises an eyebrow.
(And, to his great chagrin, feels the High Priestess grow to its final rank. Some part of him
twinges to feel underwhelmed, before remembering bonds go both ways. All that does,
unfortunately, is make him feel out of the loop.)
“Makoto,” He says.
Makoto pauses on her way out of the living room. She raises an eyebrow to match his.

Akechi rolls his eyes, “Your damn shooting was fine.”
Makoto opens her mouth, closes it. She settles on nodding stiffly, and finally leaves.
***
Sumire’s excitement for this new palace has admittedly stagnated somewhat.
From the tricks and the blatantly personal angle that Shiraishi is attempting to play, any
illusions of tearing through a cognitive realm with raucous laughter has been thoroughly
dispersed. Any illusions of any part of this remaining some semblance of fun have also
kicked it.
And with that sour mood in mind, Sumire stands with the thieves just one day after their last
infiltration outside the first of three circus tents. Joker looks stressed, Crow looks annoyed,
and Sumire is happy to see that Queen doesn’t seem all that discouraged, despite looking
pretty out of it the day prior.
In fact, she actually looks a bit smug. Sumire sees Noir give her a curious look.
“So…” Oracle drawls from above, “Still got your ticket, Crow?”
“I’d better still have my damn ticket.” Crow says threateningly, in the direction of the shadow
guarding the entrance. Shiraishi himself is yet to comment.
“I wonder what’ll be inside?” Sumire muses, as there’s a small scuffle between Joker and
Crow after the latter remembers his lack of pockets.
“Hopefully nothing too crazy.” Mona grimaces.
“I believe you’d be jinxing it, to say so.” Fox hums.
“You’re double jinxing it by pointing it out, Inari!”
“Got it,” Joker suddenly announces, holding their collective ticket aloft. The pockets of his
coat look mildly shredded.
“Yes, yes, let’s get a move on,” Crow says briskly.
“Akechi-kun has the right idea,” Shiraishi breaks his silence, “You kids have got a show to
give.”
“Do we,” Queen says flatly.
Joker walks up to the shadow guarding the tent, flicking the ticket to be caught between his
middle and index fingers. “Heya,” He says. “Ticket for, uh,” Sumire sees him do an internal
head count, “Ten.”
The shadow stares for a beat too long. Just as Joker looks like he’s about to say something
more, the shadow gives a stiff sweeping bow, and steps aside.

The thieves all exchange various glances, before Joker tentatively waves them forward.
Stepping into the tent, any lingering light from outside is quickly swallowed by the tunnel of
fabric. Sound is muffled, as well, making for a rather miserable view of bobbing shadows as
they all walk forward in relative silence.
“Very suspenseful,” Shiraishi comments.
Sumire assumes that it’s Crow who immediately swings his sword at the ceiling.
They aren’t left in suspense for much longer though, as a sharp prick of light appears at the
end of the tunnel that grows brighter and brighter, until it blooms. Sumire has to quickly duck
her head and cover her eyes, only managing to look up after blinking away the light seared
onto her eyelids.
When she does, she’s greeted with a carnival’s worth of equipment.
Knives and large balls and hoops and rings and, most eye-catchingly, a tightrope, all piled on
the sunken stage in the middle of the tent, surrounded by rings of entirely empty seats, raising
up by layers after the last.
Skull whistles.
“There’s no audience.” Noir frowns.
“…Maybe we’ll be the audience!” Panther says, which is a bit too falsely optimistic even for
Sumire.
“Afraid not,” Shiraishi says. “I’ve misplaced all my performers, y’see. I’m looking for some
new ones.”
“I don’t believe that turn of phrase quite works, here,” Fox says.
“Unless it’s something weird and convoluted,” Oracle says, still earthbound after dropping to
the ground to move through the tunnel, “Like, ‘I misplaced my gun, which then manged to
fire twenty-or-so odd bullets directly into the foreheads of all my performers.’”
“Hey, I can go with that.”
“How about we don’t?” Queen snaps, exasperated.
“No need to get so tetchy, miss,” Shiraishi chuckles, “One show is all I’m looking for,
serious.”
“And what’s stopping us from just walking right past this?” Crow drawls towards the ceiling.
“Another ticket, for one.”
On the far end of the tent, another shadow materialises, guarding a fold in the tent’s fabric
that Sumire hadn’t even seen.

“The next tent is even more exclusive, you get me?” Shiraishi explains, reasonable as
anything. “Can’t have just anyone wandering in. That’s where the real shows are. Think of
this like an audition.”
“Last time didn’t count?” Joker asks.
“I suppose if Akechi-kun wanted to waltz on past, that’s well within his power to do so.”
All the thieves blink. Crow himself tilts his head curiously, looking rather like his namesake.
“The rest of you? Well, that’s another story. You’ve given me nothing to work with! Other
than letting yourselves be stalked and hypothetically killed by our friend here.”
“That’s not fair!” Oracle blurts, “He has cloaking or some bullshit!”
“I do have that,” Crow agrees.
“Doesn’t change facts, missy.”
Oracle grumbles something likely uncharitable under her breath.
“So, what?” Skull makes a face at the equipment scattered across the stage, “You want us to
juggle?”
“You can juggle?” Panther asks, incredulous.
“Nope.”
“That’s for the best,” Shiraishi interjects drily, “Because I was hoping for something a little
more entertaining than that.”
Sumire stares the equipment down, looking for anything that might constitute entertaining.
What on earth is Shiraishi even looking for? He’s a fan of danger, clearly, fabricated or
otherwise. Emotional danger, something uncomfortable.
“Do all of us have to impress you in some manner?” Noir asks.
“How about this? If one of you extra kids does something really showstopping, I’ll consider
you all a package deal.”
Crow scoffs. Sumire’s eyes land on the tightrope.
Joker rubs a hand down his face, “It’d be great if you were a little more specific about—”
“I’ll walk across that.” Sumire blurts, pointing towards the tightrope.
Everyone stares at her. She gets the impression that Shiraishi is staring, too.
“…Would that be enough?” She tacks on, voice getting dangerously close to a squeak.

After a moment, Shiraishi bursts out laughing.
“Go for it, kid!” He cackles, “I gotta see this.”
The stares turn into a round of contemplative expressions, most of which also have the extra
effect of looking rather constipated.
“…You can do it!” Panther cheers, eyeing the tightrope warily.
“How high up d’you think that thing is?” Skull asks. Panther jabs him in the stomach.
“Well, you are a gymnast,” Mona says. “If you think you’ve got this, Violet, I say go for it.”
Sumire does not point out that none of her gymnastics exploits involve tightropes. Or beams,
for that matter. She shoots a look in Joker’s direction, dutifully ignoring whatever concerned
or dubious expression is likely on Noir and Crow’s faces.
Joker shrugs, his hands in his pockets.
What wonderful encouragement.
“Pretty sure you don’t take fall damage in the cognitive world, if it’s any consolation.” Oracle
says. “Well. So long as you don’t think too hard.”
Oh, great—
“Now that your pow-wow’s done,” Shiraishi interrupts, “Can we get this show on the road?”
“Right.” Sumire straightens up, squaring her shoulders and marching towards the ladder.
“Yes.”
Some of the thieves give cheers of encouragement. Sumire shoots them a wary smile in
response.
She holds her breath as she climbs the ladder. It’s a terrible habit, born of nervousness, that’s
caused her trouble in her routines before. Stress means she either can’t breathe, or will
hyperventilate, and both ways mean she can’t get any air.
She very purposefully takes a deep breath as she reaches the top. She takes extra care to not
look down, as much to avoid looking at the thieves as avoiding acknowledging how far down
the ground is.
It didn’t look that high, standing below.
This is why she went for floor gymnastics. Beams and bars freaked her out. Still freak her
out.
“Stalling?” Shiraishi says, addressing just her, for once.
“No,” Sumire says.

“Then hurry it up, girl. Suspense is a tool best used sparingly.”
She can’t drag this out forever. Still looking forward, she kicks off her heels, and toes the
edge of the platform, trying to find where the tightrope is. When she finds it, she delicately
shifts her whole foot out, dead centre.
The rope seems sturdy enough. She’s got good balance. She’s got this, it’s fine.
She straightens her back, tightens her core, throws out her arms, and swoops her other leg off
the platform.
She places it neatly in front of the first, and she doesn’t fall.
She thinks she hears the thieves cheering, down below. Her ears are ringing.
“Not bad.” Shiraishi says. “Might take you an hour to reach the end, at this pace.”
“Thanks,” Sumire grits through her teeth, and takes another step. The rope shifts beneath her
feet, and she pulls her back up even straighter as she just barely begins to cant forward.
She can’t let her joints shake. She can’t let her foot roll. She’s got good balance, but bad
recovery.
She puts another foot forward.
“Hm.” Shiraishi hums.
“What?” Sumire asks, eyes flitting up before she forcibly drags them back forward.
“This isn’t nearly as entertaining as I thought it would be.”
Sumire takes another step. Her foot hovers above the rope for just a moment too long, and
her stomach swoops before she properly lands. “You’re not changing your mind, are you?”
“No, no. Let me think.”
Sumire isn’t sure if she’s meant to wait. She thinks waiting would just make her sweat so
much that she’d slip and fall even while being perfectly still, so she takes another step.
Three steps later, and Shiraishi speaks again.
“I do have an idea, actually.”
Another step. “Yes?”
“A show is supposed to be stylish,” Shiraishi says. “Get some pizzaz in there, y’know? Throw
a curveball or two.”
Sumire thinks she’s getting the hang of the tightrope. “…Yes? And?”
“Think fast.”

Sumire’s chest seizes as she hears and feels the rope strain beneath her feet. Her knees
buckle, as her weight forcibly shifts and all the panic crashes back onto her in an instant.
Swooping from her left, a trapeze bar swings just out of reach.
As the rope snaps, Sumire leaps, and catches it, just barely with her left hand.
She lets out a small shriek as she scrambles to get her right hand on the bar, the wires
swinging with force applied from somewhere above. She briefly swings up to readjust her
hands, feeling her shoulders strain under the sudden weight.
“Hey, nice catch.”
Sumire doesn’t dignify that with a response. She focuses on swinging her body in time with
the trapeze, to avoid being flung off by a clash in momentum.
“Good form.”
“Thanks,” Sumire grits, with real sarcasm this time.
“Think you can do it again?”
Sumire braces, for what good it does, as she’s flung up, up, spinning upside down, the back
of her knees clanging painfully against another bar, her hair and coat left trailing toward the
ground as she’s left gripping the bar only by her legs.
Taking a sharp breath, she quickly shimmies out of her coat, letting it float away. Her arms
now free, she grits her teeth as she levers herself up, grasping at the bar and the wires
suspending it, climbing to her feet.
“Fancy.” Shiraishi whistles, “I see why the thieves guild over there let you take a crack at
this.”
Sumire does her best not to glance down at the thieves in question. “Anything else?”
“Oh, sure.”
On command, a spinning hoop comes whirling past her in an arc. She yelps, and manages to
grasp it with one hand as it tears past her, ripping her off her feet. She tucks herself into a ball
on instinct, folding her legs around the hoop and hugging it with all her might.
The hoop spins and spins, on its own axis as well as in an orbit from the ceiling. Sumire
wrests one hand free to clamp over her mouth as she feels bile rise in her throat.
Slowly, the hoop begins to loose momentum more and more, until it’s left doing an uneven
little twirl from the centre of the ceiling. Sumire doesn’t dare loosen her grip.
She squints an eye open, barely aware that she ever closed them in the first place. She peeks
upward, much closer to the top of the tent than she’d prefer. She doesn’t look down.

Drifting alongside her, a curtain of ribbons haphazardly flutter in long lines from the ceiling.
They look… sturdy enough, she supposes.
Shiraishi seems to have run out of quips and running commentary. She’s not really in the
mind to appreciate it, given that she’s stuck up here.
She slowly reaches out, and gives one of the ribbons a sharp tug.
…It doesn’t immediately detach. Whether it’ll hold her weight is another story.
Unfolding her limbs like a particularly gangly spider, Sumire fits herself to properly sit inside
the hoop. She reaches out an ankle, and winds a ribbon around it once, twice, thrice, lunging
away from the hoop to fully shift herself over to the ribbon.
Bracing her free foot over her other, she swings back and forth until she has enough force to
launch over to another ribbon that stretches further down. There’s a brief moment where she’s
holding her own weight purely by the strength of her elbows, as she clumsily wraps this
ribbon around her ankle with her other foot.
Securing herself again, she tries to chart a path.
There’s a ribbon close enough that she forgoes a jump and just reaches out to catch it. Body
working quicker than her mind can make the decision, she sends out her other arm to catch
the next ribbon, then another, and another, until she’s dancing down, twirling and throwing
out kicks just for the sake of it.
In spins and leaps, she falls to the ground with the utmost grace she can muster, catching
herself along the hoop and bars along the way, before leaping to grasp at one final ribbon that
stretches all the way to the stage, slipping down it in a tight spiral.
Her feet finally touch the floor with minimal fanfare, and she just barely remembers to throw
up her arms in some semblance of a finishing pose, rather than slumping over with immediate
relief.
The thieves are somewhere behind her, she thinks. She sees her coat on the ground a few
metres away, but doesn’t dare move until Shiraishi says something—
“Now that was mighty impressive,” Shiraishi says, somehow still sardonic.
“Was it enough?” Sumire practically begs. Everything hurts. She’d love nothing more than to
collapse to the floor in a heap. She keeps her pose.
“Ticket’s in your coat.”
Sumire immediately drops to her knees, strings cut.
She sees his shadow first, as Crow slowly walks past her to pick up her coat, rifling around in
the pockets. After a moment, he whips out a ticket between two claws.
He turns to her, walking over and offering a hand.

“Impressive,” He says flatly. He sounds like he means it.
“Thank you,” Sumire gasps. She kind of thought she was going to die. She takes his hand and
hauls herself to her feet, turning to face the rest of the thieves.
Skull whistles. Noir claps enthusiastically, though her smile is strained.
“Can we go?” Sumire chokes out.
“Was gonna suggest it myself,” Joker says. Sumire nods weakly.

Chapter 107
Chapter Summary

Interlude II, and a little bit of theatre.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

An interlude, from a time quite present.
There was a man, once, who thought he ought to have everything.
Wealth; gold and shining jewels. People, his superiors soon to be lesser. The whole world and
all its wonders, shrunk to fit in the palm of his hand.
Shrunk, to be observed from the view of a tower a very, very long way from the ground.
He heard whispers in his ear,
All this and more is exactly what you deserve, yours by right.
He agreed, certainly. He was young, handsome; people already rushed to lick his shoes, beg
him for favour.
Not everyone, though.
Listen to me, and everyone shall.
So he listened. And listened. He invested, forged, made, more, more, more, until he had a
web strung up by his hand, pulled and tugged by the slightest movement of his finger.
He wanted for nothing.
He wanted for everything, still.
Contrary to what some fools may claim, the man knew there was no such thing as enough.
Those who say they have met the end of their means are merely to cowardly to speak of their
failing worth outright. Not him.
It started as a passing fantasy. Merely an idea, really. So many already looked to him for
guidance, for navigation, that he wondered if the effort of drawing the whole country into his
thrall was really worth it.
Listen to me, and—

Of course it was worth it.
It was a long, arduous process. He had to be charming, he had to be convincing. He couldn’t
spit upon everyone he dearly wished to— He had to learn to take the measure of a man based
upon what they could give him.
Most could offer him nothing.
Some, could offer him quite useful boons indeed.
And some lingering wraiths along the path offered him curses and chains that proved awfully
difficult to shake. Had he known they were haunting him, he would have excised them long
before they could become notable problems.
Listen to—
He’s working on it.
His passing fantasy, his ultimate goal, to sit at the head of the great ship and be known far and
wide as its captain, almost entirely within his grasp.
And yet remaining: poltergeists,
The attack dog freed from his leash. The scientist and her failed endeavours. And a band of
oh-so-elusive thieves that have proven wise to being snapped up by metal jaws.
He has eight days to work with. He hasn’t made any great strides, but to his knowledge,
neither have they.
(A report sits on his desk: Two breaches of the Metaverse in as many days, both in the same
location, the reason for such entirely unknowable.
Hm.
The time for careful plays is over, he thinks.)
***
Ann is starting to think she’s maybe-probably-almost-certainly screwed.
The first time the cops called her into questioning, she managed to mostly play herself off as
a ditsy and otherwise oblivious victim of circumstance. She could practically see them
writing her off as an airhead in real time.
Infuriating, but ultimately what she wanted. She swallowed down her scowl.
The second time, they seemed a little more wise to her act. She remains a terrible liar, and
there’s only so many ways to lie about exactly how involved in the Kamoshida incident she
was.

And now, after the third time, it’s pretty apparent the jig is up.
Except, they sent her back to class, still. And even still, Ms. Kawakami gave her a worried
look when she sat back down, which confirms to Ann that getting questioned three times isn’t
normal and she definitely should be worried.
She’s not in handcuffs, and she’s not yet home free. Ann very desperately needs the scale to
tip further in one direction or the other. The indecision is going to kill her before the cops do.
Surely they’re not afraid of getting the wrong person. Certainly not from a moral standpoint.
From a logistical standpoint, then? Shido must be getting antsy, and catching someone that
isn’t actually one of the Phantom Thieves isn’t going to lessen his problem.
Maybe. Probably. None of that quite solves her problem, given she’s one of the most
suspicious people in Shujin, the only other people vying for the title having already left.
Hesitation is where weaker hearts stumble. Hecate advises. Ann thinks that’s great and all,
but that doesn’t really sway her towards the decision itself.
Except, waiting around was always stalling, wasn’t it? Hoping they could get something
done before their enemies could. So it’s a toss up between making a decision and not making
a decision. When she puts it like that—
Still, still, and still again: there’s nowhere for her to go.
“I don’t think I can keep going to school,” Ann says to the elder Niijima as soon as she gets
home.
Niijima looks up, face already contorted in a signature frown. “Has something happened?”
“Um.” Ann feels like she’s getting questioned again, with the way Niijima is looking at her.

Makoto frowns in a way remarkably similar to her sister. “…I’ll grab Akechi,” She says, and
marches back out.
“I neglected to ask,” Niijima says as there’s the sound of muffled conversation the room over.
“Will the school contact your parents, if you’re suddenly absent?”

Ann tugs at her hair a little harder. She shuffles over to take a seat on the couch. “Maybe?”
She really doesn’t know. “They can try but… I don’t know if they’re… available.”
Niijima’s eyes narrow, and Ann thinks she likes this line of questioning even less, somehow,
“There’s really no way to contact them?”
“Well.” Ann laughs nervously, “I can definitely contact them pretty easily. I just, um. Don’t.”
They’re a distant sort. They weren’t always, but then suddenly Ann was old enough to be left
at home, so as to ‘not disrupt her schooling and friends’. She does appreciate that, but, well.
Distance.

Niijima nods, which seems to be the end of that.

“Yeah.”

“Yeah.”

Shiraishi’s palace is complete, to the extent that they can complete it with their self-imposed
restrictions, and one final hurdle remains.
One final hurdle, Haru amends in her mind, of the non-godly variety. Though if she were to
be honest with herself, she considers the respective obstacles of Yaldabaoth and Maruki to be
far less complicated than Shido and his army of co-conspirators. Perhaps Sumire and Ren
might think otherwise, but she has a suspicion that she and Goro are like-minded in this
regard.
Gods do not concern themselves with politics. Gods only threaten their homes existentially,
rather than literally. Gods only leave lasting stains on their lives in the psychological sense.
To kill a god is easy. To kill an ideology, that whips the masses into a frenzy and chases them
to all the dark corners they could possibly think to hide, is much harder.
And thus, her dilemma:
How do you run from something that cannot simply be dealt with?
Haru is under no illusions that she is in quite the same position as her friends. As tenuous as
her status often feels, as quickly as the social winds shift for and against her family’s favour,
as absolutely powerless as she was with her father turning the other way and Sugimura
feeling up her hips, it was never the law that would do her in.
The only way Shido will truly catch her is if she’s bleeding out on her own carpet, which is
it’s own kind of horrifying she supposes. But, a distinctly more avoidable horrifying than
being snapped up off the street and sent to a windowless room to be questioned and beaten
until she breaks.
She could stand to exercise her power a little more liberally. She has hardly had time to fight
the tooth and nail she ought to against the various executives in Okumura Foods, but she still
remains her family’s rather sudden matriarch.
Theoretically, she could extend the safety she enjoys to her friends simply by pulling enough
strings. Now that she sits at its centre, the web afforded to her by her now-indisposed father
seems awfully grand.

Unsubtle, and untested in its effectiveness. But an option, which everyone seems so intent on
reminding each other that they lack.
Her home was initially dismissed in the list of safe options to hide away in due to the scrutiny
she’s facing, but with the police running out of excuses to rummage through her things the
longer her father’s condition remains inexplicable, does this remain the case? As Haru is
slowly coming to realise, there is very little that the police can force her to do.
A somewhat grim revelation, knowing what they can most certainly do to anyone that isn’t
her.
Being free from the police doesn’t stop her from being susceptible to bullets, though.
They’re such elegant things. Astarte titters.
Haru is inclined to agree, though less so when it’s her own blood and brains scattered against
a wall that she’s envisioning. She doesn’t envy the person who’d have to clean that up.
Shiraishi will not be truly dealt with until Shido is. And even if he were, that doesn’t stop
Shido from simply hiring someone else. She doesn’t like her chances with either option.
Fire with fire, then? Gunfire, that is.
Haru smiles, pressing a hand to her lips to hide it even with no one watching.
If she wishes to shield her friends, there isn’t much she can do but that. Buying loyalty with
money is a tenuous thing, but she does happen to have quite a lot of money.
Then, Haru supposes, it’s what she’ll do.
…
There is an ideal world that she keeps close to her heart, where she is not heiress to more
money than most could feasibly even conceive. Where the Phantom Thieves are a silly game
she plays with her friends, the threats they run from little more than shadows on the wall.
Where she runs a café like her grandfather did, where her father never stopped forgetting that
love is not a bargaining chip.
Maybe, if she were to be particularly defeatist, where he loved her at all.
She tucks the world away, somewhere to hide it from prying eyes and twisting roots. Maybe
one day, when she has beaten her life into something she wishes it was, she can unfold it
from her heart and get to work.
“Takakura-san,” She says, after ringing a seldom-used number on her phone, “Tell me. Who
did my father tend to hire for protection?”

The Tower,
The—
It’s leaning,
Cracking at the base,

He doesn’t protest when Ren says, “Out. I think that’s enough for today.”

Chapter Summary

Setbacks, monotony, and interlude III

Despite her inclination towards the more catastrophic sort of restless boredom (a trait she
finds she shares with Akechi of all people, which she avoids thinking about), Sae Niijima
doesn’t dare occupy herself with anything more than the most minor of activities.
Making a cup of coffee. Chipping away at the crossword. Making headway in that damn
book on native birds that she doesn’t know why she swiped from her own apartment so long
ago. Nothing that could fully divert her attention from straining her ears and keeping her
hand hovered over Makoto’s phone.
She isn’t sure if she expects someone to come knocking. None of the thieves who have had to
escape their homes have been around to confirm that their choice was well made. The
expectation is there, certainly, for herself, for Akechi, for the Sakuras, but will comparatively
insignificant infringements upon Shido’s conspiracy like Sakamoto and Takamaki be given
the same treatment?
Sae supposes that being a Phantom Thief is already well past the realm of insignificance. The
choice to hide is the correct one.
Not that they’ve hidden yet.
As absolutely maddening her lack of things to do is, she finds that concentrating on reading is
an impossible task. She closes the book she’ll never finish with a thump.
Maybe she should make another cup of coffee—
The sound of someone rattling the doorknob.
A moment later, a deceptively polite knock.
Sae’s breath catches.
Her hands do not shake as she reaches for Makoto’s phone.
The polite knocking pauses. It restarts as sharp bangs.

“Excuse me?! What on earth are you doing?!” A voice from the hall.
“No need to worry, ma’am, we have a warrant to search this residence.”
Sae gently, carefully, far-too-slowly (she wants to run, run, kick off her heels and kick in the
door and kick in their faces before they get the chance to do it first), lies back on their pile of
stuff, ensuring some part of her is making contact with each box and bag.
“It’s just Takamaki-san’s daughter that lives there! Do you really have to barge in on a
teenage girl? Just wait until she gets home!”
She lifts Makoto’s phone to her face,
“Ma’am, we’ll have to ask you to leave.”
“Mementos,” Sae whispers, and feels the world dissolve.

Well, she thinks again, not quite. The palace itself is something to behold. It’s just with Ren

sniper rifles trained on them from every direction.
She won’t complain. They’ve enough of that in reality, she thinks.
A point quickly proven the moment she, Makoto, and Akechi arrive home.
“Welcome back,” Niijima greets them.
Ann blinks. The room and sky are still stained red. Niijima sits perched atop all their bags
and boxes, one leg crossed over the other.
Akechi sighs.
Niijima tosses Makoto her phone back, who fumbles slightly to catch it.
“People came knocking, then?” Akechi asks.
Niijima nods, and stands, “That they did.”
Oh.
It’s not like Ann didn’t expect it. She helped plan for it.
Makoto crosses her arms. “Well. Now what?”
Everyone is silent.

“To Mementos proper?” Akechi suggests.
“To sleep?” Ann asks, incredulous.

“I suppose.” Akechi shrugs, “If you’re alright with knowing there are men intent on our death
one step past the veil of reality.”

“Bad,” is Akechi’s answer. “Not to mention it will likely start shifting quickly, depending on
how fast it’s torn apart.”
“Let’s just go to Shibuya,” Ann decides, ignoring that statement for her own sake. “We can…
find a nearby hotel, or something. Cognition should be pretty stable in one of those, right?”
“In theory,” Makoto agrees.
