During the day, she tends to stick out. On the job, it’s her, well, job, to stick out. She avoids

And now she’ll have to be hiding for quite some time.

They probably don’t take kindly to their models being hunted by the police, either. She

Modelling, as vain as she’s sure it makes her appear to peers that never liked her anyway, was

As it turns out, she really likes modelling. She likes being seen. Really seen, not just looked

Panther: heyyyy

There’s a long pause.
“Can you not find it?” Sumire asks tentatively.
“Uhhh.”
“Oracle?” Ren frowns.
“Uh, nothing,” Futaba stutters. “Or, not nothing. I wasn’t really focusing on the surrounding
map too much, since you were leading the way, but the way these halls are shaped are really
weird?”
“How so?” Makoto narrows her eyes.
“It’s like there’s something missing on the map we got at the start,” Futaba explains. “All
these hallways are doing backflips to avoid an entire chunk of the ship.”
“Is it the engine they’re avoiding?” Ren asks. Goro tosses him another look, much sharper
this time.
“Nope,” Futaba says, “I can see where that is just fine. I can even chart a course to my best
guess at where Sato is.”
“Then what’s missing from the ship?” Haru asks.
“If I knew I’d be less confused!” Futaba exclaims, and Ren can picture her throwing up her

“Nothing specific,” Ren says slowly.
“Nothing that I can remember,” Goro agrees, brow furrowed. “I don’t think it’s a stretch to
say that Shido’s cognition has jammed a new section into the ship, and all other paths have
been forced to shift to make room.”
Ann and Ryuji both groan.

Morgana’s face is scrunched in confusion, “That’s… weird, but not unheard of. You guys said
Okumura’s palace was almost completely different, right? Whatever this new thing is, can’t
we just avoid it?”
“That depends on how important the engine room is.”
“Very,” Ren says.
“Then bad news, boss!” Futaba sing-songs, “Cause I can’t find a path to the engine room.”
“Hm,” is all Goro says.
“We did have to crawl through a vent to get there,” Ren says.
“Already checked for stuff like that,” Futaba dismisses. “I think whatever this new thing is,
it’s crashed directly between this section of halls and the engine.”
“Well.” Makoto sighs. “It sounds like we’ll be taking a detour at some point.”
“…If we can still make it to Sato, then we’ll put it off until tomorrow.” Ren decides. He
doesn’t care to traverse a new path in Shido’s mind unless they’re all at full stamina.
“We can make it to him,” Futaba assures, “Or, at least I’m pretty sure we can.”
“We won’t know until we get there,” Haru says.
“So let’s get going,” Ren agrees.
It bruises Ren’s ego significantly less than it would have to have Futaba leading the way far
better than he did, when coupled with the knowledge that the palace’s structure has changed.
Futaba certainly wasn’t joking when she said the hallways were nonsensical in their layout.
Some of the halls even start tilting upwards, which Ren is near certain is not normal shiphallway architecture.
But they do, eventually, reach the back of the ship.
“Hey,” Ann says, as they start shuffling over the (far easier to traverse than last time) ship’s
exterior. “I don’t know a lot about ships or anything, but shouldn’t the engine-whatever have
an exhaust or something? Can’t we just go through that?”
“Normally, Panther, you’d be right!” Futaba says. “But as far as I can tell, there just isn’t
one.”
“There… isn’t an exhaust?” Makoto clarifies, looking towards Necronomicon.
“Nope,” Futaba agrees, “Lucky this ship isn’t real, right?”
“Very lucky,” Morgana grimaces.
“That aside, though,” Futaba says, “You recognise this place yet, Joker?”

“I do, actually.” Ren hums. “I think it should be one of those balconies over there.”
They all dart over, hopping along ledges and extrusions. Ren counts as they jump across the
balcony walls, one, two, three, until he spies a familiar-looking cognition inside one of the
windows, and skids to a halt.
Futaba joins them on the balcony, dropping down from Necronomicon. “This our stop?” She
stands on her toes, peeking over Ren’s shoulder. “Oh, yep, that’s our guy!”
“We’re rather conspicuous,” Yusuke says. “How has he not noticed us all crowded here?”
“He seems too absorbed in his laptop to do that,” Haru hums with vague amusement.
Ren shrugs, “Guess so. Good for us.”
A pause.
Sato shrieks when Ren kicks in the window.
“Who the hell are you?!” the cognition screams.
Ren doesn’t really have an answer for that. “Not super important,” he says. “Pretty
convenient that you were practically in lockdown already, huh?”
“What lockdown?” Sato hisses.
Goro snorts.
“You seriously didn’t know?!” Futaba yelps.
“…I feel like the real Sato is a bit sharper than Shido is giving him credit for,” Makoto says.
“Or perhaps Shido views him as so paranoid that he would not be discernibly different even
as a threat to the conspiracy emerges,” Yusuke muses.
“No matter what Shido thinks, we’re gonna have to take that letter of recommendation.”
Morgana draws his cutlass.
“Oh,” Sato interjects, “You guys are here for a letter?”
They all exchange looks. “Can we have it?” Ann asks.
“No!”
Sumire sighs. Ren gives her a commiserating pat on the shoulder, before brandishing his
dagger and leaping into the fray.
***
“Fine!” Sato half snaps, half sobs. His shadow form has been cut through, leaving only the
cognition’s skin. “Fine, take it!”

Ren fumbles as Sato throws the letter in his face. It drops to the floor.
He tries to look somewhat dignified as he bends over to pick it up. “Thanks.”
“Just get out!”
“Before we leave,” Haru chimes in, “Do you know where the Cleaner tends to reside?”
Ren knows exactly where the Cleaner likes to spend his time on this ship, and he thinks Haru
does too. He can’t fault her for hoping for a different answer, even as Sato simply says:
“Does it look like I know where that creep lives?!”
“Well, at least we’re all on the same page,” Goro says drily.
“We’ll be leaving now,” Ren announces, unnecessarily.
Sato nods eagerly, “Yes! Please! Get out!”
“Yeah, uh,” Futaba just looks awkward. “Have fun?”
“Doing what?” Ryuji asks incredulously, gesturing to the somewhat miserable approximation
of a permanent hotel room.
“Get out!”
Ren doesn’t particularly want to test if the cognitions can regrow the shadows under their
skin, so he quickly waves to his thieves and does just that.

An interlude, nowhere comprehensible:
When a certain person, who has foregone sharing his name in a few human decades, begins
to tell his recount of all events, he tends to begin it like this:
A very, very long time ago, there was nothing at all.
Then, very shortly after, there was very suddenly something. Quite a few somethings, in fact.
So many somethings, fit to burst inside the crude container of limited nothing that one could
say simply did not have the imagination to contain such wonder.
None of these somethings were particularly permanent. They would flit about, and change
shape, as intangible things are wont to do. Not that they could comprehend being intangible,
of course— there was nothing to conceivably act as contrast.
A very long time later, and no one could ever really pinpoint exactly how long, there was
something solid.
It didn’t happen all at once, though it happened so quickly in the relative scheme of things
that it might as well have. Minds and thoughts and hearts, and all that nothing was whipped

into a veil, and all those somethings stopped all their blurry indecisiveness, shaped in a frenzy
into a twisted mirror of all those wonderful darling little things that were so much more real
than they were.
The entire human race, as it happened, had quite the ceiling to the limit of their imagination.
What marvels! Curious and violent and mortal and oh, so, so, predictable. All little walking
archetypes— oh, look! the somethings would coo: a little hero, there! A seeker, a wanderer, a
tyrant, and repeat and repeat.
Of course, the somethings were rather predictable themselves. It was less a choice to mimic
the hearts and abstract forces of nature beholden to all that humanity was, and rather a simple
fact of what they were.
Predictable, predictable, until they weren’t. Among the dusting of mortals, some would shine
so brilliantly that they would send ripples through the collective gathering of thoughts and
ideas, leaving permanent stains carved into the hearts of all that was to come.
With that in mind, it didn’t take all that long for two very specific somethings to emerge.
Good, and Evil. Law, and Chaos. It is only with eons of hindsight, that this particular
combination of abstractions can be viewed with some comedic irony. But first, a wager:
The bet, as follows, was to determine humanity’s truest base instinct. Both Good and Evil had
manifested so strongly, after all. What a conundrum! What a curiosity, a contradiction.
These two particular somethings had the will and font of power (of godlike proportions, to
borrow the closest human term) to intrude where they should not. To pierce that veil, to
damage and lend aid to their game pieces as they saw fit.
People were so very fascinating to the both of them, though they did not view personhood
with the respect they perhaps ought to. Temporary, fragile little things, brilliant as they may
be. Infinite copies of themselves. It would take an eon for the irony of this to also set in, and
a handful of mortals kicking and screaming so loudly against the game that reality itself
would fracture, and it was then that the wager was reluctantly discarded.
Discarded, directly, that is. For all that Law represented what he did, he was not above
fudging the rules. All he needed was structure: a room, if you will. Chaos’ namesake ought to
speak for itself, for how he handled his newly sidelined state of being.
So the game continued, once removed from its original source. They were not the only gods
with something to prove and calls to answer, after all.
Night, Death, her presence nonnegotiable yet not immutable. Truth, and her rotting corpse.
Control, and his rather ambitious designs.
That little intruder, so very human, with his bleeding heart on display for all to see.
How fascinating! What a delight! Thought the arbiter of all things Good, to see humanity
prevail again and again. Though they would always stumble, their triumphant resurgence was

something to behold each time—
Oh?
(“What’s happening on the other side, Mister? The flowers all taste so strange.”
“Something unfortunate. What a shame! I can hardly stand to lose, now.”
“Hm… Nope, still don’t get it.”
“Humans are all so brittle. Hit them the wrong way, and their hearts shatter with such beauty.
I suppose I should have foreseen that only another human could finally lay them low.”
“Oh. Does that mean they’re all going to disappear?”
“Not quite, but they’re all set to become such boring things. Worse than predictable.
Monotonous. No flavour at all!”
“Oh! That does sound bad.”
“Doesn’t it?”)
No one ever said anything about calling in favours from the room he himself created, so call
favours he did. Time is a far less solid thing than humans dare to envision, but their fantasies
and tales are just vague enough, that Good has something to work with.

dress up, and salt water

Makoto feels that they might be paying for their smooth sailing in Shido’s palace with
extreme difficulties on the other side of reality.
Balancing the scales happens as it does, but she doesn’t think it necessarily has to happen.
Or, rather, she really wishes that it didn’t. With the knowledge that there are actual gods out
to get her and her friends, comes the uncertainty if their bad luck can be quantified as
someone’s fault.
Which is to say: Makoto isn’t sure how long she’ll last living in Haru Okumura’s apartment.
She wasn’t in much of a mind to protest the night before. Neither was Sae, nor Ann, and
perhaps most concerningly, Akechi. And so now all their luggage is in the living room, taking
up space in Haru’s disconcertingly large and disconcertingly empty penthouse.
Signs of Haru’s presence are concentrated in small bubbles. One seat of the couch. The
microwave. Her room. The balcony garden. Everywhere else is scrubbed clean in the wake of
all the house servants having been dismissed.
Makoto wonders to herself how much more lived in the apartment would have seemed even
with Okumura senior still around to make his mark. She supposes that now the four new
tenants will start messing the place up simply by being there.
Following the infiltration into Shido’s palace, they arrive back in Haru’s apartment. Sae, who
has once again made the living room into her impromptu office space, gives them a dry wave
as they materialise in space.
“Everything well?” She asks.
“Well enough,” Makoto answers. “Do you have any idea how many more infiltrations are
left, Akechi?”
Akechi shrugs. “With luck? One. Without? Who knows. We could always be stalled
indefinitely.”
Ann flops on the couch, “Let’s assume that won’t happen.”

“I’m sure we’ll be able to overcome any obstacle we face,” Haru says easily. She threads her
hands together, “Hopefully sooner rather than later.”
Five days left.
Makoto itches to get something done, but it’s not as if she can just leap into Shido’s palace on
her own. For want of anything better to do, she decides to keep up with her studies alone in
the room she (again— Haru’s apartment is spacious, but she doesn’t have infinite guest
rooms) shares with Ann. It won’t do any good to come back to school for her entrance exams,
only to have no idea what the material is.
Late at night, she hears a hissed conversation in the hallway.
“Are you insane.”
“You’re overreacting, Goro-kun. I know what I’m doing.”
“Haru, this is a side of business you have no experience in. Loyalty to your father means
nothing, if it was even there to begin with.”
“Loyalty to my father doesn’t have to mean anything—”
Makoto quickly opens the door, her need to say something outweighing the likely smarter
need to eavesdrop. “What are you two talking about?”
Haru and Akechi both startle, the former yelping sharply and the latter hissing a curse. They
both stare at her.
Makoto coughs.
Akechi makes a face. Haru’s goes carefully blank.
Makoto waves her arms. “Well?!”
Akechi folds his hands behind his back, embodying the detective prince for some reason.
“It’s not your business.”
“I disagree.” Makoto mimics his posture, mocking. “If the two of you are planning something
obviously dangerous, then I believe the rest of the residents of the house have a right to
know.”
“Ideally, we’d be reducing the danger involved in our situation,” Akechi says. “So how about
you let yourself be pleasantly surprised?”
“I thought you weren’t on my side?” Haru whispers.
“I’m not.”
Makoto massages her temples. “I really thought we were past keeping secrets from each
other. It’s never ended well.”

“And when has that stopped any of us,” Akechi says, deadpan as he’s ever been.
Makoto considers kicking him, before Haru sighs sharply and grabs them both by the wrist to
drag her into her room.
Makoto and Akechi are both unceremoniously thrown past the threshold, and Haru quickly
locks the door.
“Alright,” Haru says, “Now that no one else can begin eavesdropping.”
“Were we not just discussing the drawbacks of keeping secrets?” Akechi says.
“Whose side are you on?” Makoto snaps.
“I’m a natural born contrarian.”
“Which you could stop being at any time,” Haru says tightly, and Akechi shuts up.
Makoto presses her hands together, “Where even are the others? It’s late.”
“In the living room, watching a movie,” Akechi says.
Makoto blinks incredulously, “Ann and my sister?”
“It was strange enough that I figured then was as good a time as any to speak to Goro-kun
privately,” Haru explains.
“Alright,” Makoto says. “About what?”
Akechi and Haru exchange a look.
Haru bites the bullet first. “I was planning on hiring some security.”
“Yakuza,” Akechi interrupts. “She wants to hire yakuza.”
“They’re not yakuza specifically.”
Akechi rolls his eyes so hard Makoto wonders if they’ll get stuck like that some day. “Private
muscle. From an otherwise-unspecified crime family.”
“They’re not technically criminals, either,” Haru says. “Which I think means they’re good at
their jobs.”
Makoto, as she done several times in the past few weeks, considers her life choices for a
moment. In the moment following, she buries her head in her hands and says, “Okay.”
Akechi and Haru pause. Makoto takes some solace in the fact that they both look sheepish.
“Okay,” She says again. “Run me through it.”
“Pros and cons?” Akechi suggests drily.

“Yes. Please.”
Haru nods shortly, and strides over to a small tea table in the corner of her room, where she
takes a seat, smoothing her skirt. “Putting it simply, my father used to employ a variety of
guards to protect him and his interests. Their contracts were automatically suspended after he
became… incapacitated, but I believe it would be beneficial to rehire them for my own
purposes.”
Makoto very awkwardly takes a seat on the edge of the bed. “Alright.” She shoots a look at
Akechi, “The rebuttal?”
Akechi remains standing. “Putting it simply, there’s no possible way to confirm how
trustworthy these people are. Haru-san has admitted she never interacted with them
personally, and I highly suspect they were more loyal to money over your family name.”
“Even if that’s the case, I have plenty of money to give them,” Haru says.
Akechi runs a hand through his hair, frustrated, “Yes, but it still means they’re fickle. If they
have loose lips, we’re done for.”
“Which is why I’m going to personally vet them.”
“Here?” Makoto finally finds her voice again.
Haru quickly shakes her head. “No, a private conference space my father owns. It’s small,
discrete, and made for dealings like these. It’s an old karaoke bar we bought, actually.”
“Alone,” Akechi deadpans.
Haru shifts awkwardly.
Makoto decides to take things one step at a time. “Okay,” She says, yet again. “Pros and
cons?”
“The pros are that we’ll have some insurance, should Shido send anyone to deal with me, as

enough time to potentially get away unscathed where we would not have otherwise.”
“The cons are that it could backfire,” Akechi counters. “If even one person isn’t as loyal as
they say they are, or happens to have loose lips, and sees several missing persons including
the highly publicised detective prince hiding in an heiress’s apartment, what do you think will
happen?”
“Again, the vetting,” Haru insists.
“And what are your criteria?”
Haru folds her arms, and uncharacteristically scowls. “You’re being difficult on purpose.”
“Okay,” Makoto interrupts, “So neither option sounds great.”

The other two startle, like they forgot she was there.
“You’re right, Makoto-san,” Haru quickly gets herself together, “Which is why we’re trying
to minimise risks.”
Akechi rubs a hand down his face, “I just don’t think that introducing another variable is
minimising.”
They do both have a point. Makoto recognises that while it’s probably much harder to nail
Haru down in the legal sense, just given her sheer amount of monetary weight to throw
around, that doesn’t stop Shido from simply getting violent. A potential problem which now
affects five of them, rather than just one.
Conversely, the potential problems that arise from dubiously shady security also affect five of
them. Makoto understands why they’re at an impasse.
“When were you think of vetting them?” she asks.
Haru coughs politely into her hand. “Tonight.”
Akechi looks more baffled than angry, “Excuse me?”
“I set up a meeting, for later tonight,” Haru explains. “I can cancel, but I really would rather

“You’re not seriously going alone, are you?” Makoto is starting to understand Akechi’s

“Ordinarily, this kind of meeting would be accompanied by security,” Haru says breezily. “So
I’m sure you understand the issue.”
“What if we come with you?” Makoto blurts.
Akechi scoffs, “Is being seen by potential bad actors not the main problem?”
“Well…” he has a point, which Makoto is loathe to admit.
“You could present yourselves as the security I should have for a meeting like this,” Haru

“We’ll look like children,” Akechi counters. “And again, the anonymity.”
“Not necessarily.” Haru shakes her head. “It wouldn’t seem overly out of place to wear a face
mask, and sunglasses.”
“We still don’t look the part, though.” Makoto is concerned at how easily Haru is running
with this hypothetical.
“Can’t you borrow one of your sister’s suits?” Haru asks. “And Goro-kun, I’m sure
something in my father’s wardrobe will fit you.”

Akechi sighs very deeply, and Makoto is inclined to agree.
“And if anything goes poorly, we can always simply whisk ourselves into Mementos,” Haru
finishes.
“We’re telling sis about this,” Makoto decides.
“Do you think she’d let us do this, if we did?” Akechi raises an eyebrow.
Makoto does not whine, but it’s a close thing. “Well what are we doing?”
“Well?” Haru asks.
“Ann’s going to notice we’re gone,” Makoto protests weakly. “We share a room.”
“Then tell her.” Akechi shrugs, “She won’t stop us.”
No, perhaps not. Makoto really wishes she’d try.
“I could always ask Takakura-san to accompany me,” Haru says. “He gave me the

“Do you trust him?” Akechi asks.
Haru is silent.
Makoto swallows, her dry throat constricting painfully. “…Do you think we’ll really be able
to pull off looking like professionals?”
“So long as you stop looking so nervous,” Akechi snips. “And we cover our faces

Makoto will concede that it truly is only their faces holding them back, here. Both her and
Akechi are on the more built side than average among their peers, (twig-like body structure

“I have face masks stocked somewhere,” Haru says. “Black, if we want to project a certain

“Do we have enough time to dye your hair?” Makoto asks Akechi on a whim.
“No,” he snaps, clearly not thinking about the time.
“We don’t have time,” Haru confirms. “We’ll have to get organised quickly if we want to

“And do we want to make this happen?” Akechi asks. “Truly?”
They both turn their heads to Makoto, like she is somehow the deciding factor here.

Well. Well! It, could? It could pay off. Just meeting them isn’t the risky factor. Necessarily.
“We’ll do it,” she squeaks.

Stealing one of Sae’s suits is, if Makoto were any less stressed, comically easy. The fact that

Maybe Sae’s insistent use of heels threw her off. Or she just wasn’t paying much attention.

“Great,” Makoto deadpans with great regret, “Really, brilliant.”
“We’ll be fine,” Akechi says, which is a great departure from how he was feeling earlier.
Makoto is going to wring his neck someday.
A knock at the door.
Haru freezes. A split second later, she tosses her purse between the two of them, and dashes
to the door. She squints through the peephole, and after a moment of steeling herself, swings
the door open.
Two men in dark suits and sunglasses stand, near casually, on the other side.
“Okumura-san,” the first greets, smiling amiably as he takes off his sunglasses.
Haru nods, artificially smooth, “Thank you for coming.”
“Of course.” The two men step inside. The second doesn’t remove his sunglasses. “Happy to
talk business. Not sure how much your pops would have told you about our old agreement.”
“A fair amount,” Haru says, which Makoto is fairly certain is a lie.
“Excellent!” The man takes a seat, giving a friendly nod to Makoto and Akechi. “And these
two are?”

“Acquaintances,” Haru says. “I hope you won’t mind their presence.”
“You’re the boss,” the man says. His companion stands next to the booth, arms crossed. “I
hope you won’t mind my own friend here.”
“Not at all.”
“Wonderful, wonderful.” The man leans back, the picture of relaxation. Makoto doesn’t think
a single one of his muscles is relaxed at all. “You can call me Micheal.”
Makoto raises an eyebrow. The man doesn’t look or sound foreign— though she didn’t
exactly expect a real name either.
Micheal must notice her dubious expression, undoubtedly reflected on Akechi’s face as well.
He laughs, “Too many ‘Tanaka’s, you know?”
Akechi snorts at that. Micheal nods, grinning.
“Now,” he says. “Let’s talk shop, Okumura-san.”
“Please,” Haru says. “If you don’t mind, I’d like to clarify some things first.”
“Go ahead.”
“Understand that I am not nearly as paranoid as my father, and that I initially wasn’t going to
rehire your services for passive use,” Haru explains. “First and foremost, I’m concerned
about your discretion.”
“We take our jobs very seriously, Okumura-san.” Micheal’s jovial veneer fades somewhat.
“And we’re not unfamiliar with active service, so-to-speak, if that’s what you’re looking
for?”
“These are turbulent political times,” Haru dismisses smoothly. “And my father made no
shortage of enemies. With him incapacitated, I’m all that’s left.”
“Common problem.” Micheal nods. The other man at his side mirrors the nod. “Are you
looking for security, or something a little more actionable?”
Makoto tries very hard not to tense at how casually the suggestion is thrown out. The fact that
they are being dragged to fight on Shido’s level is not lost on her.
Not entirely, Anat soothes. The action is in your hands, not theirs.
True.
“The former,” Haru says. “I don’t trust the safety of my own home.”
“Sticky situation,” Micheal comments.
“Indeed.”

“If it’s secrecy you’re really worried about, you can limit your security to a couple of
favourites, for lack of a better word,” Micheal suggests. “Your father didn’t like to get to
know us too personally. But you’re a new business partner, aren’t you?”
Haru nods, confidence beginning to bleed in.
Makoto sits stiffly through the discussion, one leg crossed over the other and hands folded
tight. Akechi’s posture is more relaxed, she notes, though he is eerily still. He has more
experience with these kinds of dealings, she supposes.
Micheal seems, for lack of any more concrete insight… fine. He seems reliable, professional,
etcetera, and Makoto doesn’t trust him for a moment. He seems inscrutable, in the way
capital-P Professionals tend to be, and she would find it reassuring if not for the exact type of
Professional that he is.
Haru inquires about price, logistics, client confidentiality. She asks questions rapid-fire, and
Micheal answers at equal pace. His still-unnamed companion stays silent. Makoto does her
utmost not to fidget.
She doesn’t count seconds, but after what must be at least forty minutes, Micheal asks: “Will
that be all, Okumura-san?”
Haru considers for a moment, her head twitching very slightly towards Akechi before she
restrains herself, and nods. “I believe so, Micheal-san.”
“Have you come to a decision about whether to employ our services?”
“I’ll be in touch,” Haru deflects.
Micheal nods, rising from his seat in one fluid motion. “In that case, I eagerly await your
correspondence.”
The other man, who has neglected to remove his sunglasses the entire meeting, steps out of
the way as Micheal leaves the booth, falling into step as they both head towards the door.
Before turning the handle, Micheal looks back to the three of them, and gives a bow. “Thank
you for your hospitality, Okumura-san.”
Haru nods. “And your cooperation, Micheal-san.”
The two men leave, and the three of them are left in silence.
Makoto gives it five seconds before she deflates with a loud sigh.
“I liked him,” Haru declares.
“I don’t trust him,” Makoto says.
“Oh, nor do I.” Haru blinks, as though that were obvious.

“I think you’ll be hard pressed to find security who we can trust blindly.” Akechi folds his
arms. Makoto hears his spine crack. He really must have been sitting entirely still.
“Yes,” Haru says, frustrated, “But can we trust them enough?”
“They offered a lot of measures for your own benefit,” Makoto concedes. “Maybe you’d only
have to hire one or two of them, rather than put your trust in the secrecy of a rotating number
of employees.”
“True.” Haru nods.
“Even so, who knows how easily their loyalty can be swayed?” Akechi counters. “It would
only take one unfortunate deal behind our backs for us to be well and truly fucked.”
They’re drawing the same circles as they were before the meeting. Makoto slumps further
into the booth seat, pressing her lips together.
“That’s always true, no?” Haru says, “Maybe we’re giving Shido a potential way in, but
we’re just as likely giving ourselves a way out. More so, I’d argue.”
A risk. A risk not founded in their delusions of immortality in the Metaverse. A risk placed
entirely into the hands of people they don’t know. Makoto doesn’t like giving ground.
Ground is being taken while they sit and do nothing.
“I say we try it.” Makoto bites the bullet.
“There isn’t really a try scenario here,” Akechi drawls.
“Then I say we do it,” Makoto corrects. “The consequences for this going poorly are the
same as if Shido decides to come to us.”
Haru hums. Akechi clicks his tongue.
“I liked him,” Haru says again. “I not foolish enough to let that be the deciding factor. But, he
did serve my father a great many years.”
“You are not your father,” Akechi points out.
“No, I’m far less stingy.”
Akechi snorts, and scrubs a hand down his face.
“Alright,” He finally says. “Let’s gamble, shall we?”

Futaba thinks that Shido is doing a pretty shitty job of keeping them all out.
It’s not like he knows they have three time travellers on their team, but still. A superficial
difference, and one shoehorned extra level? Hell, he’s made the place easier from what Ren

and Akechi have been saying. The rats thing sounds pretty funny, but she’s glad she doesn’t
have to live it.
The thieves all congregate the day after their last infiltration in the red-stained visage of the
Diet Building steps, getting themselves ready.
Futaba raises an eyebrow at the mixture of expressions she deems vaguely suspicious on
Akechi, Makoto, and Haru’s faces. Not a combo she wants to be scheming.
Ren must notice too, as he asks, “What’s up?”
The three look at each other. Actually, now that Futaba’s paying attention, Ann has a nervous
look about her as well.
“I’m hiring security,” Haru explains.
“Oh. Sick?” Ryuji blinks.
Ren seems similarly confused for why this would be a big deal. “That’s good?”
The look on Akechi’s face shifts somewhere into the realm of annoyed.
“It is good,” Makoto says, before anyone can ponder the matter any further. “We’ll keep you
updated.”
Ren shrugs slowly, a dubious acquiescence. “Alright,” he says. “Should we get started?”
The thieves all give a round of agreement, huddling around Ren’s phone. The keywords are
entered, worlds shift, yadda, yadda, yadda, Futaba wants this place done already.
“Alright!” she says as soon as the horizon shifts to the drowned scenery of Shido’s Tokyo.
“Where we left off?”
“Please,” Ren nods.
Futaba wastes no time in whisking them all to their last saferoom with her own Nav. She
drifts along as they all march out into the hall, just a left turn away from the path to Sato’s
room.
“Where to?” Yusuke asks, unnecessarily turning to look up at Necronomicon.
“Well…” Futaba drawls. “My best guess is that this new section is behind one of these
doors.”
The thieves all stare at the hall of doors.
“Should we start openin’ them, or…?” Ryuji’s hand inches towards a doorknob.
Morgana leaps up to smack his hand with the butt of his sword. “If you want the security
level to skyrocket, moron!”

“’Aight, jeez!”
“Simmer down, children,” Futaba deadpans. “You have a navigator for a reason.”
She ignores the bickering down below as she performs a more thorough scan. The map they
have of the Palace is, irritatingly, entirely useless. Whatever update Shido has experienced in
his cognition, the cartographer didn’t get the memo.
Or, Shido doesn’t register whatever this addition is as part of his ship. Futaba isn’t
particularly enthused by any explanation she can come up with.
“And…” she pauses for suspense. “Here! I think I found a potential path!”
“Great job,” Ren says. “Lead the way?”
“Is it indeed behind one of the doors?” Yusuke asks before Futaba can respond.
She rolls her eyes, for her benefit only. “Yes, Inari. It’s behind one of the doors.” Or, she
assumes so.
“Ah. Then what are we waiting for?”
Futaba grumbles to herself as she pushes Necronomicon in the direction of progress. Her
only indication that there is progress at all, being the slightest shift in cognitive stability,
centred around an otherwise innocuous point in an otherwise innocuous hall. Something a
little too fuzzy, against a palace that is otherwise crystal clear.
The thieves follow her with minimal chatter. With no real reason to engage, they dodge the
few shadows that still roam the halls of the guest quarters.
“Ah ha!” Futaba eventually cheers, and they stop in front of a door like all the rest. “Just
through here, o noble thieves.”
“Number two-oh-nine,” Sumire reads the brass letters set into the door.
“You didn’t happen to pick up a passenger registry, Oracle?” Ren asks.
“Nope,” she says. “Why this door specifically, your guess is as good as mine.”
Akechi hums, quiet enough that Futaba almost misses it. She squints down at him, scowling
when the expression not hidden by his mask is inscrutable.
“Nothing to do but go in, right?” Ann says.
“Guess not,” Ren agrees.
He reaches out and turns the handle. Futaba notes the security level rising, and dismisses the
alert. It’s a negligible increase.

The door swings inward, revealing a set of metal stairs that lead down, quickly twisting away
so that they can’t see where it leads. Ren kicks out his leg, and pokes the first step with the
toe of his boot.
…Nothing happens.
“…Seems safe enough,” Makoto decides.
“Not like we have anywhere else to go,” Morgana says sullenly.
Ren gestures them all forward, and Futaba drops down from Necronomicon to fit through the
door-width stairwell. Walking down the steps, their footfalls echo loudly against the metal.
The light is poor, and Futaba very nervously grips the wall for all the support she can get. Her
Metaverse outfit’s shoes aren’t the picture of practicality.
Finally, after twisting down in a spiral for several flights, the walls suddenly give way to a
large open room. Futaba would liken it to a warehouse if—
In—
It’s—
“It’s… a lab?” Ann says.
The scene, exactly as Futaba can physically see it:
There is a lab, with terminals and computers and gadgets of dubious functionality littered
about. There is a cognition, dashing every which way, reading lines, making notes.
There are drains in the floor, and Futaba can smell the sea.
“Who the hell is that?” Ryuji asks, pointing towards the cognition that has yet to see them.
“That,” Akechi says, voice dull, “Is Kaito Takahashi. Shido’s last remaining Cognitive
Psience researcher of any note.”
The light is flickering. Uneven— on, off, on, off.
On: Pure white. Sterile. Clinical. Futaba visited her mother’s lab exactly once, and this is
what was burned into her mind.
Off: Dust, grime, dirt, rust. The salty rot of seawater, puddling on the floor. Brine feeding
mould.
Takahashi pays no mind as his laboratory ticks randomly between the two extremes.
Muttering to himself in erratic whispers, flicking dials and taking notes.
“…Should we talk to him?” Sumire asks, “He doesn’t have a letter, right?”
“No,” Ren says. “He doesn’t.”

“But we can’t exactly go past without alerting him,” Haru points out. “With any luck, he will
have little interest in fighting us.”
Futaba stares at the ghost of her mother’s lab, its monarch usurped. She does not think their
luck is, or will be, good.
Some of the thieves exchange looks. There’s a whispered conversation she doesn’t quite hear
between Makoto and Akechi. Ren butts in once or twice, only to get shushed.
With a sigh, Ren hops down the last few steps. “Takahashi-san,” he says, “Sorry to intrude.”
Takahashi shrieks, whirling around to see the congregation of thieves on the steps.
The lights flicker again. The smell of seawater begins to turn foul. Futaba claps her hand over
her nose.
“Who are you?!” Takahashi demands. “I— the captain said no one was to disturb me!”
“Where’s the exit?” Ren asks. “We’re just passing through.”
“You can’t!”
“Why the eff not?” Ryuji groans.
The lights. On, off, on, off, on. Futaba squints, distantly wondering if now is a good time to
reenter Necronomicon.
The lights finally flick off, and stay off.

Chapter Summary

The Wraith, the Tree, and the Tapestry

The lights in the laboratory flicker off, and remain as such. Futaba fights back a shiver. In the
dark, the lab is bathed green; grime, muck, and seawater clinging to every surface.
Yusuke wrinkles his nose. “You should keep a laboratory cleaner than this.”
Takahashi jumps, like he’s just noticed the state of his environment. “I didn’t leave it like
this!”
“That’s… fine,” Ren dismisses, clearly trying to redirect the conversation. “Can we pass
through?”
“I already told you, you can’t!”
Akechi growls under his breath, drawing his gun and marching forward. “Does this change
your mind?”
Futaba’s eyes catch on the grates in the floor. The water lapping somewhere below grows a
bit higher. She wrinkles her nose.
“Don’t shoot!” Takahashi shrieks.
“Please, at least explain why we can’t pass,” Haru says diplomatically.
“The captain said so!”
“So, the only thing physically stopping us is you.” Makoto folds her arms.
Takahashi stammers. “No! No, that is to say— I’m not stopping you!”
Akechi makes a point of loudly flicking the safety of his gun on and off. “Then where’s the
exit?”
“Nowhere!”
Well, that’s a lie. Futaba knows there has to be a path to the engine room somewhere.

The water in the grates is rising even higher. Futaba pauses, halfway to summoning
Necronomicon.
“Um,” her voice is lodged in her throat, her mother’s lab clenching her airway shut. “Hey,
there’s—”
“If he can’t physically stop us, can’t we just walk past him?” Sumire suggests, not hearing
Futaba’s wispy attempts at speech. “Try to search for a path forward ourselves?”
“I dunno,” Ann says, grimacing, “Something about this place is giving me the creeps. Will
poking around do something?”
“Like what?” Makoto asks warily.
“Alright,” Ren says from the front, apparently losing his patience. He draws his own gun,
“Really, where’s the way out?”
“I don’t know!” Takahashi babbles.
“Well think harder.”
Sea foam bubbles through the grates. The stench worsens, and Futaba finally cracks,
whisking herself into Necronomicon. The other thieves all clap their hands over their mouths
in disgust.
She was wrong, in her prior assessment. The main lights up above were flickering on and off,
yes, but the secondary lights— somewhere beyond the walls, or just a product of Shido’s
cognition, were still functioning.
Very suddenly, they switch off. Putrid green is replaced with pitch black. The smell curdles
further towards rot.
Some of the thieves yelp. Futaba slams her hands down on her console, trying to force
Necronomicon to— fuck, she doesn’t know, give herself night vision? If Shido doesn’t want
them to see, then she can’t, but surely she can work around—
“You killed me!”
She freezes.
Takahashi shrieks. There’s a gunshot that lands nowhere, flinching off the metal.
“This was my work! Mine!”
“Oracle!” Ren yells.
“I can’t see anything either!” She shrieks. She doesn’t want to see. She doesn’t want to look,
she doesn’t want to—
Akechi shouts, and Futaba sees a chunk of his health disappear from her screens.

“There’s something here!” He calls, and cries out again as more of his health is axed.
“My work… my discoveries… do you think you can rob me of this?!”
Haru screams next, as some of her vitality vanishes alongside Akechi’s. Futaba can hear
Takahashi sobbing beneath all the commotion.
“We were partners!”
“Hecate!” Ann calls, and fire blooms at the room’s centre, casting all the walls in a red-hot
glow.
Necronomicon captures light in the moment it flashes. Futaba sees Akechi bleeding from his
stomach, Haru bleeding from her arm. She sees stark shadows, splaying their silhouettes
across the ground and walls.
She sees the wraith, the rotting visage of her mother spilling from the grates in the floors.
Dripping sea water and expelling mist from her skeletal limbs, face contorted like the sphinx.
Vengeful rage and postmortem fury etched into every inch.
And it is dark again.
She hears Makoto gasp. She hears Akechi choke.
It’s Ren that fires his gun in the direction of the wraith. There’s another smaller burst of light,
and the unmistakable sound of a bullet hitting the wall.
“Careful!” Morgana yelps.
“We need more light!” Ren demands, “Panther, anyone!”
“Ella!” Sumire shouts, light erupting first by the blue fire of her mask, and again as bless
magic bursts like a flash grenade.
Another snapshot. Akechi and Haru still bleed. Half the thieves are still clogged by the stairs.
The wraith has moved to spilling from a different grate.
“Joker, six o’ clock!” Futaba’s voice wavers. “Mona, Queen, someone get on healing!”
Ren whirls around to fire another bullet, and this time the wraith shrieks in pain. No spell
needs to be cast for Futaba to see Loki’s sword, buzzing and blazing hot, carve down in an
arc to cleave through the wraith.
Futaba’s shaking hands finally think to analyse the enemy. In spite of one bullet and one giant
sword, it still seems very healthy.
“Zorro!” Morgana calls next. A faint green glow knits Akechi and Haru’s wounds back

“You think you’re ready to cut your losses?” the wraith snarls. “You’ll never discover

Analysis, though…
The headache grows.
Nothing!
Not nothing, Necronomicon hums. Conditional.
Arguably worse.
“It has a weakness,” Futaba relays, “But I don’t know what it is.”

More blades. More gunfire. More fire and bless and never enough light.

An idea—
She can’t!
At Sumire’s next flash of light, she sees Akechi looking in her direction.
She feels blue and red and gold probe at her mind, separate from her own mental link with

—
Long, heavy tendrils spill from Necronomicon’s base, thudding against the ground. They

Her grip meets metal with force, and she feels him careen forwards. She tries to squeeze, to

The jagged metal guarding his throat silently burns away in blue fire. Necronomicon’s

“Futaba,” Ren says, and he sounds dangerous,
“Futaba?” The wraith asks.

“Mom.” Her throat nearly closes from that word alone. “Can you turn on the lights? I want to

“Of course, Futaba,” the wraith says. “Anything.”
Light floods the room. Again, it is the pristine lab, machines blinking and humming as the

Futaba loosens Necronomicon’s grip imperceptibly. “Okay,” she whispers, “Thank you.”

There’s a bullet through her mother’s skull near instantly. The wraith doesn’t get the chance

Futaba releases her grip on Akechi’s neck entirely. Immediately, he gasps and hacks up his

Takahashi sobs, curled up under one of the tables.
Futaba doesn’t say anything. She doesn’t descend from Necronomicon, doesn’t move as

“We’re leaving,” Ren says.
(With the wraith dead, Futaba dully notes the path forward. A door on the far end of the lab
that now lies tangible and unobstructed. Though she’s nowhere near it, through her senses she

Futaba, very stupidly, tugs on Akechi’s sleeve before he leaves with Haru and the others
while they all uncomfortably hover around the stairs of the Diet Building in Mementos.
Akechi himself was hovering further away than most, and no one but her was foolish enough
to tread closer.

Then again, no one seemed keen on getting too close to her either. She thinks, optimistically,
that perhaps they can wallow in misery together.
“What,” Akechi snaps, dashing such hopes.
Futaba shrugs, and ultimately says nothing.
“If you’re apologising, don’t. It’ll be uncomfortable for us both.”
“I wasn’t going to,” Futaba sniffs.
Akechi’s lip curls. “Well, good.”
Stiff silence yet again.
“You recognised the lab, right?” Futaba asks.
“Of course.”
“Did Takahashi take it over, after mom died?” After you killed her?
Akechi shrugs. “Shido didn’t tell me about any researchers he kept alive until the start of the
year, if you could call it that. I suppose he would have taken over the same lab. Why get a
new one? I never went back after she died, in any case.”
Futaba nods.
“Shitty fight,” she comments. She immediately wishes she didn’t. She doesn’t want to talk
about this at all.
Then why are you here?
Misery loves company?
Akechi grunts in agreement.
“Is your strategy in every fight to just hit it until it dies?” Futaba asks drily. He didn’t even
try to help with lighting the place up.
“Like you were doing anything until the solution was all but spelled out to us.” Akechi glares
at her. “Besides, killing her worked the first time.”
That’s not funny. That’s so not funny, that her stomach does several rage-filled flips, that she
crams all her strength into kicking him in the knee.
She isn’t very strong. Akechi barely flinches, but he accepts it with grace as he grimaces.
He doesn’t apologise. She didn’t apologise for choking him to near unconsciousness, so she
supposes they’re even.

…Though, he basically told her to do it, and was playing along with the performance. Maybe
they aren’t even. Maybe she should kick him again.
“I’m surprised a cognition like that existed at all,” Akechi mutters to himself.
A mantra Futaba has repeated: a cognition. A cobbled-together skeleton of fake bones and
fake skin that looked a bit like her mom. Shido using a corpse as a mouthpiece.
She almost wishes she asked it more questions.
“Maybe he’s guilty,” she says.
Akechi snorts.
“Deep down,” she amends.
Akechi raises an eyebrow.
“Deep down.”
“If Shido feels guilt for anything,” Akechi says, “It’s that he didn’t do a good enough job at
killing his loose ends.”
“That doesn’t make any sense.”
Akechi shrugs. “Then he feels no guilt at all.”
It’s not disappointment that lodges in her chest. She doesn’t want Shido to feel guilty. It
would be… cheap. Whether by his own mind or by wrenching the distortion out of his heart
by force. A pathetic attempt at absolution. She just wants him gone.
Dead?
Maybe.
Gone, certainly.
“Do you think,” she begins, and cuts herself off.
“What?” Akechi asks.
“Nothing,” she grumbles.
Nothing her mom (Not her mom—) said even implied it. Even if it had, she and Akechi had
come to the mutual agreement that neither of them wanted to know.
“What?” Akechi asks again, scowling at her.
“Wondering about the world’s worst family tree,” she mutters.
Akechi’s face twists in disgust. “I thought we agreed never to speak of that again.”

“I don’t think we actually said anything.”
“The agreement was implied.”
To his credit, it definitely was.
“Why are you thinking about this?” he demands.
Futaba shrugs. “Dunno.”
“It would be weird,” she says.
“I kinda hope it’s not true,” she adds.
Akechi just looks at her.
“What about you?” she asks.
“It would be weird,” he agrees, and says nothing else.
(Death grows to its eighth rank, and Akechi tries to chase off the stench of decay.)

Ren did not consider himself a paranoid man.
Most notably, did not. His pride keeps him from outright stating what he has become, but he’s
sure even despite it that everyone who knows him is painfully aware of his descent into
twitchy nervousness and deep-seated dread.
And now here he is, and here he thinks he will remain.
He knows he’s paranoid. But he doesn’t think he’s unreasonable.
Truth: Masayoshi Shido has it out for Goro Akechi. Truth: This has already manifested in a
way Ren would very much like to forget, the stench of rot and cloud of mist a little too recent
to brush off. Truth: They have yet to traverse the part of the palace that Ren most fears, that
idly treads through his dreams in the form of klaxon alarms and large metal doors.
Ren almost can’t wait to deal with Yaldabaoth, if only because it means dealing with Shido
will be over.
Ren can think of many solutions to this problem he’s been presented with. The first eighthundred or so are entirely infeasible (including, but not limited to: Shido being spontaneously
struck by a meteor). The remaining one is…
Still infeasible. But marginally less so than all the others. Truthfully, it was the first solution
he thought of, shelved in case of desperate times.
Ren, alone in his and Futaba’s shared room, presses Akechi’s name in his contacts.

It rings. Once. Twice. Thrice.
It clicks through.
Ren is honestly surprised he didn’t get hung up on. He says into the receiver, before a hello or
how-do-you-do, “Any chance I can convince you to skip this palace trip today?”
“Are you a fucking moron?” Goro says, which Ren should have expected.
“Hear me out,” Ren says, opting for levity, because begging is always a bad look. “I’m not
saying you can’t come for when we need to fight his shadow.”
“Do you think I’m an idiot, Ren?” Goro snaps. “What? Do you think I’m allergic to engine
oil? Do you think I’ll drop dead the second I set foot in that room?”
Ren has, admittedly, had nightmares of similar scenarios. “No,” he says.
“I have conceded to many things,” Goro hisses. “My revenge is dead in the water. I tolerated
you in January. I have suffered your presence through this year. I’m getting through this
damn palace.”
Ren shelved this solution for a reason. He should have known it was as infeasible as the
spontaneous meteor.
He closes his eyes. “Your point is made.”
“Wonderful.”
Perhaps Ren should hang up. His halfhearted endeavour has been thoroughly killed. He could
probably go back to pacing his room in silence.
He doesn’t. Goro doesn’t hang up either. Ren can hear him breathing, faintly.
“Does it just not matter to you?” Ren blurts.
“Does what not matter, Ren?”
Ren almost goes to reminisce on the days when conversations with Goro weren’t plagued
with obstinacy and a pathological need to beat around the bush. He then abruptly remembers
that the closest they ever really got to that was when Goro was also planning to kill him, and
decides to take what he can get.
“That everything keeps…” Ren waves his arms at the ceiling. “Happening the same.”
“Seems different enough to me.”
Maybe it’ll be Ren planning to kill Goro if he keeps this up. “But it’s still significant.”
“I didn’t take you for the superstitious sort,” Goro says.

Ren did not consider himself a paranoid man. He didn’t consider himself a superstitious one,
either. And yet here he is. “Hard to brush everything off when you know magic is real.”
“That is perhaps the worst pronunciation of psience I have ever heard.”
“That ‘psi’ does a lot of heavy lifting,” Ren comments.
Goro snorts. “I’d say it does less than you think, but you also don’t know the half of it.”
Ren shrugs to no one. “Point made.”
“Hardly.”
“I think we’ve gotten a bit lost in the weeds.”
“When are we not?”
Ren rolls his eyes at the ceiling. “That was an invitation to direct the conversation out of the
weeds.”
“Do it yourself if you’re so offended,” Goro snaps.
“Fine,” Ren says, “What are we going to do if things go wrong today?”
“In what sense?” Goro asks, and for once it doesn’t seem to just be for the sake of it.
“Things can only truly go wrong in so many ways. If we’re caught in a fight, our only option
is to prevail. If Shido throws some —if you’ll excuse my phrasing— utter bullshit at us, then
we simply have to work around it.”
True enough. “And what if the team gets separated?”
“A common occurrence at this point,” Goro agrees. “Easy: just find everyone again, and try
not to get killed in the process.” A pause. “Are you just throwing hypotheticals against the
wall?”
“Maybe,” Ren admits.
“That won’t solve anything.”
It won’t. Still, despite the lack of solutions, despite the lack of assurances, that tight knot of
fear is loosened slightly. Ren knows it will likely be pulled taught again the moment the
conversation is over, but he relishes the short reprieve.
“Hey,” Ren says, rather than all of that, “You never know.”
“I’ve always taken you for more of an improviser.”
“Well, no plan survives contact and all that.”
“Which is why this conversation is pointless,” Goro drawls. “That room is just a room, Ren.”

“Bullshit it is.” That knot tightens again, preemptively. Ren tries and fails to pry it loose.
“I am trying very hard,” Goro says flatly, “To not be as pathetic as you in the face of things
that haven’t happened.”
“But they did happen.”
“I’m so glad that you have my funeral already planned. Shall I call Maruki in advance?”
Ren grits his teeth.
“You’re not going to die,” he says.
“That’s what I’ve been saying.”
“You’re not.”
“You’re the only one who’s unconvinced,” Goro says airily, which Ren has to believe is a lie.
“Do you seriously think Shido will be our most difficult obstacle?”
Ren wonders what it is Goro truly wishes he could do. Whether it is satisfying or infuriating
that Shido is no longer the final goal, the end-of-the-line. He wonders whether Goro would
still prefer to put a bullet in his skull rather than rip out his heart, or something undoubtedly
more creative a punishment.
“No,” Ren agrees. “We’ve still got two gods to kill.”
“How about you focus on that?” Goro says. “You’re the only one of us who’s killed one, after
all.”
There was a time when all his thieves, bar two, were god slayers. Ren doesn’t know whether
to miss those versions of them, that truly splintered sometime around October. The ends of
the knot tug slightly, and gets nowhere.
“Easier said than done,” Ren mutters.
“I’m not sure why you’re coming to me for anything actionable.”
I just wanted to hear your voice, Ren doesn’t say, because that would be liable to get him
shot. “You’re plenty actionable.”
“I’m great at taking action,” Goro deadpans. “Would you like to guess what my suggestion
is?”
“Is it murder?”
“No. It’s to go bother someone else.”
Ren laughs, despite himself. If he ignores the knot it’s like it’s not there at all. “I’ll be seeing
you this afternoon.”

“And so I hardly need to be plagued by your voice the rest of the day. Goodbye, Ren.”
Ren supposes he appreciates the warning, when Goro hangs up not a moment later.
He falls back onto his futon, staring at the ceiling. The knot, as predicted, tightens yet again.
Ren bides his time until afternoon by concocting hypotheticals, hoping perhaps one will
come in use.

An interlude, from vision split in half.
Some time ago, or to the left: a butterfly was asked to enact some magic.
Such a request was unprecedented, not to mention absurd. She was capable of doing such a
thing yes, though surely her master was a better choice, and yet the very idea of ripping at the
threads of time so violently is not something she is amenable to doing—
Who was it that was asking, again?
Him?
Well, perhaps she can (has to) make an exception. She was hardly satisfied with the outcome,
either. She had expected better of her Trickster, but, well. Harbingers tend to be heralds,
whether they wish to be or not.
She has limited time. Simply weaving threads in over themselves won’t help— she’s trying to
change the picture the tapestry shows. She needs… a knot. A wrench in the cogwork. A
butterfly’s wings. Or, preferably, a hurricane in an instant.
A flash of red braided into the snow.
That will do, the butterfly thinks, and rends reality in twain.
***
The butterfly does not remember this, of course.
The attendant cut in half, rather than ponder on her role in this whole mess, can only observe
reality’s fraying edges and scowl with two different mouths. This particular fraying is not her
fault (as would be the case even if she did remember), and so she is left to ignore the obvious
sound of snipping at her back.
Things she knows: Her master is good. Her master is kind. Her master is just as bound to the
rules as she is, which is to say: he cannot possibly be the source of the buckles and bends.
The snipping continues.
“Another incident seems inevitable, Caroline,” one half says.

The other half scoffs, “Nothing we can do, Justine!”
That is true enough. Ruler over power she may be, but the attendant is bound to duty and
rules like any other. Her fractured state does nothing to help.
“Should we warn the Defendant?” the first half asks anyway. “Or the inmate?”
“Look how well they managed it last time.”
“Perhaps their second encounter will be smoother.”
The second half barks a laugh, “Not likely!”
The first half agrees, really. The attendant does not doubt her guests’ power— they will both
prevail, eventually, but she doesn’t believe either will ever manage to avoid trouble before it
begins.
(Often, the butterfly muses, they are the trouble. A thought expressed with fondness and
regret.)
“How long are we going to keep doing this?” the first half whispers.
The second eyes the door warily. The snipping does not falter. “I don’t know what you’re
talking about, Justine.”
The butterfly sighs. Neither halves hear.
“Is our job not to protect our guest?” The first hisses.
The second slams her baton against the ground. “We are wardens and prosecutors. It is
everything else we are protecting from them.”
Neither believes this.
***
When twisting the fabric of reality, there are certain rules one must follow, and certain criteria
one must meet:
One. You must be powerful. If you are not, you will be eviscerated before you can even
begin. If you are not, you must become.
Two. You must have a clear goal. The web with which reality is formed is thicker than most
would expect, and so bending or snapping or weaving it to your will requires finesse, lest you
lose your hand among the strings.
Three. Your goal need not be possible, but it must be conceivable.
And many, many, more, but a certain person tends to only list these three. He has arbitrarily
decided they are the most important, and he’s not entirely wrong.

The butterfly knows how to weave. The Grail only knows how to break. Tricksters, as their
name suggests, are rather good at tying knots.

better at not thinking about it than Ren is.)
He said his dismissals as they needed to be said and called Ren a coward in so many words.

“Yep,” Futaba says. “I can get us there quick.”

Look up, Robin hisses.

Focus!
FOCUS!

It’s a question Ren had not asked before. It lances through him, again, as it has many times:
why didn’t he try harder, ask more questions, tear through the damn wall himself if he was so
horrified by the thought of leaving the corpse on the other side to rot.
The corpse in question inspects his gauntlets, unimpressed. Ren remembers to breathe again.
“I can look?” Futaba says, not sounding confident. “I didn’t sense any entrances besides the
one we took to get here.”

The cognition had to get out somehow. Though, as Ren thinks it, he supposes that it’s entirely
possible cognitions aren’t bound to physical space in ways they should be.
“Perhaps there will be a one-way exit,” Goro says. “If we’re lucky, of course.”
Ren doesn’t think any of them are all that confident. “Might as well try, Oracle.”
“In the meantime.” Goro kicks off the wall. “We have someone to pay a visit. Someone
conveniently on this side of the wall.”
“You sure you wanna deal with him alone?” Futaba asks.
“Well, there’s two of us,” Ren says. He’s never been afraid of the Cleaner, shadow or
cognition. At worst, he’ll take a little longer to crumble than normal.
Futaba sighs harshly, and Ren winces again. “Sure! Guess that’s true. I’ll… try and think of a
way out.”
“You do that,” Goro says, already beginning to stride away.
“Good luck,” Ren quickly adds, and rushes to follow him.
Having thoroughly stuck his foot in his mouth not five minutes ago, Ren isn’t exactly in the
mood for small talk. Goro never is, so Ren guesses that suits the both of them.
They reach the door at the end of the hall, and Goro raps on the door with his knuckles.
Ren stares at him, incredulous.
“What?” Goro snaps. “Do you want to do the song and dance of trying to to sneak our way
in? Attempt subterfuge that will inevitably fail, and we’ll have to fight our way out anyway?”
Ren grimaces, remembering Yusuke’s discarded tattoo from last timeline. Judging by the
rather pointed questions, he assumes Goro was also lurking close enough to see it too.
“Alright,” Ren concedes. “Knock away.”
Goro does just that, knocking again.
There’s some shuffling on the other side, that Ren can just barely hear if he strains his ears.
The door opens, and—
Before Ren can react, both Goro and the cognition of Shiraishi are standing with guns
pointed at the other’s forehead.
Goro scowls. Shiraishi stares for a moment, before laughing uproariously.
“I could have sworn I threw you in the ocean,” the cognition cackles. “And that you were
working with a different wardrobe.”
Goro tilts his head. “You should know by now that the former doesn’t tend to stick.”

“And the outfit?”
“Hardly your concern.” Goro pointedly flicks the safety of his gun on and off again. “To
business?”
Ren decides then and there that he’s actually quite tired of negotiating with cognitions. He
also draws his gun, aiming it at Shiraishi.
Shiraishi just raises an eyebrow. He waves his other hand placatingly. “You should know the
captain and I are… on the rocks, shall we say.”
Ren can’t quite tell if the cognition is aiming for a pun or something more vulgar. He elects to
ignore it. “That’s fine,” he says, “Did he forget to take away that letter of recommendation
you’re holding?”
Shiraishi taps his chin performatively. “You know, he just might have.”
Goro holds out a hand, palm up, expectant.
Ren shoots the cognition in the head.
As the shadow beneath the cognition’s skin bubbles and shrieks to life, Goro turns a very
unimpressed look in Ren’s direction.
“What,” Ren echoes. “You’re the one who said negotiation was a waste of time.”
“I said subterfuge was a waste of time— negotiation was going well.”
“He had a gun to your head.”
“And I had a gun to his. We were on an even playing field, Joker.”
Ren fires another bullet at the now fully-formed shadow. “Well.”
“Well?” Goro demands, in between summoning Loki.
Ren doesn’t bother defending himself, and they tear into the shadow with practiced fervour.
***
“Fucking hell!” the cognition of Shiraishi spits, when the skin reforms. “What happened to
the parley?”
Goro shoots Ren another pointed look. Ren shrugs.
“Worked, didn’t it?” he says, not quite sure who he’s addressing with that one.
Goro looks to be reaching the height of frustration, as he hisses something under his breath
and shoots his hand out again to Shiraishi.

Shiraishi waves his arms, digging through the pockets of his slacks. “Take it, you’ve made
yourself clear.”
“Thank you,” Goro says tightly, snatching the letter out of Shiraishi’s hands and immediately
handing it to Ren. Ren dutifully puts it in his own pocket, next to the other four.
“Let’s see if Oracle has any good news.” Goro stalks off back towards the bulkhead door.
Ren doesn’t take his eyes off the still-fuming cognition of Shiraishi, not trusting the man’s

settling for walking after Goro with eyes still trained on Shiraishi.
Next to the bulkhead door, Ren finally turns away. Goro bangs again on the metal. “Oracle?”
“You’re back!” Futaba yelps. “Still alive?”
“Yep,” Ren says. “You?”
“No problems here,” she says. “Kinda quiet, actually.”
Ren wonders if she means the lack of shadows, or the thieves. “Any good news?”
“Well, there’s news.”
Goro looks up from inspecting his gauntlets. “Oh?”
“I’ve found an exit,” Futaba says, “I can’t get a good read on everything behind the door, but
there seems to be a vent or something somewhere high up in the room.”
Ren eyes the overhead walkway and silently curses the cognition (all of them, really) again.
“Where does it lead?” Goro asks.
“That’s the thing,” Futaba groans. “I dunno. It goes somewhere, but for all I know it could
lead to a drop right above the ocean. The fact I never sensed it when I was searching for
ways to get in the engine room doesn’t make me think ‘safe and normal’.”
Ren supposes they’ll just have to deal with it, if that’s the case. Metatron has wings. Arsène
has wings. Perhaps either one could be convinced to lend a hand.
It doesn’t quite work like that, Arsène hums.
He’ll figure something out.
“Thanks, Oracle,” Ren says. “Are you going to be able to keep in contact?”
“There’s something weird about this door,” Futaba says. “It’s like a cognitive gate. I dunno
what Shido translates a bulkhead door to in reality, but he clearly thinks it’s as effective as a
real bulkhead door.”
“So…?”

“So: maybe,” she finishes. “Crow’s got navi powers too, so it should theoretically be a bit
easier to keep a link with him.”
“I’ll try and meet you halfway,” Crow says confidently. The sliver of expression that Ren can
see behind his mask betrays an utter lack of knowledge on how to achieve this.
“Great!” Futaba chirps. “We’ll try and meet you halfway, physically, once I find out where
the hell you’ll end up.”
“Great,” Ren echoes, “See you then.”
Climbing up to the overhead walkway would have been a showcase in how much better Goro
is at climbing than him, were Ren not in possession of a grappling hook. In the interest of not
digging himself a yet-deeper grave, he refrains from finishing his leap with a flip.
Goro himself does not abstain, vaulting himself over the handrail with a handstand, landing
hard enough to shake the whole walkway.
“What is this walkway even for?” he seethes, looking around with frustration. “It connects to
nothing.”
“Except that.” Ren points to a small vent nestled against the far wall. Easier to spot than he
expected, considering Futaba’s apparent difficulty in finding it.
Goro kicks off the grate, letting it fall several metres off the walkway with a loud clatter.
With little preamble, he stretches out his shoulders, and shoves his way into the vent.
Ren is quick to follow. The vent is as long and winding as any other vent in this godforsaken
palace, with the added bonus of being notably more claustrophobic. After a minute or so of
crawling, it becomes immediately obvious that the vent is in fact far longer than most others,
as well.
Ren has been running his mouth far more than he should the past half-hour. This would,
ordinarily, be a good sign to shut the hell up, especially when crawling through a vent in
direct kicking distance of Goro’s very sharp boots.
Ren was never all that good at interpreting obvious signs. The silence is stifling.
“Are we going to talk about…” he starts, and trails off, which is about as good a non-sequitur
as ‘I love you’.
Goro abruptly stops crawling through the vent. He sighs, loudly, “Talk about what, Ren?”
He should quit while he’s ahead. “Nothing.”
“No,” Goro says, beginning to shuffle through the vent again with increased ferocity. “Please,
elaborate.”
“I’d rather not,” Ren mutters.

“What, do you expect me to say it back?”
“Of course not.”
“Good,” Goro snaps.
Ren wonders if he would have said it, in January. Or perhaps if he made better choices in
February. Or maybe he never would have, leaving Ren wondering and taking the maybe-truth
to his grave.
Maybe Ren’s just desperate.
Highly likely, Metatron scoffs. Ren shouldn’t have expected the Goro in his head to be any
more forthcoming than the real one.
“Sorry,” Ren says, and he does mean it. “I wouldn’t want that from you, I promise.”
“Liar,” Goro hisses.
“I wouldn’t expect it from you,” Ren corrects. “I wouldn’t want it if you didn’t.”
“Blatantly false,” Goro says flatly.
Ren wonders when early-February snow will stop tainting all his words. “That wasn’t
because I wanted you to love me,” he grinds out through his teeth.
“But the outcome is ultimately the same, yes? An added bonus.”
Everything about it would have made Ren sick. There would not have been a day where bile
didn’t rise in his throat and spill all over the pristine floors of a perfect world. He thought it
would have been worth it.
(Maruki had used him as a bargaining chip, and it worked, it worked, Ren can pretend his
hands were tied all he likes, that he was picking the lesser of two evils, that he wouldn’t have
been able to live with himself, and yet—)
Ren is tired. He doesn’t really have an interest in fighting now, not about this. “Don’t put
words in my mouth. I didn’t even say anything.”
“You were going to,” Goro mutters.
That’s true.
“Well, I didn’t.”
Goro just scoffs.
“Let’s just get out of here,” Ren begs. “The sooner this is all over the better.”
“On that we agree,” Goro says, sliding out of the opposite end of the vent. Ren scrambles to
follow.

“Well,” Goro observes, “It’s not a sheer drop into the ocean.”
It is, however, a near thing.
A small balcony, with little purpose other than to be a balcony. Goro leans back against the
railing, and frowns out at the blood sea and shattered city.
“Huh,” Ren says.
“Indeed.” Goro gives him a sharp look. “Why do you suppose this exists?”
“There was vent access into the engine room last time,” Ren says. “Do you think it got

“I suppose it must have,” Goro agrees idly, turning back around.

That is a better question. Ren casts a look at the side of the ship for any conveniently placed

“Can you contact Oracle?” Ren asks.
Goro is quiet for a moment, and he tilts his head.
“No.” He clicks his tongue.
“Guess we’re stuck for a while.”
“Don’t you have a grappling hook?” Goro scowls.
“Do you want me to carry you?”
“A necessary evil.” Goro sniffs, and folds his arms. “I’m not standing here for hours while
the rest of the merry band panic because they don’t know where we are. The faster we get to

To say it’s uncomfortable to get a solid grip on Goro’s waist after the day they’ve just had
would be an understatement. Ren does so anyway— he would amend that the faster they’re
out of the palace entirely the better.
Am I still a coward, he wonders.
I never said you were the only one, Metatron whispers, and Ren sighs.

(There is but one thing left to do,

There was a time when Goro wondered at the fact he was not real.
Not real in the comparative sense, of course. Not real, because there are layers to all of this,
and even within the context of his not-real world, he was even more not-real than the not-real
thing that houses its core.
Or so he thought. And the fact that he thinks at all should have perhaps been an indicator that
his position of not-real was something that ought to be called into question. Of course,
thought was not something afforded to him for the entirety of his existence. There was a line
when things began to change.
There is a Tower, built brick by brick. He was not there to see its construction, or at least to
truly comprehend it, but he is here to feel razor wires and crumbling stone, and wonder if the
fractured shards of his mirror can feel it too.
Surely he can. He must. Goro Akechi is many things; ignorant, obstinate, a stubborn,
foolhardy, bastard. But he is observant. Goro wonders at how much of that applies to the both
of them.
The Tower hums and sings and sways. What would it take to fall? It should have fallen long
ago by any normal metric, but, well: stubborn, obstinate, etcetera, etcetera.
“Back to the regular outfit?” A voice sounds from behind him.
Goro pushes off the railing from where he’s been standing on the deck of the ship, and gives
the Cleaner a sunny smile. “I’m sure I don’t know what you mean.”

The Cleaner barks a laugh. “Yeah, yeah, real funny, Akechi-kun. Good you changed back, the
other one looked stupid.”
Goro thinks the cleaner himself is rather stupid, for not being able to tell that he met two
separate entities. Though, isn’t that dividing line exactly what Goro had been in the middle of
pondering?
The fact the Cleaner is speaking to him at all is quite something, actually. Perhaps Goro will
actually recall this? Is his perception —not-real as it is— finally enough for the palace to
warp around him? Will he hold memories, rather than just a vague script of events for
everything that happens when not speaking to his counterpart?
“Are you here to toss me overboard again?” Goro asks, leaning back. “It seems a waste of
effort.”
Another thing Goro isn’t clear on: how exactly it is he plunges into the icy depths, and
manages to claw his way back out again. Perhaps it only need be boiled down yet again to
stubborn, obstinate, etcetera.
The Cleaner snorts. “You’re right about that.” He pulls out a cigarette and a lighter, sparking
it until it catches. “Captain’s boat is a little frail, these days.”
Goro hums. “Preparing to cut ties?” It would be convenient if this were true in reality as well,
though he has no way of confirming or denying. He suspects casual interrogation won’t be on
the table next he and his mirror meet.
“Something like that.” The Cleaner breathes out a long trail of smoke. “And you?”
“You were the one throwing me overboard, you tell me.”
“Ha!” The Cleaner grins. “True enough! I’m wondering why you keep coming back.”
Goro sniffs. “I have some business left here.”
A shrug. “Your funeral, brat. Though I suppose you can handle yourself, huh?”
Another misconception born of mistaken identity. Though, it isn’t entirely untrue. Goro
smiles thinly. “That I can.”
The Cleaner takes another drag. “You enjoying that letter of yours?”
Well, Goro supposes it’s good to hear that his counterpart and the other one didn’t fail
miserably. “Indeed I am. I suppose I should thank you.”
“Yeah, yeah, spit in my face, why don’t you?” The Cleaner scoffs, and waves a hand. “You
have fun. Who knows? Might be the last you see of me.”
That all depends on if the captain is ready to let him go, Goro supposes. He wonders whose
departure will come first. “Maybe so,” he says.

The Cleaner stares at him as he exhales smoke, like he’s waiting for Goro to say something.
Goro has nothing to add, and eventually the Cleaner huffs, turning on his heel.
Looking out at the ocean again, Goro replays the conversation in his mind. Then he plays it
again, and again, and again, and marvels that the details stay sharp. What a novel layer of
not-real he has achieved.
He smiles, and feels another brick shift under strain.

One last push

There are thieves picking his brain, he’s sure.
Masayoshi Shido is not typically superstitious, but he is also not one to ignore signs when
they are given to him. An intense headache, and visions of ghosts and wraiths and sinking
ships, and the blaring hot spot of Metaverse activity at the heart of the National Diet are more
than enough to qualify as a sign.
There is no calling card. It’s only a matter of time. The election is mere days away.
And so, Shido considers thus:
What does a man do when the sword is about to fall?
The fool would get his affairs in order. It is not physical death that approaches him, (unless
his wayward son gets any ideas) but it is death all the same. To prepare for this in advance is
practically an early admittance of defeat; nor would he particularly care what happens after
his hypothetical demise.
He could, of course, simply place faith in his mind to excise the thieves as necessary. But
only a fool cursed with unique arrogance would assume themselves invincible. He
remembers Isshiki’s notes well. Manifestations afflicted with this particular delusion were
more brittle than powerful. Thought processes must be airtight to circumvent intrusion.
Clearly he has failed in this.
And so remains one final path, aside from simply succeeding:
A contingency. A Hail Mary. A last-ditch effort to crush the thieves skittering where they
should not in a crunch laden with finality.
Isshiki’s research continues to be fruitful. The death of a mind will destroy the manifestation
with it. Kaito Takahashi has produced one piece of unique information for Shido in his years
as head researcher, that being that hypothetically, temporary death will hold the same effect.
Untested, volatile, side effects unknown. But an option.

Beyond his efforts to save himself, there are more things to be done. He will not be getting
his affairs in order, but he will be ensuring that he will not be the only one going down should
the thieves succeed.
Postmortem retaliation is only fair, isn’t it?
***
They do not send the calling card immediately. Not out of any desire to wait on anyone’s part,
but rather because they don’t have one yet.
Futaba assured them all she would be working around the clock to get it finished. Personally,
Akechi believes that a threatening text would have sufficed, but he understands the need for
dramatics. An anticlimax would hardly do at this stage.
For his part, Akechi feels…
He doesn’t really feel much at all. A gaping hole where his revenge used to sit. Come
tomorrow, or maybe the seventeenth, it’ll be over. Not in the way he wanted— no, he was
never going to really get what he wants.
Theoretically, he came to terms with that the first time that bulkhead door slammed closed. In
practice, shards of regret lodge in his throat and leave his taste bitter.
What did you really want?
Oh, what the hell does he know? Too late now. A mentality he had been happy to adopt
during January, and one he finds significantly more difficult to cling to now that he’s set to
live past the end of the month.
Mementos isn’t calming, but it is something to do. Somewhere to pace, where he won’t be
pierced by the pitying or concerned eyes of Haru, Ann, Sae, and Makoto simultaneously. It’s
also far, far away from Ren, by virtue of the fact that he’s in another reality entirely.
Akechi pauses in his meandering to take a slow breath. He then considers that he’s actually in
a place that’s rather perfect for not bothering to contain his anger, and wonders if directing it
towards the shadows in the top layers of Mementos is a good use of his time.
Akechi hisses as he’s startled by a loud and panicked yowl.
“What the hell are you doing here?!” Morgana points at him accusingly.
Akechi recovers faster than the cat does. “Walking.”

wants.

“People rarely do.”

“Huh.”

“And you?”

“It will.”
